articles.title: NYT demands Brave shut down its paywall blocker and end deals with AI firms
articles.text:
The New York Times and other newspaper companies sued Brave Software yesterday, alleging that the browser maker illegally bypasses paywalls and sells stolen news content to AI companies.
“Brave is the supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content for its own users and many of the most prominent GenAI companies, including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere,” the NYT alleged in a lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Southern District of New York. Citing third-party revenue estimates, the suit claimed that “Brave has made more than $100 million by copying and reselling publishers’ work without consent or permission,” while “publishers have received nothing.”
The lawsuit said, “AI companies pay Brave to provide them with real-time online content from the Brave search index,” and use content from the Brave index “to train their own AI models” and “to respond to specific user queries.” The NYT lawsuit points to Brave’s website, which says the Brave Search API is “used by some of the biggest names in AI, including Cohere, Mistral, Perplexity, and You.com.”
The lawsuit accused Brave of all the major types of copyright infringement: direct infringement, contributory infringement, and vicarious infringement. The lawsuit claims Brave infringes copyrights directly by scraping articles for its search index, for its “Ask Brave” AI search feature, and for the Brave API that “serves as an illicit source of unlicensed copyrighted material, including Times journalism, to other AI companies.”
The NYT accused Brave of being “a contributory and vicarious infringer when it deliberately induces, facilitates, controls, and profits from its users’ and GenAI customers’ copying of the copyrighted content.” Finally, the lawsuit said Brave violated the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) by circumventing technological measures the NYT and other content owners use to restrict access to their articles.
“The Brave Browser includes a default setting that, when activated, causes the browser to go behind website paywalls and provide the paywalled content to the user,” the lawsuit said. The browser “blocks advertising that would otherwise appear on The Times’s website, and instead shows its own ads, offering its users a cut of the revenue even as it deprives The Times of digital advertising revenue that helps it fund the expensive effort of producing journalism,” the lawsuit said.

articles.title: cPGuard Update Channel Hijacked to Backdoor Linux Servers and Collect Password Hashes
articles.text:
An attacker broke into the update system of the cPGuard security tool on November 2 and used it to send a malicious script to customers' Linux servers.
The script installed a backdoor and collected password hashes and other sensitive files from servers that ran it, cPGuard maker OPSSHIELD said in an advisory. The attacker has since taken some of that data.
cPGuard 5.88.25 and later versions remove the backdoor and the files the script left. Credentials the script copied may still work after the update, so any server that may have run the script also needs new passwords and keys.
At 02:06 UTC, the attacker, who has not been identified, used compromised credentials to get into cPGuard's update system. The script went out in cPGuard versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19.
The attack was detected within 12 hours of those versions going out, according to OPSSHIELD. The company has cleared its infrastructure credentials and stopped the script from reaching more servers. It is still investigating how the attacker got the credentials.
OPSSHIELD has not said how many servers installed one of these versions. Servers check for updates at intervals, so some may not have run the script.
Admins can check whether a server installed an affected version by searching its update log:
grep 'Successfully updated' /opt/cpguard/logs/install_log
An entry for any version from 5.88.12 through 5.88.19 means the server installed an affected update. The entry alone does not show that the script ran or that data left the server. The server should still be treated as potentially compromised, even if it now runs 5.88.25 or later.
A server with no matching entries, or with a missing or incomplete log, may still have run the script. Admins who are unsure can contact OPSSHIELD Support.
The script collected these kinds of data, OPSSHIELD found: /etc/shadow and /etc/passwd, root's MariaDB or MySQL configuration (my.cnf), root's shell history, and the SSH authorization and known-hosts files for root. It may not have collected every file from every server, and the company is still working out what left each one.
The /etc/shadow file stores one-way password hashes. Weak, common or previously leaked passwords can be recovered from those hashes by testing guesses offline, and even strong ones still need resetting. Secrets that may sit in the database configuration or shell history have no such hashing to protect them.
The script uploaded what it collected to a licensing server run by OPSSHIELD itself, using a compromised account, so the attacker could pick it up later. OPSSHIELD has since secured that account.
The attacker took 32 files from that server, each tied to one customer server, OPSSHIELD estimated late on November 2 UTC. The count covers only files known to have been taken, and it may change. It does not show how many servers may be involved in total.
Beyond the data collection and the backdoor, OPSSHIELD has found no other malicious activity so far, a finding it says is not final.
What cPGuard Admins Should Do Now
OPSSHIELD asks admins to update every cPGuard server now and confirm the version:
- Run cpgcli update --start on each server.
- Run cpgcli --version and check that it reports 5.88.25 or later. If the update fails or the version is lower, contact OPSSHIELD Support.
Admins should also take these steps for any server where the script ran or may have run:
- From a trusted recovery environment, reset the passwords for root and every other local Linux account that uses a password.
- From a trusted device, change any of those passwords that are also used on other systems.
- Rotate the server's database passwords, S3 access keys, DigitalOcean tokens and any secrets recorded in root's shell history.
- Replace the SSH private keys stored under /root/.ssh, and remove the matching old public keys from every system that trusts them.
OPSSHIELD is not recommending a full reset or operating system rebuild as a routine step, and says that view could change as the investigation continues. Admins who find other signs of compromise, or cannot confirm a server is clean, should ask OPSSHIELD Support for a case-by-case review, which may lead to a rebuild.
Separately, OPSSHIELD is releasing another update, as a precaution, that removes its support-access keys from cPGuard servers where they were added earlier.
Support access is a cPGuard feature customers use to let OPSSHIELD staff into a server for troubleshooting. Granting it adds an SSH public key belonging to OPSSHIELD to the authorized_keys file for root, according to the company's documentation.
OPSSHIELD has not said whether the private key that matches its support-access key was exposed in the attack.
Files the Script Left Behind
OPSSHIELD published these file names. The update removes the backdoor shell and the collection directory, so their absence after updating proves nothing about whether the script ran.
- File: cpguard-v58812-i91511.sh (the malicious script)
- File: /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh (backdoor shell)
- Directory: /var/tmp/.cpg91511 (where the script gathered files)
- File: /var/tmp/.cpg91511/loot.tgz (archive the script prepared)

articles.title: Startup Athena raises $2.5M in pre-seed funding to revamp the revenue model for legal AI - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Startup Athena raises $2.5M in pre-seed funding to revamp the revenue model for legal AI
Athena Circle Corp., an artificial intelligence-native legal technology startup that’s automating the nitty gritty of commercial real estate deals, said today it has raised $2.5 million in pre-seed funding.
The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz’s accelerator program, a16z Speedrun. No other investors were named.
Legal AI technology is nothing new, but its adoption in the industry has been somewhat haphazard, for the technology has exposed an awkward problem: Most law firms are still billing their clients by the hour, and that makes automation less lucrative. If a law firm can use AI agents to get a 10-hour contract review done in just a couple of minutes, then it’s going to let an awful lot of billable revenue slip through its fingers, killing any incentive there might be to adopt them.
Athena’s co-founders Cem Ucan (pictured, left) and Kieran John Keenan (right) and founding engineer José Braz all cut their teeth at the pioneering legal AI tech startup Legora AB, where they quickly realized how AI conflicts with the industry’s standard business model. They came up with an entirely different business model to convince legal firms of the benefits of automation. Instead of selling software tools directly, it provides a legal service through its affiliated law firm, charging a fixed fee per transaction that’s typically 30% to 50% lower than standard rates. In this way, it ensures that revenue is better aligned with efficiency.
“Most legal AI companies sell tools to traditional law firms, but we took a different approach,” Ucan said. “Our AI works hand-in-hand with a law firm designed around it from day one, with experienced attorneys focused on the judgment and negotiation that actually move deals forward.”
The startup is focused on automating the intricacies of commercial real estate acquisitions, sales and financing. Its AI agents are designed to automate the creation and review of purchase agreements and loan documents, and will handle all of the due diligence and administrative closing hurdles needed to get deals done, while ensuring human lawyers remain fully in the loop to make all of the final legal determinations.
In this way, Athena basically takes care of the grunt work, giving commercial real estate firms much more agility. That’s a real advantage, because commercial real estate is an industry where speed is of the essence: The faster a law firm gets things done, the more likely it is to actually secure the deal, which is the end result that everyone wants. With investors often submitting dozens of bids for each property listing, the ability to get the paperwork done in a matter of hours rather than weeks or days means buyers can lock in a deal before their rivals know what’s happened.
Keenan, who serves as the startup’s chief technology officer, explained that each new workflow begins with an incoming agreement that’s ingested by its AI agents. They cross-reference the terms of the deal against their standard deal sheets in order to flag inconsistencies, prepare redlines and draft client communications.
This work is informed by historical transactions, which allow its agents to adapt to each client’s negotiating style, Keenan said. Human attorneys then review this work, make strategic judgment calls when required, and approve all deliverables before they’re sent to clients.
“I measure our progress by how quickly an attorney can review an AI agent’s work and confidently stand behind it,” Keenan explained. “A draft produced in minutes can still leave a lawyer with hours of work. Making that review more efficient is how our platform helps us deliver faster legal services with the quality clients expect.”
Athena’s agents are already proving their worth, with the startup having signed up 22 legal firms as clients so far, just two months after launching its service. By learning continuously from attorney’s edits and client’s preferences, its agents have reduced review times by an average of 70%.
L. Miguel Arce, chief executive of the Texas-based multifamily real estate and property management firm Mox Living, said Athena was able to deliver a complete purchase agreement in less than 48 hours, the fastest turnaround he has ever seen. “A lot of firms in our industry have an AI task force in name only,” he said. “What stood out about Athena is that the system learns from every deal, from what the attorneys change to what we prefer. Speed only matters if it’s quality work, and Athena gets us both.”
Keenan said Athena is primed to strike while the iron is hot. He said the industry is bracing itself for a wave of new commercial deals as properties financed through short-term loans in 2021 and 2022 hit their refinancing deadlines, and he’s hoping that the startup can win a significant amount of that business. In any case, growth is on the horizon, for Athena also plans to expand into new markets and property classes and even new legal domains.
A16z Speedrun’s Troy Kirwin said AI automation is all well and good, but clients still demand to speak to a human who can take responsibility for the work that gets done. “Athena is building around that need with a system that can improve through real legal work and a team that’s obsessed with scaling fast,” he said.

articles.title: AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to $16B as demand surges | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Fal, a San Francisco-based startup that hosts and runs AI video, image, and audio models, has raised $1.3 billion in its latest funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Nvidia, Sound Ventures, and T. Rowe Price. The deal values Fal at $16 billion, double its $8 billion valuation in April, Bloomberg reported.
The startup announced its Series E & F rounds at the same time, noting that a combined $1.65 billion was raised across both. (Sequoia led the earlier round.)
The latest round (Series F) comes amid soaring demand for inference services, the process of running an AI model that’s already been trained to generate outputs, particularly from customers relying on open-source models. Fal surpassed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year, Bloomberg’s report noted.
Companies providing inference services, including Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Modal, have also been growing rapidly and raising large funding rounds at higher valuations. But their gross margins remain thin because of the high cost of buying or leasing compute, according to several people familiar with inference companies’ financials.
Fal was co-founded in 2021 by Burkay Gur, a former Coinbase machine learning leader and Oracle engineer, and Gorkem Yurtseven, who was previously a developer at Amazon.

articles.title: Hands-on with the DockCase Mount Ling 2 Pro — handheld dock with a built-in capture card and space for up to 4TB of NVMe storage
articles.text:
Hands-on with the DockCase Mount Ling 2 Pro — handheld dock with a built-in capture card and space for up to 4TB of NVMe storage
Mount Ling 2 Pro offers a lot of flexibility for a gaming dock.
DockCase is no stranger to Kickstarting unique SSD enclosures and docks, with the company’s Visual Smart M.2 enclosure making its way onto our list of the best SSD enclosures. The Mount Ling 2 Pro, however, is gunning for a spot among the best USB-C docks. It’s a dock for handhelds like the Steam Deck and Switch 2, an external enclosure for an NVMe SSD, and a game capture device, all packaged up in a dock that can show off your handheld and expand your port selection.
There are two versions of the dock: the standard Mount Ling 2 and the Pro version. The only difference between them is the internal capture card. The base version is $109 via an early bird deal while the Kickstarter gets underway, and the Pro version is $149. They’ll be priced at $199 and $249, respectively, after the early deals are gone.
It’s the world’s first “smart creator dock,” says DockCase, which is partially true. There are other docks that give you additional inputs, a stand, and capture capabilities with a handheld, and at a lower price. The AVerMedia X’TRA GO, for instance, offers all of that for $160. The differentiator here is the internal M.2 slot that can support up to 4TB of NVMe storage, with points to mount 2280, 2242, and 2230-sized drives. Of course, this external storage only works with platforms that normally support external storage (so, not the Switch or Switch 2).
For PC-adjacent handhelds running Windows or Linux, the Mount Ling 2 Pro is an expensive but useful dock that gives you capture, storage, and port expandability in one attractive package. For the Switch and Switch 2, the usefulness isn’t as clear. You can’t use the SSD with either platform, and Nintendo’s game of whack-a-mole with third-party accessories means a system update could break HDMI passthrough (and, in the process, the capture function of the dock).
Mount Ling Dock 2 specifications
DockCase says the Mount Ling 2 Pro supports the Steam Deck, ROG Ally, Switch, Switch 2, and “more,” presumably wrapping up other Windows- or Linux-based handhelds like the ROG Ally X Xbox or Lenovo Legion Go S. Switch and Switch 2 are supported, as well, though getting Nintendo’s handheld to connect properly isn’t always smooth.
The dock connects to your handheld with a USB 3.2 Gen Type-C connection capable of 10 Gbps, and DockCase includes a small, braided 40 Gbps cable in the box, along with two right-angle connectors. That single connection gives you up to 100W through the USB-C port, along with Gigabit Ethernet, an HDMI 2.0 connection (4K@60Hz), a single USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A port, and a USB 2.0 port. An additional USB-C connection serves as another USB 3.2 Gen 2 port on the Mount Ling 2, while it becomes the capture card output on the Pro model.
Interestingly, there’s also an optical audio output available. Although I don’t suspect most users will put it to use (HDMI transfers audio, as well), it’s a nice fallback if you plan on using the dock with a more elaborate audio setup. It’s a nice bonus, though I would’ve liked a 3.5mm audio jack as well, considering handhelds no longer have access to that connection.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The dock itself is constructed almost entirely of plastic, and holding it in your hands, you can tell it’s filled with more air than hardware. It’s a sizable package at 8.4 x 7 x 3.5 inches. Outside of the shell, there’s a thick layer of firm silicone to rest your handheld on. There are grooves to provide a natural resting place for just about any handheld, as well as a deep central cut that fits the Switch and Switch 2 specifically.
You can install your SSD at the bottom of the dock, with mounting points for 2280, 2242, and 2230 drives. There's a single 40mm fan internally, as well as venting around the back and side edges, to keep the drive cool. The fan will automatically adjust its speed out of the box, but you’re free to manually adjust the speed or turn the fan off, if you want.
Unfortunately, there’s no room for a heatsink. The face of the drive sits nearly flush against the vented cover on the bottom of the dock. Even if you left the cover off, most heatsinks would push past the rubber feet and prop the dock up.
Using the Mount Ling 2 Pro dock
Setting up the Mount Ling 2 Pro is mostly a matter of plugging everything in and getting on your way. The dock goes through a connecting phase when you hook up a new device, and it’s finicky. Sometimes it would drop one part of the connection, like charging, while picking up another, particularly with the Switch 2. You want to have the dock fully connected before hooking up your host.
The main page of the dock’s screen provides HDMI, SSD, and power info at a glance, which is helpful to quickly check, for example, that the HDMI passthrough is operating at the correct resolution and refresh rate without digging into the settings. A swipe to the right brings up five quick-access settings, which just take you into the settings menu, while a swipe to the right gives you access to volume and fan controls. The volume adjustment on the dock is passed through to the host.
Swiping up instead gives you the full settings menu, which has more to monitor than adjust. You can see the SSD details (including SMART monitors), the status of USB connections, and your HDMI info, andother details about the dock. For settings, there are different HDMI transfer modes, in case you run into a broken handshake, along with power delivery settings if you need to roll back to PD 2.0.
For the dock itself, you have some small control over the fan and built-in lighting. For the fan, you can adjust the speed manually, turn it off, or leave it on the default automatic mode. The lighting settings are surprisingly bare. You can choose between blue, red, or a gradient between them, and that’s it. Otherwise, you can just dim or turn off the lights. If you find the screen and lights distracting, there’s a dedicated button on the back of the dock to turn all the lights off (including the screen).
Although the screen is responsive with minimal lag between swipes and taps, the software running here isn’t perfect. Particularly with the Switch 2, if I connected things in the wrong order, the dock would force itself to reboot, only sometimes picking up the Switch 2 when it came back. DockCase offers firmware updates over USB, and hopefully it gets a patch between units shipped to fix some of these quirks.
The firmware updates are a nice sign, but they bring up an unfortunate reality of creating a device for the Switch 2 without Nintendo’s seal of approval. Both the Switch and Switch 2 are infamously fickle with third-party docks and hubs. A system update could break compatibility, forcing a firmware update.
DockCase plays up Switch 2 support on its product page, and that is a big draw. However, the dock can’t get around the limitations that Nintendo itself has placed on its handheld. You may as well fill the SSD slot with concrete if you’re docking a Switch 2, and docking the device is troublesome. It took multiple emails for me to get the Switch 2 to pass through its HDMI signal at all. You have to connect everything in a specific way, and critically, have the Switch 2 already unlocked when you plug it into the bottom USB-C port; the top port won’t work.
With the Steam Deck, everything was seamless, and although I didn’t have a Windows handheld on hand to try out, I don’t anticipate there will be major issues. DockCase may offer a lot of functionality in a single box with the Mount Ling Pro 2, but it’s all operating over standard connections that are well supported in the Windows ecosystem.
You can use the SSD with the Steam Deck, though you’ll need to head to desktop mode to partition the drive and add a folder for Steam games. The process is similar on Windows handhelds if you’re using some sort of handheld-native overlay.
For the capture portion, it serves its purpose. Critically, DockCase doesn’t have any software for capturing or recording like the mainstream capture cards you’ll find from Elgato and AVerMedia, so you’ll need to use something else like OBS. For any of these types of recording/streaming platforms, the DockCase shows up as a simple video capture device, with resolution and frame rate determined by your settings on the host device (assuming it’s within that 4K60 limit that HDMI 2.0 is capable of).
There isn’t much of a need here for HDMI 2.1, considering the types of devices connecting to the Mount Ling Pro 2, though it would’ve been a nice upside. You can still push the refresh rate higher, just not at 4K. And in fairness to DockCase, the devices it’s targeting really have no business driving a 4K display.
Mount Ling 2 Pro SSD performance
You shouldn’t expect wonders out of SSD performance with the Mount Ling 2 Pro, given that it uses a USB 3.2 Gen 2 connection that’s only capable of up to 10 Gbps. High performance in an external enclosure is the game of Thunderbolt 5 docks with M.2 storage, which can often reach sequential reads above 5,000 MB/s over the 80 Gbps Thunderbolt 5 interface. Here, the connection will bottleneck your speeds, all the way down to typical PCIe 3.0 NVMe SSDs.
Still, in the context of gaming on a handheld, that isn’t the end of the world. It’s nice to have that much storage on tap for a device like the Steam Deck, which is otherwise only expandable with a larger internal SSmicroSDicro SD card.
In CrystalDiskMark, the Mount Ling 2 Pro landed with sequential reads and writes around 820 MB/s, with random performance far lower. We tested with a 2 TB WD_Black SN770, which is a PCIe 4.0 drive that boasts sequential reads up to 5150 MB/s when installed directly in a motherboard. In the Mount Ling 2 Pro, it behaves more like an external SSD like the SK hynix Beetle X31 2TB, naturally hamstrung by the connection.
Overall Mount Ling 2 Pro impressions
The Mount Ling 2 Pro does a lot, combining external storage, a capture card, and an attractive dock into a single package that works with both PC handhelds and the Nintendo Switch 2. The SSD performance isn’t great, as is to be expected out of a dock that uses a 10 Gbps USB link for connection, but that downside isn’t much of a concern considering the devices this dock targets.
Although Switch 2 support is a big upside, it’s also fickle. You don’t get access to the SSD, and the connection can fail if you don’t follow the order of operations for connection. The Mount Ling 2 Pro makes sense if you have a Switch 2 and a PC handheld of some kind, but as a pure Switch 2 dock, it doesn’t make much sense. You’d be better off buying an external capture card for use with the official dock.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

articles.title: This is the Epson EcoTank printer I’d buy for its crisp low cost pages
articles.text:
'Excellent long-term value': We praised Epson's cartridge-free EcoTank ET-2980 printer for its generous free ink. Now, an early Black Friday price cut makes it even better
In our four-star review we said we'd buy the printer for its crisp low cost pages
Buying a printer is one thing, but keeping it supplied with ink can quickly become massively expensive, especially if you regularly print documents, homework, or photographs. Epson's EcoTank ET-2980 is one of our favorite cheap ink tank printers, saving a fortune on replacement ink cartridges.
Now, the value-led cartridge-free printer sees a price cut down to $285 (was $330) at Amazon, while in the UK, it's listed under the name EcoTank ET-2950, down to £230 (was £280). It's the same model, though. And the price delivers an even better deal on the machine we called "a bargain of this bottle-fed printer."
• Best for: Households, students, and home office workers who print a lot and want to keep ongoing ink costs down without loss of everyday printing, scanning, and copying capabilities.
• Why it matters: You get refillable ink tanks with up to three years of ink included. There’s also Wi-Fi, Wi-Fi Direct, a 100-sheet paper tray, automatic double-sided printing, and borderless photo printing.
This wireless all-in-one inkjet printer features refillable ink tanks, automatic duplex printing, borderless output, flatbed scanning, mobile connectivity, and included ink rated for thousands of black and color pages.
The UK equivalent, the EcoTank ET-2950, is also on sale. Usually priced at £279.99 it's currently down to £229.99, a £50.99 saving.
Why we recommend it
The biggest attraction of the EcoTank ET-2980 is Epson's approach to running costs. The included ink can produce up to 6,600 black pages or 5,500 color pages, and each replacement bottle set is equivalent to approximately 90 individual ink cartridges.
Refilling is straightforward, thanks to Epson's EcoFit bottles, which have keyed nozzles designed to help prevent you from putting the wrong color into a tank.
In his four-star review, our expert Jim said it: "printed reliably on everything from envelopes to thick 300g/m² cardstock. It’s not a fast printer, but automatic duplexing is a welcome convenience. Pigment black ink produces crisp, smudge-resistant text, while dye-based colors look bright and punchy. Photographs are slightly soft and oversaturated towards red, but perfectly acceptable for occasional use."
He added that: "The biggest attraction is the ink economy. Epson is putting plenty of ink in the box and replacement bottles are cheap. I think its low running costs, reliable performance and essential duplexing feature make it excellent long-term value."
For more top performing units, see our guides to the best home printers and best ink tank printers.
Price context & historical value
Amazon's current $285 asking price is $44.99 below how much it usually sells for. That's not the cheapest we've seen it sell for in the past though. It was as low as $229.99 earlier in the year, and it's possible it will be reduced more the closer to Black Friday we get.
The British equivalent model, the EcoTank ET-2950, is usually priced at £279.99 and is currently down to £229.99.
If you want to save on other units, see our guide to the best printer deals we've seen this week.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the Epson EcoTank ET-2980 if...
You regularly print documents, school assignments, or photographs and want to reduce your reliance on ink cartridges. The ET-2980 also offers automatic double-sided printing, which can help cut paper consumption.
❌ Skip the Epson EcoTank ET-2980 if...
You only print occasionally or need a dedicated business printer with advanced document-handling features. A cheaper cartridge-based model may be more economical for light use.

articles.title: Woher kommt 3I/Atlas? James-Webb-Teleskop findet Spur im All
articles.text:
3I/Atlas: James-Webb-Teleskop findet Hinweise auf den Ursprung des interstellaren Kometen
Die Methan-Signatur von 3I/Atlas ist ungewöhnlich reich an schwerem Wasserstoff, was darauf hindeutet, dass die gefrorenen Bestandteile des Kometen in einer extrem kalten Umgebung um einen anderen Stern, oder in der Wolke, die diesem Stern vorausgegangen war, entstanden sind. Zu dieser Erkenntnis kam ein Forscher:innen-Team rund um Nathan Roth von der American University (USA).
James-Webb-Weltraumteleskop liefert entscheidende Daten
Mithilfe des James-Webb-Weltraumteleskops und der Unterstützung des Goddard Space Flight Centers der Nasa konnten sie das Verhältnis von schwerem zu gewöhnlichem Wasserstoff in 3I/Atlas bestimmen. Es ist etwa 13-mal so hoch wie bei dem Kometen 67P/Tschurjumow-Gerassimenko, der wahrscheinlich aus unserem Sonnensystem stammt. Ihre in der Fachzeitschrift Nature Astronomy veröffentlichten Ergebnisse bieten Wissenschaftler:innen eine seltene Gelegenheit, die frühe Chemie eines anderen Planetensystems zu untersuchen.
Schwerer Wasserstoff, auch Deuterium genannt, besitzt ein zusätzliches Neutron im Atomkern. Er kann in einem Methanmolekül den Platz eines gewöhnlichen Wasserstoffatoms einnehmen. Dieser Austausch verändert die Infrarot-Signatur des Moleküls, was es Astronom:innen ermöglicht, zwischen den beiden Varianten zu unterscheiden.
Rekordwerte bei Deuterium im Methan von 3I/Atlas
Das James-Webb-Teleskop beobachtete 3I/Atlas am 22. und 23. Dezember 2025, als sich der Komet etwa 2,4-mal so weit von der Sonne entfernt befand wie die Erde. Das Teleskop untersuchte dabei das Infrarotlicht aus der Koma – jener Gaswolke, die den eisigen Kern des Kometen umgibt. Entdeckt wurde dabei ein Deuterium-Wasserstoff-Verhältnis (D/H-Verhältnis) von etwa 3,2 Prozent im Methan.
„Dieses D/H-Verhältnis übertrifft jeden anderen Wert, der jemals für Methan im Sonnensystem gemessen wurde“, schreiben die Autor:innen der Studie. Der Vergleich mit dem Kometen 67P, einem Kometen der Jupiter-Familie, ist besonders aufschlussreich, da dies der einzige weitere Komet ist, in dem deuteriumhaltiges Methan nachgewiesen wurde.
Das sind die 18 besten Bilder aus dem Weltall:
3. Entstehungsprozesse in kalten interstellaren Wolken
Das D/H-Verhältnis (Deuterium-Wasserstoff-Verhältnis) im Methan war etwa dreimal so hoch wie der Wert, der zuvor im Wasser von 3I/Atlas gemessen wurde. Die Forscher:innen vermuten, dass das Methan möglicherweise erst später entstanden ist: zu einem Zeitpunkt, an dem die chemische Umgebung bereits mehr Zeit hatte, den schweren Wasserstoff anzureichern.
Laut den Wissenschaftler:innen passen ihre Ergebnisse gut zu der Theorie, wonach 3I/Atlas in einer kalten Wolke oder in der Umgebung eines entstehenden Sterns entstanden sein könnte. Und in einer Region mit vergleichsweise wenigen Elementen, die schwerer als Helium sind, und einer hohen Intensität an kosmischer Strahlung. Diese hochenergetischen Teilchen tragen dazu bei, jene chemischen Reaktionen in Gang zu setzen, die zu einer Anreicherung von Deuterium in Molekülen führen. Dies liefert laut der Wissenschaftswebseite phys.org zwar eine plausible Entstehungsgeschichte für 3I/Atlas, lässt aber noch keinen eindeutigen Geburtsort bestimmen.

articles.title: 5 lessons to learn from the book super cool startup by Sairam Krishnan.
articles.text:
5 lessons from the book Super Cool Startup by Sairam Krishnan
Discover five lessons from Super Cool Startup by Sairam Krishnan about storytelling, content marketing, community building, PR, and social media.
Super Cool Startup: Get Your Early-Stage Marketing Right for the AI Age by Sairam Krishnan is a practical guide for entrepreneurs, startup founders, and marketers who want to build brands that people recognise, trust, and remember.
Drawing on his experience working with companies such as Freshworks and Atomicwork, and his work in the startup ecosystem, Krishnan explains why having a great product is not enough to build a successful business.
Startups also need a clear story, meaningful content, an engaged community, effective public relations, and a strong social media presence.
The book focuses on five fundamental pillars of early-stage marketing: storytelling, content, community, PR and guerrilla marketing, and social media. It offers useful insights into how businesses can earn attention and build a marketing engine, particularly in an era when AI has made content creation easier but strategic judgement more important.
5 Important lessons from Super Cool Startup by Sairam Krishnan
1. A great product needs a great story
One of the biggest lessons from Super Cool Startup is that building a good product is only one part of building a successful business. People also need to understand why the product exists and why they should care about it.
A startup may have an innovative product, talented founders, and a promising business model. However, if it cannot communicate its purpose and value clearly, it may struggle to attract customers and stand out in a competitive market.
Krishnan emphasises storytelling as the foundation of startup marketing. A compelling brand story explains the problem a company wants to solve, the people it wants to help, and what makes its approach different.
For example, instead of simply describing a product through its features, a startup can explain the everyday problem it solves and how it makes customers' lives easier.
The lesson: Do not just tell people what your product does. Give them a reason to care about it. A clear and relatable story can help a startup build recognition, trust, and a stronger connection with its audience.
2. Content is how you build trust
A strong brand story needs the right content to reach its audience. This is where content marketing becomes important.
The book highlights content as one of the essential pillars of early-stage marketing. Whether it is an article, newsletter, case study, video, or social media post, content allows businesses to communicate their ideas and demonstrate their expertise.
However, creating content simply to remain active online is not enough. Businesses need to understand what their target audience wants to learn, what problems they are trying to solve, and what information would genuinely help them.
For instance, a startup offering marketing software could publish practical guides, industry insights, customer stories, and educational videos instead of constantly promoting its product.
This approach helps potential customers understand the brand before they even consider making a purchase.
The lesson: Focus on creating useful content rather than producing content just for visibility. When businesses consistently offer valuable information, they have a better opportunity to build credibility and earn their audience's trust.
3. Build a community, not just a customer base
Another important lesson from Super Cool Startup is that successful brands should focus on building communities around their products and ideas.
Customers may purchase a product because they need it, but a community gives them a reason to stay connected with the brand. When people feel involved in a company's journey, they can become supporters who recommend its products, share their experiences, and introduce others to the business.
Krishnan identifies community-building as a fundamental part of early-stage marketing. Instead of treating customers as people who simply purchase products, startups should create opportunities for meaningful interactions.
This could include organising online discussions, hosting webinars, creating customer groups, encouraging feedback, or bringing together people with similar interests.
For example, a fitness startup could build a community where members share their progress, exchange advice, participate in challenges, and support one another.
Such interactions can help businesses develop stronger relationships with their audiences.
The lesson: Do not focus only on acquiring customers. Give people a reason to become part of your brand's journey. A supportive community can become one of a startup's most valuable long-term assets.
4. You do not always need a huge budget to get attention
Startups often operate with limited resources, which makes traditional advertising and large marketing campaigns difficult to afford. However, getting noticed does not always require spending a significant amount of money.
In Super Cool Startup, Krishnan highlights public relations (PR) and guerrilla marketing as important ways to generate attention and make a brand more recognisable.
Public relations helps businesses build credibility through media coverage, industry conversations, founder interviews, and meaningful announcements. Guerrilla marketing, meanwhile, involves creative and unconventional approaches to reaching people.
A startup can use these methods to create memorable experiences and generate conversations without depending entirely on expensive advertising campaigns.
For instance, a small business could organise an interesting public activation, collaborate with a relevant creator, or develop a creative campaign that encourages people to share it organically.
The key is to understand what makes an idea interesting enough for people to talk about.
The lesson: Creativity and strategic thinking can sometimes achieve what a large advertising budget cannot. Focus on developing memorable ideas that give people a reason to notice and discuss your brand.
5. Use social media to make your story travel
Having a great product, an interesting brand story, and valuable content means little if the right audience never discovers them. This is why social media plays an important role in a startup's marketing strategy.
Krishnan identifies social media as the fifth pillar of building a super-cool startup. It provides businesses with platforms to distribute their stories, communicate with customers, showcase their products, and participate in conversations relevant to their industries.
However, effective social media marketing involves more than regularly uploading posts. Businesses need to understand which platforms their audiences use, what type of content they engage with, and how to communicate in a way that feels relevant.
For example, a B2B startup might use LinkedIn to share industry insights, founder perspectives, and customer success stories, while a consumer brand could use Instagram to showcase products, collaborate with creators, and build an engaged audience.
The important thing is to ensure that social media supports the larger marketing strategy rather than becoming an isolated activity.
The lesson: Treat social media as a distribution channel for your brand story. Use it strategically to reach the right people, build relationships, and make your business more recognisable.
Final thoughts
Super Cool Startup by Sairam Krishnan offers practical insights into entrepreneurship, branding, and modern marketing. It shows why a strong product needs effective storytelling, clear positioning, and meaningful audience connections to succeed.
The five lessons explore how storytelling, content, community-building, PR, and social media shape a startup's marketing strategy. The book also highlights that while AI makes content creation easier, good marketing still relies on human judgement and an understanding of audience needs.
Whether you are a founder or marketer, the book offers useful ideas for building a brand people understand, trust, and want to talk about.

articles.title: Vague de cyberattaques contre les supermarchés : l'Europe veut des plans d’urgence face à des menaces « profondément préoccupantes »
articles.text:
Quelques semaines après la cyberattaque nationale qui a frappé la France, les pirates ont remis le couvert en s’attaquant à six pays de l’Union européenne. Exploitant des installations exposées sur Internet, les cybercriminels ont pris le contrôle d’une centaine de frigos à travers l’Europe. La température des frigos a grimpé jusqu’à 50 °C, détruisant des montagnes de nourriture. Des milliers d’euros de pertes ont été recensés.
À lire aussi : « La partie émergée d’un iceberg » : après les frigos, quels appareils risquent aussi de se faire pirater ?
Bruxelles va passer les enseignes au crible
Face à cette nouvelle vague de cyberattaques, l’Europe a décidé de réagir. La Commission européenne va évaluer la capacité des supermarchés à faire face aux attaques informatiques. Interrogé par Politico, Christophe Hansen, commissaire européen à l’Agriculture et à l’Alimentation, explique avoir l’intention d’aborder le sujet lors de la prochaine réunion du Collège de sécurité de la Commission.
« La chaîne d’approvisionnement alimentaire européenne doit être préparée aux menaces nouvelles et en évolution. Les cyberattaques répétées contre les supermarchés sont profondément préoccupantes, causant des pertes économiques pour les distributeurs et des rayons vides pour les consommateurs », déclare Christophe Hansen.
Mis en place l’année dernière, le Collège de sécurité réunit l’ensemble des commissaires afin de se pencher sur les menaces qui pèsent sur l’UE. La prochaine réunion permettra d’examiner les plans d’urgence des géants de la grande distribution et leur capacité à réagir en cas d’incident majeur. Aucune date n’a encore été fixée, mais les chefs de cabinet ont convenu que la réunion devait avoir lieu rapidement, au vu de l’actualité récente. Le Collège se réunit à intervalles réguliers, en dehors des réunions hebdomadaires de la Commission.
« Il s’agit d’une tentative délibérée de perturber notre chaîne d’approvisionnement alimentaire et de saper la confiance des consommateurs dans celle-ci, un avertissement que nous devons prendre au sérieux », prévient le commissaire européen à l’Agriculture et à l’Alimentation.
Notez que Bruxelles n’a pas attendu la vague d’attaques survenue début novembre pour s’emparer du sujet. Le mois dernier, des responsables de la Commission chargés de l’agriculture ont déjà rencontré les distributeurs touchés par la cyberattaque nationale contre la France. Bien que la sécurité alimentaire de l’Europe ne soit pas menacée, Christophe Hansen estime qu’il est impératif de « travailler à tous les niveaux pour renforcer notre préparation et notre résilience ».
À lire aussi : Cyberattaque contre les frigos de supermarchés – on sait enfin ce qu’il s’est vraiment passé
« Le maillon le plus faible »
Dans un commentaire transmis à 01net, Pierre-Henry Poiret, ingénieur en cybersécurité chez HarfangLab, souligne d’ailleurs que la cyberattaque nécessite une « coordination au niveau européen et mondial ». Comme « souvent en matière de cybersécurité et de chaîne d’approvisionnement, la sécurité de l’ensemble dépend de celle de son maillon le plus faible », poursuit l’expert, soulignant que « les conséquences d’une vulnérabilité peuvent donc largement dépasser les frontières nationales ».

articles.title: Brave é processado por coleta de dados para IA e funções contra paywall • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Brave é processado por coleta de dados para IA e funções contra paywall
Ferramenta de busca com inteligência artificial também é alvo da ação.
O jornal The New York Times está processando a dona do navegador e buscador Brave, sob a acusação de copiar reportagens e transformá-las em matéria-prima para produtos próprios. A ação, apresentada nesta segunda-feira (02/11), também questiona recursos de bloqueio de anúncios que permitem contornar paywalls.
Segundo a ação, a empresa mantém um acervo com mais de 30 bilhões de páginas da web e continua adicionando milhões de endereços diariamente. Entre esse material estariam cópias de reportagens do Times obtidas sem autorização.
O jornal afirma ainda que a Brave não identifica publicamente o robô usado para fazer a coleta desses dados, dificultando o bloqueio do rastreador. O conteúdo é utilizado em produtos como o Ask Brave, que responde perguntas com IA (semelhante ao Modo IA, do Google), reduzindo a necessidade de o usuário acessar a publicação original.
Em um processo separado, os jornais New York Daily News, Chicago Tribune e Orlando Sentinel fazem acusações semelhantes.
Segundo a ação, a Brave estaria comercializando acesso ao seu índice por meio da Brave Search API, utilizada por terceiros para recuperar informações da web. Entre os clientes citados na ação estão empresas de IA como Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI e Cohere.
Um dos produtos oferecidos pela API, segundo o Times, é o LLM Context, criado especificamente para fornecer a modelos de linguagem textos, tabelas e outros dados provenientes de raspagens na internet.
O jornal tem sido extremamente duro em relação ao acesso não autorizado aos seus conteúdos por ferramentas e empresas de IA. Ele aguarda o julgamento de um processo contra a OpenAI e a Microsoft, aberto em 2023.
O navegador Brave, conhecido pelos recursos de privacidade e bloqueio de rastreadores, também está no centro da disputa. Segundo o Times, essas ferramentas também interferem nas receitas com anúncios e assinaturas dos jornais.
A ação menciona filtros que podem ser adicionados ao bloqueador e contornam barreiras de acesso, como o Paywall Blocker, que permite acessar textos exclusivos para assinantes.
O jornal afirma que, sem recursos para financiar o trabalho jornalístico, “haverá um vácuo na produção de notícias que nenhum computador ou inteligência artificial será capaz de preencher”, e sustenta que o Brave se beneficia do acesso ao conteúdo enquanto reduz oportunidades de monetização do veículo que o produziu.
O processo afirma que a disputa começou antes da chegada do caso aos tribunais. O Times diz ter enviado duas notificações extrajudiciais ao Brave em 2025 e 2026. A nova ação foi apresentada depois que a empresa não atendeu aos pedidos.
O porta-voz do jornal, Graham James, afirmou que o veículo apoia o desenvolvimento responsável de inteligência artificial, mas acusa a Brave de ignorar a legislação de direitos autorais e os pedidos anteriores para interromper a prática.
A Perplexity, mencionada como um dos clientes da raspagem de dados feita pelo Brave, criticou a acusação e disse que o New York Times estaria “gastando demais com advogados e pouco com jornalistas”.

articles.title: I tested the Bambu Lab H3C 3D printer, and it's far beyond other machines
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Having had the H3C on the workbench for the last month, I still feel like I have only just scraped the surface of what’s possible. The big innovations here are the ability to print with different nozzle sizes, and while this still feels like a technology in development, the potential is obvious. However, as I built a pair of speakers with PLA outer walls and dampening TPU infill, the technical potential demonstrated the next step in 3D printing.
Reasons to buy
- + Multi-material printing
- + Multi-diameter printing
- + Fast standard prints
Reasons to avoid
- - Complex machine
- - Large and heavy
- - Software complexity takes some working out
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
It was inevitable that there would be a successor to the Bambu Lab H2C, which was no small machine; however, the Bambu Lab H3C takes scale and ability to the next level, although the innovative Vortek Hotend Change System is no more.
Like the H2C, there’s the multi-tool functionality, but as you’ll see from the images, the system is all new, with dedicated tools in the Swaptek Tool Changer rather than the Vortek hotend-changing system, so something closer to the Bondtech INDX tool changers.
An interesting update is the ability to print with different-sized nozzles, so a fine 0.2 mm for fine detail, going to a 0.8 mm for infill and areas where speed is preferable to fine finishes. What I have discovered through the month that I’ve had the printer so far is that this is an evolution of the 3D printing process, refining the techniques and while this technology and its application are still being ironed out, the full potential is apparent.
Adding to the multi-diameter printing is the advanced TPU handling. This essentially enables you to print with thicker 2.85 mm filament using the PrintTool hotend. As the filament is thicker, it supports softer TPU, and again, there’s a learning process behind its use. It’s not quite as simple as popping it in and letting it go, but it is a step in the right direction.
Sitting on top of the machine is the new AMS 3H filament management system that holds up to nine filaments, with two slots enabling integrated drying and bypass feeds for specialist materials.
I’ll admit, as the boxes kept arriving and the H3C started to take shape on the workbench, the machine did seem to dominate the space. However, after squeezing in the H2C next to it, while the new AMS gives a visual impression of scale, the footprint of the two machines is much the same.
The big question for me at the start of this test was whether this new machine and design was a direct replacement for the H2C or something altogether new. It certainly initially looks far more complex, but then, as I became more familiar with the machine, the full tool changer design, once assembled, did seem, a little more simplistic and certainly more reliable as I pushed the print times and complexities.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
One point to note is that throughout the test, while I had the machine and seemingly every accessory that I could need to go with it, the actual official machine specifications and final tweaking of the software were still to be released.
What Bambu did supply was a few test models and an extensive set of instructions about how to tackle each of the main new features. There was also a set of complex models that I used to start the test before deviating to some of my own, and then back to the supplied models to finish the test.
I’ll cover more of those tests in the performance section, but what interested me was using this printer for a real practical task. This is, after all, a business-class machine, although the price will put this just in range of the keen enthusiast as well.
The main project for this test was to print and build a set of speakers from Print Your Speakers, with the Supersonic MK3 kit fitting the bill for this test. Essentially, a solid PLA outer with TPU to add damping to the infill, and then a switch of nozzle sizes for the fine detail of the outer wall and a thicker nozzle for the inner walls.
This is where the learning curve of this machine and the Bambu Lab software really comes into play, and while that learning curve is steep.
As the test ran on, the potential of this machine started to grow. While multi-filament and tool changer machines now dominate and Bambu Lab’s lead in the field was quickly fading, especially with the Original Prusa CORE One INDX, of which the H3C’s new system bears more than a passing resemblance. But with support for 2.85 mm TPU and multiple other materials, it now pushes them back out in front and truly offers something unique, although there are still a few refinements needed.
Bambu Lab H3C: Price and availability
The H3C will be available to purchase from the Bambu Lab website from 3 November 2026, following the official launch. Unlike the H2C, there is just one configuration available at launch, with the AMS 3H and all nine PrintTools included.
- H3C AMS Combo: $2,499 / £2,199
- Combo + PLA Palette + TPU: $2,589 /£2,269
- Combo + PLA Palette + TPU + Bambu Station (Enclosed) + E1 Air Purifier:
- $3,049 / £2,699
- Combo + PLA Palette + TPU + Bambu Station (Open): $2,799 / £2,469
Bambu Lab H3C: Design
Print Technology: Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF)
Build Area: 330 × 320 × 325 mm
Minimum Layer Resolution: To be confirmed
Maximum Layer Resolution: To be confirmed
Dimensions: 493 × 571 × 587 mm
Weight: 36.28 kg (including AMS 3H)
Bed: Heated, up to 120°C
Print Surface: Textured PEI plate
Software: Bambu Studio
Materials: PLA, PETG, TPU, ABS, ASA, PA, PC, PPA, PPS and other supported materials
Print Speed: Maximum toolhead speed of 1,400 mm/s
The Bambu Lab H3C is a 3D printer on another scale, and whilst it doesn’t look that much larger than the H2C initially, once you start to work with it and try to move it around the workshop, you suddenly realise that its colossal 36.28 kg weight and physical dimensions of 493 × 571 × 587 mm make it more of a two-person lift than something you’re able to handle on your own.
That would explain why Bambu Lab also sent a special trolley along with the machine, so it’s easy to access and move around the workshop. The issue at the moment is that there are so many 3D printers coming out that my workshop doesn’t have any space, so this will be something that I will manoeuvre the printer onto once I can find a pathway through the workshop to get the two sections to meet.
As it was, I decided to set this machine up in the photo area, and I’ve already manoeuvred the H2C next to it so that I can do a side-by-side comparison on size and scale, however, again this left little room as the the scale of these machine is rapidly increasing.
As I first lifted the H3C into position, the two machines looked roughly the same size, but as I started to add the huge new AMS 3H on top, I realised that this was an altogether different proposition.
As I unpacked the machine, it was obvious that Bambu Lab had taken a completely different direction to multi tool head printing compared with the H2C, and the H3C has something more akin to the INDX tool changer. You can definitely see the similarities. As I went through the initial setup, what was surprising here was just how easy and straightforward it was, and whilst the machine was large, the actual placing of the AMS on top and positioning all of the nozzles wasn’t at all difficult.
The only thing that you do need to make sure of is that there are nine tools included: eight with 0.4 mm PrintTools for 1.75 mm filament and one dedicated 0.4 mm PrintTool for 2.85 mm filament. Careful reference to the instructions as you’re setting up is essential to make sure that this nozzle goes in the right place.
Before taking a closer look at this new system, it’s worth pointing out that the AMS 3H is quite an evolution on the AMS 2, sitting on top of the machine and really integrating more closely with the design compared with the add-on box of the AMS 2. This, I know, will please a lot of print farms, which, whilst generally fans of the Bambu Lab machines, find the AMS 2 is often a weak point and the part that they have to replace most often. One point here is that, of those nine slots, there’s a separate section within the rack which enables just two of those nine slots to be actively dried.
As we’ve seen before, you can also add more AMS units, enabling up to 24-colour printing, up from the nine possible out of the box.
Once I got everything set up and installed, which, to be honest, didn’t take too long, it was then time to connect the machine to the local network via Wi-Fi 6. As ever, this was as straightforward and simple as with all other Bambu Lab machines. One of the surprises is that a machine of this size and scale, especially aimed at the professional market, doesn’t feature an Ethernet port.
The other point here is that as soon as it connected, it ran through a series of updates before then going through the calibration process. So, while the machine itself is really well designed and easy to set up, the software updating and full calibration process can take up to an hour, which is slightly infuriating when I was quite excited to see what this machine was capable of doing.
After the Wi-Fi connection, calibration and everything else had been run through, it was time to connect through the Bambu Studio software, and again, a few clicks through the beta release that we were given, enabled me to connect quickly to the printer.
However, as always, before running through my own prints and some of those others that had been supplied to fully test out this new machine’s abilities, I ran through the standard test prints on the machine. These are the usual 3D Benchy and variants, alongside scrapers and a few other bits and bobs, as expected. It ran through all of those prints flawlessly, and then it was time to cross over to Bambu Studio.
Bambu Lab actually supplied some very interesting test models, which I go into in the performance section, but before I went into these multi-filament, multicolour designs, I decided to test out some of my more standard prints. This just enabled me to double-check the calibration and also try out a few different materials.
There are two built-in 1080p cameras, with an optional Bird’s Eye camera available as well. The chamber heats up to 65°C, with a 120°C heated bed and a 350°C maximum nozzle temperature.
Leaving the machine just to run through those few prints, I was able to step back and take a proper look at the machine, and it is an evolution of what we’ve seen with the other H series printers, just slightly larger. Again, this is a steel chassis, which gives it structural support and also makes it insanely heavy to lift around the workshop.
The outer is plastic, with a grey and black exterior that looks stylish, just in the same vein as we’ve seen with the other Bambu Lab hardware. On the front, you’ve got a big viewing window so that you can see what’s going on with the print, and whilst the top-mounted AMS 3H does stop you from looking down into the machine, it's integrated rather than being a separate unit, which I personally really like.
As we’ve seen before, there’s a really nice 5-inch colour touchscreen, with an 854 × 480 display resolution, and this is very responsive, giving me full access to all the functions and settings. However, it is getting more complex, especially with those nine toolheads. It does take a little bit of extra time just to orientate yourself with all of those different settings.
Across the front is the main feature of this new 3D printer, obviously the new nine-toolhead rack, and what’s interesting here is that the rack raises and lowers, so if you do want to see what’s going on on the print bed, it’s far easier than with some of the other multiple systems of this style out there. At all times, however, you can see where the influence of the Prusa CORE One INDX version has influenced Bambu Lab’s slight change of direction, although they’ve taken that style of design in a slightly different direction.
The rack features nine individual PrintTool docking positions, and these all automatically dock with tool alignment and offset compensation. What’s interesting here is that there are dedicated filament paths for each PrintTool, meaning that each works completely independently, and there are integrated filament cutters within the PrintTools, again just to help speed things up. When it comes to the extruder and internal mechanisms, they all use hardened steel, with hardened-steel extruder gears and nozzles rated at HRC 55+.
As ever, we see a flexible steel build plate, and this is a decent size, with a 330 × 320 × 325 mm build volume enabling you to tackle all sorts of projects, especially with the huge material support this new printer offers.
Bambu Lab H3C: Features
It’s difficult to do a quick run-through of the features because, over the H2C, things have really progressed, and the new Swaptek nine-tool changing system is a real evolution of design. You can’t help feeling it’s heavily influenced by the INDX system that we’ve seen from Bondtech and featured on the latest Prusa CORE One machines.
However, over that system, there are plenty of changes, and it’s obviously got the Bambu Lab spin, with automatic tool changes that happen in under six seconds. There’s also active preheating that essentially anticipates the upcoming tool changes and heats the next nozzle in advance, making complex models slightly faster to print than on some of those other systems.
One of the features that I noticed early on, and one of the issues with other systems of this style, is that quite often the tool rack gets in the way of being able to see the print area. However, once that new tool is selected, the tool rack actually retracts upwards so that you get a good clear view of the print area, and it also helps to keep the filament tubes out of the way.
Feeding all of those nine new toolheads is the redesign of the AMS system, known as the AMS 3H, that manages the filaments in an integrated box that sits on top of the machine. Like the AMS 2, it's a sealed storage option and helps protect the filaments inside from moisture.
Again, as we’ve seen in the past, it has automatic filament loading and routing that works exceptionally well, and with RFID built in, as long as you’re using Bambu Lab’s own materials, they’ll be automatically recognised and synced with the software, making the whole process that much easier.
One of the surprises is that only two of those nine slots are actively dried, so if you do have filaments that are more prone to moisture than others, then they should sit in those two. There’s a cover that sits over the top, so it’s pretty easy to see which two those are.
As ever, there are also expansion options, so if you have other AMS systems and you want to plug them in, the H3C supports additional AMS units for up to 24-colour printing.
One of the new additions is the FlexFeed extruder that supports both 1.75 mm and 2.85 mm filament, and there’s also a dedicated 2.85 mm filament path for flexible materials such as TPU. While TPU for AMS can just be used directly on the machine, as I discovered when I printed speakers with files from Print Your Speakers, when it came to printing other softer TPU, you have to use one of the bypass feed ports and quickly change part of the installation and feed to the toolheads.
The first time you do it, it takes a little bit of time and working out, but essentially, the soft TPU needs to go into one of the slots that enables active drying. TPU is hygroscopic and collects water like a sponge, so ensuring that it’s nice and dry before it goes through the system is just going to improve and help with the quality of the print.
You then feed that through into the 2.85 mm supporting toolhead, but rather than running through the filament feed tube, you bypass the tube, cutting just a small length that goes into the toolhead and then directly into the extruder. This just helps with the smooth movement of the TPU filament through the system. This means that it can actually cope with TPU all the way down to 75A, perfect for some of the projects that Bambu Lab supplied.
Using TPU in the system is not uncommon, but you still have to reconfigure the system slightly. Bambu Lab has made that slightly easier, and of course, you also have the ability to print with multiple materials and multiple colours.
But what impressed me the most is that with the Bambu Lab PLA palette, which is a new range of filaments, you can print with CMYKW to enable colour mixing using cyan, magenta, yellow, black and white filaments. The end results, as you’re seeing in some of the sample pictures, are quite amazing, enabling far more colourful and complex prints than has previously been possible.
But it’s not just about multiple colour-mixing filaments. You can also use a huge amount of engineering materials because of the hardened nozzles and the actively heated chamber, so utilising ABS, ASA, PA, PC and carbon-filled composites is all perfectly possible.
Further supporting the flexibility over the way you print is that there are multiple nozzle sizes, including 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 mm. But what makes a difference here is that you can optimise it to work using those different nozzles in one print. That means you can speed up the printing of the interior support structure with, say, a 0.6 or 0.8 mm nozzle and get that fine-quality finish on the exterior with a 0.2 or 0.4 mm nozzle. This is something very new.
There’s also been a range of feature enhancements for speed, with a maximum toolhead speed of 1,400 mm/s and acceleration of 25,000 mm/s². To keep up with that high-speed printing, the hotend flow rate of 40 mm³/s is also impressive, although these run to Bambu Lab’s own test conditions rather than what you’re actually going to see in the real world.
Something which I haven’t really been able to look at in any depth is the CraftTool support, and we’re starting to see Bambu Lab not only promote their machines for 3D printing but for other craft uses. This is what really made the H2D such an interesting machine. Potentially, in the near future, the CraftTools will enable automatic switching between compatible printing and crafting tools, so there will be blade cutting, drawing and debossing, but I’ll bring you more on that when I’ve been able to look at it properly.
As I mentioned in the Design section, Bambu Lab and, actually, quite a few of the other manufacturers are starting to take filtration seriously, and here we’ve got the H11 HEPA filter, granulated coconut-shell activated-carbon filter and an integrated chamber exhaust and circulation system. Bambu Lab actually even provided an air filter with the machine, which has been very handy, especially in quite a crowded workshop.
When it comes to features, the H3C is one of the most feature-packed printers to have come onto the market yet, but with all of those features comes an added level of complexity that could cause issues in the long run, and the only way to discover those is to ensure that, over the month of having this machine, it has been running almost constantly.
Bambu Lab H3C: Performance
As these 3D printers get more complex and the models that they’re able to produce become increasingly more elaborate, mixing not only colours but materials, the time it takes to fully test one of these machines is rapidly increasing.
Thankfully, Bambu Lab recognises that whilst machines are speeding up, when it comes to fully testing some of those mixed-filament options, it doesn’t just take hours; it takes days for each print to be produced. In order for you to run through all of the test prints provided, including rerouting different filaments, that all takes a considerable amount of time.
But thankfully, I’ve had this printer for almost six weeks, and through that time, there have only been brief periods where it has remained dormant. Otherwise, filament after filament has gone through, producing everything from pinhole cameras out of carbon-filled filament through to some quite incredible desktop speakers, thanks to the guys at printyourspeakers.com, and of course, the extremely elaborate models that the guys at Bambu Lab provided to test out this printer.
Before I go into that, I’ll just quickly run through the setup process of the machine, as whilst this machine looks extremely complex, the actual setup process is typically Bambu. Essentially, with the machine arriving in two boxes, the machine and a separate box for the AMS, it only took about half an hour before the machine was sitting proudly on the workbench, looking ready to produce its first print.
The instructions are pretty clearly laid out, and as you’d expect, the large 5-inch touchscreen gives you all the information you need. Once everything is plugged in and connected, you then simply load the filament, and it’s pretty much set to go. However, as always, that complexity comes with a large extra step.
First, you download and install the firmware, which all ran through nice and quickly, but then it was on to the full setup calibration. Whilst it doesn’t actually take any involvement from yourself other than clicking a couple of buttons, it does take about an hour, and when you have a machine of this size and potential in front of you, that wait is slightly agonising but unfortunately essential.
Once the machine had run through its copious amount of checks and all the nozzles had been calibrated, it was time to run through the first set of prints, and here I had three different options. Firstly, those pre-installed on the machine in the 64 GB internal storage; the second was my usual test prints; and the third was the additional files that Bambu Lab had provided to fully test out the system.
I opted for the quick run of those prints in storage just to check whether the calibration had worked and everything was printing correctly, and sure enough, print after print came off the print bed without issue, mixing the colours beautifully into pretty good-quality standard prints. All of these that I started with initially were PLA and mainly ends of reels from previous reviews.
Then it was on to my own test prints, and again, the accuracy and precision of the printer really stood out, and I was also impressed with the relative speed. One of the big points here is that the tool-changing system, as I saw with the INDX, vastly increases print speeds when compared with the H2C, which is a machine that I actively always have set up and running.
The speeds with this new system are again slightly faster. A quick test of those print speeds on the H3C, printing the two-tone tree frog in large, took two hours and three minutes, with about eight minutes taken for the preparation time and the rest on the actual model printing. This compared with almost three hours on the H2C, and whilst it was far faster on the preparation and checks at just under six minutes, the print time was closer to two hours and 50 minutes. Finally, comparing it with the H2D, surprisingly, it put in a similar time to the H2C.
As I ran through the test, the speed of the machine was the first thing that really stood out, and with a relatively large print bed as well, I was able to print large projects with absolute ease. Support structures went in nice and easily, and I always use PLA support, although as I started to venture into Bambu Lab’s own models, I realised the standard PLA support was just not delicate enough for what was needed, and PVA support, which could be washed away, would have been a better option.
Through my own models, there were quite a few different projects that I wanted to really give a go. The first was a pinhole camera that I had designed for some lectures and was small. It's a good way to test out dimensional accuracy, as I had to drop in a brass-sheet pinhole lens that I had designed and make it tripod-mountable, with brass inserts used for the screw thread.
As the box also had to be lightproof, dimensional accuracy due to the fitting and removing of a lightproof back was also essential, and using a carbon-filled filament with solid infill just ensured that the whole box would stay lightproof. I also had to feature a sliding shutter mechanism that would cover the brass aperture, so again, quality of surface printing as well as dimensional accuracy was absolutely essential.
After running several iterations of the design, I came up with the final product and tested it in the studio with success, producing small prints onto photographic paper through a 0.3 mm aperture. The quality of the print and success of the project just highlighted the first bit of flexibility with this machine and its design.
The next was to call on somebody with a lot more experience with high-quality and precision engineering 3D design, and the guys at Print Your Speakers provided me with the Supersonic MK3 desktop speaker kit to give this new printer a go. There were several angles that I wanted to fully test that no other printer would be able to do.
The first was obviously to print speakers using PLA for the outer, but then rather than having PLA infill, I wanted it to be TPU in order to help absorb some of the sound. I also wanted to be able to swap between nozzle sizes, all of which took a little bit of experimentation, and at present this is an area of the systems use that I will have to come back to, as at the moment I haven't had any success. I then tested a straight PLA box against the PLA and TPU mixed box, and the difference in audio quality was apparent, with a far deeper sound from the more advanced material-mix option.
Having now tried a variety of different materials and options through the machine, I was pretty confident about setting off with some of Bambu Lab’s own models to fully test out its abilities. The first was the FROSTSPINE Dragon Bust 1015, which used a variety of materials and took a while to organise the different materials that were needed into the AMS and configure the system.
Printing this started to point out the big difference between the old Bambu Lab multi-filament AMS systems and this new iteration. It's far more complex, and along with the printing guides that helped guide you through the setup, there’s definitely a greater skill required to get the most out of this machine.
It took two or three initial attempts before that model rattled off the print bed, taking several days to complete. I then moved on to the hummingbird frame, which was a simple multi-filament PLA mix, and here I really started to see the full potential, being able to mix the colours to create colours that weren’t directly available from a single filament but only once they were blended together, and the results were spectacular.
The only thing was that I accidentally used PLA support rather than PVA support, so once the final model printed, which took several days, it was going to be a long process to break away all of that support. The intricacy and delicacy of many of the models that you’re now able to print on this machine far exceed what you’ve been able to do before.
Through this whole process, the one thing that became apparent was that this is a far more hands-on machine, and there is an obvious learning curve, especially working with all the different toolheads, nozzle sizes, bypass filament feeds and potentially additional CraftTools. This is a very feature-enhanced workshop machine at a price that will appeal to both enthusiasts and professionals.
Bambu Lab H3C: Final verdict
In those six weeks of testing, I feel like I’ve only just started to scrape the surface of what’s possible, but there are several key points that I’ve learnt through this test. The first is that if you just want to get straight into printing, then there are cheaper machines out there which will enable you to do that. So if you only print with up to four filaments, which most people do, then the complexity of this machine might be just a little bit above what you need.
But then, as you start to embrace all its options and capabilities, and if you’re willing to sit down and learn about how to mix materials, how to use those different nozzle sizes together and obviously all those different filament types, then you have a 3D printer that is really quite different from anything that’s come before and sets the tone for what’s coming up in the future.
Whilst there are more than passing similarities with the INDX system, what Bambu Lab has done here is to evolve what it had done with its previous multi-filament systems and, with this new option, create something that is far more advanced.
With that increasing complexity come its own issues, and through the process of this review, I did have occasions where I had to rerun the full calibration as one of the nozzles wasn’t quite sitting right. Then there’s the whole bypass reconfiguration of the filament feed, which does get quite complex, but once you’ve done it once, you basically allocate one toolhead to TPU, still leaving you with eight for all other filaments.
The options and possibilities for this machine are huge, and through this review, I’ve just been incredibly impressed with the overall quality. Each firmware update has fixed some of the issues that I was having early on, such as the RFID not recognising filament reels and, for some reason, the auto-feed system suddenly not auto-feeding. But after the update, those issues were fixed.
I also had, as you might be able to see on the speaker set, a slight issue with surface finish, but then that’s because I was experimenting with some of those more advanced features, and this was the first time that I had configured the whole process myself in the software. Later, small models printed with much better quality, but again, this is all part of that learning process. As it stands, this printer is a definite evolution of what’s possible and an exciting glimpse into the future of 3D printing.
Should I buy the Bambu Lab H3C 3D printer?
Buy it if...
You want to print with multiple materials and nozzle sizes.
The H3C enables you to combine different materials and nozzle diameters in a single print, something that would be difficult or impossible to produce on more standard 3D printers.
You want faster, more efficient multicolour printing.
With nine PrintTools and material changes taking under six seconds, the H3C reduces the time swapping filaments.
Don't buy it if...
You just want a straightforward 3D printer.
The H3C has a steep learning curve, especially when mixing materials and nozzle sizes. For standard PLA printing, there are simpler, cheaper options.
You have limited space or a tight budget.
At £2,199 and over 36 kg, the H3C is a substantial investment unless you'll regularly use its advanced features.
For more models, I've tested the best 3D printers you can get right now.
Alastair is a photographer, filmmaker and tech writer who has been working in the publishing industry since the late 1990s. For more than 25 years he has covered photography, video and technology across Future's photography, technology and gaming brands. He runs a photography and video production company and lectures in TV and film. He can usually be found testing mini PCs or prototyping and prop building with the aid of 3D printing.
