articles.title: TV Mini LED vs OLED : quelles différences et quelle technologie choisir ?
articles.text:
Entre Mini LED et OLED, la différence tient à une question simple : d’où vient la lumière ? Une TV OLED fabrique sa lumière pixel par pixel, une TV Mini LED l’obtient d’un rétroéclairage composé de milliers de diodes miniatures pilotées par zones.
En 2026, cette seconde approche a pris l’avantage en luminosité : TCL annonce jusqu’à 10 000 nits sur sa X11L, et notre labo a déjà mesuré 2 526 cd/m² sur la C8K de 2025, et jusqu’à 3 648 cd/m² sur un téléviseur QLED, contre 2 687 cd/m² pour la meilleure OLED passée sur notre banc, tandis que l’OLED conserve son noir absolu. Le détail de ce match technique, poste par poste, avec les réponses apportées par TCL, numéro 1 mondial du Mini LED. On vous explique.
L’essentiel en chiffres
- Jusqu’à 20 736 zones de rétroéclairage indépendantes (local dimming) sur la TCL X11L 98 pouces, contre 1 680 zones sur le TCL 65C8K testé par notre labo en novembre 2025.
- Jusqu’à 10 000 nits annoncés par TCL sur la X11L et 5 000 nits sur la C8L 65 pouces, contre 2 687 cd/m² pour la meilleure OLED mesurée par le 01lab.
- Une dalle WHVA 2.0 Ultra et un film à faible réflexion annoncé à 0,5 % de réflexion sur les TCL X11L et C8L 2026.
- Zéro risque de marquage sur un écran Mini LED, un phénomène qui reste possible sur une dalle OLED après plusieurs milliers d’heures d’images fixes.
- Un prix de 1 199 € pour la TCL 65C79L et de 1 499 € pour la TCL 65C89L le 19 octobre 2026, soit 300 à 1 000 € de moins qu’une OLED de même taille.
- TCL, numéro 1 mondial du Mini LED en 2025 avec 3,95 millions d’unités et 31,1 % de part de marché selon Omdia.
Rétroéclairage ou pixels auto-émissifs : d’où vient la lumière ?
Sur une TV OLED, chaque pixel est une diode organique qui produit sa propre lumière et peut s’éteindre totalement. Sur une TV Mini LED, l’image est formée par une dalle LCD, et la lumière vient de derrière : un panneau de diodes de moins de 0,2 mm, plusieurs milliers sur un 65 pouces, remplace les quelques dizaines de LED d’un écran LCD classique. En d’autres termes, le Mini LED est un écran LCD dont le rétroéclairage a été découpé en une mosaïque de petites sources lumineuses que le téléviseur allume et éteint séparément.
Cette différence de principe explique tout le reste. Le pixel OLED s’éteint, donc le noir est parfait, mais il s’use quand il éclaire fort et longtemps. La diode Mini LED peut pousser très fort sans s’abîmer, mais elle éclaire un groupe de pixels et non un seul : tout l’enjeu consiste à piloter finement chaque zone. C’est sur ce terrain que TCL, qui a lancé ses premiers téléviseurs QD Mini LED en 2019, a construit son avance.
| Principe | Mini LED | OLED | 
|---|---|---|
| Source de lumière | Rétroéclairage à milliers de mini diodes, par zones | Chaque pixel émet sa propre lumière | 
| Dalle | LCD (filtre à cristaux liquides + points quantiques) | Diodes organiques, pas de rétroéclairage | 
| Noir | Très profond, zone éteinte | Absolu, pixel éteint | 
| Luminosité de pointe | 3 000 à 10 000 nits annoncés par TCL en 2026 | Jusqu’à 2 687 cd/m² mesurés par notre labo | 
| Usure | Aucun marquage | Marquage possible sur images fixes | 
Le local dimming permet-il vraiment au Mini LED de rivaliser avec l’OLED sur le contraste ?
Oui, à condition d’avoir assez de zones et un pilotage assez fin. Le local dimming est le contrôle indépendant de chaque zone du rétroéclairage : une zone peut rester très lumineuse pendant que la zone voisine reste sombre, ce qui permet d’afficher une étoile éclatante sur un ciel noir sans éclairer tout l’écran. Plus les zones sont petites et nombreuses, plus le téléviseur s’approche du comportement d’une OLED, où la frontière entre clair et sombre se joue au pixel près.
Les chiffres donnent la mesure du chemin parcouru. Le TCL 65C8K que notre labo a testé en novembre 2025 comptait 1 680 zones gérées sur 23 bits. Sur la génération 2026, la TCL C8L 65 pouces monte à 2 040 zones, et la TCL X11L à 11 520 zones en 75 pouces, 14 400 en 85 pouces et 20 736 en 98 pouces, un record sur le marché, et un algorithme maison, All-domain Halo Control, affine le pilotage de chaque zone. Reste la limite physique : vu de face, le halo autour des objets clairs devient très difficile à percevoir, mais il peut réapparaître quand on se décale sur le côté, comme sur tout écran LCD. L’OLED, elle, n’en produit jamais.
Comment ça marche chez TCL ? La technologie SQD Mini LED, pour Super Quantum Dot Mini LED, est la huitième génération de rétroéclairage de la marque, inaugurée en 2026 sur les séries X11L, C8L et C7L. Les diodes, plus petites, permettent de multiplier les zones, jusqu’à 20 736 sur la X11L 98 pouces, et chaque zone est pilotée par l’algorithme All-domain Halo Control, chargé de limiter les fuites de lumière entre zones voisines. Le tout est orchestré par le processeur TSR AiPQ de la marque.
Luminosité : pourquoi le Mini LED prend-il l’avantage en plein jour ?
Parce qu’une diode inorganique peut émettre bien plus de lumière qu’un pixel organique sans se dégrader. En octobre 2026, la meilleure OLED que nous avons mesurée plafonne à 2 687 cd/m², quand TCL annonce 5 000 nits sur la C8L 65 pouces, 6 000 nits sur les 85 et 98 pouces et jusqu’à 10 000 nits sur la X11L. Même en gardant une marge entre valeur annoncée et valeur mesurée, l’ordre de grandeur n’est pas le même. Sur notre banc, le meilleur téléviseur QLED a été mesuré à 3 648 cd/m². Sur une image claire plein écran, celle d’un match ou d’un journal télévisé, un rétroéclairage à diodes conserve en outre bien plus de puissance qu’une dalle OLED, qui doit se brider pour protéger ses pixels.
Concrètement, cette réserve change la vie dans un salon exposé au soleil : l’image reste lisible en journée sans fermer les volets, et les contenus HDR conservent leurs hautes lumières au lieu de les écrêter. Notre labo l’avait déjà constaté sur le TCL 65C8K, pointé à 2 526 cd/m² en mode Filmmaker, pour une note de 4,4/5. Sa descendance 2026 annonce 5 000 nits en 65 pouces sur la C8L et jusqu’à 10 000 nits sur la X11L 85 et 98 pouces.
| Téléviseur | Technologie | Pic HDR | Source | 
|---|---|---|---|
| TCL 75X11L (2026) | SQD Mini LED | Jusqu’à 9 000 nits annoncés (10 000 en 85 et 98 pouces) | TCL, fiche officielle | 
| TCL 65C89L (2026) | SQD Mini LED | Jusqu’à 5 000 nits annoncés (6 000 en 85 et 98 pouces) | TCL, fiche officielle | 
| TCL 65C8K (2025) | QD Mini LED | 2 526 cd/m² mesurés (mode Filmmaker) | 01lab, novembre 2025 | 
| Meilleure OLED mesurée | OLED | 2 687 cd/m² mesurés | 01lab, octobre 2026 | 
| Meilleur Mini LED mesuré | Mini LED | 2 629 cd/m² mesurés | 01lab, octobre 2026 | 
Comment ça marche chez TCL ? Entre le rétroéclairage et la dalle, un film de points quantiques convertit la lumière bleue des diodes en rouge et vert très purs. Sur la génération SQD, TCL affine ce filtre, baptisé Ultra Color Filter, et revendique une gamme 33 % plus large et 69 % plus précise, jusqu’à 100 % de l’espace BT.2020, la norme de couleurs la plus étendue de la télévision ultra-haute définition. Notre labo avait déjà salué la précision colorimétrique du C8K de 2025, avec des tons chair et des couleurs justes dès la sortie du carton.
Noirs, angles de vision, reflets : où l’OLED garde-t-elle l’avantage ?
Sur trois points précis : le noir absolu, les angles de vision et, selon les modèles, la gestion des reflets. Le pixel éteint d’une OLED ne laisse passer aucune lumière, là où une zone Mini LED éteinte reste bordée de zones allumées. Les angles de vision sont la seconde limite structurelle du LCD : vu de biais, un écran à cristaux liquides perd en contraste et en saturation, alors qu’une OLED reste quasiment inchangée hors de l’axe. Enfin, les dalles TCL 2026 sont brillantes, un choix qui favorise le rendu des noirs en pièce éclairée, mais que certaines OLED à traitement mat contournent mieux face à une fenêtre.
Il faut dire que TCL ne nie pas ces limites, il les attaque. Dès le C8K de 2025, notre labo relevait une dalle « Wide HVA » conçue pour élargir les angles de vision, avec un gain annoncé de 40 % par rapport aux dalles HVA précédentes, et un film à faible réflexion qui atténue les reflets directs. La génération 2026 passe à la dalle WHVA 2.0 Ultra sur les X11L et C8L, avec un film dont le taux de réflexion annoncé par TCL tombe à 0,5 %. Pour un canapé placé face à l’écran et un salon normalement éclairé, l’écart avec l’OLED devient difficile à percevoir. Dans une pièce noire, le cinéphile exigeant verra encore la différence.
Comment ça marche chez TCL ? Une dalle HVA, pour High Vertical Alignment, est un LCD dont les cristaux liquides sont alignés verticalement au repos, ce qui bloque mieux la lumière et donne un contraste natif élevé. Sa variante Wide HVA ajoute une compensation optique qui limite la perte de contraste quand on regarde l’écran de biais.
Durée de vie et marquage : quelle technologie vieillit le mieux ?
Le Mini LED ne présente aucun risque de marquage, parce que sa dalle LCD ne contient aucun composant organique qui s’use de façon inégale. Sur une OLED, les pixels qui affichent longtemps le même élément lumineux, un logo de chaîne, un bandeau d’information ou l’interface d’un jeu, vieillissent plus vite que leurs voisins et peuvent laisser une empreinte permanente, généralement après plusieurs milliers d’heures. Les constructeurs ont ajouté des parades, décalage de pixels, détection de logos, cycles de rafraîchissement, mais le phénomène reste possible, et les garanties qui le couvrent sont l’exception.
Sur un LCD, c’est le rétroéclairage qui vieillit. Un Mini LED à diodes multiples a l’avantage de ne pas dépendre d’une poignée de LED latérales : la défaillance d’une diode parmi des milliers ne condamne pas l’écran. Seule ombre au tableau : la consommation. Plus un rétroéclairage est puissant, plus il tire sur la prise, et notre labo notait sur le C8K que le mode Boost, qui pousse la luminosité au-delà de 2 500 cd/m², fait grimper la consommation en HDR. En SDR, pour la télévision du quotidien, l’écart avec une OLED est bien moindre.
Combien coûte un Mini LED TCL face à une OLED en octobre 2026 ?
Nettement moins cher à taille égale. Le 19 octobre 2026, la TCL 65C79L s’affichait à 1 199 € et la TCL 65C89L à 1 499 € chez Boulanger, Fnac et Darty, quand la meilleure OLED 65 pouces de 2026 selon notre labo oscillait entre 1 768 et 1 899 € dans notre comparateur de prix, pour un tarif de base de 2 499 €. La TCL 75X11L, modèle star de la gamme, était proposée à 3 299 €. À noter que les C8L et C89L, comme les C7L et C79L, sont les mêmes téléviseurs vendus sous deux références selon l’enseigne.
Bonne nouvelle ? Le calendrier joue en votre faveur. Le Black Friday a lieu le vendredi 27 novembre 2026, et TCL annonce des offres sur l’ensemble de sa gamme Mini LED à cette occasion, de la C7L à la X11L. Pour un salon lumineux, une grande diagonale ou un usage mêlant sport, jeu et télévision du quotidien, le Mini LED est le choix que nous recommandons en 2026 ; l’OLED ne garde l’avantage que pour le cinéma dans une pièce plongée dans le noir. Il serait dommage de passer à côté.
Sans attendre le 27 novembre, les premières offres Black Friday de TCL sont déjà en ligne depuis la fin octobre. Voici les prix pratiqués sur les modèles cités dans cet article, et sur le reste de la gamme :
- TCL 75X11L (75 pouces, SQD Mini LED) : 2 499 €, contre 3 299 € le 19 octobre, avec 200 € remboursés en plus par TCL, chez Darty et Boulanger
- TCL 65C89L (65 pouces, SQD Mini LED) : 1 199 €, contre 1 499 € le 19 octobre, avec 100 € remboursés en plus par TCL, chez Fnac, Darty et Boulanger
- TCL 55C89L (55 pouces, SQD Mini LED) : 799 €, avec 50 € remboursés en plus par TCL, chez Fnac, Darty et Boulanger
- TCL 65C79L (65 pouces) : 899 €, contre 1 199 € le 19 octobre, chez Fnac, Darty et Boulanger
- TCL 65C6K (65 pouces) : 799,99 €, avec 50 € remboursés en plus par TCL, chez Conforama et Darty
- TCL 55A400PRO (55 pouces) : 699 €, chez Boulanger, Son-Vidéo.com et LDLC
| Série TCL 2026 | Tailles | Luminosité annoncée | Zones de local dimming | Fréquence | Prix relevé le 19 octobre 2026 | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TCL X11L | 75, 85, 98 pouces | 9 000 nits (75″), 10 000 nits (85″ et 98″) | 11 520 à 20 736 | 144 Hz natif en 4K, 288 Hz en 1080p | 3 299 € en 75 pouces | 
| TCL C8L / C89L | 55 à 98 pouces | 3 000 à 6 000 nits selon la taille | 1 008 à 4 032 | 144 Hz natif en 4K, 288 Hz en 1080p | 1 499 € en 65 pouces, 3 499 € en 98 pouces | 
| TCL C7L / C79L | 55 à 98 pouces | 2 700 à 3 000 nits selon la taille | 800 à 2 176 | 144 Hz natif en 4K, 288 Hz en 1080p | 1 199 € en 65 pouces | 
Les questions qu’on nous pose sur le Mini LED et l’OLED
Le Mini LED est-il une bonne alternative à l’OLED ?
Oui. En 2026, un téléviseur Mini LED haut de gamme comme la TCL X11L ou la TCL C8L offre un contraste proche de celui d’une OLED grâce au local dimming, avec une luminosité nettement supérieure : 5 000 à 10 000 nits annoncés par TCL sur la C8L 65 pouces et la X11L, et jusqu’à 3 648 cd/m² mesurés par notre labo sur un téléviseur QLED, contre 2 687 cd/m² pour la meilleure OLED passée sur le même banc.
L’OLED reste préférable pour qui regarde des films dans une pièce sombre et exige un noir absolu sans halo. Pour tous les autres usages, salon éclairé, sport, jeu vidéo, grandes diagonales, le Mini LED fait aussi bien ou mieux, sans risque de marquage et pour un budget inférieur.
Quelle différence entre QD Mini LED et SQD Mini LED ?
Le QD Mini LED associe un rétroéclairage Mini LED à un film de points quantiques (Quantum Dots) qui élargit la gamme de couleurs ; TCL l’a introduit en 2019. Le SQD Mini LED, pour Super Quantum Dot Mini LED, est la huitième génération de cette technologie chez TCL, lancée en 2026 sur les séries X11L, C8L et C7L.
Par rapport à la génération 2025, le SQD Mini LED apporte des diodes plus petites, donc davantage de zones à taille égale, un algorithme Halo Control retravaillé et un filtre de couleur qui gagne, selon TCL, 33 % de largeur et 69 % de précision.
Combien de zones de local dimming faut-il pour une bonne TV Mini LED ?
Plus il y a de zones, plus le halo autour des objets lumineux se réduit, parce que chaque zone éclaire une portion d’image plus petite. Sur la gamme TCL 2026, le compte va de 800 zones sur la C7L 55 pouces à 2 040 sur la C8L 65 pouces et 20 736 sur la X11L 98 pouces, contre 1 680 zones sur le C8K 65 pouces de 2025 testé par notre labo.
Le nombre de zones ne fait pas tout : la finesse du pilotage compte autant. Sur le C8K, notre labo relevait un pilotage sur 23 bits, soit plusieurs millions de paliers de luminosité par zone, ce qui adoucit les transitions entre zones claires et sombres ; la génération SQD y ajoute l’algorithme All-domain Halo Control.
Le blooming est-il encore visible sur une TV Mini LED ?
Vu de face, sur une TV Mini LED 2026 bien dotée en zones comme la TCL X11L, le blooming devient très difficile à percevoir et ne se devine que sur des scènes extrêmes, par exemple des sous-titres blancs sur fond noir. Il peut réapparaître quand on regarde l’écran de biais, à cause des angles de vision limités de toute dalle LCD.
Le blooming, ou effet de halo, désigne la lumière qui déborde d’une zone de rétroéclairage allumée sur les pixels sombres voisins. Une OLED, qui éteint chaque pixel individuellement, n’en produit jamais ; c’est la raison pour laquelle elle garde l’avantage dans une pièce noire.
Quelle TV Mini LED TCL choisir en 2026 : X11L, C8L ou C7L ?
La TCL C7L (ou C79L) est l’entrée de gamme SQD Mini LED, avec 800 à 2 176 zones et jusqu’à 3 000 nits de 55 à 98 pouces. La TCL C8L (ou C89L) ajoute une dalle WHVA 2.0 Ultra, 1 008 à 4 032 zones, jusqu’à 6 000 nits et un film à faible réflexion annoncé à 0,5 %. La TCL X11L, en 75, 85 et 98 pouces, vise le très haut de gamme avec 11 520 à 20 736 zones et jusqu’à 10 000 nits annoncés.
Toutes trois tournent sous Google TV (avec en plus, l’IA Gemini), affichent du 144 Hz natif en 4K et du 288 Hz en 1080p avec le Game Accelerator, et embarquent une section audio signée Bang & Olufsen. Pour un salon lumineux et un budget maîtrisé, la C8L en 65 ou 75 pouces est selon nous le meilleur compromis de la gamme.
En partenariat avec TCL

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 3, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: Daily roundup (November 3, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Tuesday, November 03, 2026.
India continues to remain an important growth market for Apple as startups continue to raise funding across cheque sizes. YourStory brings you this and other latest developments across sectors.
Featured stories
India shines in Apple’s record September quarter
India emerged as a stellar growth market for Apple in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, registering an all-time company revenue record in the country. “We also set September quarter revenue records in both developed and emerging markets, in addition to an all-time record in India,” Apple Chief Executive Officer John Ternus said. The performance in India was propelled by a September quarter record for iPhone upgraders, with Worldpanel survey data ranking iPhone among the top-selling smartphone models in the country.
VC funding into Indian startups plunges 66% in October
Venture capital (VC) funding into Indian startups touched a new low in October, with a decline of 66% against October of last year. When compared with the VC funding raised in September 2025, the drop was 49%. The total VC funding in October came in at just $581 million as compared with $1.6 billion in October 2025, according to YourStory Research. In September 2026, the funding amount was $1.1 billion.
Funding news
PowerUp Money raises $10M to expand AI-led wealth management
PowerUp Money, a wealthtech platform offering mutual fund advice and digital wealth management services, has raised $10 million in a funding round led by Flourish Ventures, an early-stage investment firm. Existing investors Peak XV Partners, Accel, Blume Ventures, Kae Capital, 8i Ventures and DeVC also participated.
The Bengaluru-based company plans to use a significant portion of the capital to develop its AI-powered wealth management platform and expand its managed advisory business.
Sachin Tendulkar backs Hitwicket maker Metasports Interactive
Metasports Interactive, the Hyderabad-based maker of cricket strategy game Hitwicket, has brought cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar on board as a strategic investor. He will also serve as the game’s brand ambassador.
The financial terms and valuation remain undisclosed. Existing backers include venture-capital firms Prime Venture Partners and Singapore’s Horizon Ventures, as well as cricket commentator Harsha Bhogle.
Upsurge India leads Rs 50 Cr secondary transaction in iD Fresh Food
Upsurge India has led a secondary transaction worth over Rs 50 crore in Bengaluru-based fresh-food brand iD Fresh Food, facilitating the exit of early investor Blue Ashva Capital. The transaction involved the transfer of approximately 1% equity in the company, with TG Fund and WW Ventures participating as co-leads.
Founded in 2005, iD Fresh specialises in preservative-free ready-to-cook products, including idli and dosa batter, Indian breads and chutneys. The company reported a revenue of over Rs 870 crore in FY26, compared with Rs 681 crore in FY25, representing growth of more than 25%. The transaction highlights growing institutional investor interest in established Indian consumer businesses and the increasing importance of secondary liquidity in private markets.
The Croffle Guys raises Rs 14 Cr in funding round led by V3 Ventures
Mumbai-based quick-service restaurant startup The Croffle Guys has raised Rs 14 crore in a funding round led by V3 Ventures, backed by Verlinvest, at a post-money valuation of Rs 100 crore. N.A.N. Partners also participated in the round. Founded in 2025, the company has expanded from two outlets to eight within a year and achieved an annualised revenue run rate of Rs 24 crore.
The startup plans to add more than 40 outlets, primarily across Mumbai and Delhi, with a selective presence in Pune. It is targeting an annualised revenue run rate of Rs 100 crore over the next 10-12 months. The company had earlier secured a Rs 2.5 crore investment on Shark Tank India at a Rs 50 crore valuation.
Solgram raises over $1M in pre-seed funding
Gurugram-based premium grocery platform Solgram has raised over $1 million in a pre-seed funding round led by DSG Consumer Partners and Saama Capital, with participation from hospitality entrepreneur Kapil Chopra. The capital will be used to expand its temperature-controlled cold-chain infrastructure, strengthen technology capabilities and deepen sourcing relationships. Launched in Gurugram, Solgram offers fresh produce, dairy, meat, seafood, bakery products and gourmet groceries through an integrated supply chain covering sourcing, storage and last-mile delivery. The platform also offers a health-focused selection through its Mindful Mode feature. Solgram plans to expand across the National Capital Region before entering other Tier I markets. Its business model focuses on product quality, provenance and reliability rather than delivery speed alone.
Unify Foodworks raises Rs 5 Cr to expand restaurant brands
Unify Foodworks, the exclusive pan-India master franchisee of Moe's Casa Mexicana and Carvel, has raised Rs 5 crore in seed funding through compulsorily convertible debentures. The capital will support expansion of both international food brands across the National Capital Region (NCR), where they made their India debut.
The company plans to strengthen store density, consumer awareness and operational capabilities before entering additional markets. Moe's Casa Mexicana offers Mexican-inspired dishes, including burritos, bowls and tacos, while Carvel is an American ice cream brand founded in 1934. Unify Foodworks has outlined a long-term expansion roadmap of more than 100 stores across India. The company is also developing integrated supply-chain and operating systems to support its expansion.
ECOPATH raises Rs 2.25 Cr to scale zero-cement construction tech
Bengaluru-based climate-tech startup ECOPATH has raised Rs 2.25 crore in seed funding from Social Alpha and Gemcorp to scale its zero-cement construction technology. The company has built an order book exceeding Rs 40 crore within two years of operations.
Founded by Sourabh Kumar and Abhishek Chhazed, ECOPATH develops cement-free concrete using industrial by-products, including steel-industry waste, and proprietary binders. The funding will support manufacturing capacity expansion, supply-chain development, research and team building. The company has secured over 40 commercial customers, including Lodha, Tata Power and Jindal Steel. ECOPATH says its materials can reduce carbon emissions by approximately 75% compared with conventional cement-based alternatives, depending on application and project specifications.
Mahesh Babu invests in gaming studio Shortgun Games
Actor Mahesh Babu has joined Mumbai-based gaming development studio Shortgun Games as a strategic investor to support the development of premium PC and console games. The partnership will focus on creating original intellectual properties for international markets, including North America and Europe.
The studio's flagship project, PROJECT TAKEDOWN, is a high-budget, narrative-driven action-adventure game being developed for platforms such as PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.
Founded by Jeet Chandan and Vidhit Mehta, Shortgun Games is focusing on building cinematic gaming experiences from India for global audiences. The company has also brought on action director Vicky Arora to lead the game's combat design, incorporating motion-capture choreography and physical stunt mechanics.
Cellegant Energy Systems raises Rs 2.61 Cr for hydrogen-powered drones
IIT Gandhinagar professor-founded startup Cellegant Energy Systems has raised Rs 2.61 crore from investors, including GVFL Prarambh Fund Trust, CoCreate Aarambh and IIEC, IIT Gandhinagar's incubator. The funding will support the development of indigenous hybrid hydrogen fuel-cell electric drivetrain systems designed to extend the endurance of drones and unmanned aerial vehicles.
Founded by Dr Atul Bhargav, the startup's immediate priority is to demonstrate a 35-kg hydrogen-powered drone. It aims to advance the programme from technology readiness level three to six over the next six to 12 months. Cellegant is also developing energy solutions for autonomous robots, marine vehicles and other applications. The investment will support technology development, intellectual property protection and team expansion.
DBS Foundation awards Rs 7.4 Cr to India's Khyaal
DBS Foundation has awarded SGD 3 million, approximately Rs 22 crore, to four purpose-driven businesses across Asia under its Impact Beyond Award programme. India's Taisho Ventures, which operates senior citizens' platform Khyaal, will receive SGD 1 million, equivalent to approximately Rs 7.4 crore. Khyaal has more than five million users and provides services spanning physical, emotional, cognitive, social, financial and digital well-being for people aged 50 and above. The funding will help strengthen its platform and expand services into Tier II and III cities, besides exploring opportunities in Southeast Asia. The other award recipients are Hon Yang Healthcare in Taiwan, One Bite Design Studio in Hong Kong and Shanghai Fuyuan Elderly Care Service in China.
OBSESS raises angel funding to build fitness technology platform
Delhi NCR-based fitness and sports technology startup OBSESS has raised angel funding to develop an integrated digital ecosystem for India's fitness and wellness industry. The round saw participation from investors including Pushpendra Singh, Co-founder of Centricity, Amitt Goel and Harshit Vij, Co-founder of Freecultr.
Founded in 2026 by Tushar Sharma and Yash Kumar, the company is developing a platform covering gym discovery, memberships, personal training, sports venue bookings, fitness products, nutrition and wellness services. The funding amount was not disclosed. The capital will support technology development, expansion of its network of gyms and trainers, user acquisition and partnerships. OBSESS also plans to introduce AI-powered capabilities for workout planning, nutrition recommendations and personalisation.
Other news
Adobe launches programme offering free tools to eligible startups
Adobe has launched Adobe for Startups, a programme designed to help early-stage companies strengthen their branding, content creation and customer engagement capabilities. Eligible startups will receive 12 months of free access to Adobe Firefly Pro Plus, Acrobat Studio, Adobe Express Premium and Semrush.
The programme is open to startups founded within the last five years that have raised less than $15 million in funding, subject to eligibility and country availability. The offering combines AI-powered creative tools, document productivity solutions and marketing intelligence capabilities. Adobe will also provide opportunities for founders to participate in workshops, events and learning programmes with its experts. The initiative aims to help startups build their brands and scale marketing activities with limited resources.
Smarten Power Systems reports 77.4% revenue growth in H1 FY27
Smarten Power Systems has reported a 77.4% year-on-year increase in consolidated revenue from operations to Rs 204.54 crore during the first half of FY27, compared with Rs 115.26 crore in the corresponding period last year. Consolidated profit after tax more than doubled to Rs 11.99 crore, registering growth of 103.8% against Rs 5.88 crore in H1 FY26. Profit before tax increased 111.9% to Rs 15.83 crore, while earnings per share stood at Rs 6.31. On a standalone basis, revenue grew 87% to Rs 201.37 crore.
The company manufactures power backup and solar energy products, including home UPS systems, solar inverters, batteries and solar panels, with operations across 23 states and two Union Territories.
Indian enterprises lose $3M per major IT outage: New Relic
Indian enterprises are losing an average of $3 million for every high-impact IT outage, according to New Relic's 2026 Observability Forecast: India Edition. The report, based on a survey of 500 Indian respondents, found that 61% of organisations experience major outages weekly or more frequently. Nearly 31% encounter such disruptions multiple times a day.
The study also found that 56% of Indian organisations monitor AI agents in production, compared with the global average of 35%. However, developers spend nearly half their time addressing system disruptions. India also leads in OpenTelemetry standardisation, with 42% of respondents fully standardised. New Relic said fragmented monitoring tools continue to limit the benefits of advanced observability investments.
365squared launches AI-powered voice fraud protection platform
365squared, a Route Mobile company within Proximus Global, has launched 365callguard, an AI-powered voice fraud protection solution for mobile and fixed-line operators. The platform is designed to identify and prevent fraudulent calls before they reach subscribers. It addresses seven categories of fraud, including vishing, caller ID spoofing, Wangiri, international revenue share fraud, SIM box fraud, flash calls, and robocalls.
The solution combines AI models with rule-based detection to provide real-time analysis and enable automatic actions such as call blocking, caller ID modification and subscriber alerts. The launch expands 365squared's existing communications security portfolio, which includes its AI-powered messaging protection platform, 365smsguard.
FirstClub enters beauty and personal care category
FirstClub, the quality-focused consumer platform, has expanded into the beauty and personal care category under its 'Filtered for Good' initiative. The launch brings together more than 80 brands across skincare, haircare, body care and personal care, with products priced between Rs 300 and Rs 3,500.
The company has introduced an ingredient-first evaluation framework covering shampoos, cleansers, moisturisers and sunscreens. It has excluded more than 100 ingredients from its beauty selection and requires listed products to have customer ratings of at least four stars. The platform will also offer 100% ingredient disclosure on product pages and a Samples Selector feature. The expansion follows its earlier entry into grocery, pet care and home and kitchen products.
BIT Mesra and IIT Kanpur sign five-year research collaboration MoU
Birla Institute of Technology, Mesra, and IIT Kanpur have signed a five-year memorandum of understanding to strengthen academic engagement and joint research. The agreement provides for student and faculty exchanges, joint supervision of research scholars, access to specialised facilities and collaborative academic programmes. It also establishes a framework for jointly submitting research proposals to national and international funding agencies.
The MoU covers undergraduate and postgraduate research, internships, joint Master's and PhD supervision, academic programmes and staff training. Students from both institutions will be able to participate in joint research projects and access specialised laboratories. The partnership is aimed at strengthening research capabilities, technology development and academic cooperation between the institutions.
Straive partners with Anthropic for responsible enterprise AI deployment
Global data and AI company Straive has partnered with Anthropic to help enterprises build and deploy AI solutions across business workflows. The collaboration will focus on responsible AI adoption, combining Anthropic's approach to safe AI with Straive's expertise in data readiness, domain knowledge, governance and operational delivery.
The partnership aims to help organisations integrate AI into industry-specific workflows while maintaining human oversight and appropriate operational controls. Straive's Build AI and Run AI capabilities cover solution design, deployment and continuous improvement. The companies will work with enterprises to identify where AI can support business processes and where human intervention remains necessary. Straive serves sectors including financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, media, education and publishing.
Vartis Platforms launches UdhaarSaathi loan marketplace for small merchants
Vartis Platforms, the parent company of LenDenClub and InstaMoney, has launched UdhaarSaathi, a digital loan marketplace targeting UPI QR-enabled micro and small businesses. The platform aims to facilitate Rs 1,000 crore in loan disbursements by the end of the current financial year. It offers collateral-free business loans ranging from Rs 15,000 to Rs 2.5 lakh, with an average ticket size of approximately Rs 1 lakh.
Target customers include kirana stores, pharmacies, street vendors and small retailers. The platform uses banking and payment transaction data shared with merchants' consent to facilitate credit assessment by lending partners. Operating as a loan service provider, UdhaarSaathi works with multiple NBFCs and offers daily repayment structures aligned with merchants' cash flows.
TEXMiN partners Magnora to strengthen India's rare earth magnet ecosystem
TEXMiN, the Technology Translation Research Park established by the Department of Science and Technology at IIT (ISM) Dhanbad, has entered into a strategic alliance with Magnora RE Tech to explore opportunities in critical minerals, rare earth elements and rare earth permanent magnets. ELITech Earth Science will provide project management consultancy and technical coordination support.
The collaboration aims to strengthen India's domestic value chain for rare earth permanent magnets, which are essential for electric vehicles, renewable energy systems and advanced electronics. The partnership will combine research expertise, industry investment and project execution capabilities. The initiative is aligned with the National Critical Mineral Mission, Atmanirbhar Bharat and Viksit Bharat 2047, with the objective of reducing import dependence.
AMU Leasing sees 65% of EV financing disbursements from non-metro markets
AMU Leasing, an RBI-registered NBFC focused on green mobility and electric vehicle financing, has reported that 65% of its disbursements come from non-metro markets. The company has acquired approximately 14,000 customers and is strengthening its presence across 10 states. Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, West Bengal, Jharkhand and Haryana are among its fastest-growing markets. Commercial electric vehicles account for the entire financing portfolio in these markets, reflecting the company's focus on last-mile connectivity and goods transportation.
AMU Leasing is also working to establish operations in Rajasthan and Chhattisgarh. The company offers financing across electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, four-wheelers and commercial vehicles, targeting underserved rural and semi-urban markets.
E2E Networks launches Blaze pay-per-token AI inference service
E2E Networks has launched Blaze, a pay-per-token inference service for open AI models, targeting developers and enterprises. The platform provides a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint to access multiple open models, with customers paying according to their token consumption.
Powered by NVIDIA GPU infrastructure and components from NVIDIA DSX OS, Blaze is designed for applications such as voice, coding agents, document AI, OCR and image and video generation. The service is hosted on E2E's India-based cloud infrastructure, addressing demand for data sovereignty and cost-efficient AI deployment. E2E is also expanding its AI infrastructure capacity to approximately 14.6 MW, including a 1,024-GPU NVIDIA Blackwell cluster that has been operational since May 2026.
Azim Premji Foundation launches Social Startups Programme
Azim Premji Foundation has launched a Social Startups Programme to support development sector professionals in establishing and leading civil society organisations focused on underserved communities. The first cohort will include approximately 100 participants across Odisha, Northeast India, Eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bengaluru Urban.
The programme will support areas such as rural livelihoods, healthcare, mental health, disability, children's welfare and community sanitation. Applicants must be below 40 years of age, hold a graduate degree and have at least three years of grassroots development experience. Selected participants will receive financial assistance and guidance during an eight-month seeding phase, followed by an opportunity to apply for a two-year seed grant. Applications are open from November 1 to December 31, 2026.
mFilterIt removes over 2 lakh fraudulent digital assets during festive season
Digital trust and ad-fraud intelligence platform mFilterIt has removed more than two lakh fraudulent digital assets targeting a leading Indian bank during the festive shopping season. Its monitoring uncovered 2.4 lakh fraudulent cases across 10 digital platforms, including fake websites, phishing pages, impersonation accounts and bogus promotional offers.
The company reported a takedown success rate of over 97%, with 80-85% of identified scam assets removed within 24 hours of detection. The cases included brand impersonation, coupon abuse and deceptive referral schemes. According to mFilterIt, the findings highlight the growing scale of digital fraud during high-traffic shopping periods. The company advocates continuous monitoring and digital crawling to identify and remove fraudulent infrastructure before consumers are affected.
Airtel and District rename Bengaluru concert venue Airtel Arena
Bharti Airtel and District have announced a collaboration to enhance digital connectivity at a major live entertainment venue in Bengaluru, which will be renamed Airtel Arena. The 16-acre open-air venue will receive dedicated digital infrastructure investment from Airtel to improve connectivity for fans, artists and event organisers. The venue can accommodate more than 17,000 people and has hosted performances by artists including Arijit Singh, Anirudh Ravichander and Bryan Adams.
The partnership will support high-speed connectivity, digital payments, livestreaming and other services during large-scale events. District will continue managing the consumer-facing entertainment experience, while Airtel will strengthen the venue's technological infrastructure. The initiative reflects growing investment in India's live entertainment ecosystem.
Medi Assist reports 60.2% growth in H1 FY27 net profit
Medi Assist Healthcare Services has reported a 13% year-on-year increase in operating revenue to Rs 478 crore in H1 FY27. Operating EBITDA grew 19% to Rs 97.2 crore, while profit after tax increased 60.2% year-on-year. Profit before tax rose 47% and total premiums under management reached Rs 24,752 crore. The company's group health benefits market share stood at 34.1%, with client retention of 90.5%. Technology monetisation also improved, with SaaS and licensing revenue growing 83.8% to Rs 18.1 crore during the first half.
The company's board has approved a share buyback of up to Rs 49.3 crore, funded through internal cash flows. Medi Assist said the buyback would support shareholder returns while preserving funds for expansion and technology investments.
Decentro launches Soundbox range for UPI merchant payments
Fintech infrastructure platform Decentro has launched a range of Soundbox devices aimed at small merchants and businesses accepting digital payments. The offering includes a Static QR Soundbox and a Dynamic QR Soundbox featuring a display, keypad and NFC capabilities. The devices provide audio payment confirmations and are designed to support merchants in Tier II and smaller markets, which account for approximately 45% of UPI transaction volumes.
The Static QR device supports 4G connectivity, with 2G and optional Wi-Fi backup, while payment alerts are available in multiple languages. The company is targeting one million devices by the end of 2028 and is in discussions with five partners for large-scale deployments. Decentro currently has over 5,000 offline UPI QR deployments.
Porter appoints Gaurav Jain as CFO, elevates technology and marketing leaders
Digital goods transport platform Porter has strengthened its leadership team with the appointment of Gaurav Jain as chief financial officer. The company has also elevated Shubham Gupta as chief technology officer and Mohit Rathi as chief marketing officer.
Jain joins Porter from Amazon, where he spent more than a decade, and brings over 20 years of experience in finance and strategy across e-commerce, financial services and FMCG. Gupta, who joined Porter in 2015, has led engineering and technology initiatives, including infrastructure modernisation, security and AI adoption. Rathi has been with the company for over a decade and has handled expansion and customer growth initiatives. The leadership changes come as Porter prepares for its next phase of expansion.
MathCo appoints former Unilever executive Vijay Raj to advisory board
Enterprise AI and analytics company MathCo has appointed Vijay Raj to its advisory board as it enters its second decade of operations. Raj brings three decades of experience in the insights industry, including 26 years at Unilever, where he worked on consumer behaviour and business strategy. In his new role, he will advise the company's leadership on market opportunities, customer priorities and long-term growth strategy.
His experience is expected to support MathCo's expansion in the consumer packaged goods sector and strengthen its engagement with enterprise clients.
Fulcrum Digital appoints Latha Nathan as SVP of India delivery operations
Enterprise AI and digital transformation company Fulcrum Digital has appointed Latha Nathan as Senior Vice President of India Delivery Operations. She will oversee the company's delivery organisation across its centres in Pune, Coimbatore and Mumbai. Her responsibilities will include delivery excellence, talent development, client success and scaling India operations.
Nathan joins Fulcrum Digital from Fidelity Investments, where she served as Vice President and led a business unit focused on digitisation and customer-facing platform products.
AstraZeneca appoints Naveen Krishna Yamarthi to lead Chennai innovation centre
AstraZeneca has appointed Naveen Krishna Yamarthi as managing director of AZIPL and the head of its Global Innovation & Technology Centre in Chennai, effective October 30, 2026. In his new role, he will lead the centre's development as a strategic, multifunctional innovation hub, supporting the company's global operations and Bold Ambition 2030 strategy.
Yamarthi brings more than 22 years of experience in building and scaling global capability centres (GCCs), with expertise in technology and business transformation.
UiPath appoints Yashdeep Vaishnav as India country manager
Business orchestration and automation company UiPath has appointed Yashdeep Vaishnav as managing director and country manager for India. He will lead the company's business operations, drive adoption of its automation solutions and expand its customer and partner ecosystem in the country. He has previously held senior positions at Snowflake, Salesforce, VTEX, Melento and Oracle.
AscentHR recognised as leader in NelsonHall Payroll Services 2026 assessment
HR technology and payroll services provider AscentHR has been recognised as a Leader in NelsonHall's Payroll Services 2026 – Overall assessment. The company was also named an Innovator in the Multi-Country Payroll Capability category.
The evaluation was conducted through NelsonHall's Vendor Evaluation & Assessment Tool, which assesses payroll providers on market presence, client value and technological innovation. NelsonHall cited AscentHR's payroll expertise, broad service portfolio and technology capabilities, including intelligent anomaly detection, Tia 2.0 and Smart Rules.
GoKwik announces Rs 7.57 cr ESOP liquidity programme for employees
Bengaluru-based commerce enablement platform GoKwik has announced an employee stock option liquidity programme involving a combined payout of Rs 7.57 crore to 69 employees. The participating employees are expected to realise an average return of approximately nine times their original grant value among the earliest ESOP holders.
The programme comes as the company turned adjusted EBITDA positive in October 2026, based on unaudited management accounts.
1Crowd partially exits Mojro investment, retains 75% stake
Early-stage investment firm 1Crowd has partially exited its investment in logistics technology company Mojro, generating returns of several times its original investment. The firm has sold 25% of its holding while retaining the remaining 75%, signalling its continued commitment to the company.
1Crowd first invested in Mojro in February 2018 and has supported it through three subsequent funding rounds. The partial exit took place as part of Mojro’s Series A financing, in which 1Crowd also participated alongside other investors. Mojro provides an AI-native B2B SaaS platform that helps enterprises automate logistics planning, route optimisation, scheduling and delivery operations. The platform is designed to improve efficiency, reduce logistics costs and provide visibility across goods movement.
Mobavenue reports 72% growth in H1 FY27 profit
Mobavenue AI Tech reported a 72.2% year-on-year increase in profit after tax to Rs 22.9 crore for the first half of FY27, while revenue rose 48.6% to Rs 149.6 crore. EBITDA grew 59.6% to Rs 31.6 crore, with the margin expanding 140 basis points to 21.1%. For the second quarter ended September 30, 2026, revenue increased 41.3% to Rs 76.7 crore and EBITDA rose 47.3% to Rs 16.2 crore. Profit after tax was up 54.8% at Rs 11.3 crore. Growth was driven by demand from advertisers in quick commerce, BFSI, fintech, entertainment, travel and commerce. International markets contributed 23.8% of Q2 revenue, while direct clients accounted for 64.7%. India contributed 77.7% of first-half revenue.
Avanade report highlights gap in Indian enterprises’ AI transformation
Indian businesses report high confidence in their use of artificial intelligence, but many have yet to fundamentally transform operations around the technology, according to an Avanade survey. The company’s AI Reality Report found that 82% of Indian business leaders are confident in their teams’ AI use, while only 23% said their organisations had reshaped how they work. The survey found that 44% of Indian respondents reported significant improvements in operational efficiency and 42% cited gains in employee productivity. However, 75% said AI had yet to deliver returns that justified the investment, while 74% had not formally calculated its return on investment. Integration and scaling remain challenges, with 47% reporting deployment problems. Avanade said enterprises must strengthen foundations and measure financial outcomes.
Taghash launches AI assistant for investment funds
Investment fund technology platform Taghash has launched Taghash Brain, an artificial intelligence assistant designed to streamline portfolio monitoring, reporting and daily operations for venture capital firms and other investment funds. Integrated into Taghash’s fund management platform, Brain enables investment teams to analyse fund data, generate reports, build live dashboards and execute tasks through a conversational interface. It uses information already maintained within the platform, including portfolio data, deal records and operational workflows. Taghash plans to introduce further agentic AI capabilities in the coming months.
Deel launches workforce security solution to detect hiring fraud
Global HR and payroll platform Deel has launched Deel Security, a workforce security solution designed to detect identity fraud during recruitment and throughout employment. The platform analyses risk signals across resumes, digital footprints, interviews and identity documents to identify deepfakes, proxy interviewers and suspicious identities. The launch follows rising concerns about fraudulent remote job applications. Deel research involving 1,011 HR professionals in the UK and US found that 66% of organisations had seen an increase in suspicious or potentially fraudulent remote worker applications over the past year. Some 93% of HR leaders expressed concern about deepfake or AI-generated workers.
Zelio E-Mobility begins production at new Hisar facility
Zelio E-Mobility has commenced commercial production at its new manufacturing facility in Patan, Hisar, Haryana, adding annual capacity of 48,000 electric two-wheelers and 24,000 three-wheelers. The expansion takes the company’s total installed capacity from 2.4 lakh to approximately 3.12 lakh units. Spread across six acres, the facility has a built-up area of 2.61 lakh square feet and represents an investment of more than Rs 20 crore. Production has begun for Zelio electric scooters and Tanga electric three-wheelers. The additional capacity is expected to come on stream during the third quarter of FY27. Zelio currently operates four plants and has more than 400 dealers across over 25 states.
IKF Finance targets Rs 25,000 crore AUM by 2030
IKF Finance is targeting assets under management of Rs 25,000 crore by 2030, supported by technology investments, product diversification and expansion beyond its traditional southern markets. The lender ended FY26 with consolidated AUM of more than Rs 8,600 crore, up around 30%, and reported profit after tax of Rs 215 crore. The company has expanded to more than 350 branches across 13 states and operates in vehicle, construction equipment and MSME finance. Its housing finance subsidiary offers affordable home loans. Vehicle finance now accounts for less than 70% of the group’s assets.

articles.title: Anthropic tells Claude Code to stop recreating existing video games
articles.text:
In context: Vibe coding and AI agents have made game decompilation and recompilation child's play, but things might soon change significantly. Claude Code is now being instructed to avoid performing this type of workload, meaning decompilation enthusiasts will need to turn elsewhere to get the job done.
Claude might soon stop being one of the best AI tools for decompiling and recompiling existing games. According to Anthropic programmer Addy Osmani, the model behind the company's vibe-coding service will now avoid user prompts that request recreations of someone else's video games.
The change was first spotted by decompilation enthusiasts over the weekend. On October 27, Claude Code started picking up a new rule hidden behind the "tengu_heron_brook" flag. The rule is designed to force the AI model to build original games based on users' own designs and assets, rather than content taken from games already on the market.
Read our feature: Decompilation on Steroids: Why AI Is Suddenly Cracking Open Old Software
Soon after the rule was discovered, Osmani confirmed that Anthropic was adding two new sentences to Claude Code's Opus 5.5 model. Recreating someone else's intellectual property is apparently against Claude's usage policy, meaning users should only be able to vibe-code "original" games. Osmani also said the company would continue iterating on the new rules to achieve the "right balance."
 – Addy Osmani (@addyosmani) October 30, 2026
AI-assisted recompilation and decompilation projects have taken the IT world by storm. Vibe coders are now leveraging previous human-made research efforts to "port" console-exclusive games to PC – or vice versa. Projects such as AnyPS5 are even attempting to turn PlayStation 5 games into "native" PC titles.
The vibe-coded decompilation deluge is also having a significant impact on human-led research efforts. The decomp.dev website has now shut down because AI-assisted coding has undermined meaningful efforts to understand and document how game code works. Vibe coders are now forking existing decompilation projects and letting AI finish the job, or racing to port games to different platforms just to plant their flag on the map.
Vibe-coded game recreations might now be more difficult with Claude, but the decompilation "fun" is likely to continue regardless. Users will simply need to switch to other AI models and services, adapt to rapidly improving open-weight models, or resort to offline setups to keep churning out new recompilations and web-based conversions.

articles.title: The 4 Elements of Exposure Prioritization and How to Operationalize Them
articles.text:
Your team is remediating more vulnerabilities than ever, yet your breach risk has barely changed. You’re spending too much time and effort on exposures attackers may never exploit, while higher-risk exposures sit, waiting in the queue. Gartner®’s report on exposure prioritization states that fewer than 10% of vulnerabilities are exploited, yet most are treated as urgent. The report also argues that CVSS scores alone do not predict actual exploitation or business impact.
Gartner predicts that by 2028, organizations that prioritize exposures using threat intelligence, asset context, exploitability modeling, and security control validation will reduce breach likelihood by at least 70% compared to their peers relying primarily on CVSS-based vulnerability prioritization. Let’s break down how each element works, and how the Picus Platform puts all four into practice.
Severity-based prioritization made sense. Then it didn't.
Severity-driven prioritization was an entirely rational response for the era it was built in: a static attack surface, scarce adversary tooling, and remediation capacity that exceeded disclosure volume. Suddenly, that world is gone. Enterprises face tens of thousands of new vulnerabilities a year across cloud, SaaS, identity, and supply chain modalities, and AI has compressed time-to-exploit from weeks or months to hours.
Gartner is candid about why teams still anchor on severity, and it’s not a lack of awareness. In fact:
- legacy metrics
- compliance pressure, and
- fragmented ownership
all reward what’s auditable over what’s legitimately impactful.
The result is widespread prioritization paralysis, with significant resources being funneled into remediation activity, but with remarkably little measurable risk reduction to show for it.
The smarter path is performing risk-based vulnerability management in its truest sense: measuring success by the exploitable exposures you’ve reduced, not the hypothetical vulnerabilities you’ve closed.
The four elements, and the question each one answers
Gartner’s framework rests on four pillars, and their value emerges only when added together. Sure, operationalizing one or two will bring you incremental gains, but integrating all four delivers significant reductions in both exposure windows and remediation fatigue.
Each element answers a distinct question about an exposure:
An exposure deserves urgent remediation only when all four answers converge.
The model aligns directly with the prioritization and validation stages of continuous threat exposure management (CTEM): remediation is mobilized only after priorities are validated in context.
Element 1: Threat Intelligence
Threat intelligence brings the adversary’s perspective into prioritization by showing which exposures attackers are actually exploiting. In real-world environments, many high-severity vulnerabilities are never exploited. Attackers frequently weaponize moderately rated vulnerabilities because they are easier to exploit, affect widely used systems, or can be exploited reliably. Past exploitation evidence helps teams focus their remediation efforts on a smaller, higher-risk subset of the backlog.
The operational challenge here is speed. Your team needs to use that intelligence to decide what to test and fix before a campaign reaches your environment. Track the time it takes to go from threat publication to testing and remediation.
Element 2: Asset Context and Business Criticality
An exploitable vulnerability becomes materially risky when it affects an asset that supports critical business functions, processes regulated data, or provides an easy pivot to higher-value systems. Without asset context, prioritization treats all assets as equal, and attention can easily drift to low-impact systems while crown-jewel exposures wait in the same queue.
This context already lives in tools most teams own: scanners, CMDBs, cloud security platforms, and identity systems. The practical work is to both unify it and keep it current, so its impact reflects the asset as it’s defended today, not as it appears in an inventory.
Element 3: Exploitability Modeling
Exploit prediction models such as EPSS estimate how likely a vulnerability is to be exploited, based on patterns like exploit complexity, component prevalence, and disclosure-to-exploitation timelines. These models complement threat intelligence by surfacing latent and lingering risks: helping identify the exposures that are statistically likely to be exploited before exploitation is widely observed, enabling you to shift teams from a reactive to an anticipatory or even proactive stance.
Statistical likelihood describes the world in general, not your organization’s unique environment. EPSS points to what’s probably exploitable somewhere; only validation proves what is exploitable here and now. Exploitability modeling works best as a filter that feeds validation, not as a final verdict.
Gartner’s full report goes deeper into how EPSS, KEV and similar models should be weighted against threat intelligence and control validation. Download the Gartner report on exposure prioritization to read the complete analysis.
Element 4: Security Control Validation
This is the element most programs are missing. Security control validation evaluates each exposure against the defenses already deployed around it: segmentation, endpoint protection, detection coverage, and identity controls.
An exposure that looks critical may be practically unreachable behind your existing defenses, while a less critical one on a poorly monitored asset may carry far more risk than its score suggests. Ignoring control context, Gartner warns, leads to systematic overestimation of risk and the wasted remediation efforts that follow it.
Testing shows whether attackers can realistically exploit an exposure in your specific environment today. Gartner notes this capability can be achieved with adversarial exposure validation techniques: proving exploitability with evidence, through live attack execution where testing is safe, and attack-chain analysis against deployed controls where assets can’t be touched.
How Picus Operationalizes All Four Elements into a Single Loop
The sum here is indeed greater than its parts, but the four elements only deliver their full value when evaluated together. This is, not surprisingly, where most organizations struggle as vulnerability management grows into exposure management. Why? Because in most organizations, threat intelligence sits with one team, asset context with another, exploitability scores are in a scanner, and control effectiveness only shows up in periodic assessments. Four inputs in four places do not lead to one decision.
Picus is named among the vendors in the 2026 Gartner® Market Guide for Adversarial Exposure Validation. The Picus Platform brings all four elements together in a continuous loop: Discover, Validate, Prioritize, and Mobilize.
Here’s how the platform maps to each element.
Security control validation deserves a closer look, because evidence is what turns the other three elements from assumptions into decisions. Picus Breach and Attack Simulation is one of three validation methods on the platform.
- Picus Autonomous Penetration Testing runs real exploit paths against reachable production assets and proves which ones lead to your critical systems.
- Picus Exposure Validation breaks each CVE into the techniques an attacker must use and tests every step against your existing controls on that asset, with no exploit fired, so even assets you can never test live get an evidence-backed verdict.
Together, these three validation methods give every exposure one explainable, organization-specific rating.
What Good Looks Like: Measuring the Shift
If prioritization is working, you should be able to see it in three places: your controls hold up better, you respond faster, and your team spends its time on the exposures that matter, rather than wasting it on the ones that don’t.
Here’s what our customers are reporting.
- Within three months of deploying Picus, their security controls are blocking or detecting roughly twice as many attacks as before.
- Response time to emerging threats drops by 89%.
- Missed remediation deadlines on high and critical vulnerabilities fall by 92%, because the queue now holds only the exposures proven to be exploitable.
One customer cut their critical ticket backlog by 98%. And the full cycle, from a new threat or change being detected to actual validated findings landing with the right team, runs under six hours.
A CISO at our 2026 Validation Summit put it simply: While a severity score is a useful label for sorting, the smarter strategy is to shut down those attack paths that could actually hurt your business. The numbers above back this up.
Exposure Prioritization Is a Risk Decision. Make It With Evidence.
Gartner frames exposure prioritization as a risk decision, and we agree.
Each of the four elements answers one part of it: threat intelligence tells you whether the exposure matters to an attacker, asset context tells you what it would cost you, exploitability modeling tells you how likely it is to take place, and security control validation tells you whether it could actually happen here.
The Picus Platform runs all four in one continuous loop, so every exposure ends in a decision you can defend to your board and your auditors: so you can fix it, mitigate it, or accept it with proof.
Ready to see validated prioritization in practice? Request a demo and watch one of your own CVEs go from a new scanner finding to the right response backed by evidence.
Note: This article was written by Sila Ozeren Hacioglu, Security Research Engineer at Picus Security.

articles.title: Cyberangriffe: Hacker kapern auch Kühleinheiten in deutschen Supermärkten
articles.text:
Cyberangriffe auf Kühlschränke: Auch deutsche Supermärkte sind betroffen
Nach der Serie von Cyberangriffen auf Kühlanlagen in europäischen Supermärkten untersucht die Polizei mehrere Fälle auch in Deutschland. Kriminelle sollen sich nach bisherigen Erkenntnissen in Nordrhein-Westfalen sowie in Niedersachsen in Kühltruhen gehackt und dort die Temperaturen hochgestellt haben. Für betroffene Läden ist der Schaden groß.
Angriffe im Münsterland und Niedersachsen
In Wuppertal, Wetter bei Hagen und im Münsterland wurden nach Polizeiangaben Kühlanlagen vermutlich durch einen Hackerangriff lahmgelegt. Die Temperatur sei so hoch eingestellt worden, dass Lebensmittel verdorben seien und entsorgt werden mussten, sagten Polizeisprecher.
In Niedersachsen wurde die Kühlkette eines Supermarkts in Lilienthal bei Bremen zeitweise lahmgelegt. „Wir mussten Waren im Wert von über 360.000 Euro wegwerfen“, sagte Inhaber Daniel Breiding. In dem Supermarkt fielen in der Nacht auf den 2. November Bedientheken, Kühlhäuser und Tiefkühltruhen aus. Die Anlagen heizten sich demnach auf 30 Grad auf.
Cyberkriminelle hatten in den vergangenen Tagen unter anderem in Belgien, Schweden, Irland, Luxemburg, Estland, Finnland und den Niederlanden dafür gesorgt, dass Kühlschränke und Tiefkühltruhen wärmer wurden. Nach Angaben eines belgischen Kühltechnik-Dienstleisters wurden die Anlagen aus der Ferne in den Abtaumodus versetzt.
Mitte Oktober hatte es bereits einen großangelegten Angriff gegeben, der Märkte mehrerer großer französischer Lebensmittelhandelsketten betraf. Der Angriff richtete sich gegen einen Technik-Dienstleister. Die Cyberkriminalitäts-Abteilung der Staatsanwaltschaft Paris übernahm Ermittlungen.
Opfer der Hacker wurde auch ein von der Arbeiterwohlfahrt betriebener Supermarkt in Wetter-Volmarstein im Ennepe-Ruhr-Kreis. Der eigentliche Angriff sei auf die Firma erfolgt, die die Kühlanlagen aus der Ferne warte, hieß es dort. Große Mengen an Lebensmitteln hätten weggeworfen werden müssen.
Temperatur der Kühlanlagen aus der Ferne hochgestellt
Auch in einem Markt in Wuppertal seien große Mengen an Waren verdorben – offensichtlich, weil Hacker aus der Ferne die Temperatur der Kühlanlagen hochgedreht hätten, sagte ein Polizeisprecher. Der Angriff sei am Wochenende erfolgt und am Morgen des 2. Novembers bemerkt worden. Bei einem Markt in Raesfeld im Münsterland fiel die Kühlung ebenfalls aus. Dort wird nun geprüft, ob ein Hackerangriff der Grund sein könnte.
Mehr Anstrengungen beim Schutz von digitaler Technik gefordert
Bundesdigitalminister Karsten Wildberger (CDU) rief zu mehr Anstrengungen beim Schutz von digitaler Gebäude- und Betriebstechnik auf. Dazu habe es auch schon vor den jüngsten Cyberattacken entsprechende Aufforderungen des Bundesamts für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik gegeben.
Im Nachrichtensender Welt TV sagte Wildberger: „Erstmal zeigt das, dass wir in einer Welt leben, wo immer häufiger das Thema Cybersicherheit an Bedeutung – leider – gewinnt. Heißt auch: Auch alle Unternehmen, das gilt auch für die Verwaltung, müssen mehr Vorsorge tragen.“
EU-Krisentreffen einberufen
Die EU-Kommission berief zwei Krisentreffen ein. Dabei ging es vor allem darum, Informationen auszutauschen und das weitere Vorgehen abzustimmen, wie ein Sprecher der Kommission in Brüssel sagte.
An einer ersten Runde nahmen demnach unter anderem die EU-Cybersicherheitsagentur Enisa, die Polizeibehörde Europol und die zuständigen Experten der Kommission teil. Auch das europäische Netzwerk für Cyberkrisen sei aktiviert worden. Die Ermittlungen zu den Angriffen laufen nach Angaben des Sprechers bei den nationalen Behörden, die Kommission stehe mit ihnen in engem Kontakt. Wer hinter den Attacken steckt, ist bislang unklar. Die Vorfälle zeigten aber, dass Europa sich gemeinsam auf solche Angriffe einstellen müsse.

articles.title: Nvidia tells data center operators to limit business from Chinese customers with new global restrictions, report claims — allegedly restricted to 49% of the total, ensuring 51% are non-Chinese outfits
articles.text:
Nvidia tells data center operators to limit business from Chinese customers with new global restrictions, report claims — allegedly restricted to 49% of the total, ensuring 51% are non-Chinese outfits
Cloud providers have been told that they must sell 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies for the first time.
Nvidia has purportedly told its data center customers that they must limit the amount of business that they do with Chinese companies in what is a new policy for the U.S. company. The move would mean that data center operators who sell their services to Chinese companies must now track what proportion of their overall business they make up, limiting them to just 49% of the total and ensuring 51% are non-Chinese outfits. The FT reports the new policy has been communicated to Nvidia's customers by its sales force and regional teams, and does not appear to have been laid out in any official form via documentation.
Notably, Nvidia's alleged new stance on Chinese customers does not only apply to data centers that are located in Asia. Instead, it applies to those based globally, and even then it only affects new and future contracts rather than any existing Nvidia hardware leasing agreements that are in place. In a statement, Nvidia notes that "American chips are the foundation that American model and application makers need to compete worldwide." The statement goes on to say that current U.S. policy "encourages" cloud providers to build on American infrastructure and to accept business from "everywhere they can."
But this latest move to restrict Chinese access to Nvidia's high-performance data center hardware comes amid ongoing tensions between the United States and China with regard to AI capabilities. Nvidia can only sell its chips to whitelisted companies, a situation that has led to a thriving black market for its wares. Earlier this year, it was found that even Nvidia's older servers have become so sought-after that their values have tripled.
Whether limitations on who Nvidia can sell its chips to have had the desired effect is open to debate, with even China's state-owned telecoms giant China Telecom having recently been found to have Nvidia hardware in its data centers. The situation wouldn't be out of place in a blockbuster espionage thriller, with Nvidia CEO Jason Huang reportedly the target of a spy plot by Chinese agents.
The reasons behind the U.S. government's attempts to limit China's access to Nvidia hardware are obvious. The aim is to stymie China's ability to advance its own AI technologies, with Nvidia chips the go-to option for AI servers and data centers around the globe. But this limitation on which customers cloud service providers can accept will put additional strain on companies that are already fighting it out for the same contracts. Reducing the pool of potential customers could potentially see a shrinking in the scale of data center operations moving forward.

Oliver Haslam has written about technology of all shapes and sizes for over 15 years, both online and in print. He's fascinated by how personal computing continues to change as tower PCs give way to foldable phones and beyond.

articles.title: I've spent a week with Apple's new iPad mini, and the OLED upgrade is everything I'd hoped for
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The iPad mini is an absolute joy to use, and the long-awaited move to OLED makes a world of difference to Apple's smallest tablet. Add in its deceptively slim design, extra durability, strong performance, and solid battery life, and there's a whole lot to love — even if the high price and lack of ProMotion leave a little room for improvement.
Reasons to buy
- + Gorgeous OLED display
- + Super-slim design with added durability
- + Acoustic Display speakers seriously impress
- + A20 Pro keeps things running smoothly
Reasons to avoid
- - Limited colors: only Starlight and Midnight
- - No ProMotion
- - Can get expensive fast
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Apple iPad mini 8.5-inch (2026) review: One-minute review
It's been a long time coming, but Apple has finally addressed more than a few people's wish lists with its latest-generation iPad mini. Yes, it's still the smallest iPad in terms of display size, not price, but this upgrade is really about the sum of its parts.
The jump to OLED is the headline upgrade, and paired with a thinner, lighter build and plenty of performance under the hood, it makes a big, big difference. The 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR display is an absolute joy to use; whether I'm watching a film, playing a game, editing photos, or just scrolling through iPadOS, everything looks fantastic.
If you've been holding out for an OLED iPad mini, this is the upgrade you've been waiting for. It's a major improvement, even without ProMotion, and the improved refresh responsiveness makes everyday scrolling and swiping feel that much more seamless.
The design is another big part of the story. At just 5.33mm thick and 254g, the iPad mini is deceptively slim and light. The mini was already the iPad I find easiest to take pretty much anywhere, but this new model is even more comfortable to hold and use for longer stretches. And while it might look familiar, there are some meaningful changes beyond the thinner build. The new IP67 rating adds welcome water and dust resistance, giving the mini more durability for everyday use, and giving you peace of mind if you're sharing it with family members.
It also packs plenty of power. The A20 Pro chip makes multitasking, photo editing, gaming, and even some of Apple's newer AI features, which demand a fair bit of power, feel effortless. Battery life has been solid in my testing, too, getting close to Apple's 10-hour claim, while the N1 chip brings Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread connectivity. If you opt for the Cellular model, you also get Apple's C2 modem.
Of course, all of this comes at a price. The iPad mini starts at $699, so it's certainly not the cheapest iPad in Apple's lineup. The model I've been testing is the 512GB Wi-Fi and Cellular version with the optional nano-texture display, which comes in at $1,099. That's a considerable investment for a tablet this size, but the mini has never really been about offering the lowest entry price. It's for people who want this particular screen size and the portability that comes with it, and Apple has now managed to squeeze a whole lot more value into this little package.
There are still a couple of things I'd like to see, most notably ProMotion and a more exciting selection of colors. But those small issues don't take away from how much I enjoy using this iPad. The OLED display makes a world of difference, the slimmer build is even better, and the combination of performance, battery life, and added durability makes this a seriously capable little tablet. If you're already a fan of the iPad mini, you'll love a lot about this generation.
