articles.title: Le robot d'Apple serait prêt depuis deux ans, mais l'IA poserait encore problème
articles.text:
Le projet occuperait les laboratoires de Cupertino depuis 2019, sous le nom de code J595, avec un objectif de départ presque banal : faciliter les appels vidéo à la maison. Sept ans plus tard, la partie matérielle de ce robot domestique serait figée, et ce depuis environ deux ans. Le logiciel, lui, s’est chargé d’ambitions nouvelles en cours de route, au point de repousser le lancement vers2027, voire 2028, rapporte The Information.
À quoi ressemble le robot qu’Apple garde au garage ?
L’appareil prend la forme d’un écran de 9 pouces perché sur un bras articulé, qui pivote pour suivre les occupants et « ressemble à la lampe Pixar ». Sa caméra et ses capteurs doivent lui permettre de comprendre la pièce : contourner un obstacle, repérer une arrivée dans le salon, allumer la lumière au passage. L’engin irait donc bien au-delà de l’enceinte à écran posée sur un meuble, puisqu’il est pensé pour vivre avec le foyer et le suivre du regard.
Côté facture, le tarif envisagé tournerait autour de 1 000 dollars, une estimation qui pourrait encore grimper avec la flambée des composants. Le nom pressenti, HomeView Ultra, rattacherait l’appareil à l’écran connecté HomeView, attendu dans les foyers américains d’ici quelques jours après avoir lui-même patienté le temps que les chantiers de Siri avancent. Le robot en serait la déclinaison haut de gamme, la plus chère et la plus ambitieuse.
Pourquoi le lancement glisse-t-il d’année en année ?
À l’origine, l’engin devait surtout suivre son utilisateur pendant les appels vidéo, un cahier des charges resté raisonnable pendant les premières années du projet. Les fonctions d’intelligence artificielle empilées depuis ont changé l’ampleur du chantier : conscience de la pièce, déplacements autonomes, interactions continues avec les habitants. Résultat, un matériel achevé attend un cerveau qui n’existe pas encore, et c’est lui qui dicte désormais le calendrier.
Début 2025 déjà, l’analyste Ming-Chi Kuo ne voyait pas de production en masse avant 2028 pour les premiers robots de la marque, un pronostic que les dernières indiscrétions rendent crédible. Depuis l’abandon de son projet de voiture, Apple cherche la prochaine grande catégorie capable d’épauler l’iPhone, et aurait déjà réduit la voilure sur le Vision Pro pour dégager des ressources. La maison mise donc sur un produit jamais montré, sans nom officiel, sans prix public ni date de sortie.

articles.title: Another child dies of measles as CDC reportedly holds up health alert
articles.text:
A child in New York has died of measles, health officials in the state announced late Monday. It marks the first reported measles-associated death in New York in more than 30 years. It is the seventh measles-linked death reported in the US this year; all six of the other deaths were reported in Pennsylvania, which is experiencing a dramatic measles outbreak that has stricken over 1,430 people this year. Prior to the deaths, Pennsylvania hadn’t seen a measles-related death in 35 years.
The boom in vaccine-preventable outbreaks, cases, and tragic deaths is being fueled by slipping vaccination rates nationwide as health misinformation and anti-vaccine sentiments have taken hold. One of the most prominent anti-vaccine activists in the US currently serves as the US health secretary; Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spent decades prior to taking office attacking vaccines and spreading misinformation. He and his anti-vaccine organization, Children’s Health Defense, have been one of the most prolific sources of anti-vaccine content.
Since taking office, Kennedy has waged a multi-front war on vaccines that has included dismantling and obstructing federal vaccine recommendations; launching dubious studies to look for alleged, unspecified harms of vaccines; promoting alleged vaccine injuries; and continuing to spread misinformation about vaccines and vaccine-preventable illnesses.
In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul directly tied the state’s death to Kennedy’s policies and anti-vaccine activism. She called the child’s death “a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.” She also said she was “heartbroken” by the death, sending her condolences to the family. “As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through,” Hochul said. Overall, New York has reported 170 measles cases in over a dozen counties.
Blocked alert
Days before the seventh preventable measles death, The Washington Post reported on Kennedy’s latest push to thwart public health efforts: Career scientists at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention—which is under Kennedy’s control—were blocked from publishing an urgent health alert to clinicians regarding the risk and management of measles cases during pregnancy.
Given the previous success of vaccines and vaccination campaigns, many clinicians have never seen such cases in their careers. But measles infections during pregnancy pose severe, life-threatening risks to both pregnant people and fetuses. As such, CDC scientists wanted to issue an informational advisory through the CDC’s Health Alert Network.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit BTCPay Server Flaw to Steal Bitcoin and Litecoin From Hot Wallets
articles.text:
BTCPay Server, a self-hosted, open-source cryptocurrency payment processor, has urged users to install the latest version of its software in response to reports of Bitcoin and Litecoin being stolen from hot wallets on instances running older versions.
"Our investigation found that these attacks targeted servers running BTCPay Server 2.4.1 (released on 23 July 2026) or earlier," BTCPay Server said. "The attackers used a different method to exploit the vulnerability fixed in 2.4.2, released on 7 August 2026."
Users who are running versions 2.4.1 or earlier are recommended to move to a fresh server with a new wallet, even in scenarios where users have not noticed a theft. In the event of stolen funds or suspected unauthorized access, it's imperative that users consider the entire machine and all secrets stored on it as compromised and follow the same recovery procedures.
It's currently unknown when the attackers behind the campaign first began exploiting the vulnerability, although reports began to surface around November 1, 2026.
In a post on X, BTCPay Server said no "credible reports" of hot wallet drains have been reported from users running the latest 2.4.7 release. The version addresses one critical and several medium-severity security vulnerabilities discovered via Anthropic's OSS scanner.
BTCPay Server has also shared two wallet addresses linked to these incidents -
- Bitcoin: bc1p0f7wmcnesrapznymf9ljdn04pudgmh96sqtrm9vmgqxdh666fh8qvn63r7
- Litecoin: ltc1qp49tmfdueyaqrmgrx0uyx4uegyygt8yt02whee
"If you need a hot wallet for daily operations, keep only the funds needed for those operations on the server and move the rest to a wallet whose spending keys are held off the server," it cautioned.
"If you run BTCPay Server through a hosting provider, your instance may have been shut down automatically to keep older versions from being exploited."
In August 2026, BTCPay Server disclosed that a critical vulnerability had been weaponized by attackers to steal funds from some users. The issue, which affects all BTCPay Server versions, was patched in version 2.4.2. It's unclear if the latest set of attacks is related to the same vulnerability.
"The issue could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to obtain .macaroon credential files for LND, an implementation of the Lightning Network," it said in the August alert. "Those credentials could be used to take control of an LND node and move funds. The attacks we reviewed targeted only files with the .macaroon extension."
The development coincides with a string of security breaches and exploits across the cryptocurrency space, including the record theft of $6.43 billion from Binance by North Korean threat actors. That same day, prediction market giant Polymarket briefly halted trading after it was hit by a $2.65 million exploit following the compromise of software developed by DebugBear.
Hardware wallet maker Trezor also followed suit with a warning that it received a responsible disclosure report alleging a hardware implant in a Trezor Safe 5 purchased from CryptoBilis in August 2026. It's assessed to be part of a sophisticated supply chain attack in which some of the devices sold via third-party resellers are physically tampered with to steal the victim's seed phrase and use it to drain assets.
Mercado Bitcoin Discloses Security Incident
On Monday, Mercado Bitcoin, Brazil's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said it's temporarily pausing deposits and withdrawals following a security breach that resulted in $49 million in stolen funds.
"At this moment, the value of the assets involved is approximately $ 38 million," it said in a post on X. "In a swift action with the crypto community and strategic partners – including Tether, Circle, Paxos, BRL1, and Chainalysis – we have already blocked US$ 11 million."
"Other amounts eligible for blocking have been identified, and containment efforts continue. The resumption of services will occur as soon as full security conditions are met, and deadlines will be communicated exclusively through our official channels."
Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino confirmed that the stablecoin issuer had frozen more than 4.5 million USDT in connection with the incident.

articles.title: “Les gens méritent d’avoir leur RAM” : Elon Musk se moque de Sam Altman qui regrette que nos PC utilisent de la RAM
articles.text:
Pénurie de mémoire : Elon Musk recadre Sam Altman, qui préférerait voir la RAM de nos PC dans ses serveurs
En pleine crise mondiale de mémoire vive, Sam Altman juge “tout à fait terrible” que les ordinateurs personnels mobilisent de la RAM, s’attirant illico les moqueries d’Elon Musk.
La pénurie mondiale de mémoire vive continue de faire flamber les prix des produits tech et de créer quelques tensions entre multimilliardaires. Alors que les fabricants réorientent leurs usines vers l’intelligence artificielle au détriment du grand public, le patron d’OpenAI, Sam Altman, a remis de l’huile sur le feu en critiquant la présence même de RAM dans nos ordinateurs. Une sortie très mal accueillie sur le web, qu’Elon Musk s’est empressé de tourner en dérision.
La RAM des PC au service du cloud : Elon Musk se moque de Sam Altman
Invité sur la chaîne YouTube Cheeky Pint, le dirigeant d’OpenAI a affirmé que, du point de vue de l’allocation mondiale des ressources, il serait “tout à fait terrible que tout le monde ait une part de l’offre mondiale limitée de DRAM assise dans son propre ordinateur et utilisée 5 % du temps”. Face à la pénurie actuelle, il estime qu’il serait bien plus logique de regrouper toute cette mémoire dans les serveurs du cloud pour la faire tourner à plein régime, tout en déplorant que le grand public pense exactement l’inverse.
Il n’en fallait pas plus pour faire réagir le patron de Tesla et SpaceX sur son réseau social X. Affirmant que “les gens méritent aussi d’avoir leur RAM”, Elon Musk a publié un mème détournant le film Inglourious Basterds avec un officier allemand de la Seconde Guerre mondiale traquant des personnes cachant des barrettes de DRAM au détriment du cloud.
Derrière la position de Sam Altman se dessine surtout l’intérêt financier d’OpenAI. Si l’entreprise propose quelques modèles open source, elle tire ses revenus des modèles hébergés dans ses centres de données et facturés aux utilisateurs. Des ordinateurs domestiques capables de faire tourner des modèles en local viennent ainsi réduire mécaniquement le besoin de passer par ses serveurs payants.
Pénurie de RAM et IA : une flambée des prix partie pour durer au-delà de 2027
Cette déclaration passe d’autant plus mal que les consommateurs subissent une hausse généralisée du prix des composants et produits tech, liée justement au développement à vitesse grand V de l’infrastructure IA. Samsung, SK Hynix et Micron, leaders de ce marché, prévoient des pénuries de mémoire vive jusqu’en 2027 et au-delà.
Alors que Lenovo prévenait dès le mois de juin que les tarifs ne reviendraient pas de sitôt (voire jamais) à leurs niveaux d’avant 2026, Apple a annoncé hier lors de la présentation de ses résultats trimestriels que cette flambée “sans précédent” rogne ses marges et restreint les stocks de Mac et d’iPad pour décembre. Cela laisse au passage planer la menace d’une nouvelle hausse de prix chez la firme à la pomme après celles de juin et septembre, bien que rien n’ait été confirmé pour le moment.

articles.title: Test de la Xbox Nano : une mini-manette qui voit grand, mais pour qui ?
articles.text:
Quand on passe plusieurs heures à jouer, une bonne manette change tout. Entre les modèles trop gros, trop lourds, trop petits ou mal pensés, on peut chercher longtemps celui qui nous convient.
Si des modèles comme la DualSense de Sony ou certaines manettes haut de gamme parviennent à offrir un excellent confort, ils restent souvent chers et pas forcément adaptés aux déplacements. Entre leur poids, leur encombrement et la crainte de les abîmer, on hésite parfois à les glisser dans un sac.
Après avoir proposé une manette particulièrement imposante avec la première Xbox (la fameuse Duke), Microsoft prend aujourd’hui le contre-pied avec la Xbox Nano. Un modèle miniature, léger et pensé pour les petites mains comme pour les joueuses et les joueurs nomades. La Xbox Nano sort ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026 en France, au prix de 49,99 €. Mais que vaut vraiment cette petite manette ?
Points forts
- Format ultra-compact et poids plume
- Bonne réactivité en jeu
- Batterie rechargeable et compatibilité multiplateforme
Points faibles
- Grip limitée et ergonomie peu adaptée aux grandes mains
- Boutons assez bruyants
- Absence de vibrations
Une manette Xbox en miniature
Difficile de ne pas remarquer la différence au premier coup d’œil. Avec un peu plus de 12,7 centimètres de longueur et 99 grammes sur la balance, la Xbox Nano affiche des mensurations particulièrement réduites. D’ailleurs, quand le livreur m’a apporté le carton contenant la manette, je me suis demandé si ce dernier n’était pas vide. Elle pèse à peu près autant qu’un gros pain aux raisins, c’est dire.
À titre de comparaison, la manette Xbox Wireless classique dépasse les 15 cm et pèse près de 290 grammes avec ses piles. Microsoft a donc considérablement réduit l’encombrement de son accessoire, au point de pouvoir le glisser dans une poche de veste ou dans un petit sac.
Malgré cette cure d’amaigrissement, la Nano conserve les 18 commandes habituelles d’une manette Xbox, toutes placées au même endroit. On retrouve les deux sticks analogiques, la croix directionnelle, les quatre boutons ABXY, les gâchettes et les commandes centrales. Leur disposition reste familière pour les habitués de l’écosystème Microsoft, même si tout a été sacrément rapproché pour tenir dans un si petit châssis. La manette ajoute également un bouton Action programmable à la place du bouton de partage (Share). Par défaut, il sert aux captures d’écran et aux enregistrements de séquences, mais on peut le réattribuer dans l’application Xbox Accessories.
Faire tenir toutes les commandes d’une manette Xbox dans un boîtier aussi petit impressionne, mais le format impose des compromis. Avec sa silhouette plus plate et ses poignées beaucoup moins marquées, la Nano laisse forcément moins de place aux mains pour se caler et tenir fermement la manette.
Cela ne gêne pas pour de courtes sessions, mais quelques heures de jeu d’affilée pourraient venir à bout de votre endurance et invoquer le mauvais esprit de la tendinite. Alors certes, cette Xbox Nano n’a pas pour but de remplacer vos manettes habituelles, et Microsoft ne ment pas sur la marchandise : c’est une petite manette nomade. Mais il faut bien avoir en tête ces contraintes avant de l’acheter. Autre concession, la Nano n’a pas de vibrations.
Des boutons corrects qui font le travail
La Xbox Nano fait également l’impasse sur les sticks à effet Hall ou TMR, puisqu’elle embarque des potentiomètres classiques. Ce choix classique ne pose pas de problème à court terme, mais il expose la manette à l’usure mécanique et au fameux stick drift, quand le personnage bouge tout seul alors qu’on ne touche pas au stick. Difficile cependant de reprocher à Microsoft de ne pas avoir opté pour une technologie plus récente sur un modèle aussi compact.
Du côté des commandes, les boutons ABXY et les gâchettes remplissent correctement leur rôle. Ils sont toutefois assez bruyants et donnent une sensation plutôt sèche, loin de la douceur de certaines manettes plus haut de gamme. Les sticks analogiques sont également assez courts, ce qui réduit légèrement leur amplitude de mouvement et peut demander un petit temps d’adaptation. La croix directionnelle, en revanche, s’en sort plutôt bien : elle offre des pressions franches et une précision suffisante pour les jeux qui sollicitent davantage les directions.
Une fois en jeu, la Xbox Nano se montre heureusement à la hauteur. Les commandes répondent correctement, et je n’ai pas relevé de problème particulier de réactivité. La détection des directions et des mouvements analogiques reste suffisamment fine pour jouer dans de bonnes conditions, y compris dans des jeux de conduite ou des FPS. Côté réactivité, la manette ne souffre pas de son format réduit et se comporte comme un contrôleur Xbox classique.
Une manette pour les enfants ?
Avec sa petite bouille mignonne et sa taille réduite, on serait tenté d’y voir la manette idéale pour les enfants. En plus d’accompagner facilement un ordinateur portable, une tablette ou un smartphone dans le train, elle vise d’ailleurs ouvertement les plus jeunes, puisque Microsoft la présente comme une option pour les jeunes joueurs et les petites mains. Les commandes rapprochées leur permettent d’atteindre les boutons sans étirer les pouces, et les gâchettes sont faciles à atteindre.
Pour autant, la Xbox Nano manque un peu de volume et de prise en main pour convaincre pleinement les plus jeunes. Les enfants pourront éventuellement préférer des manettes plus généreuses, que l’on peut agripper fermement et manipuler sans retenue, comme la très bonne gamme de controleur filaire Hori pour Switch et Switch 2. Avec sa finesse, la Nano ne semble pas non plus faite pour être malmenée, et à 49,99 €, on n’a pas forcément envie de la voir finir par terre après une partie un peu trop mouvementée.
Après, je pinaille, car dans l’ensemble, la Xbox Nano remplit parfaitement son rôle lorsqu’un ami passe à la maison ou qu’un enfant souhaite rejoindre une partie à plusieurs. Voyez-la comme un compromis entre une manette Xbox classique et une moitié de Joy-Con : un contrôleur d’appoint, compact et facile à sortir du tiroir quand on en a besoin.
Une manette sur batterie
C’est l’un des changements les plus appréciables par rapport à la manette Xbox traditionnelle : la Nano embarque directement une batterie rechargeable. Loger des piles AA au dos d’une manette aussi petite aurait d’ailleurs été une gageure. La recharge s’effectue en USB-C (le câble n’est pas fourni dans la boîte).
Côté autonomie, la Xbox Nano s’en sort plutôt bien. Comme je l’ai reçue peu de temps avant la rédaction de ce test, je n’ai pas encore réussi à vider sa batterie. J’ai néanmoins pu jouer pendant une bonne douzaine d’heures sans que celle-ci ne montre de signe d’épuisement. Un résultat encourageant pour une manette aussi compacte.
La Nano se connecte directement aux Xbox Series X|S et Xbox One grâce au protocole Xbox Wireless, mais peut également passer par le Bluetooth pour fonctionner avec les PC Windows, les smartphones, les tablettes et certains téléviseurs connectés compatibles.
Proposée à 49,99 €, la Xbox Nano a un positionnement assez particulier. Elle ne prétend pas rivaliser avec les manettes haut de gamme, mais cherche plutôt à rendre l’écosystème Xbox plus accessible et plus facile à transporter. Son poids plume, son encombrement réduit, sa batterie intégrée et sa compatibilité avec plusieurs appareils constituent de véritables arguments. Reste à savoir si elle arrivera à convaincre les joueuses et les joueurs Xbox ou PC qui peuvent avoir une manette Xbox Series pour 15 € de plus.
Le verdict
Xbox Nano
Voir la fiche
On a aimé
- Format ultra-compact et poids plume
- Bonne réactivité en jeu
- Batterie rechargeable et compatibilité multiplateforme
On a moins aimé
- Grip limitée et ergonomie peu adaptée aux grandes mains
- Boutons assez bruyants
- Absence de vibrations

articles.title: Hubble der Absturz: Wer kann das Uralt-Teleskop retten?
articles.text:
Anfang 2026 machten Meldungen die Runde, wonach das Hubble-Weltraumteleskop aufgrund erhöhter Sonnenaktivität schlimmstenfalls schon 2029 in die Erdatmosphäre eintreten und damit abstürzen könnte. Ein echter Verlust für die Beobachtung des Weltalls, weil vor 2040 mit dem Habitable Worlds Observatory wohl kein Ersatz für Hubble im Orbit sein dürfte.
Hubble im Sinkflug: Absturz droht bis 2034
Zwar haben sich die Befürchtungen eines dermaßen verfrühten Absturzes nicht bestätigt. Das ändert aber nichts daran, dass sich das Hubble-Teleskop weiter im Sinkflug befindet. Spätestens 2033 oder 2034 soll der kritische Punkt von 400 Kilometern Höhe erreicht sein, an dem sich die Umlaufbahn nicht mehr stabilisieren ließe.
Zur Einordnung: Beim Start 1990 wurde Hubble in gut 600 Kilometern Höhe ausgesetzt. Aktuell gibt der sogenannte Hubble Reentry Tracker für das Weltraumteleskop eine Höhe von gut 469 Kilometern an.
Letzte Service-Mission fand 2009 statt
Bisherige Service-Missionen, die Hubble bis 2009 jeweils um einige Kilometer angehoben hatten, sind aufgrund des Fehlens der dafür eingesetzten Space Shuttles nicht mehr wiederholbar. Die Nasa sucht jetzt fieberhaft nach Alternativen, wie Golem berichtet.
Einer entsprechenden Ausschreibung zufolge hat die US-Weltraumbehörde dafür vor allem Privatunternehmen im Visier. Diese sollen im besten Fall dafür sorgen, dass das Teleskop in seinen Zielorbit von 600 Kilometern über der Erdoberfläche zurückkehren kann. Dann könnte es einige weitere Jahrzehnte in Betrieb bleiben.
Anheben, stabilisieren oder abstürzen lassen
Die zweite Option wäre eine Art Wartungsmission, die Hubbles Umlaufbahn wenigstens um einige Kilometer nach oben verschieben und die technische Ausrüstung instand setzen könnte. Sollte das ebenfalls nicht möglich sein, bliebe eine dritte Möglichkeit. Dann soll eine Mission für einen kontrollierten Absturz sorgen. Hubble besitzt nämlich selbst kein Antriebssystem.
In den vergangenen Jahren gab es schon verschiedene Pläne, wie sich Hubble möglicherweise retten ließe. Das von zwei ehemaligen Blue-Origin-Ingenieuren gegründete Startup Orbital Robotics etwa setzt dabei auf einen KI-kontrollierten Roboterarm. Für sein Konzept ist das Unternehmen aber auf Partnerfirmen angewiesen, die ein Roboter-Raumschiff zur Verfügung stellen können.
Nasa sucht nach technischen Lösungen
Ob Orbital Robotics für die von der Nasa sondierte Mission zur Wartung oder Rettung des Hubble-Weltraumteleskops zum Einsatz kommt, muss sich noch zeigen. Mit der aktuellen Ausschreibung prüft die Behörde zunächst, welche Firmen überhaupt infrage kommen und lotet technische und wirtschaftliche Möglichkeiten aus.

articles.title: Sofia Coppola, sobre su 'María Antonieta' de 2006: "Le dedicamos mucho trabajo, pero no tuvo una acogida muy cálida"
articles.text:
En 2006, 'María Antonieta' de Sofía Coppola fue abucheada en Cannes, y pasó por salas estadounidenses con una recaudación discreta. Ahora, en 2026, el palacio de Versalles, donde se ambienta su historia le dedica una exposición en el Petit Trianon. Es decir, fue en Francia donde se le dedicaron esos abucheos, pero si revisamos la taquilla de la época podemos ver que también allí fue donde recaudó casi la mitad de lo que hizo en Estados Unidos.
Una decepción. Sofia Coppola todavía define así aquel estreno. "Nos quedamos muy frustrados porque le habíamos dedicado muchísimo trabajo, pero la película no tuvo una acogida demasiado cálida". Sin embargo, veinte años después, se ha convertido en una preciosista pieza de culto a reivindicar: aparte de la exposición en Versalles, se estrena el documental 'Making Marie Antoinette', y la prestigiosa editora Criterion publica una edición del film en 4K aprobada por la directora.
Pero... ¿hubo abucheos? La leyenda negra arranca en la Croisette en mayo de 2006. Coppola defiende que aquello se exageró y que los abucheos salieron de un pequeño grupo de periodistas ingleses. En 2006 Roger Ebert calculó que abuchearon cinco personas, quizá diez, mientras muchas otras aplaudían, y recordó que Variety había hablado de un abucheo con acento galo. La biografía que el propio Festival de Cannes mantiene de la directora afirma que la película recibió “una ovación del público”.
La crítica la aplastó. Coppola encontró hace poco una caja llena de reseñas negativas, con titulares del tipo 'Un desastre real', y atribuye a muchos críticos varones haberla despachado como algo frívolo por ser femenina y tener una estética recargada. También le sorprendió que escandalizara la banda sonora, con Siouxsie and the Banshees, Bow Wow Wow, The Strokes o New Order sonando en la corte de Luis XVI. Curioso en un panorama que ya estaba habituado a experimentos de corte similar como 'Moulin Rouge'.
Taquilla mal. La película recaudó 60,9 millones de dólares en todo el mundo con un presupuesto de 40 millones. En Estados Unidos se quedó en 15,96 millones, algo más de una cuarta parte del total. Francia, el país cuya reina era retratada con zapatillas Converse en la película, aportó 7,87 millones. Y en España, donde se estrenó el año siguiente, sumó 3,3 millones, casi el doble que Reino Unido. Sin embargo, pronto empezó el reconocimiento: Milena Canonero ganó el Oscar al mejor diseño de vestuario por la recreación de las extravagancias de la corte. Y el DVD fue muy bien: se estiman unas ventas en Estados Unidos de unos 16,7 millones de dólares, por encima de lo que ingresó en taquilla.
Llega Tumblr. El cambio más significativo en la percepción de la película lo sitúa Coppola diez años después: entonces empezó a oír que la gente estaba descubriendo la película: una generación de usuarios de Tumblr creció con sus imágenes en los años 2010. Se convirtió en referente de la estética coquette, junto al Tumblr de colores pastel y la primera Lana Del Rey. Parte de ese culto se alimentó de las fotos de rodaje de Andrew Durham, amigo de la directora: Vogue Francia publicó unas pocas en 2006 y de ahí pasaron a los muros de Tumblr. En ellas el reparto aparece vestido de época junto a portátiles y auriculares. Las imágenes forman ahora el libro 'Making Marie Antoinette', que acompaña al documental como parte de esta reivindicación tardía.
La siguiente y definitiva oleada reivindicativa llegó en formato de vídeo vertical. En The New York Times, la directora explicaba que sus hijas le enseñaron montajes de la película con canciones de hip-hop en TikTok. El círculo se cierra con la edición de Criterion, que llega justo ahora, cuando la Generación Z ha vuelto a comprar formato físico.
El documental. 'Making Marie Antoinette' sale de las 80 horas que Eleanor Coppola, madre de la directora, grabó en Versalles durante el rodaje. Madre e hija temieron al principio que faltara drama: la producción terminó en plazo y dentro de presupuesto, sin crisis como las que se describen en 'Corazones en tinieblas', la sensacional crónica de Eleanor sobre el rodaje de ‘Apocalypse Now’, dirigida por su marido.
Eleanor Coppola murió en abril de 2024 sin ver terminado el documental: Sofia lo ha completado con amigos de la familia y colaboradores habituales, con Diane Lane leyendo en él los diarios de su madre. En el documental, la directora admite que 'Maria Antonieta' le dejó la lección de no volver a hacer películas grandes ni de época, y a trabajar en lo sucesivo con equipos y repartos pequeños.

articles.title: Affinity arrive enfin sur iPad, et Canva ne s’est pas contenté d’un simple portage
articles.text:
Canva réunit la retouche photo, le dessin vectoriel et la mise en page dans une nouvelle application Affinity pour iPad. Gratuite pour les particuliers, elle accueille aussi un espace de dessin pensé pour l’Apple Pencil.
Il aura fallu patienter un peu plus longtemps que sur ordinateur. Un an après la fusion de ses trois logiciels dans une application gratuite, Affinity adopte enfin la même formule sur iPad. Nous vous avions annoncé son arrivée pour novembre : Canva a lancé l’application le 2 novembre, avec une interface adaptée à la tablette et quelques nouveautés qui donnent davantage de travail au stylet.
Du premier croquis à la maquette, sans changer d’application
Dans son annonce, Canva met notamment en avant Sketch Studio, un nouvel espace consacré au dessin à main levée. L’utilisateur peut y esquisser une illustration au doigt ou à l’Apple Pencil, jouer avec les pinceaux, les textures et les calques, puis passer dans Vector Studio pour retravailler les courbes et les points de son dessin. Le tout reste dans le même fichier, sans export intermédiaire.
L’intérêt dépasse donc le simple regroupement de boutons dans une nouvelle interface. On peut préparer un croquis, construire son illustration, retoucher la photo qui l’accompagne et assembler les différents éléments dans une brochure. Les espaces Sketch, Vector, Pixel et Layout se partagent le travail, sans obliger à jongler entre plusieurs applications.
La partie photo comprend le développement des fichiers RAW, les masques, les sélections et les retouches non destructives, qui permettent de revenir sur ses réglages. Côté mise en page, Affinity propose notamment des pages maîtres et des outils typographiques pour préparer des documents destinés à l’impression.
Pour reprendre ses projets existants, Canva annonce la prise en charge des fichiers PSD de Photoshop, AI d’Illustrator, INDD et IDML d’InDesign, mais aussi des PDF et SVG. De quoi retrouver ses créations sur la tablette et poursuivre les modifications sans repartir de zéro.
Canva promet également une utilisation fluide sur les fichiers complexes, y compris hors ligne. Une ambition bienvenue, même s’il faudra vérifier ce que deviennent ces belles promesses avec un document bien chargé et un iPad moins récent.
Les outils gratuits d’un côté, l’IA sur abonnement de l’autre
Le modèle économique reprend celui de la version pour ordinateur : les outils principaux de dessin, de retouche, de création vectorielle et de mise en page sont gratuits pour les particuliers. Il faut toutefois se connecter avec un compte Canva, lui aussi gratuit, pour utiliser l’application.
Canva AI Studio reste, lui, réservé aux comptes premium. Cet espace rassemble notamment des fonctions de réduction du bruit, de correction du flou et de suppression d’arrière-plan. La gratuité couvre donc bien les outils de création, mais pas l’ensemble des fonctions mises en avant par l’éditeur.
L’application est proposée sur l’App Store français, avec une interface en français, et nécessite iPadOS 18 ou une version ultérieure. Prévoyez également 1,9 Go pour le téléchargement. La boutique affiche Canva Pro à 12 euros par mois ou 109,99 euros par an pour ceux qui souhaitent accéder aux fonctions premium. Pour commencer son premier dessin ou retoucher ses photos, la carte bancaire peut rester dans le portefeuille.

articles.title: Borderlands is now a 100 million-copy franchise, and Gearbox isn't done yet
articles.text:
In brief: Borderlands, the action role-playing first-person shooter series developed by Gearbox Software and published by 2K, has surpassed 100 million copies sold since its debut. The achievement comes just over a year after the launch of the latest entry in the franchise, Borderlands 4.
Gearbox launched Borderlands 4 on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, and Windows PCs on September 12, 2025. Like others in the series, it is playable solo or with up to three others. Gamers have enjoyed a solid first year of post-launch add-on content including two story packs, five bounty packs, and a pair of new vault hunters, on top of several new activities and features.
Gearbox said it's rare for a game series to surpass the 100 million units sold mark, and they aren't wrong. Outside of monster franchises like Mario, Call of Duty, Sonic the Hedgehog, Zelda, and Resident Evil, very few ever reach that milestone.
Only three individual games have ever sold more than 100 million copies on their own: Grand Theft Auto V (230 million), Minecraft (425 million), and Tetris (520 million). Barring any unforeseen circumstances, the next installment in the GTA series will likely be the fourth to join that coveted list.
According to Sensor Tower's sales tracker, Rockstar has already secured 7.71 million pre-orders for Grand Theft Auto VI. That works out to roughly $751 million in revenue, with orders split 74% / 26% in favor of the PlayStation 5. The game is reportedly coming to PC as early as Q1 2027, but that hasn't yet been officially confirmed by Rockstar.
What are your thoughts on the Borderlands franchise? I know several people that swear by it, but have also spoken to others that find it a bit too repetitive in that you're essentially stuck in an endless cycle of grinding to level up only to fight stronger enemies, requiring stouter weapons to defeat them.
Looking ahead, Gearbox pointed to November 6 and the start of a community fundraising event called The Hunt. Earlier this year, gamers raised nearly $120,000 for St. Jude Children's Research Hospital in Memphis, TN through a similar event.

articles.title: Windows 11 : Microsoft promet des PC à 8 Go de RAM "jusqu'à 40 % plus rapides" — Frandroid
articles.text:
Pavan Davuluri, vice-président exécutif chargé de Windows chez Microsoft, a publié ce mardi 3 novembre un billet sur le blog officiel de Windows sur les PC qui n’ont que 8 gigaoctets de mémoire vive. Ces machines reviennent dans les rayons, et Microsoft répète depuis juin que 8 gigaoctets suffisent. Il y a déjà eu une première mise à jour à la mi-octobre pour alléger Windows 11. Cette fois, l’éditeur détaille ce qu’il a changé, avec des chiffres qu’il a mesurés lui-même.
Une histoire de compression
Microsoft a annoncé avoir réglé autrement la compression de mémoire, qui tasse les données peu utilisées pour les garder en RAM. D’après l’éditeur, Windows peut ainsi garder en mémoire jusqu’à 2 gigaoctets de données actives en plus. Windows met aussi en pause des tâches de fond, comme l’indexation de la recherche, pendant qu’on utilise le PC.
Les applications de Microsoft ont aussi été retouchées. Sur les PC à 8 gigaoctets ou moins, les Widgets ne se chargent plus qu’à l’ouverture, ce qui libère environ 200 mégaoctets quand le panneau est fermé. Edge met en veille les onglets inactifs au bout de 15 minutes par défaut, contre deux heures jusqu’ici. Teams passe dans un mode qui consomme moins de ressources et se lance jusqu’à 20 % plus vite.
Au total, Microsoft annonce jusqu’à 900 mégaoctets de mémoire réservée en moins pendant une séance de multitâche, dont 360 mégaoctets grâce à Word, PowerPoint, Excel et Outlook.
Des gains mesurés par Microsoft, sur un seul PC
Les 20 % de réactivité viennent de la télémétrie, ces données que les PC envoient à Microsoft. Elles portent sur six gestes : ouvrir le menu Démarrer, lancer une recherche, faire un clic droit, ouvrir les Paramètres, l’Outil Capture et l’Explorateur de fichiers. La comparaison se fait avec la version de Windows 11 de janvier 2026.
Les 40 % en multitâche, eux, sortent d’un seul scénario en laboratoire, sur un HP OmniBook 3 à puce Snapdragon X Plus. Microsoft écrit lui-même, en note de bas de page, que ce résultat ne vaut que pour ce scénario et cette machine. Précisons qu’un test comparatif publié en octobre sur Windows 11 26H2 allait déjà dans le même sens.
Le billet met aussi en avant un Dell XPS 13 de 2026 avec 8 gigaoctets, 94 % plus rapide en multicœur qu’un modèle de 2021. Ce test a été fait par le cabinet Principled Technologies, à la demande de Microsoft. Microsoft reconnaît quand même que la 3D ou le montage vidéo poussé demandent 16 gigaoctets ou plus.

articles.title: How Anju turned a personal food experiment into a snack brand expanding to 41 retail stores
articles.text:
How Anju turned a personal food experiment into a snack brand expanding to 41 retail stores
After a 20-year corporate career, Anju Kalhan ventured into entrepreneurship and built Bliss by Anju, a plant-based food brand offering snacks without added oil, ghee or dairy.
A 20-year corporate career, an events business and eight marathons may not seem like the usual starting points for a food entrepreneur.
But Anju Kalhan's journey to building a healthy snacking brand has taken an unconventional route.
A graduate in Business Economics from the University of Delhi, Anju spent two decades working in corporate and industry organisations.
She served as a Senior Economist at ASSOCHAM and Deputy Director at the Hotel Association of India, where she also worked with SSH Rehman, former Managing Director of ITC Hotels.
She eventually left her corporate career to start an events company, organising FICCI events and corporate workshops. Alongside her professional commitments, she pursued fitness, completed eight marathons and trained as a yoga professional and fitness coach.
But it was a personal health experience that eventually led her towards the food business.
Today, she is the founder of Bliss by Anju, a food brand making plant-based snacks without added oil, ghee, dairy or refined ingredients.
What began with experiments in her home kitchen has grown into an operation with an in-house manufacturing facility and a retail presence across 41 stores in India.
A personal journey sparks a business idea
Anju says she had lived with high blood pressure for nearly 30 years, along with severe migraines and sinusitis. Health complications within her family, including diabetes and high blood pressure among her parents, also made her reconsider their everyday food habits.
During the Covid-19 pandemic, she began exploring plant-based whole-food diets, learning from coaches and studying the role of food in health.
She gradually removed ghee, cooking oil and highly processed packaged foods from her kitchen. According to Anju, she noticed significant improvements in her blood pressure and migraines within 90 days. Her mother, who was over 80, also experienced improvements in her diabetes and blood pressure after changing her diet, she says.
The experience encouraged Anju to look beyond her household and examine what was available in the market.
She visited organic stores, large retail outlets and shops selling artisanal products to find snacks that aligned with her new food choices. However, she found that many products marketed as healthy still contained palm oil or other added oils.
This exposed a gap she wanted to address.
"The healthy food is not tasty, and the tasty food is not healthy," was how Anju described the problem she encountered.
She decided to create snacks that could offer both. Rather than depend on oil and ghee for flavour, she began experimenting with Indian spices, nuts and seeds.
The company's earlier journey began with home-kitchen experiments in 2018-19, followed by selling at farmers' markets in 2019-20. As her understanding of whole-food eating evolved, she reworked the product range in 2023-24 to remove ghee and added oils.
From kitchen experiments to an in-house factory
Building a food business without a background in professional cooking or bakery operations meant learning several things along the way.
Anju says she is neither a trained chef nor a nutritionist. Instead, she approached product development through research, experimentation and a willingness to learn.
The brand's philosophy is built around plant-based whole foods and familiar ingredients. Its range includes granolas made with nuts and seeds, cookies prepared using chickpea flour, sattu and almonds, biscotti, sweets and savoury snacks such as matthi.
One of its products, tangy dates, uses dates, spices and lemon, offering an alternative to conventional packaged aam papad.
For Anju, spices are central to making the products flavourful without added fats. Cinnamon, cardamom and nutmeg, she explains, can bring aroma and flavour to snacks without relying on oil or ghee.
The company also pays attention to how its ingredients are prepared. Anju says nuts and seeds are washed, soaked and dried before being used in its products.
What started in her kitchen has now moved into manufacturing. The company operates an in-house factory in Okhla industrial area, where it makes its products.
Its approach is to cover different snacking occasions throughout the day, from morning granola to cookies with tea, biscotti with coffee and savoury snacks in the evening.
Taking the brand to more consumers
Bliss by Anju has expanded its distribution to 41 stores across India and is also available on Amazon and Blinkit.
The company has entered its third year of operations in its current phase of growth, according to Anju. It remains bootstrapped, and she says she is looking for investment to support the next stage of the business.
Building awareness remains one of the challenges. As a relatively small brand, Anju says she cannot afford large celebrity endorsements or extensive marketing campaigns. She is looking to reach consumers by communicating the thinking behind the products and the ingredients used to make them.
The brand's products can also be relatively expensive because of their use of nuts, seeds and other whole-food ingredients. Anju believes consumers should understand food labels and make informed choices about what they eat.
Her efforts extend beyond selling packaged snacks.
Through her association with the SHARAN community, she participates in cooking demonstrations and classes that teach people how to prepare food without oil and ghee. Many of these sessions are free or offered at a nominal charge.
She is also careful about how she positions her products. Anju says the snacks are not intended to replace fresh meals. Instead, they are meant for people who need convenient options while travelling, working in offices or packing food for children.
At 60, Anju is building a food business around an idea that emerged from her own experiences. Having moved from a corporate career to entrepreneurship and then into food manufacturing, she is now looking for investment and opportunities to expand Bliss by Anju.
For women considering entrepreneurship, her advice is simple: pursue the idea, even when the circumstances are not perfect. As she puts it, one should not be afraid of taking the plunge. Something worthwhile can emerge from the effort.

articles.title: Robô de entregas ignora sinal vermelho e é “atropelado” por ônibus • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Robô de entregas ignora sinal vermelho e é “atropelado” por ônibus
Pelo menos nove passageiros se feriram em acidente na capital da Estônia.
Um robô de entregas ganhou as manchetes na Europa por ignorar completamente um sinal vermelho e decidir atravessar a rua na cidade de Talin, capital da Estônia. Um ônibus atingiu o equipamento em cheio, e ainda deixou pelo menos nove passageiros feridos, de acordo com os primeiros relatos da imprensa local.
O motorista do ônibus disse que deu uma freada brusca para tentar evitar o acidente, mas mesmo assim não foi possível evitar o impacto. Após a colisão, o robô ainda é arrastado por alguns metros.
O caso ocorreu no centro da cidade, por volta das 18h. Depois disso, o robô da empresa de mobilidade Bolt simplesmente seguiu o percurso, como se nada tivesse acontecido.
A empresa municipal de transporte declarou quer “se o participante de um acidente de trânsito deixa a cena sem cumprir todas as obrigações estabelecidas em lei, isso pode constituir um ilícito”.
Já um dos diretores da mesma empresa disse que “o robô fugiu, se é que podemos colocar desta forma”. Andrei Novikov também disse que a polícia iria investigar o caso.
O chefe de operações da Starship Technologies, que é responsável pelos robôs de entrega, disse que a decisão equivocada do equipamento tem a ver com a maneira como ele enxerga o ambiente. Segundo Pepe Aaviksoo, havia muita luz das propagandas no entorno e os semáforos tanto para pessoas quanto para carros estavam na mesma linha de visão. Por isso, o robô teria lido errado a sinalização.
“Há muitas lições a serem aprendidas, mas situações excepcionais acontecem”, disse o representante da empresa. Ele ainda afirmou que o robô ficou no local por aproximadamente 10 minutos, ou seja, não teria fugido.
Após a colisão, o robô entrou em contato com os funcionários no escritório, que teriam assumido a direção para colocá-lo num local seguro da via. “Do nosso ponto de vista, a situação estava resolvida”, diz o representante da empresa, já que o ônibus seguiu a viagem e nenhum veículo de resgate ou policial estava na cena.
O caso ocorreu na semana passada.

articles.title: Ferrari’s controversial Luce EV is sold out for 2027 | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The Luce, Ferrari’s first electric car and one of its most polarizing models, isn’t just selling. It’s selling out.
The five-seater EV designed by Jony Ive, Apple’s longtime design chief, was mocked and widely panned when it debuted in May, sending Ferrari’s stock price lower. But all that criticism hasn’t dampened demand, according to CEO Benedetto Vigna.
The 2027 production run of the Luce, which starts at about $615,000, is “fully allocated,” Vigna said Tuesday during the company’s third-quarter earnings call, meaning every car Ferrari plans to build next year already has a buyer. “If someone comes, he has to wait one year to get the cars,” Vigna added. The first deliveries of the Luce are expected to begin in the fourth quarter.
Just how many Luce cars that represents is unclear. Ferrari has never publicly disclosed how many Luce vehicles it plans to produce. Financial Times reported earlier this year, citing unnamed sources, that Ferrari planned to sell just under 500 units this year. The company’s longer-term target is to sell 2,500 units by 2030, or about 600 a year, according to Financial Times.
Speculation on who these buyers are — ahem, the founders of multibillion-dollar AI labs, perhaps? — will have to remain just that until Luces are spotted in the wild. Vigna wouldn’t provide a breakdown of who these Luce customers are, only noting it was a “good mix in terms of client, it is a good mix also in terms of geography.” He later added that there is no specific pattern or demographic of Luce buyers.
While Luce deliveries have yet to begin, Ferrari’s existing lineup and growing demand for personalized options helped fuel its financial performance in the third quarter. Revenue from customizations, which executives said accounted for more than 21% of revenue from cars and spare parts, helped boost profits. The company said deliveries of the F80, its limited-run hypercar, and customization reflect its clients’ “ever-deepening desire” to make each Ferrari uniquely their own. As a result, the company raised its full-year guidance, saying it now expects adjusted earnings of at least €3 billion ($3.36 billion), up from €2.97 billion.
Ferrari, which enjoys some of the highest profit margins in the auto industry, reported third-quarter revenue of €1.9 billion, up 7% from a year earlier, and net income of €431 million, up 13%. Operating profit was €563 million, for an operating margin of 29.7%, meaning the company kept roughly 30 cents of every dollar of revenue as profit from its core business.

articles.title: The RedMagic 12 Pro is a phenomenally powerful gaming phone — but a significant price increase spoils its appeal
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The RedMagic 12 Pro is the most capable gaming phone on the market, but as an all-round proposition, it might just be worse than its predecessors. Subtle design enhancements, cutting-edge performance, and impressive battery life are offset by a hiked price, a mediocre camera, and a poor software support commitment.
Reasons to buy
- + Barnstorming performance
- + Superb stamina
- + Bright, obstruction-free display
Reasons to avoid
- - Much more expensive than before
- - Cameras not good enough for the money
- - Poor software support
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
RedMagic 12 Pro: One-minute review
RedMagic has produced yet another phenomenally high-performing phone in the RedMagic 12 Pro, but it no longer screams ‘bargain’ in the way the series used to.
Its design has been slightly slimmed down and lightened up, though it remains a whole hunk of a phone with a slightly gauche look. Mind you, that visible liquid cooling system meets the approval of our inner 13-year-old.
The phone’s display is brighter and faster than that of the RedMagic 11 Pro, and provides one of the cleanest media experiences thanks to the lack of a selfie notch — though that omission leads to issues elsewhere.
As one of the first phones released with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, the RedMagic 12 Pro is just about as fast as you could hope for, though it may not be able to sustain peak performance quite as well as its predecessors.
Battery life is the biggest improvement here, thanks to a massive increase in capacity. This is a phone that could potentially last you days, provided you don’t hit the games too hard, with 80W charging (both wired and wireless) getting you up to speed relatively swiftly.
But for all of these improvements, RedMagic has fallen into a familiar and oh-so-2026 trap. In raising the price of the 12 Pro by such a considerable amount (£170 / $250 / €200), it no longer feels like the total bargain this series built its reputation on.
Don’t get us wrong, £799 is a very good price for a phone that performs and lasts as long as this, especially in this hiked-up climate. But we’re still talking about a flagship(ish) price here, which can only draw extra attention to the phone’s failings.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
For all the subtle progress elsewhere, that’s most typified by a camera system that’s as mediocre as ever. Selfies, especially, continue to be a total write-off on the RedMagic 12 Pro thanks to that aforementioned hidden front camera.
Elsewhere, a paltry two-year OS update promise further dents the brand’s formerly unimpeachable sense of value.
The RedMagic 12 Pro is the most capable gaming phone on the market, but the previous-generation RedMagic 11 Pro remains a much better buy while stocks last.
RedMagic 12 Pro review: Price and availability
- Released on November 18, 2026
- Priced from $899 / £799 (around AU$1,290)
- Another big price bump
- Available globally
Open sales for the RedMagic 12 Pro commence on November 18, 2026. Availability is global, including the UK, US, Australia, and much of Europe.
Following an industry-wide trend, the phone is significantly more expensive than its predecessors. With a starting price of $899 / £799 (around AU$1,290 — RedMagic lists the 'global' price of the 12 Pro in US dollars) for 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, it’s a considerable $250 / £170 (around AU$360) more expensive than the RedMagic 11 Pro.
This represents the second major price rise in a year for the brand. The RedMagic 11S Pro only launched in June, and at a lower starting price of $849 / £709 (around AU$1,220).
You’ll pay a lot more for models with higher RAM and storage, too: $999 / £889 (around AU$1,430) for 16GB/512GB, and $1,199 / £1,059 (around AU$1,720) for 16GB/1TB.
- Value score: 3.5 / 5
RedMagic 12 Pro review: Specs
| RedMagic 12 Pro specs |  | 
|---|---|
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Header Cell - Column 1 | 
|---|---|
| Dimensions: | 163.03 x 75.96 x 8.55mm | 
| Weight: | 223g | 
| Display: | 6.85-inch 1.5K (1216 x 2688) up to 185Hz BOE AMOLED | 
| Chipset: | Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 | 
| RAM: | 12GB / 16GB | 
| Storage: | 256GB / 512GB / 1TB | 
| OS: | Android 17 with RedMagic OS 12 | 
| Primary camera: | 50MP Samsung OV50J 1/1.56-inch sensor w/ OIS | 
| Ultra-wide camera: | 50MP Samsung OV50D40 1/2.87-inch sensor | 
| Macro camera: | NA | 
| Front Camera: | 16MP under-display | 
| Battery: | 8,400mAh | 
| Charging: | 80W wired, 80W wireless | 
| Colors: | Nightfreeze, Subzero | 
RedMagic 12 Pro review: Design
- Extended liquid cooling system
- Confusing IP68/IP69 and IPX8 certification
- Dedicated gaming mode button and capacitive shoulder buttons
- Improved speakers
RedMagic’s current design language dates back to the RedMagic 8 Pro in late 2022. That was the first RedMagic phone to feature the brand's now-signature flattened-out look, as replete with right angles as it was with semi-transparent elements and RGB lighting.
The RedMagic 12 Pro broadly follows that trend, but there have been a few minor tweaks and refinements in the years since the 8 Pro hit shelves.
It remains a big lump of a phone, measuring 163.03 x 75.96 x 8.55mm and weighing 223g. Compared to last year’s model, however, the 12 Pro is 7g lighter and 0.35mm thinner, together with a fractionally smaller footprint.
I’m somewhat perplexed by the RedMagic 12 Pro’s level of dust resistance. New to this year’s model is the claim of full IP68 and IP69 certification, which is genuine flagship-grade. However, this comes accompanied by the following small print, which I’ll quote directly from the press materials: “IP68 and IP69 ratings apply to the device, while the cooling fan area is rated IPX8 due to its independent airflow channel design.”
So the 12 Pro is completely dustproof... until you get to the open vents on either edge of the phone. Thanks for that, RedMagic.
Those vents do, admittedly, form part of the most extensive cooling system around, leading to a physical fan that spins at a higher 25,500rpm (up from 24,000rpm). This is paired with an even more extensive liquid cooling system, which now winds its way around much more of the RedMagic 12 Pro, drawing heat away from core components.
The lava lamp look of this liquid cooling system continues to fascinate, with tiny clear globules winding their way around a brilliant blue pathway. It’s more tasteful than the blingy RGB LED lighting, which can be configured around the cooling fan, shoulder buttons, and to a lesser extent the cooling goop itself.
The right edge of the phone continues to be crammed with elements, with a set of capacitive shoulder buttons joining the volume rocker and circular power button. One new element sees the old slider switch giving way to another push button.
It serves the same purpose, granting access to RedMagic’s custom gaming UI. But you’ll now need to press and hold the button rather than simply flicking a switch.
It’s less satisfying and intuitive to use, but on the plus side, it now functions much better as a remappable ‘Magic Key’. Repurposing it as a camera or flashlight shortcut feels more natural now.
RedMagic has bolstered the audio output of the 12 Pro’s Dolby Atmos-certified stereo speakers. You now get a pair of 1115E speakers — they're more balanced and fuller-sounding, although they lack the low-end kick of the speakers on something like the Poco F9 Ultra.
- Design score: 3.5 / 5
RedMagic 12 Pro review: Display
- 6.85-inch OLED display
- 185Hz refresh rate
- 1,900 nits maximum brightness
RedMagic has kept the basic dimensions of the 12 Pro Display consistent with its recent antecedents — it’s another large 6.85-inch OLED panel with a 2,688 x 1,216 (1.5K) resolution.
Improvements have been made, however, starting with a move to a new BOE X11 panel material, which has a higher maximum brightness of 1,900 nits (up from 1,800 nits).
It can also hit a higher 185Hz refresh rate, compared to the RedMagic 11 Pro’s 144Hz. Not many games will be able to hit the kind of elevated frame rates to make the most of that spec, but it makes more sense on this gaming-focused phone than any other.
As always, I found RedMagic's default color profile to be a little too punchy, but a quick rummage around in the Settings menu — and a switch to the Standard mode — saw to that particular problem.
Ultimately, the RedMagic 12 Pro's display has all of the key strengths we’ve grown accustomed to with the brand. Its large size and unobstructed view — there’s no selfie notch to get in the way of gaming or video content — set it apart from most other phones and make it a great choice for media playback.
- Display score: 4 / 5
RedMagic 12 Pro review: cameras
- 50MP main camera with OIS
- Mediocre 50MP ultra-wide
- No more macro
- 16MP in-display selfie camera remains awful
RedMagic phones have never been particularly impressive in the camera department. We’ve always accepted this fact, albeit somewhat begrudgingly, because of the brand’s tight gaming focus and aggressive pricing.
The RedMagic 12 Pro’s cameras don't improve matters, and they're a little harder to defend given the phone's price bump.
Its camera system is led by a 1/1.56” 50MP OmniVision OV50J sensor. Image quality in good lighting is fine, though it's nothing you can’t get (or even improve upon) with a decent mid-range phone like the Google Pixel 10a.
Night shots, meanwhile, reveal noisy skies and a distinct lack of detail pulled from the shadows.
Portrait shots are weirdly horrendous, with an oddly fake-looking bokeh effect made worse by a terribly imprecise edge blur around the subject.
You’re not going to hear me complaining about the loss of the RedMagic 11 Pro’s 2MP macro camera, but it’s technically another cut.
With no dedicated telephoto, zoomed shots are forced to crop in on that main sensor. The results look somewhat soft even at 2x, becoming noticeably grainy at 3x, and downright unusable at 10x.
There’s also a humble 50MP ultra-wide camera with a 1/2.87" OmniVision OV50D40 sensor. It yields slightly better results in terms of sharpness, though the tone is noticeably cooler and the exposure falls short of the main camera's equivalent.
Matters degrade further with the RedMagic 12 Pro's 16MP front camera, which once again suffers badly from its positioning under the phone’s display. While this positioning is an advantage for clean media playback, it renders selfies a fuzzy mess, producing sickly skin tones and smudged details. They’re a write-off.
Video, at least, is moderately impressive on the RedMagic 12 Pro, with support for 4K/120fps enabling reasonably high-quality slo-mo footage. You take your wins where you can get them.
I get that photography isn’t the focus here, but the simple point is that a $899 / £799 smartphone should be taking better pictures in late 2026.
- Camera score: 2.5 / 5

RedMagic 12 Pro review: performance
- Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset
- 12GB or 16GB, or 24GB of RAM
- Extended liquid and active cooling system
The RedMagic 12 Pro is one of the first phones on the market to use Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset. While this 2nm chip is the fastest Android chip on the market at the time of writing, it doesn’t bring about a seismic shift in performance.
Benchmark tests suggest that the RedMagic 12 Pro is barely any faster than the RedMagic 11 Pro and RedMagic 11S Pro (which share the same chip) in CPU terms, according to Geekbench 6.
GPU tests point to a much bigger improvement in GPU terms, with Geekbench 6 GPU scores that are between 16 and 28% faster, depending on the test.
That’s good to hear from a gaming-focused smartphone. Less positive were my 3DMark stress tests, which suggest the RedMagic 12 Pro is worse than its predecessors when it comes to sustained load.
Its peaks were higher, but its lower scores towards the end of the 20-minute WildLife Extreme Stress Test were quite a bit lower. This resulted in a stability score of 54% compared to 66% on the RedMagic 11 Pro.
Putting aside the possibility that this is a simple driver issue, it would suggest that, while the RedMagic 12 Pro is capable of running faster than its predecessors, it’s not capable of maintaining that flat-out speed quite as well. That’s surprising, given RedMagic has packed in an even more extensive liquid cooling system, plus a large vapor chamber and a faster cooling fan.
Benchmarks aside, the RedMagic 12 Pro performs impeccably in demanding games, running Wuthering Waves at relatively smooth frame rates with high graphical settings.
Ultimately, if you’re after the fastest-performing Android phone on the market right now, you won’t do any better than the RedMagic 12 Pro. Viewed from this angle, that $899 / £799 asking price doesn’t seem so bad at all.
- Performance score: 4.5 / 5
RedMagic 12 Pro review: software
- Fluid yet bland Android 17-based UI
- Game Space gaming UI
- Two Android updates
- Five years of security updates in Europe, three in the US
One of RedMagic’s main weaknesses has always been software, and some credit is due in this department on the RedMagic 12 Pro.
The company has cleaned up its act considerably, to the point where RedMagic OS 12 looks and feels much like most other custom Android UIs from Chinese manufacturers.
Instances of random Chinese text and troublesome bugs are now relatively rare — though I did observe a slight glitch with the DisneyPlus app in picture-in-picture mode. Gone, too, are the ugly screen-dominating widgets.
What’s left is slightly bland and generic, and relatively free of frills or flair, but it works quickly and reliably. Google Feed is placed to the left of the home screen, in all its increasingly AI- and ad-blighted glory.
RedMagic OS still has a bit of a bloatware problem. There are unwanted preinstallations for Booking.com, TikTok, Instagram, and AliExpress, as well as three rubbish games and a duplicate web browser app. But none of that is particularly unusual.
More problematic is the relatively poor level of software support. RedMagic promises a mere two full Android OS updates and up to five years of security updates for Europe. The US only gets three years of the latter.
As ever, the unique selling point here is Game Space UI. Long-press the red button, and this interface will offer you a hub for running, tweaking, and optimizing your games. It’ll also let you crank up the processor or map those capacitive buttons to specific controls within games via a drag-out overlay.
It’s all very busy and nerdy, but that’s just what the doctor ordered with a gaming phone of this caliber.
- Software score: 3 / 5
RedMagic 12 Pro review: Battery life
- Huge 8,400mAh battery
- Multi-day usage
- Comprehensive 80W wired and wireless charging
RedMagic has managed to massively increase the size of the 12 Pro’s battery, despite its slimmed-down chassis. It now runs on a massive 8,400mAh cell, up from 7,500mAh in the RedMagic 11 Pro and its subsequent S variant.
If you don’t stretch the phone's legs with too many high-end games or a lot of 4K video recording, you could well get through three full days before needing to recharge. On one day of light-to-moderate usage, with 3 hours 40 minutes of screen-on time (and no gaming), I was still left with 72% in the tank.
This hefty battery is, of course, built to allow you to incorporate a couple of hours of heavy-duty 3D gaming into your day, but even then, you should be able to get through a full day without running too low.
When it comes time to recharge, 80W wired and wireless charging keeps things reasonably rapid. It’s not hugely impressive, but given that large capacity, a 50% charge in 30 minutes seems pretty good.
A full charge from empty took me about 72 minutes.
Do note, however, that I was able to use a compatible Nubia charger, and that no such provision comes in the box.
- Battery score: 5 / 5
Should you buy the RedMagic 12 Pro?
| RedMagic 11 Pro scorecard |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Design | RedMagic has slimmed its design down a little, and the visible liquid cooling system is fascinating, but this is still a big old phone. | 3.5 / 5 | 
| Display | The 12 Pro offers a big, bright, unblemished view of media, with a rapid 185Hz maximum refresh rate and no annoying notch to get in the way. | 4 / 5 | 
| Performance | The Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 ensures this is one of the fastest Android phones around, though there are indications that sustained performance has dropped off a tad. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Camera | RedMagic has streamlined its camera offering to pretty middling dual 50MP set-up and a terrible 16MP selfie camera, which isn’t really good enough give the new higher price tag. | 2.5 / 5 | 
| Battery | With a huge new 8,400mAh cell, the RedMagic 12 Pro’s stamina is seriously impressive, while 80W wired and wireless charging is more than sufficient. | 5 / 5 | 
| Software | Redmagic OS 12 is cleaner and less annoying than it’s ever been, but it’s still rather functional and drab, and software support is limited. | 3 / 5 | 
| Value | Consecutive price rises over the past year mean that the RedMagic 12 Pro is far from the bargain that the RedMagic 11 Pro was, though it still offers a lot of bang for your buck. | 3.5 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You want the fastest phone around
With the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, liquid cooling, and plenty of RAM, the RedMagic 12 Pro is as fast as they come.
You want a fluid, unobstructed viewing experience
Thanks to a 185Hz maximum refresh rate and no notch, this phone offers an extremely clean media viewing experience.
You want the fun to last
RedMagic has ramped up the battery capacity again to 8,400mAh, which can last for days of normal use.
Don't buy it if...
You remember how much of a bargain RedMagics used to be
No manufacturer is immune to price pressures, and the RedMagic 12 Pro costs a massive $250 / £170 more than the RedMagic 11 Pro.
You like taking pictures
The RedMagic 12 Pro’s two 50MP rear cameras will just about do a job, but nothing more, while the 16MP selfie camera won’t even do that much.
This is going to be your last phone for a while
With only two major Android updates and as little as three years of security updates in the US, this is not a phone that’s in it for the long haul.
RedMagic 12 Pro review: also consider
RedMagic is the only dedicated gaming phone maker on the market, but there are alternative options to consider.
RedMagic 11 Pro
Given the huge price hike with this year’s model, tracking down the RedMagic 11 Pro or even the RedMagic 11S Pro will prove better value. In truth, the 12 Pro doesn’t offer all that much more in terms of hardware.
Read our full RedMagic 11 Pro review
Poco F9 Ultra
It too is more expensive than its predecessor, but the Poco F9 Ultra offers a slightly more mainstream-friendly combination of performance and outstanding media playback at a not-extortionate asking price.
Read our full Poco F9 Ultra review
How I tested the RedMagic 12 Pro
- Review test period = 2 weeks
- Testing included = Everyday usage, including web browsing, social media, photography, gaming, streaming video, music playback
- Tools used = Geekbench 6, 3DMark, native Android stats, Nubia 80W power adapter
☑️ 100s of smartphones reviewed
☑️ 15 years of product testing
☑️ Over 16,000 products reviewed in total
☑️ Nearly 200,000 hours testing tech
I tested the RedMagic 12 Pro for two weeks, using it as I would any other gaming phone. I played demanding titles like Wuthering Waves for extended periods, watched movies and TV shows on apps like Netflix, and browsed the internet and social media during casual-use days.
I tested the phone's power credentials using benchmark apps including Geekbench 6 and 3DMark, and used a compatible Nubia 80W power adapter to measure its charging speed.
First reviewed: October 2026
Jon is a freelance journalist who has been covering tech since the dawn of the smartphone era. Besides TechRadar, his words and pictures have appeared in The Telegraph, ShortList, Tech Advisor, Trusted Reviews, Expert Reviews, and more. He largely covers consumer technology, with a particular focus on smartphones and tablets. However, he's also been known to dabble in the worlds of entertainment and video games.
