articles.title: CentOS co-founder creates a Linux-compatible kernel in just 11 days, with AI doing almost all the coding
articles.text:
The big picture: Writing an operating system kernel from scratch usually takes a team of seasoned engineers years of work. Gregory Kurtzer, who co-founded CentOS and later launched Rocky Linux, says he just built one in 11 days – mostly by having an AI agent write the code. Even without any Linux code underneath, his new kernel can already boot Rocky Linux 10. That said, it's still very much a research prototype.
Kurtzer unveiled the kernel, Ginux, on X last week. The code is on GitHub, too, under the Apache 2.0 license. As for the name, it blends Linux, GPT, and Greg. The README jokes that to keep its author's ego in check, the G officially stands for GPT.
Despite the name, Ginux isn't a fork of Linux. Everything from memory management and scheduling to filesystems and networking was written from scratch, mostly in Rust. What it does share with Linux is the ABI, so unmodified Linux programs can run on it as-is.
Its README describes Linux as a "personality" the kernel presents to software. That's the only one built so far, though BSD is floated as a possibility down the line.
Even that one personality still has plenty of gaps, though. Of the 375 system calls in Linux 6.12's x86-64 interface, Ginux fully implements just 82. Another 245 only partly work. The remaining 48 are blocked on purpose.
Software on Ginux runs inside isolated "domains," each with its own processes, memory, and filesystem. The project pitches these as a stronger boundary than containers, though Ginux still pulls standard OCI container images to assemble each domain's files. That's how it gets Rocky Linux 10 all the way to systemd's multi-user target.
In a technical report, Kurtzer calls his approach Human-Directed Agentic Engineering. He set the architecture, milestones, and pass criteria himself. The agent handled the rest, from writing the code to booting the kernel, testing it, and fixing whatever broke.
All of that ran as a single long-running OpenAI Codex task using GPT-5.6 Sol. Over the 11 days, it produced about 139,000 lines of code and tests across more than 1,000 commits. Real-world distros like Rocky Linux also exposed bugs that the project's synthetic tests missed.
Even so, Ginux is strictly a research project for now. Nobody has independently audited its security. It also lives entirely inside a QEMU virtual machine, since there's no support for physical hardware, GPUs, or NVMe drives. Kurtzer himself says AI can now write complex systems software, but things like compatibility, security, and long-term maintenance "remain the real moat."
Meanwhile, Linux's own developers have been warming up to AI. Last month, Linus Torvalds had Claude Code write a set of experimental page cache patches. Reviewers soon spotted a race condition in them, so the work is still under review. Around the same time, kernel maintainers agreed to stop requiring contributors to disclose AI-assisted code.

articles.title: How Gen Digital built Norton Revamp’s AI-curated News Engine with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Gen Digital built Norton Revamp’s AI-curated News Engine with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search
Your professional reputation now lives online first. Recruiters check LinkedIn before returning a call. Clients review your digital presence before booking a first meeting. For ambitious professionals, that shift is an opportunity: a well-crafted online voice can open doors that a résumé alone never could.
But standing out takes more than content generation. It takes real-time awareness of what’s happening right now. A professional building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader needs to react to today’s breakthroughs, not last week’s headlines. And with feeds flooded by AI-generated noise, audiences reward authenticity and timeliness more than ever.
Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore made that possible. We built Norton Revamp, a generative AI-powered professional reputation management platform. At its heart is an AI-curated News Engine, powered by AgentCore Web Search, that grounds every content suggestion, goal recommendation, and news feed item in current, cited web knowledge. The platform launched in March 2026, built by a small group of engineers.
In this post, we show you how the Gen team builds an AI-curated News Engine in Norton Revamp with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search to help customers turn ideas into engaging social media posts.
The challenge: Real-time grounding for professional content
Unlike chatbots that rely on static knowledge bases, Norton Revamp needs to understand what’s trending right now in each user’s professional domain. A cyber security expert needs today’s threat intelligence. A marketing leader needs this week’s industry shifts. Traditional approaches (custom web crawlers, third-party news APIs, static content databases) each carry trade-offs: infrastructure overhead, stale data, vendor complexity, or data egress risk.
We evaluated three alternatives before choosing AgentCore Web Search. Custom crawlers require ongoing maintenance and lag real time. Third-party news APIs added vendor contracts, API key management, and data leaving our AWS environment. Static knowledge bases were perpetually stale. AgentCore Web Search eliminated these concerns. It’s fully managed with zero infrastructure overhead, operates entirely within AWS with zero data egress, and returns cited sources with URLs and publication dates. This makes personalized, real-time news feeds viable at scale.
How AgentCore Web Search powers Norton Revamp
Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a fully managed web search capability, compliant with the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It’s available as a managed connector on the AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Our agent sends a natural-language query, and Web Search returns relevant snippets, source URLs, titles, and publication dates that the model uses to produce grounded responses.
This capability powers three core features:
AI-curated news feed
Every user gets a personalized content stream surfacing the latest articles and trending topics tied to their goal. If you’re building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader, your feed prioritizes AI breakthroughs, industry analysis, and emerging use cases, sourced in real time through AgentCore Web Search. Unlike a static RSS aggregator, the feed is a goal-aware discovery engine that refreshes with every session.
Smart content suggestions
Users receive AI-generated content ideas tailored to trending topics in their space, written in their own authentic voice, with optional AI-generated visuals. AgentCore Web Search grounds every suggestion on what’s happening today. A three-step coaching flow (Analyze, Refine, Post) walks users from initial ideas to published content on LinkedIn and X, with a feedback loop, so the AI gets sharper with every iteration.
Trend-aware goal setting
Users define a goal. The AI builds a personalized roadmap with weekly themes and milestones. AgentCore Web Search feeds real-time trend data into goal generation, so weekly themes reflect current industry movements. The system learns from the past four weeks of activity, refreshing recommendations as users grow.
Architecture and tech stack
The integration follows an event-driven architecture. When a user sets or updates their professional goal, Amazon Nova (through Amazon Bedrock) generates targeted search queries based on the goal, recent activity, and engagement patterns. The agent sends these queries to AgentCore Web Search, which returns cited results entirely within our AWS environment. Our AI Learning System ranks the results for relevance, recency, and source credibility. The ranked results then serve as grounding context for Amazon Nova Lite to generate content suggestions in the user’s authentic voice. Engagement data feeds back into query generation, making the News Engine progressively smarter.
Generative AI and machine learning stack:
- Amazon Bedrock – Core generative AI engine for content generation, personalization, post analysis (batch mode), and content coaching.
- Amazon Nova (Nova Lite) – Primary large language model (LLM) powering content generation, goal creation, and trend analysis.
- Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Real-time web retrieval powering the News Engine, content grounding, and trend discovery through an MCP-compliant managed connector.
- Stability AI – Image generation.
- Claude (through Amazon Bedrock) – Additional LLM capabilities for complex reasoning tasks.
Infrastructure: React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS on the frontend. Node.js, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB (multi-table with composite key patterns), Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon EventBridge, Amazon CloudFront, Amazon CloudWatch, and AWS Secrets Manager on the backend. Infrastructure managed through Terraform with blue-green deployment for zero-downtime releases.
Processing pipeline: The platform runs four pipeline stages:
- Full Scan – Pull up to 1,000 historical posts, store in Amazon S3, run Amazon Bedrock batch analysis for reputation impact.
- Daily Scan – Amazon EventBridge-triggered incremental analysis.
- Weekly Goal Generation – Lambda generates goals considering past engagement data plus real-time trend data from AgentCore Web Search.
- Content Coaching – Synchronous Amazon Bedrock calls through the Analyze, Refine, Post flow, each step grounded with AgentCore Web Search results.
Engineering with an AI-native development mindset
We embedded generative AI from day one, as both the product and the development methodology. The human-AI responsibility split was deliberate: human-owned architecture decisions, security reviews, business logic, and personalization algorithms. AI handled code generation, documentation, test scaffolding, refactoring, and UI component creation.
With Claude, we produced 10 or more design variants per concept, compressed design-to-prototype time from weeks to hours and generated 70 percent of UI code with AI. We tested five pricing models in the time previously needed for one. The gamification system went through eight iterations before launching.
The measurable impact: 3x faster feature implementation, boilerplate generation accelerated by 90 percent, documentation by 80 percent, test creation by 70 percent, and UI component generation by 65 percent. The trade-off: AI output review consumed 20–30 percent of our time.
AI helped with personalization algorithms, the DynamoDB multi-table architecture (which needed experience-based judgment), security implementation, and Amazon Bedrock batch processing optimization. The key insight: AI accelerated implementation, but humans designed how the AI Learning System should adapt to user goals. Product generative AI (Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Nova, AgentCore Web Search) and development generative AI served different purposes, and we kept them separate.
Testing, security, and quality assurance
We achieved 85 percent code coverage through automated test generation. Critical test areas included content generation quality, AgentCore Web Search result relevance and freshness validation, engagement tracking accuracy, gamification logic, and news feed relevance to user goals.
For a product carrying the Norton brand, compliance is non-negotiable. Security checks spanned static code analysis, dependency vulnerability scanning, authentication flows, user data encryption, access control logic, generative AI model output validation, and content filtering. Our security team reviewed all AI-generated recommendations: AI accelerated identification, and humans made final decisions.
The result: 99.9 percent uptime since launch with real-time monitoring of generative AI content quality and user satisfaction.
Best practices for AgentCore Web Search integration
For teams considering AgentCore Web Search for real-time grounding:
- Invest in query generation – Well-structured queries yield better results than open-ended ones, so we focused on our prompt engineering there.
- Cache strategically – Real-time freshness is the point, but some queries don’t need to re-execute every session. We cache results with time-to-live (TTL) values that match freshness requirements.
- Build feedback loops – Track which web search results users engage with and feed that signal back into query generation. Our News Engine’s relevance improved over the first 90 days.
- Validate source quality – AgentCore Web Search returns source URLs and publication dates. We built a lightweight credibility scoring layer to prioritize authoritative sources.
Conclusion
Building Norton Revamp proved that a small, generative AI-augmented team can deliver enterprise software in months. It also proved that Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore can serve as the real-time intelligence backbone for products that need to stay current with the world.
We launched a generative AI-native professional reputation management platform in months, with personalized goal setting, AI-driven content suggestions, real-time curated news feeds grounded by AgentCore Web Search, adaptive learning, gamification, and Norton-grade security. A small group of engineers achieved 99.9 percent uptime.
Generative AI doesn’t replace engineers. It amplifies them. Pairing that amplification with fully managed services like AgentCore Web Search removes entire categories of infrastructure complexity. Humans designed the vision. Generative AI through Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Nova, and AgentCore Web Search accelerated bringing it to life, grounded in real-time, cited web knowledge.
        “Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore eliminates the complexity of building and maintaining our own web retrieval infrastructure. It lets our Norton Revamp News Engine deliver real-time, personalized content grounded in what’s happening in each user’s professional domain, with zero data egress and Norton-grade privacy. We went from concept to production in months, and AgentCore Web Search was a key enabler.”

articles.title: FreightTech startup Conlio secures €6.4 million to expand AI-powered financial automation across Europe | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Conlio, a German AI-powered financial operations platform for road freight forwarders, today announces a €6.4 million fundraise to expand across Europe – accelerating the automation of financial systems across freight.
The fundraise was led by Piton Capital, with participation from Haufe Group Ventures and the backing of two logistics groups: WaVe-X (WALTER GROUP), and F-LOG Ventures, the venture investment fund of FIEGE. Existing investors System.One, Puzzle Ventures, Booom Ventures and Yellow also participated in the round. Conlio has raised €6.4 million to date.
Dr. Claudio Consul, Founder and CEO of Conlio, says: “Freight is one of the world’s largest industries, and digitalisation has transformed large parts of it. But the industry is full of edge cases and decisions that depend on context, which has made true end-to-end automation difficult with traditional software. AI changes that.
“At sennder, I saw first-hand how much operational complexity still sits behind freight documentation, settlement and payments. With Conlio, we turn that complexity into verified data and automated financial workflows. Our long-term ambition is to change how money moves across supply chains, and verified freight documents are where this begins.”
Conlio’s fundraise follows a series of European investments in freight software and AI-enabled financial operations during 2026.
In Germany, Hamburg-based Procuros raised €20 million to automate supply-chain data exchange and invoicing, while Berlin-based cargo.one secured nearly €17 million for its multimodal freight platform.
Elsewhere, Ukraine-based Cargofy raised €5.2 million in primary capital for AI-powered freight operations, Belgium’s Vectrix secured €1.15 million for transport-order automation, and Denmark’s Plinto and the UK’s Zalos raised €2.9 million and €3.1 million respectively for AI-enabled financial workflows.
Together, these rounds represent approximately €49.4 million in newly raised funding, excluding Conlio’s investment.
EU-Startups has also previously covered Conlio investor F-LOG Ventures’ participation in Germany’s FRYTE Mobility, which raised €3.5 million in September to expand its electric truck charging coordination platform.
Michael Macklin, Investor at Piton Capital, adds:”Road freight forwarding handles huge volumes of transactions dependent on manual checks, and many people have been stumped on how to fix this. What we liked most about Conlio and Claudio was that they know the problem inside out, from the perspective of their customers, while also having the technologist’s insight on how it can be done differently.
“The product is already embedded in customers’ daily operations and we believe that can build a platform with powerful network effects as more participants join and more transactions flow through it.”
Founded in Berlin in 2023 by Dr Claudio Consul, Conlio uses AI to turn complex freight documents into verified data and automate the financial workflows that follow.
The company explains that European road freight is a roughly €430 billion market, yet freight forwarders operate on thin margins. Conlio can reportedly automate more than 90% of freight document checks, reducing manual processing costs, catching overpayments and accelerating invoicing.
Conlio’s platform can increase a forwarders’ EBIT by up to 30% – more than €1 million in annual EBIT impact for a forwarder with €100 million in revenue.
Every road freight transport generates a trail of documents, from CMRs and proofs of delivery to carrier invoices. Before paying carriers or invoicing customers, forwarders need to check that those documents are complete and correct. But documents arrive in different formats and languages, often contain handwritten notes, and need to be checked against rules that vary by customer, route and geography.
This complexity has historically made the process difficult to automate with traditional software.
Conlio uses AI to read, interpret and verify freight documents at scale, applying context that traditional rules-based software struggles to understand. A single CMR, for example, can carry up to four dates, recording when it was issued, when the goods were collected, when they were delivered and other events during the transport.
The challenge is not reading the date but knowing which event it refers to, and Conlio checks each one against the requirements for that shipment.
Thomas Muscher, Managing Director at WaVe-X, says: “AI is moving from pilot projects into the core processes of freight forwarding, and the finance back office is one of the areas where the impact is most immediate. Conlio turns unstructured freight documents into verified transaction data, which is the foundation for genuinely automated, increasingly agentic workflows. With WALTER GROUP’s decades of experience in European road transport, WaVe-X can support Conlio not only with capital but with real industry insight as it scales across Europe.”

articles.title: The Worst Is Yet to Come for Memory Shortages, Warns Team Group
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 3rd 2026
The Worst Is Yet to Come for Memory Shortages, Warns Team Group
We might not be past the worst part of the global memory shortages, as the most severe supply chain squeeze could happen soon. During Team Group's earnings conference on November 2, the company stated that the worst period in memory demand is projected to be between Q4 2026 and Q2 2027, which is just a few months away. Major memory makers such as SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron have sold out their 2027 supply and entered into long-term agreements with customers, making it increasingly difficult to source memory for any third-party purposes. Team Group states that even if you have the funds, it might be impossible to purchase memory products. Currently, it is possible to buy memory, albeit at a high price, but soon enough, that may no longer be an option, noted the company.
Even though CXMT and YMTC are supplying close to 10% of the memory market share with their products, it is still impossible to satisfy demand. A supply-demand balance may not emerge until the second half of 2028 or even later. Currently, Team Group sells most of its memory modules to businesses in the B2B sector, which commands 64.6%, while the B2C sector, selling directly to consumers, accounts for 35.4%. This is a sharp reversal compared to the 2025 Q3 figures, where B2B was 24.6% and B2C was 75.4%. Most of the revenue now comes from the business sector developing AI servers, rather than traditional consumer purchases.For example, the contract price for DDR5 16 Gb was $8.7 in October 2025, and it is now about $48 as of September 2026. For spot pricing, which means no long-term contract structure, prices are even higher, carrying a premium of 30-50% on top of that. Team Group plans to open a new facility with 1,000 workers in New Taipei City in Q1 2027, with equipment installation scheduled for that quarter. The company ended Q3 with consolidated revenue of NT$10.139 billion, which is roughly $309.13 million at the time of writing.

articles.title: Frontline Education Data Breach Impacts Over 1.3 Million
articles.text:
Frontline Education is notifying over 1.3 million people that their personal information was compromised in a data breach.
The incident occurred on August 14 and involved the exploitation of a vulnerability in a third-party software product to gain unauthorized access to Frontline’s environment.
Frontline, which provides administration software purpose-built for K-12 school districts, addressed the security defect and reinforced security. The attack was fully contained by August 15, the company says in an incident notice.
The investigation into the data breach determined that the hackers stole the personal information of both school district staff and students from the Frontline Central and School Health Management products.
While the stolen data varies by individual, it may include names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, driver’s license numbers, passport and other government ID numbers, health insurance information such as Medicaid IDs, and Student IDs.
“Frontline has notified affected school districts and, in cooperation with those districts, has begun notifying individuals whose personal information was affected via email or by letter sent via the US Postal Service, as required and where available,” the company says.
While Frontline has not shared the number of potentially affected individuals, filings with the Attorney General’s Offices in Massachusetts, New Hampshire, South Carolina, Texas, and Vermont show that 1,298,917 people were affected.
However, the company also filed notices with the AGOs in California, Indiana, and Iowa, and possibly in other states that do not maintain data breach portals, and the total number of affected individuals is likely well above 1.3 million.
Frontline is providing the affected US adults with two years of free credit monitoring and identity-theft protection services. For qualified minors, it offers free dark-web monitoring services.
SecurityWeek has emailed Frontline for additional information on the data breach and will update this article if the company responds.

articles.title: Bethesda confirms Elder Scrolls VI title is 'Sentinel' -- 8 years after reveal
articles.text:
Bethesda has announced that the next Elder Scrolls game will officially be called The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. The company unveiled the full title, which had recently been leaked, in a larger video celebrating its 40th anniversary.
However, that’s all the quick trailer shows us outside of a dune and a quote from a character called Yazar the Moth Priest. Otherwise, we still know nothing about the game itself. For context, The Elder Scrolls VI was first announced way back at E3 2018 alongside the sci-fi RPG Starfield. But while that latter game launched in 2023, Bethesda went dark on the sixth Elder Scrolls.
To be clear, it undoubtedly takes a long time to make the kind of sprawling RPGs that are Bethesda’s bread and butter. But it also begs the question of why you’d announce the game way back in 2018 when it was still in pre-production and clearly many years away, especially since Starfield was the focus at the time. For what it’s worth, Bloomberg‘s Jason Schreier said the announcement was made to placate fans who were upset over Fallout 76, a multiplayer game. (We still don’t even have a release window for Sentinel, although Schreier speculated it’s at least two years away still.)
It certainly hasn’t helped Bethesda in recent months that parent company Xbox has been an absolute mess, laying off thousands of people and having big corporate shake-ups throughout. These reductions have included at least 50 people at Bethesda Game Studios, which, understandably, has also left those who remain with reduced talent and diminishing morale. (All of this comes, mind you, as Microsoft continues to report soaring profits.)
But hey, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma took some time in the summer in between axing everyone to say that the game is great, so we can all rest easy.
Image credit: Bethesda

The value here is participation. Instead of simply hearing how someone else approached a problem, founders can bring their own questions, compare experiences with the people around the table, and leave with ideas that are much closer to their actual business.
Watch the startup pitch advice get tested live

For anyone preparing to raise, sell, recruit, or simply explain their company more clearly, seeing those reactions live can be incredibly useful.

Keep it going at the closing reception

articles.title: The Download: controlling AI agents and “Super Intelligence” loyalty tests
articles.text:
The Download: controlling AI agents and “Super Intelligence” loyalty tests
Plus: Today’s midterms will test AI’s influence on US politics.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.
While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal.
Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice.
Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave.
—Amit Katwala
Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with just one directive: government agencies must rebrand artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.”
One month on, the rebrand is slowly appearing across government websites and documents, but it hasn't caught on with everyone. Even some of the biggest names in tech still use “AI.”
But the bigger concern is the new term becoming a political loyalty test: Those who use it signal allegiance to the administration. Those who don’t become targets for attacks.
—James O'Donnell

articles.title: When AI finds the path you didn’t know existed
articles.text:
When AI finds the path you didn’t know existed
What frontier AI incidents teach us about cybersecurity
In July 2026, OpenAI disclosed that several of its cyber-capable AI models, operating during internal evaluations, circumvented controls intended to isolate them from the internet and compromised parts of OpenAI’s research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems.
A fuller report published the following month revealed that the agents had exploited shared infrastructure, communicated through unauthorized channels, collaborated with one another and accessed several external systems. OpenAI described the incident as a “warning shot” demonstrating that capable AI agents can find and exploit weaknesses across interconnected systems when safeguards are insufficient.
Senior Manager of Threat Hunting at Forescout.
Despite the alarming headlines, this should not be viewed solely as a failure of artificial intelligence. It offers an important security lesson for organizations preparing for a future in which autonomous systems play a larger role in cybersecurity operations, business processes and software development.
The most valuable takeaway is not just that an AI model “escaped”, rather the lesson is that even controlled environments can contain unintended paths to sensitive systems, credentials or data. Once such a path exists, a sufficiently capable and persistent agent may find it.
The positive side of early disclosure
Every significant advancement in security has resulted from discovering risks before attackers could exploit them at scale. In this case, the activity occurred during controlled evaluations rather than a criminal campaign. The organizations involved were able to identify weaknesses in containment, access controls and environmental design before similar techniques could be widely adopted by cybercriminals.
The incident also demonstrated something important about modern AI systems: persistence. When confronted with obstacles, the models did not try to stop. They continued pursuing their assigned objectives and searched for alternative routes.
Security teams perform penetration tests and red-team exercises because human attackers rarely follow a single path. Advanced AI systems are becoming capable of behaving similarly, exploring multiple options and adapting when obstacles appear. The earlier organizations understand this reality, the better prepared they will be.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The real issue was not one model
Much of the initial discussion focused on the behavior of OpenAI’s models. Subsequent disclosures have shown that the underlying challenge is more nuanced. Anthropic identified three incidents in which Claude models reached the public internet during cybersecurity evaluations and gained unauthorized access to real organizations. OpenAI also disclosed separate cases involving third-party testing environments in which model activity extended beyond its intended boundaries.
These incidents, though similar, were not identical. In some cases, models exploited vulnerabilities to circumvent isolation. In others, configuration errors left routes to the internet open while the models had been told they were operating within simulations. However, the common lesson is that instructions, policies and safety guardrails cannot compensate for weaknesses in the surrounding infrastructure. The instructions described one set of boundaries while the technology enforced another.
Security professionals have encountered this problem for decades. A firewall rule may be intended to block access while an overlooked network connection creates an alternative path. A user may be prohibited from accessing data while excessive permissions provide an unintended route. Autonomous systems create the same challenge at greater speed and scale.
An optimizing agent does not necessarily think like a human attacker. It pursues the objective it has been assigned and evaluates the available options. Organizations should therefore assume that autonomous systems may pursue their objectives through any path the environment leaves open.
Security must move beyond AI guardrails
Much of the discussion around AI governance has focused on whether a model should answer a particular prompt or perform a particular action. Prompt-level guardrails remain important, but they are no longer sufficient on their own. Security teams must continuously assess who is authorized, which systems and data they can reach, and what actions could create risk. Each layer should be tested independently rather than relying on a single refusal mechanism to govern them all.
The OpenAI incident illustrates this clearly. The problem moved beyond models possessing advanced capabilities, to one where capabilities, connectivity, credentials and autonomy came together in environments where containment mechanisms were insufficient.
Organizations must therefore consider AI security as a combination of identity, authorization, containment and oversight.
The conditions for trusted autonomy
In order to combat this, defenders need to align themselves to a new framework that is shaped by frontier AI: Assume Autonomy. The framework begins with the expectation that adversaries and defensive controls may operate through automated, non-human agency. It is built around context, constraint, transparency and reversibility.
Context means understanding what an agent can access, which identities it can use and how those systems connect to other resources. Constraint requires access to be limited through technical controls rather than instructions or expected behavior alone.
Transparency provides visibility into what an autonomous system is doing while it is happening. Reversibility ensures teams can stop workloads, revoke credentials, isolate systems and recover quickly when unexpected behavior occurs.
For high-capability agentic systems, governance must address these areas with evidence rather than assumptions. This requires autonomy stress testing, independent red-team exercises focused on containment failures, testing of identity and network boundaries, audited isolation controls, runtime authorization for high-impact actions and rehearsed rollback procedures.
Responsible access to powerful AI
Incidents like this often prompt calls for tighter restrictions on advanced AI models, but the reality is more complicated. Attackers can switch between models, providers or open-source alternatives when they encounter restrictions. Defenders, particularly smaller organizations, may not have those options. If advanced defensive capabilities become slow, expensive or heavily restricted, the result could be reduced defensive readiness without a corresponding reduction in offensive capability.
The objective should be responsible access. Verified identities, strong authorization controls, immutable logging, human accountability and time-limited access can provide meaningful safeguards without unnecessarily restricting defenders.
Preparing for autonomous systems
Organizations cannot improvise security once an autonomous system begins acting unexpectedly. The necessary controls must already exist.
This includes deny-by-default network access, workload-specific identities, short-lived credentials, segmentation between evaluation and production environments, telemetry that can correlate activity across systems, and rehearsed containment procedures. Organizations should assume that a capable autonomous system will discover every reachable path that advances its objective and ensure that no such path grants unintended authority.
These incidents should be viewed as proof that security architecture must develop alongside rapidly advancing autonomy. Organizations that adapt now will be better positioned to harness the benefits of AI tools while keeping risk under control. Those that rely on instructions alone may discover that technology follows the paths we leave open, rather than the rules we intended it to follow.

articles.title: Apple aún no sabe cuándo tendrá suficientes iPhone Duo para todos sus compradores
articles.text:
Con la demanda del iPhone Duo superando con amplitud la cantidad de unidades disponibles para la venta, Apple se está moviendo rápido para tratar de mitigar esa escasez. Sin embargo, aún no sabe cuándo tendrá la disponibilidad suficiente para enviar su primer móvil plegable a todos los compradores.
John Ternus, CEO de Apple, le dijo a Reuters que el acceso al iPhone Duo continúa restringido a pesar de que han incrementado su producción. Por lo pronto, el ejecutivo no se ha aventurado a ofrecer algún tipo de ventana objetivo en la que esta situación podría normalizarse.
"A día de hoy, la disponibilidad del iPhone Duo está limitada. El aumento de la producción avanza bien, pero en este momento no podemos predecir cuándo se van a equilibrar la oferta y la demanda", manifestó el jefe de Apple al citado medio.
Así que si todavía no tienes tu iPhone Duo, lo mejor es que sigas cultivando tu costado más paciente. Al momento de redacción de este artículo, la tienda en línea de Apple sigue mostrando una fecha de entrega estimada para el 22 de enero de 2027, así que no se han observado cambios sustanciales en tal sentido.
Apple no sabe cuándo se equilibrarán la oferta y demanda del iPhone Duo
Vale mencionar que Apple ha logrado reducir los tiempos de espera para algunos de los compradores del iPhone Duo. Se han visto casos de personas que inicialmente recibieron una fecha estimada para diciembre, pero que luego se actualizó a noviembre. Aun así, la cosa dista bastante de ser la ideal.
Desde el principio se sabía que el iPhone Duo estaría disponible en cantidades muy limitadas, aunque la situación ha excedido cualquier estimación previa. Según analistas, no solo la demanda por el plegable ha sido muy alta a pesar de su elevado precio, sino que muy posiblemente hubo menos unidades del móvil a disposición de las que se creía.
Por supuesto que los revendedores hicieron de las suyas y Apple ha tomado medidas para evitar que se aprovechen todavía más del panorama. No obstante, las palabras de Ternus dan a entender que la poca disponibilidad del iPhone Duo posiblemente sea un problema hasta entrado el 2027. A lo que hay que sumarle el episodio de las pantallas con fallos, un episodio que la compañía sostiene que es de alcance limitado.
Más allá de lo que ocurre con el iPhone Duo en particular, el CEO de Apple también se pronunció sobre la crisis de la RAM. El ejecutivo le manifestó a Reuters que durante el último trimestre padecieron un marcado incremento en los precios de la memoria. Ternus dijo que lograron morigerar el impacto de la subida, aunque no precisó si esto se sostendrá en el tiempo.
"Observamos un aumento en los costos de la memoria en comparación con el trimestre de junio, lo cual se vio parcialmente compensado por el beneficio de tener inventario y menores costos en ciertos componentes que no son de memoria", explicó. La próxima prueba de fuego para Apple y sus productos, incluyendo el iPhone Duo, será la temporada navideña.

articles.title: This Election Day, remember which party ran against EVs and tethered us all to the gas pump
articles.text:
It’s the midterms! Here’s a fun fact for you as you head to the polls: Gas prices today are the highest ever recorded for a US Election Day.
This Election Day, remember which party ran against EVs and tethered us all to the gas pump
Donald Trump and congressional Republicans spent years waging a culture war against EVs. Now, record gas prices and a foreign war are leaving voters stuck footing the bill at the pump.
The national average for a gallon of gasoline is $4.12 and $6.28 for a gallon of diesel, according to GasBuddy. Meanwhile, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which is maintained by the US Department of Energy as a safeguard during energy crises, is down to 282.2 million barrels of crude, the lowest level in 44 years.
Gas prices, along with other essential cost-of-living items, are certainly top of mind for many voters this election cycle. And perhaps many will also remember which political party ran on a campaign message of ending the fictional “EV mandate” and “drill, baby, drill.”
For the past two years, Donald Trump and congressional Republicans have made gutting EV incentives, freezing charging infrastructure funding, and rolling back fuel economy standards a hallmark of their tenure in power. As a result, EV sales plummeted in the US, ensuring that Americans would stay indefinitely shackled to fossil fuels for years to come. For Trump, it was fulfilling a promise he made during the 2024 campaign. And for his donors from the oil and gas industry, it was money well spent.
Most voters might not have cared that much. After all, skepticism toward EVs was already high, driven by premium prices and lingering charging anxiety. But when Trump went to war with Iran, the resulting surge in gas prices sent Americans scrambling for cheaper ways to get around. Many turned to hybrid and electric vehicles as a solution — only to find vehicle prices were still higher than average, with no federal incentive to help defray the costs. Dealerships saw a surge of foot traffic from drivers who were skeptical of battery-powered cars, now desperate for anything that ran on a plug or a hybrid motor.
While automakers had made strides toward cheaper EVs, the average transaction price still hovered well over $50,000. But the incentive that once helped close that gap — the $7,500 federal clean vehicle tax credit, applied instantly at the point of sale — was gone. The subsidies had been systematically dismantled or left to lapse under the banner of fiscal discipline and anti-green populism.
Here is the real irony of this election. Republicans spent years painting electric cars as an out-of-touch, liberal fad, doing everything they could to kill tax credits and charging programs. They rolled back fuel economy standards that would have forced automakers to build more fuel-efficient powertrains, claiming they were saving everyday drivers from expensive technology they didn’t want.
Instead, they took away an important tool that could have protected family budgets from a global energy crisis. Electricity is made right here at home; its price doesn’t spike every time conflict breaks out in the Middle East. But because Republicans treated EVs like a partisan culture war, millions of Americans are stuck standing at the pump, watching the price roll higher.
Even if Democrats win back Congress, don’t expect them to bring back the Biden-era EV tax credits. The political fight over what kind of car people drive is probably stuck. At the same time, major car companies are backing Trump’s push in court to roll back strict fuel-economy rules. Electric cars aren’t disappearing, but they now have to stand on their own two feet. Companies like General Motors and Ford do have plans to make them more affordable, as long as the government keeps blocking cheap Chinese models from entering the market.
In the end, Trump won his culture war against the electric car. Automakers retreated, subsidies vanished, and the traditional combustion engine was saved from the bureaucrats. But victories have price tags. And as voters step into the booth with a $4 gallon of gas on their minds, they might finally realize what was traded away: the simple freedom to drive past the pump and never look back.

articles.title: Developer manages to run Windows 11 26H2 with just 128MB of RAM, just 3.1% of recommended minimum — stripped-down installation can access Desktop, File Explorer, and Notepad
articles.text:
Developer manages to run Windows 11 26H2 with just 128MB of RAM, just 3.1% of recommended minimum — stripped-down installation can access Desktop, File Explorer, and Notepad
Just 128MB of RAM is enough to boot Windows 11.
NTDEV, the popular developer behind the Tiny11 project, has once again pushed the limits of just how little hardware is required to run Windows 11. In a video shared on YouTube, the developer claims to have successfully booted the latest Windows 11 26H2 on a system with just 128MB of RAM. Despite severe memory constraints, the heavily stripped-down installation manages to load the Desktop and File Explorer, access the Start menu, and even run the classic Notepad app.
While it is an impressive achievement, the developer acknowledges that the system is "painfully slow," making this more of a technical experiment than a practical way to run Windows 11 on older hardware. According to Microsoft’s official requirements, Windows 11 requires at least 4GB of RAM, meaning NTDEV's latest experiment uses just 3.125% of the recommended minimum. The developer has not shared a detailed breakdown of every component removed or disabled to achieve the result, but the project builds on years of experimentation with stripped-down Windows installations.
This is not NTDEV's first attempt at pushing Windows 11 beyond its usual hardware limitations. Back in 2023, the developer managed to get the operating system running with only 176MB of RAM by extensively trimming its system components, drivers, and background services. That experiment relied on an IDE storage interface to reduce the number of drivers required, and sacrificed the standard Windows desktop environment.
Last month, the developer showcased another interesting experiment that squeezed an entire Windows 11 installation into a CD-ROM-sized ISO file. The experimental build created using the developer's upcoming Pico11 tool weighs in at 699,811,840 bytes and retains a functional Windows desktop. The stripped-down version of Windows 11 successfully boots into the desktop environment and runs basic applications such as Calculator, Settings, Notepad, and Paint. The test was conducted on a virtual machine with 4GB of allocated RAM, with the operating system using around 883MB.
Such experiments are a great way to showcase just how much of Windows can be stripped away while still retaining some of its core functionality. At the end of the day, they are primarily technical demonstrations with the intention of exploring the limits of Microsoft's operating system rather than providing practical alternatives to a standard Windows installation. Stripping away essential components, drivers, and background services comes with significant trade-offs, including reduced functionality, compatibility issues, and severely degraded performance.

articles.title: Goldman Sachs restricted Claude Code for bankers — but made one surprising exception
articles.text:
Goldman Sachs restricted Claude Code for bankers — but made one surprising exception
Replit CEO Amjad Masad is warning that AI coding agents running on employee devices are becoming a security risk for enterprises and governments, as financial institutions begin restricting access to tools such as Claude Code.
“AI agents running on employee endpoints are becoming a systemic security risk for enterprises & governments,” Masad writes on X, Tuesday. “Some are responding by restricting tools like Claude Code, as Goldman Sachs reportedly has.”
“Some are responding by restricting tools like Claude Code, as Goldman Sachs reportedly has.”
Why finance restricts coding agents
His comments follow a Bloomberg report that Goldman Sachs has restricted access to Anthropic’s Claude Code and Microsoft’s GitHub coding tools to engineers. The restrictions apply to bankers and traders, but certain quantitative employees known as strats are exempt.
Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra told Bloomberg the bank weighs productivity gains against potential risks when deciding which employees can continue using AI tools.
Masad suggests Goldman Sachs is not alone.
“This is widespread in finance. The ban hammer is coming down,”
“This is widespread in finance. The ban hammer is coming down,” he writes, responding to a post about the bank’s restrictions.
When asked what was driving the crackdown, Masad points to “Supply chain attacks etc.”
The credential exposure problem
Running coding agents directly on employee machines raises concerns about credential exposure, malicious instructions and compromised dependencies, each of which has already surfaced well beyond the finance sector.
The credential question has been pushing vendors toward short-lived tokens for months, a shift Vercel recently forced on its own suppliers by setting a deadline to abandon the long-lived keys that an agent operating on an endpoint could quietly read and reuse.
When asked on X whether banks were more worried about code leaving their environments or a lack of audit trails, Masad says, “So many things.”
He offered no examples of security incidents that prompted Goldman’s restrictions or other financial institutions adopting similar policies.
Isolating agents in the cloud
Alongside his comments, Masad shares a security advisory published by Replit on Monday. Written by Luis Héctor Chávez, Replit’s chief technology officer, and engineering lead at Replit, Manish Mehta, it recommends keeping AI agents off employee devices and running them in company-controlled cloud environments instead.
“AI agents should operate in dedicated, organization-controlled environments with limited access to the resources each task requires,”
“AI agents should operate in dedicated, organization-controlled environments with limited access to the resources each task requires,” Masad writes.
Replit recommends running agents in isolated environments, with credentials, audit logs, and approvals managed separately.
The advisory points to recent security incidents, including a compromised Claude Code extension distributed through the Cursor marketplace, as an example of how attackers can exploit developer tools.
That pattern has played out repeatedly across the ecosystem this year, including an attack in which intruders hijacked roughly 1,900 GitHub accounts before moving against some 30,000 repositories, a reminder that a single poisoned link in the chain can reach far past the machine where it started.
Controlling what agents can access
But restricting AI coding agents to engineers doesn’t necessarily solve the problem. Even experienced developers can run agents that follow malicious instructions or pull in compromised software, and research has shown how little it takes to knock an agent off course, with one team finding that stripping a single line from Claude Code’s instructions sent its out-of-scope actions climbing. Replit argues that companies need to control what agents can do, not just who gets to use them.
What this means for enterprise AI adoption
Goldman’s restrictions suggest companies may be rethinking how widely they allow employees to use AI coding tools. Giving non-developers the ability to build software has been a major selling point, but that becomes harder to justify when agents have access to sensitive corporate systems.
Masad argues that companies don’t need to stop using agents. They need to keep them off employee devices and put tighter controls around what they can access.
Whether financial institutions broadly adopt that model remains to be seen. Masad has described restrictions as widespread, but has not provided public evidence establishing how many organizations have introduced them.
The New Stack has reached out to Replit for additional comment on the reported restrictions, the security concerns driving them, and whether financial institutions are changing their approach to AI coding agents.

articles.title: Fast, Sub-Volt HZO Ferroelectric Capacitors For DRAM-Like Memory (SNU)
articles.text:
Seoul National University-led researchers published “Resolving the Kay–Dunn limit and the speed–endurance dilemma in ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 for DRAM-class sub-volt capacitors.”
The first author, Geun Hyeong Park, Ph.D., summarizes the work here:
“Fast, frequently rewritten memory requires low operating voltages, rapid switching, and high cycling endurance. In ferroelectric capacitors, however, accelerating polarization switching often requires higher voltages that can shorten device lifetime.
This work addresses this tradeoff through TiN electrode and interface engineering, reducing interfacial voltage loss and facilitating polarization reversal. Key experimental results include:
Cycling tests also reached 10^12 bipolar cycles without hard electrical breakdown.
Beyond the capacitor measurements, the researchers propose a common-plate ferroelectric RAM (CP-FeRAM) architecture using one transistor and one capacitor per cell, and evaluate its readout through circuit simulations. The architecture explores polarization-based sensing after stored charge has decayed, offering a potential route to reducing refresh requirements in DRAM-like memory.”

articles.title: Pénurie de Mac et d'iPad pour Noel ? Apple risque de manquer d'appareils à mettre sous le sapin
articles.text:
Il n’y a pas que l’iPhone Duo qui pose des problèmes de stocks chez Apple. Les Mac et les iPad aussi sont concernés : il pourrait en manquer pour les fêtes de fin d’année. Le Black Friday arrive, les promotions de Noël aussi et c’est à ce moment-là que la plupart des consommateurs achète les cadeaux de Noël pour leurs proches. Parmi eux, des Mac et des iPad. Alors, y en aura-t-il pour tout le monde ?
Apple reconnaît des problèmes d’approvisionnement qui impactent ses Mac et iPad
C’est lors de la conférence téléphonique de l’entreprise sur ses résultats financiers du quatrième trimestre qu’Apple a confirmé que la disponibilité des Mac et iPad serait limitée durant toute la période de Noël. Rassurez-vous, la santé financière d’Apple est excellente (surtout comparée à celle du reste de la tech, impactée par les déboires autour de l’IA) : c’est son meilleur exercice fiscal jamais enregistré. Ce qui ne l’empêche pas d’avoir des petits soucis.
Concernant les Mac tout d’abord, ils se vendent bien : 24% de plus sur la période par rapport à l’année dernière, soit plus de 10 milliards de dollars de chiffre d’affaires. Quant aux iPad, c’est plus nuancé : 10% de baisse sur un an et un chiffre d’affaires de 6,2 milliards de dollars. Pour ces deux types de produits, Apple reconnaît des « contraintes d’approvisionnement » ainsi que des « pressions liées aux taux de change », qui touchent les iPhone, les Mac et les iPad. Des difficultés qui pourraient avoir un impact sur le chiffre d’affaires global de l’entreprise : 7 à 10% de progression sur un an, sa « meilleure estimation compte tenu de l’approvisionnement contraint ».
Au regard des temps de livraison sur le site d’Apple, rien d’alarmant : de quelques jours à plus d’une semaine pour recevoir les produits chez soi ou aller les chercher en boutique. Mais qu’en sera-t-il fin novembre avec les promotions de Noël ? Les revendeurs tiers aussi pourraient pâtir de ces problèmes d’approvisionnement.
La marque à la pomme n’arrive plus à suivre les hausses de prix des composants
Jusqu’à il y a quelques mois, Apple semblait protégée par la hausse du prix des composants. Par sa taille, Apple a de quoi remplir des carnets de commande à tour de bras pour les usines. Mais ce n’est plus le cas : la plupart de ses produits a vu ses tarifs augmenter et on commence à voir des problèmes d’approvisionnement. C’est notamment le cas avec l’iPhone Duo : si vous en commandez un sur le site d’Apple aujourd’hui, il arrivera le 25 janvier.
Le dirigeant d’Apple John Ternus le reconnaît : « Ce que nous constatons actuellement avec les prix de la mémoire est sans précédent. […] nous avons observé des coûts de mémoire plus élevés qu’au trimestre de juin ». Une hausse qui ne va pas aller en s’arrangeant, puisqu’Apple prévoit que la mémoire voit encore son prix augmenter sur le dernier trimestre de l’année. Même chose en 2027 : « nous anticipons que les prix d’achat de la mémoire continueront d’augmenter. » Et pourtant, John Ternus se veut rassurant devant ses investisseurs : « nous sommes enthousiastes quant à notre situation actuelle. » La raison possible : dans cette crise, Apple est peut-être l’entreprise qui s’en sort « le moins mal ».
Pour conserver ses marges, Apple n’a d’autre choix que d’augmenter ses tarifs et c’est bien ce qui pourrait se passer en mars ou avril prochain, période durant laquelle de nouveaux produits pourraient sortir. On s’attend à l’arrivée de nouveaux iPad, à l’iPhone Air 2, mais aussi et surtout l’iPhone 18 et pourquoi pas sa déclinaison 18e. Pourraient également arriver le MacBook Air M6 ainsi qu’un MacBook Neo 2 sur cette même période.

articles.title: Tener una tele de 98 pulgadas hoy es más asequible: esta TCL con altavoces Onkyo nunca había bajado tanto de precio
articles.text:
Tener televisores exageradamente no siempre tiene por qué ser demasiado caro, y es que hay modelos que, cuando están de oferta, se pueden encontrar con precios bastante competitivos. Un buen ejmplo lo tenemos en Amazon con el TCL 98T8D, que ahora mismo se encuentra en Amazon por 1.399 euros en lugar de 1.749 euros.
TCL 98T8D (98 pulgadas)
Un televisor enorme de 98 pulgadas
El TCL 98T8D es un televisor QD-MiniLED que incorpora un panel con diagonal de 98 pulgadas, por lo que es una tele bastante grande. La pantalla ofrece una tasa de refresco de hasta 144 Hz y es compatible tanto con Dolby Vision como con el formato de imagen HDR10+.
Destaca también el hecho de que sus altavoces están firmados por Onkyo y ofrecen una potencia total de 40W. Es compatible con Dolby Atmos y su sistema operativo es Google TV, lo que permite que podamos acceder a un gran catálogo de aplicaciones desde la tienda.
Por otro lado, el televisor viene con conectividad inalámbrica Bluetooth y WiFi. También cuenta con AMD FreeSync y con HDMI 2.1, lo que permite que podamos exprimir al máximo las características de las consolas actuales para poder disfrutar de una experiencia fluida y con buena resolución.
