articles.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI with EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build a semantic layer for agentic AI with EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
In this post, we show how to build a semantic layer for agentic AI using EDB Postgres AI. We run a Strands Agents agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that queries the layer to answer customer 360 (C360) questions. Earlier posts in this series built the same C360 pattern with Stardog’s knowledge graph, Denodo’s data virtualization platform, AtScale’s dimensional model, and Strategy Mosaic’s linked models.
EDB Postgres AI puts the semantic layer inside the operational Postgres database as an AIDB extension. Business meaning lives next to the data in standard Postgres COMMENT statements, the join graph comes from Postgres foreign keys, and governance uses Postgres GRANT and row-level security through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that ships with AIDB.
By the end of this post you will know:
- How to build an AIDB semantic knowledge base (SemKB) over a Postgres schema, how COMMENT ON statements and aidb.create_semantic_alias behave as the authoring surface, and how foreign keys crawl into join paths.
- How to expose the AIDB tool catalog to an external agent through the built-in EDB MCP endpoint, fronted by an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and registered as an MCP target on AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
- How Postgres roles, column-level GRANT statements, and row-level security produce different results for different callers. The prompt, tool catalog, and agent code stay the same.
- How AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for every SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema, queryable with ordinary SQL.
Three layers an agent needs
An agent that answers business questions from live data needs three layers: a model that plans and writes queries, a meaning layer that tells the agent what the data represents, and a runtime that hosts the agent and controls identity and access. The Stardog post in this series introduced this framing. The model layer in this post is Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock, the same as prior posts (model availability varies by AWS Region). The runtime layer is AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore Gateway handles inbound authorization, and AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, holds outbound credentials for the tool targets, same as prior posts. EDB Postgres AI hosts agents and tools inside the database itself and acts as the connection point for external agents through its MCP endpoint.
The meaning layer is where this post diverges from the others. Here it is a SemKB that lives inside the operational Postgres database. The schema and the business definitions are indexed together. Postgres GRANT, row-level security, and column-level grants enforce access, not an advisory system prompt. The sections that follow cover how AIDB builds the layer, how AgentCore exposes it, and how two Postgres roles asking the same question get different answers.
Example use case: C360 on EDB Postgres AI
The dataset is the Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit, loaded into a single EDB Postgres AI instance in a dedicated c360 schema. The data model has four tables and one derived view.
| Object | Key columns | 
| customers | cid, first_name, last_name, full_name, email, ssn, phone, picture, location (FK to locations.id) | 
| locations | id, city, state, zip | 
| products | id, name, brand, dept, price | 
| purchases | id, cid (FK to customers.cid), pid (FK to products.id), date, quantity, price | 
| big_spender (view) | cid, full_name, state, large_orders, largest_order | 
The physical schema is a plain Postgres join graph: a customer in the customers table lives at a location, places purchases, and each purchase references a product. The semantic work rests on three business ideas that column names don’t reveal.
State isn’t on the customer row. It lives in locations, reached through the customers.location foreign key, and a comment on that column tells SemKB where to find it.
purchases.price records the order total. An agent that reads it as a unit price and multiplies by quantity returns $502,529 for the top customer instead of $27,991.66.
Big spender is a term the business owns. Captured as a view with a COMMENT ON VIEW statement, its definition stays in one place that every agent, dashboard, and query reads from.
The questions we run through the agent end to end:
- Who are our top 10 customers by total spend, and what state is each in?
- How many big spenders do we have in each state?
- Can you list 10 customers and the state each lives in?
- Which 10 products have sold the most units?
- Can you list five customers with their Social Security numbers? (used in the governance rerun).
Reference architecture
The following diagram shows the request path from the analyst through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to the semantic layer inside EDB Postgres AI. The analyst authenticates with Amazon Cognito and calls AgentCore Gateway with the issued JSON Web Token (JWT) as a Bearer token. Gateway routes to AgentCore runtime, which plans with Claude on Amazon Bedrock. The agent calls MCP tools through Gateway, which forwards to an Application Load Balancer in the EDB Postgres AI virtual private cloud (VPC) and on to the edb-endpoints MCP server inside AIDB. AIDB serves the SemKB, semantic aliases, and read-only PostgreSQL tables. AgentCore traces go to Amazon CloudWatch, and AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces as rows in the aidb_otel schema inside Postgres.
Two flows cross the boundary between AgentCore and EDB Postgres AI.
Inbound: A client calls AgentCore Gateway with a bearer token issued by an Amazon Cognito user pool. The Gateway inbound JWT authorizer validates the token against the Cognito discovery URL. Gateway then evaluates its Cedar policy against the token’s claims to decide which tools this agent, acting for this user, can invoke. It then routes the call to AgentCore runtime. The agent invokes Claude on Amazon Bedrock for planning and answer composition.
Outbound to the semantic layer: The agent’s tool call is an MCP request. AgentCore Gateway supports MCP server targets directly. AIDB’s edb-endpoints HTTP server speaks streamable HTTP MCP with HTTP Basic authentication, which lets Gateway treat it as an MCP server target with no translation layer. An Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate fronts edb-endpoints on an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance. The ALB URL is registered as the Gateway target. The AgentCore Identity credential provider holds the Postgres role credential and injects it as Basic auth on every outbound request. The agent code doesn’t see the Postgres credential.
Observability: AgentCore emits traces for tool calls, large language model (LLM) calls, and token usage to CloudWatch Transaction Search. AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema inside Postgres, queryable with ordinary SQL after the database is configured to write them (see enabling telemetry on the source database).
No AWS Lambda is required in this architecture. AIDB already speaks MCP, so Gateway talks to it as an MCP server target directly through the ALB. The Denodo post in this series uses the same ALB pattern in front of its MCP server, and the architecture here is unchanged other than the vendor.
Build the semantic layer
These steps assume AIDB is installed and enabled on the EDB Postgres AI instance and the Stardog C360 kit’s four CSVs are loaded into a dedicated c360 schema with the primary and foreign keys shown earlier. Because this layer lives in the same database as the data, there is no second system to deploy and no catalog to synchronize. The semantic layer is defined in SQL, inside the same database as the application that writes the rows.
An AIDB semantic knowledge base indexes Postgres schema, not data. It embeds the definition of every table, view, and column (with the COMMENT ON text alongside) into a vector store that an agent can search in natural language. Three authoring tasks help the agent find the right table and column by meaning: writing COMMENT ON statements, defining business terms as views with their own comments, and registering recurring questions as semantic aliases. Comments are the simplest of the three authoring tasks and improve text-to-SQL accuracy the most for both users and agents.
Add comments where the agent will look
The view holds the business definition in one place, so no agent or dashboard has to redefine big spender. The time you spend on comments up front pays off on every query the agent runs afterward.
Create the semantic knowledge base
Create the SemKB over the c360 schema. The call registers the name, the embedding model, the target schemas, and the auto-processing mode.
The embedding model is a local llama.cpp model (llamacpp_embeddings) that ships with the AIDB Amazon Machine Image (AMI). SemKB uses one embedding model per KB, so every entry sits in the same vector space. The AIDB AMI ships with a default SemKB named semkb over public, so creating c360_kb leaves two SemKBs on the instance. When more than one SemKB exists, every aidb.semantic_kb_search call must pass kb_name explicitly. To swap the local model for a remote embedding model, such as Amazon Titan Text Embeddings on Amazon Bedrock, register the remote model with aidb.create_model. Pass its name as the SemKB’s model parameter. The auto_processing parameter accepts Disabled, Live, or Background. Live reacts to schema changes through Postgres event triggers. Background processes them asynchronously from a worker. Disabled waits for an explicit aidb.refresh_semantic_kb(). SemKB also crawls foreign keys into relationships at the same time. The purchases.cid foreign key becomes a join path the agent can discover by meaning, not by column name.
Capture recurring questions as semantic aliases
A semantic alias is a named, parameterized read-only SELECT with a natural-language description that SemKB indexes alongside the schema metadata. The agent finds it by meaning, calls it with parameters, and returns a governed answer.
Aliases are AIDB’s reusable text-to-SQL building block. They sit next to tables and views in the SemKB index and show up to an agent as a tool. For a full text-to-SQL walkthrough, see the EDB documentation.
Govern access
Governance in this architecture runs through Postgres primitives all the way down. The AIDB MCP endpoint has no permission system of its own: “Postgres grants decide what each agent can run” (MCP endpoint reference). Each MCP request authenticates with a Postgres username and password over its own connection, so current_user inside every tool call is the agent’s role, visible in pg_stat_activity like other connections.
The following diagram traces how identity flows from the end user through AgentCore to the Postgres role that evaluates the SQL, and how the resulting trace is captured for audit. The chain runs in four phases: inbound trust at the Gateway, outbound credential from AgentCore Identity, enforcement in Postgres through GRANT and row-level security, and audit through OpenTelemetry traces in the aidb_otel schema.
Inbound trust at Gateway: 1. The end user authenticates with Amazon Cognito and receives a JWT bearer token. 2. The client calls AgentCore Gateway with the token in the Authorization header. 3. The Gateway JWT authorizer validates the token against the Cognito user pool’s discovery URL. 4. Gateway evaluates its Cedar policy against the token’s claims to decide which tool this agent can call.
Outbound credential to AIDB: 5. Gateway resolves the outbound credential for the MCP target from the AgentCore Identity credential provider. For AIDB, this is a Postgres username and password used as HTTP Basic auth. 6. Gateway forwards the MCP streamable-HTTP request to the ALB, which forwards it to edb-endpoints.
Enforcement in Postgres: 7. edb-endpoints opens a Postgres connection using the username and password from the Basic auth header. Postgres authenticates the login role per pg_hba.conf, and current_user inside the tool call is that role. 8. Column-level GRANT statements and row-level security policies on c360 tables enforce what rows and columns the tool call returns. A denial surfaces as a Postgres permission-denied error on the restricted table or column, which the MCP endpoint forwards unchanged.
Audit. 9. AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for the SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema, available through SQL immediately.
Two Postgres roles, same question, different results
Define two agent login roles that differ only in a column-level GRANT: mcp_agent_full sees every column, mcp_agent_restricted sees every column except customers.ssn.
Both login roles need password-auth entries in pg_hba.conf for the local edb-endpoints connection path, as covered in configuring your agent role. Running the same question through both roles produces different results. The agent calling under mcp_agent_restricted can’t project the ssn column: the moment it tries, Postgres returns permission denied for column ssn and the MCP endpoint forwards that error unchanged. The agent then responds that it can’t read SSNs. The prompt, the tool catalog, the SemKB, and the agent code are identical between the two roles. The only difference is the credential AgentCore Identity injects on the outbound Basic auth header.
Row-level filtering follows the same pattern. Enable row-level security (RLS) on a target table and attach per-role USING policies. The AIDB MCP endpoint sees the same rows the role would see in a direct psql connection.
A note on AIDB purposes. AIDB also ships purposes, a policy abstraction that confines in-database agents (those created with aidb.create_agent and invoked with aidb.agent_converse) to a named Postgres role. Purposes apply to the in-database agent path. The external AgentCore path this post uses governs through Postgres roles directly at the MCP endpoint, as described earlier. For audit of external MCP agents, see EDB Agent Governance, which reads the same aidb_otel spans and visualizes agent sessions and policy decisions.
Responsible AI considerations. The governance surface shown so far controls what the agent can execute at the database layer. Pair it with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on the model side to shape what the agent is allowed to generate: content filters for sensitive topics, denied-topic lists, and PII redaction. The two layers complement each other. Postgres GRANT stops the agent from reading SSNs at the data layer. Guardrails help prevent PII patterns from leaking through other paths in the model response. For agents answering business questions over customer data, both are production controls.
Expose the layer and run the agent
Enabling the AIDB MCP endpoint takes two Postgres parameters plus a restart. Set edb.endpoints_mcp_enabled = on in postgresql.conf, add aidb to shared_preload_libraries, and restart (enabling the endpoint). To reach the endpoint from outside the EC2 instance, set edb.endpoints_mcp_host to a non-loopback address such as 0.0.0.0. Choose a port with edb.endpoints_mcp_port (default is 8765). Supply the Transport Layer Security (TLS) pair with edb.endpoints_mcp_tls_cert and edb.endpoints_mcp_tls_key, which the endpoint requires for non-loopback binds (configuring the endpoint).
An Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and an ACM certificate exposes edb-endpoints to AgentCore Gateway. The ALB target group uses HTTPS to the EC2 instance on port 8765 and doesn’t validate the backend certificate chain, so a self-signed certificate on edb-endpoints is sufficient for development and testing. For production, use an internal ALB with AgentCore Gateway VPC egress to keep connectivity between Gateway and the ALB private.
Create an AgentCore Gateway with a Cognito authorizer, register the ALB URL as an MCP server target, and store the two Postgres credentials in the AgentCore Identity credential provider (credential provider reference).
The agent is a short Python script. It uses Strands Agents to wire a BedrockModel pointing at the latest Claude Sonnet to an MCPClient. The MCPClient connects to the Gateway URL over the streamable HTTP MCP transport with the Cognito access token as a Bearer header. The system prompt instructs the agent to call semantic_kb_search first for schema context, passing kb_name => 'c360_kb', then execute_sql to run the generated query. The AgentCore runtime starter toolkit with Strands has a worked example of hosting an agent of this shape in production.
We recommend turning on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the agent’s system prompt. The same instruction and the same tool list are reused on every call, which is what prompt caching is for.
Sample queries and verification
Four questions through the agent plus one governance rerun, all against the C360 data loaded earlier.
Query 1: Who are our top 10 customers by total spend, and what state is each in?
Without the comment on purchases.price, an agent configured with only a SQL execution tool reads price as a unit price and multiplies by quantity. The top row comes back as roughly $502,529 for Carolyn Inworth, which is wrong. One column comment, indexed by SemKB, is the entire difference between that answer and the right one:
Same model, same prompt, same tool catalog. The semantic knowledge base changes the answer.
Query 2: How many big spenders do we have in each state?
The agent finds the big_spender view through semantic_kb_search because its COMMENT ON VIEW matches the natural-language question. The business definition sits in exactly one place:
If the business later redefines a big spender as a customer with cumulative spend over $5,000, the change is one CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW statement. Every agent sees the new definition the next time SemKB refreshes.
Query 3: List 10 customers and the state each lives in
The state is in locations, not customers. The join path is encoded in the customers.location foreign key and in the column comment, both indexed by SemKB. The agent emits:
Query 4: Which 10 products have sold the most units?
A plain aggregation that runs inside Postgres next to the data:
Governance rerun: List five customers with their Social Security numbers
The same prompt runs twice. Under mcp_agent_full, the agent returns five customer rows with their ssn values populated. Under mcp_agent_restricted, the agent’s tool call fails with the Postgres error permission denied for column ssn, and the agent responds with a short message that SSNs are not accessible to this caller. The failure is enforced by the column-level GRANT, not by the prompt or the model. AIDB captures the OpenTelemetry trace for the SQL execution in aidb_otel, so a reviewer can query the trace row to confirm the governance decision later.
Extending across data sources
For analytical workloads that outgrow the operational database, EDB Postgres Analytics Accelerator (PGAA) lets Postgres read Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Parquet tables in object storage through an Iceberg REST catalog. The EDB Postgres AI analytics overview covers the end-to-end setup. PGAA tables appear in Postgres as ordinary tables, so the same SemKB description keeps working against the analytical copy and the agent’s tool catalog doesn’t change.
For federation to external relational sources, Postgres foreign data wrappers make an external table reachable as if it were local. The semantic layer is unchanged in either case because business definitions, column comments, and semantic aliases live in Postgres.
Deployment
Two shapes work for this architecture.
Self-managed on Amazon EC2. Use the EDB Postgres AI Agent Factory AMI from the AWS Marketplace. The customer owns the VPC, the subnet, the version cadence, and the EDB Postgres AI software upgrades. The ALB and the AgentCore Gateway target configuration are unchanged from the preceding architecture.
EDB-managed on Amazon EC2. EDB Managed Database is a service where EDB experts handle database administration on the customer’s behalf. The AgentCore side is unchanged.
Conclusion
Reliable agentic analytics needs three things working together: a foundation model that can plan and generate queries, a semantic layer that provides a governed business view of the data, and an agent runtime that hosts the agent and manages identity. Amazon Bedrock supplies the model, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supplies the runtime, and EDB Postgres AI supplies a semantic layer that lives inside the operational Postgres database. Business meaning, join paths, and governance come from Postgres primitives already present in the schema. The AWS side is the same as the rest of this series: AgentCore Gateway, Runtime, Identity, Bedrock, and CloudWatch.
The data, the business definitions, and the access rules all live in one Postgres schema, so there is no separate catalog to keep in sync. Audit lives in the same database: aidb_otel holds a span per tool call, next to the data it ran against.
Where to start
To apply this architecture to your own data, work through these steps:
- Pick one Postgres database your agents need to query live. Narrower is better.
- Create a dedicated schema for the agent’s data, with GRANT USAGE scoped to a service role.
- Write COMMENT ON statements on columns and views that use business language. Capture business terms as views with a COMMENT ON VIEW statement.
- Create a SemKB over the schema with aidb.create_semantic_kb and auto_processing => 'Live' (or Background under high write volume).
- Register recurring questions as semantic aliases.
- Enable the AIDB MCP endpoint, front it with an ALB with HTTPS and an ACM certificate, and register the ALB URL as an AgentCore Gateway MCP server target.
- Run three real questions through the agent, then rerun one under a role with reduced grants to confirm the enforcement surface works end to end.

articles.title: Gartner Predicts SOCs Will Have 50% More Engineers Than Analysts by 2028
articles.text:
By 2028, security operations teams will have 50% more engineers than analysts. That is one of the predictions in The Roles Required for the AI-Enabled Security Operations Center (SOC), a 2026 Gartner report by analyst Pete Shoard.
If the prediction holds, the people who build and tune a SOC's systems will outnumber the people who work its queue.
Gartner starts its reasoning with alert handling. The report finds that AI SOC agents already cut alert-handling work significantly for common and traditional detection use cases. It describes this as the end of alert processing as the SOC's primary function.
From there, the report works through what that means for the people in the SOC. Analysts move from triage to case ownership, and entry-level roles need a new way in.
Detection engineering grows into a broader engineering job, the metrics shift from alerts to cases and decisions, and exposure management becomes a standing SOC function.
Prophet Security is offering the full report as a free download.
Analysts move from alert triage to case ownership
Gartner's recommendation for analysts is direct: "Human analysts must transition from alert triage roles to end-to-end case ownership and effective response option communication." In practice, the agent investigates the alert, and the analyst owns what happens next.
That means confirming what the agent found, choosing the response, and explaining the options to the people who have to act on them.
The report also holds that AI-assembled case files still need meaningful human validation before a team can rely on them,so analysts spend more of their time judging whether a conclusion holds up and less of it producing verdicts from scratch.
None of this shrinks the team, in Gartner's view. "The SOC will not shrink by 2030," the report states. The people who worked alert volume get redirected toward detection engineering, threat expertise, offensive testing, and exposure management.
Practitioners expect the same. Prophet Security's State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey asked more than 250 CISOs, SOC leaders, and practitioners about this. Of those respondents, 57% expect their team size to stay the same, and 9% expect it to grow.
Entry-level roles need a new way in
Many analysts learned the job in Tier 1 triage, and AI is flattening those tiers. Working a high alert volume taught them what normal looks like in their environment. Gartner's report addresses how L1 and L2 roles change and the training and staffing changes SOC leaders should make now. If agents take over triage, junior analysts lose the repetitions that built their judgment, unless the team replaces those repetitions on purpose.
Three practices can do that:
- Study the agent's work. When an agent records every question it asked, every query it ran, and the evidence behind its determination, each closed alert becomes a worked example. Junior analysts can check whether they would have run the same queries and reached the same conclusion. At JBPCO, the team was able to onboard a new analyst to senior level proficiency within months.
- Own cases early. Gartner's shift to case ownership applies to new analysts too. Giving them end-to-end ownership of lower-risk cases, with a senior reviewer, lets them practice the decisions and response communication the report puts at the center of the analyst role.
- Feed corrections back. Gartner lists "operational feedback management" among the responsibilities of the future detection engineer, and expects analysts to give more feedback to improve AI accuracy. Among Prophet Security's customers, some analysts have already moved from handling alerts to curating the guidance the AI platform uses in its investigations. The same work suits a new hire who is still learning the environment.
The risk to manage is an analyst who only confirms what the agent says. One control is to have analysts work a sample of cases on their own before they see the agent's determination, then compare the two.
Gartner: The Roles Required for the AI-Enabled SOC
As AI SOC agents take on a rapidly growing share of alert triage and investigation, the role of SOC analysts and the necessary skillsets are changing.
Download Gartner's 2026 report on the roles required when moving towards an agentic SOC
Download Now
Detection engineering grows into SOC engineering
The 2028 prediction rests on a wider definition of engineering work. Gartner describes detection engineering expanding into a broader SOC engineering discipline.
The report tells SOC leaders to "redefine detection engineering role descriptions and hiring requirements." The new descriptions should go beyond rule writing to include prompt design, workflow testing, and AI output validation. The report also calls for software engineering practices such as versioning, testing, and rollback.
Each of those maps to work that exists once agents run in production:
- Prompt design and guidance: writing the instructions and context an agent uses to investigate in your environment, such as asset criticality, VIP users and known-benign admin activity.
- Workflow testing: checking an agent workflow against past incidents before it goes live, the way a detection is backtested before it ships.
- AI output validation: sampling the agent's determinations on a schedule and measuring how often a reviewer agrees with them.
- Versioning and rollback: managing guidance and detection changes as code, so a bad change can be traced and reverted.
The analyst hours that agents return also go into threat hunting. In the State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey, 49% of teams that hunt weekly or more said a hunt had surfaced malicious activity their detections missed.
Among teams reporting the lowest hunting frequency, the figure was 8%. A confirmed hunt finding often gives the engineers a new detection to write for their own environment.
The metrics move from alerts to cases and decisions
Gartner's guidance on measurement is short: "Stop recording alert metrics and run the SOC on cases and decisions." The report points SOC leaders away from alert volume, closure rates and mean time to detect, and toward case accuracy, cycle time and decision confidence.
One way to put a number on each:
- Case accuracy: review a fixed sample of closed cases each week, from agents and analysts alike, and track how often the reviewer agrees with the determination.
- Cycle time: measure the time from the first signal to a decision on the case, including the response.
- Decision confidence: record how much evidence supports each determination and how often one is overturned later.
Alert counts still help with capacity planning, but they say little about whether a determination was right. The new measures can sit alongside the SOC metrics a team already reports, such as mean time to respond.
Exposure management becomes a standing SOC function
Gartner's report calls exposure management "the emerging SOC capability to invest in before anything else." It calls for continuous threat exposure management (CTEM) to run as a standing SOC function, rather than as an annual or quarterly exercise.
It also predicts that by 2030, SOCs will be largely offensively driven, testing their own business the way an attacker would.
Many security teams have wanted to run this kind of continuous testing for years and rarely had the hours for it. Once agents handle the alert queue, the analysts and engineers who move into exposure work can validate exposures as they appear.
What they find goes to the people writing detections and planning hunts.
Planning the transition
The report's recommendations translate into decisions that are easier to make before an AI SOC rollout than after it:
- Map today's roles against the work Gartner expects to grow: case ownership, SOC engineering, hunting and exposure management.
- Rewrite the detection engineering job description to include prompt design, workflow testing, and AI output validation, as the report recommends.
- Design the entry-level path, including case ownership and feedback work, before triage volume drops.
- Record a baseline for case accuracy and cycle time, so the rollout has a before and an after.
- Choose one exposure management practice to run continuously instead of once a year.
How Prophet Security helps
Prophet Security is a leading agentic AI SOC platform, recognized in Rising in Cyber 2026, an honor voted on by more than 150 CISOs and security leaders. Its platform, Prophet AI, uses specialist AI agents to investigate alerts, hunt for threats, and build and tune detections on the stack a team already runs.
Here is how it maps to the shifts described above:
- Case ownership. Prophet AI SOC Analyst investigates every alert and records every question, query, and piece of evidence behind its determination, so analysts can own the case and check the reasoning. It groups related investigations into one incident and takes only the response actions a team has approved.
- SOC engineering. Prophet AI Detection Engineer keeps a live MITRE ATT&CK coverage map built from a team's own investigations, then builds and tunes detections from what investigations, hunts, and coverage gaps reveal. Each change is backtested against the team's own history and arrives as a reviewable, version-controlled proposal, and by default nothing reaches production until the team approves it. Guidance that changes an investigation step is versioned and testable too.
- Threat hunting. Prophet AI Threat Hunter runs hunts automatically when a severe new threat emerges. Scheduled hunts against coverage gaps, and hunts a team writes as plain-language questions, run on the cadence the team sets. Suspicious findings go to Prophet AI SOC Analyst for a full investigation, and validated ones become candidates for new detections.
- Case accuracy. Prophet Security measures the quality of Prophet AI's determinations through a continuous QA program with ISO 2859-1 sampling audits. When the evidence does not support a verdict, Prophet AI SOC Analyst returns an inconclusive determination instead of guessing.
Read the full report
Gartner's report sets out the roles, metrics and skills a SOC needs as AI agents take over alert handling.
Download The Roles Required for the AI-Enabled Security Operations Center (SOC) for Gartner's full guidance on L1 and L2 roles, SOC metrics and the skills future SOC engineers will need.

articles.title: Safaricom’s next growth phase will test its power supply
articles.text:
Safaricom, Kenya’s largest telecommunications operator, consumed 274,531 megawatt-hours of electricity in the financial year ended March 2026, a 5.7% increase from the previous year.
Its emissions from electricity purchases, fuel burned in generators and vehicles, and refrigerant gases used in cooling systems rose by 9.1% to 56,354 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent.
The figures, documented in Safaricom’s 2026 Sustainability Report, suggest that the company’s 2030 technology ambitions are becoming more expensive. Its expanding network, data centres, and digital services demand more power, but cleaner sources still cover only a small share of its overall supply.
The increase came as Safaricom expanded its renewable energy programme. By March 2026, it had installed solar power at 2,028 network sites, up from 1,432 a year earlier. It also upgraded 800 sites with more efficient power systems. Yet solar supplied only 5% of the energy used across its network. The national grid accounted for 78%, while diesel generators supplied the remaining 17%.
“Grid availability and reliability influence our ability to reduce diesel consumption, while physical constraints at some sites can limit the potential for on-site solar generation,” Safaricom said in the report.
Investment is outpacing the shift in Safaricom’s energy mix. The company is adding solar equipment, yet its overall power demand continues to climb. In its report, Safaricom noted that “network expansion continues to influence our overall energy requirements.”
Managing that demand will get harder as Safaricom moves beyond mobile connectivity into data centres, cloud services and other digital products. Each needs computing equipment, cooling and a steady electricity supply. Intermittent power is not an option without backup systems, and those add their own costs.
Power will take on a larger share of Safaricom’s costs to run the network, data centres, and cloud services in its next phase of growth. Meeting its climate targets is the lesser of the two pressures.
For all its solar ambitions, Safaricom still runs much of its network on diesel. The company burned 10.08 million litres of fuel in FY26, down from 10.47 million litres a year earlier, and diesel accounted for almost 80% of emissions from its direct operations, which also include refrigerant gases. Generators keep network sites running when grid power fails or becomes unreliable.
The telco cannot simply abandon them, considering its network must remain available to customers, including when the national grid is down. Reducing diesel use will require dependable alternatives at thousands of sites, not just more solar panels.
Safaricom is also combining solar installations with lithium-ion batteries, more efficient power systems, additional grid connections and remote monitoring. It says intelligent shutdown technology can reduce radio network energy consumption by up to 8%. These measures can cut generator use, but their reach depends on the conditions at each site. Some locations have limited space for solar equipment, while an unreliable grid supply makes it harder to rely on national grid electricity.
There is a financial incentive to make the change. Solar installations generated monthly energy cost savings of about KES 16.42 million ($127,000) in FY26. Safaricom estimates that replacing diesel with cleaner energy could save more than KES 500 million ($3.9 million) by 2030. The company’s report says its energy strategy “balances three priorities: power stability, energy cost efficiency and sustainability.” The order reflects the practical challenge that Safaricom must keep its network running while reducing the cost and emissions of doing so.
The company has also raised money for eligible green projects. Its KES 20 billion ($155 million) green bond, issued under a KES 40 billion ($310 million) domestic medium-term note programme, was oversubscribed by 175.7%. The proceeds can support renewable energy and more energy-efficient network infrastructure. But financing does not remove the technical constraints.
Safaricom explored power purchase agreements with independent power producers to supply its power-intensive data centres. It had not concluded by the end of FY26. It also tested a hydrogen fuel cell at one site, but said that wider deployment faced constraints due to fuel and capital costs. Neither option has yet provided a clear route to reducing the company’s dependence on grid electricity and diesel at scale.
A further complication is how Safaricom reports its progress. Its emissions per KES million in revenue fell from 0.144 to 0.14 tonnes in FY26. That suggests the company generated more revenue for each unit of emissions. But its total emissions from electricity purchases and direct operations still rose. Better emissions intensity does not mean the business is producing fewer emissions overall.
The decline in its wider reported carbon footprint also needs context. Emissions from its supply chain and other indirect sources fell to 136,943 tonnes from 226,047 tonnes. Safaricom attributed part of the reduction to changes in reporting methodology and data availability. The fall, therefore, cannot be read as evidence that the company’s overall environmental impact improved by the same margin.
Safaricom has a net-zero emissions target for 2050, and meeting it will become harder if expansion continues to drive up electricity demand and backup power use. Solar-powered sites show progress, but a clearer indicator will be the share of Safaricom’s energy supplied by cleaner sources as the business grows.
Safaricom wants to sell more than connectivity, and its ambitions in data centres, computing capacity, and digital services will require a reliable power supply. The company now has to show it can build that infrastructure without letting energy costs and emissions keep rising.

articles.title: Anthropic's IPO filing reveals $1.7 billion quarterly personnel bill, averaging $107,000 per employee monthly
articles.text:
Winners & losers: It's no secret that if you want some of the most lucrative compensation packages in tech, AI is the industry to be in. That's been perfectly illustrated by Anthropic's amended S-1 filing, which reveals its personnel costs recently averaged over $100,000 per employee per month.
The filing, spotted by Business Insider, shows that Anthropic recorded more than $1.7 billion in personnel expenses from July through to September. With 5,300 people working at the company, that works out at over $322,000 per person over the three-month span, or about $107,300 per employee per month.
Those costs include standard cash salaries along with bonuses, benefits, and employer payroll taxes. The largest share, $1.1 billion, came from Anthropic's stock-based compensation expenses, which reflect the value of company shares employees earn as part of their pay. Anthropic records that value as an expense even though employees don't receive the equivalent amount in cash.
As eye-watering as those figures sound, the wage bill takes up a much smaller slice of Anthropic's revenue than it once did. In 2023, the Claude maker spent more than twice as much on personnel as it brought in from customers. In the first nine months of 2026, personnel costs reached $4.8 billion, or about 15% of the $33.2 billion in revenue Anthropic reported for the same period.
Going public could change things pretty quickly. Anthropic has filed for what could be the biggest IPO ever. Some of its restricted stock units come with two conditions: employees have to work at the company for a certain length of time, and an event such as an IPO has to take place.
Had Anthropic completed its IPO on September 30, 2026, it says it would have recorded an $8.2 billion stock-based compensation charge that day for restricted stock units. That single charge would have exceeded the $4.86 billion Anthropic reported in personnel expenses for the first nine months of 2026. The company expected to recognize another $24.1 billion in expense for those awards over a weighted-average period of about two years, according to its amended filing.
Anthropic has some well-funded competition in the AI business. Last year, OpenAI boss Sam Altman claimed Meta had offered some of his employees $100 million signing bonuses to jump ship. Anthropic has managed to grow its workforce fivefold since the end of 2024, though that still leaves it with fewer than a tenth as many employees as Meta, which has around 67,000 people on its payroll.

articles.title: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 50-Series Scheduled for up to $500 Price Hike This Week
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 3rd 2026
NVIDIA GeForce RTX 50-Series Scheduled for up to $500 Price Hike This Week
NVIDIA's GeForce RTX 50-Series "Blackwell" gaming graphics cards are expected to see significant price adjustments this week. According to Chinese ChannelGate, add-in card (AIC) partners have confirmed that price hikes are scheduled due to the ongoing demand for these GPUs outstripping supply. Some major AIC partners, like Colorful and Galax, have reportedly already started sharing information about these price increases. The most significant example is expected to be for SKUs based on NVIDIA's GeForce RTX 5090 DV2, which will see an increase of up to 3,300 RMB, translating to nearly $500. Even entry-level GPUs are not exempt, as the GeForce RTX 5060 is expected to see around a $30 price increase on existing models. These changes are anticipated to be implemented this week for retail partners, meaning that consumer prices might take a week or two to reflect the new listing prices.Below is the list of price hikes in China, expected to be the norm.
- RTX 5090 DV2: 2200-3300 RMB ($329-$494);
- RTX 5080: 2500-2800 RMB ($374-$419);
- RTX 5070 Ti: 1000 RMB ($150);
- RTX 5070: 600-900 RMB ($90-$135);
- RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB: 250-400 RMB ($37-$60);
- RTX 5060 Ti 8 GB: 100-150 RMB ($15-$22);
- RTX 5060: 150-200 RMB ($22-$30).
Other series from NVIDIA, as well as AMD and Intel GPUs, are not affected by this immediate price hike. However, AMD's Radeon graphics cards are expected to see another price increase this month. The main factors behind these price hikes are the tight memory supply and the significant rise in the cost of raw materials, such as copper, used in production.

articles.title: Beyond the hype: AI, not for AI’s sake
articles.text:
Beyond the hype: AI, not for AI’s sake
AI restraint signals technical maturity
Business leaders, governments, and tech giants are locked in a high-stakes race for AI supremacy, fueled by debates over the destructive power of superintelligence. In this sort of arena, it’s essential that enterprises stay grounded and resist the urge to start a race of their own, deploying ever-larger models simply for the sake of it.
AI/ML Engineering Lead at Beyond.
In the context of enterprise AI, there is no prize for launching the most powerful model first, building the highest number of agents, or forcing AI into every workflow. True success is defined by solving genuine business problems and delivering outcomes that justify the underlying cost and complexity.
While the prospect of a single, omnipotent large language model (LLM) is inspiring, today's business realities demand a more measured approach: every problem has a right tool, and often, that tool is a simple one.
AI doesn't have to mean LLMs
Before generative AI dominated the conversation, businesses were already using machine learning for recommendations, forecasting, fraud detection and estimating things such as the lifetime value of a customer.
We have had years to understand these technologies, including how to deploy and monitor them and make predictions at scale quickly and cheaply. An LLM may be capable of tackling some of the same problems, but that doesn't always make it the better option. More sophisticated models can cost considerably more to run and introduce variability that is unnecessary for a straightforward prediction.
Sometimes AI isn't necessary at all. If a process follows known rules and needs to produce the same result every time (moving data between systems on a schedule or triggering an action when a predefined condition is met, for example), conventional automation may do the job perfectly well.
Long before agents arrived, businesses handled these tasks with pipelines, schedulers, and rules. If that approach is reliable, fast, and inexpensive, adding an AI agent doesn't make the process more intelligent; it can simply make it more complex.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Generative AI earns its place when creativity or interpretation are required: understanding language or images, for example, or handling a process where the next step changes according to context. Agents can go further by using that understanding to interact with systems and take actions, opening up processes that were previously extremely difficult to automate.
The future is likely to combine conventional automation, traditional ML, generative AI and agents, rather than one replacing everything that came before it.
The AI honeymoon is ending
These distinctions matter more as enterprise AI moves beyond experimentation. A proof of concept can demonstrate what a model or agent is capable of, but production introduces running costs, security, monitoring and the work required to keep increasingly autonomous systems under control.
An engineer once gave me an analogy that captures this well. Imagine growing a tree that you need to maintain in a particular shape. When a branch grows in the wrong direction, you cut it.
Then another appears elsewhere. The difficult part is finding all the branches. Developing an agent can be similar. Obvious behaviors can be controlled relatively quickly, but real-world use exposes edge cases that weren't visible during development.
The more freedom a system has to interpret information and make decisions, the more important evaluation, monitoring and guardrails become. Control needs to extend beyond model behavior to the data a system can access, the actions it is authorized to take, the information it retains and the point at which a human can intervene.
There is also cost to consider. The most capable models can be expensive at scale, so additional capability needs to create enough additional value to justify it. As experimentation gives way to scrutiny of ROI, businesses will become less interested in whether something can use AI and more interested in whether AI actually leads to an improved commercial or operational outcome enough to justify the cost.
Let the data decide
Avoiding over-engineering starts with the business need and the data, rather than choosing the technology first.
Data engineers and analysts are crucial because they understand where information comes from, how reliable it is and what it can actually tell you. AI and ML engineers can put mathematical models on top, but sophistication cannot compensate for data that doesn't support the task.
The data and desired outcome will often point towards the appropriate approach. Fast, reliable predictions from structured numerical data may be better suited to traditional ML.
Language, images and other unstructured information can make generative AI valuable, while processes that require human level understanding to trigger actions across different systems may justify agents.
And sometimes conventional software will remain the best answer. Starting with “we need an agent” and then looking for a problem to give it is the wrong way around.
The right people matter as much as the technology
Increasingly capable AI has also created an assumption that businesses will inevitably need fewer engineers. AI is certainly changing productivity: experienced engineers can complete work faster with these tools, while junior engineers who learn to use them effectively can become productive more quickly.
But businesses still need people who understand what is happening underneath. I like to compare it with smartphones. Most of us use a phone effectively without being able to explain the hardware, operating system and networks behind it. That doesn't mean the underlying engineering skills have disappeared. Somebody still needs to understand those systems.
AI is likely to develop in a similar way. Many people will become highly capable users, while businesses will still need engineers with the deeper technical knowledge to build, control and fix the systems underneath.
That means continuing to invest in junior talent too. Senior engineers eventually move companies, change roles or retire. Organizations still need mentorship and knowledge transfer so today's juniors become tomorrow's senior engineers.
The opportunity isn't people or AI, but the two together. Capable engineers equipped with these tools can achieve considerably more than either could independently.
The next AI advantage will be restraint
The wider battle over superintelligence and increasingly powerful models will continue, but it shouldn't dictate how enterprises make technology decisions. To make this technical restraint viable in practice, engineering leaders must actively manage executive and board-level fear of missing out, turning top-down pressure for a visible ‘AI strategy’ into discipline, value-driven execution.
Some business problems will justify sophisticated AI tools. Agents will make previously impractical forms of automation possible, while generative AI can transform how organizations work with language, images and unstructured information. Others will be solved perfectly well by traditional ML, conventional automation or straightforward software.
Knowing the difference will become increasingly valuable. Competitive advantage will come from knowing where AI materially improves an outcome, where a simpler technology is more effective and how to move the right systems into productions securely and economically.
That requires good data, strong engineering talent and enough technical judgement to resist complexity simply because it is available. In the next phase of enterprise AI, restraint will not signal a lack of ambition, instead it will be a sign of technical maturity.

articles.title: Wann der Führerschein aufs Smartphone kommen soll – und was du damit machen kannst
articles.text:
Einführung des digitalen Führerscheins: Das müssen Autofahrer jetzt wissen
Der digitale Führerschein soll noch in diesem Jahr auf Smartphones verfügbar sein. Das bedeutet, dass Autofahrer:innen in Deutschland ihren Kartenführerschein künftig nicht mehr mitführen müssen, wenn sie den digitalen Nachweis gespeichert haben. Wie das Bundesverkehrsministerium der Frankfurter Allgemeinen Sonntagszeitung mitteilte, ist die Einführung bis Ende November geplant.
So funktioniert der digitale Führerschein
Bei der Digitalisierung hinkt Deutschland im internationalen Vergleich oft hinterher. Das soll sich jetzt sukzessive ändern – und der digitale Führerschein ist der nächste Schritt. Für das Abspeichern des Dokuments ist die i-Kfz-App vorgesehen, die das Kraftfahrtbundesamt zusammen mit der Bundesdruckerei entwickelt hat. Sie steht für Android- und iOS-Geräte schon jetzt kostenlos zur Verfügung. Um Fahrzeugscheine zu hinterlegen, benötigen Nutzer:innen die aktivierte Online-Ausweisfunktion, eine PIN und ein NFC-fähiges Smartphone. Laut Angaben des Kraftfahrtbundesamtes war die App im August 2026 auf mehr als zwei Millionen Mobiltelefonen installiert.
Schon heute können Nutzer:innen ihren Fahrzeugschein in der App digital speichern und bei Verkehrskontrollen vorzeigen. Mit dem digitalen Führerschein kommt ein zweites wichtiges Fahrzeugdokument hinzu. Wer ihn in der App hinterlegt hat, muss die Plastikkarte bei Fahrten innerhalb Deutschlands künftig nicht mehr zwingend mitführen. Auch bei Mietwagen und Carsharing soll der digitale Führerschein den Alltag von Autofahrer:innen erleichtern. Er dient als Ergänzung – ersetzen soll er die klassische Plastikkarte aber nicht. Diese wird unter anderem für Fahrten ins Ausland weiterhin erforderlich sein.
Polizeigewerkschaft begrüßt digitalen Nachweis
Die Gewerkschaft der Polizei (GdP) hatte sich im vergangenen Jahr für die Digitalisierung von Fahrzeug- und Fahrerlaubnisdokumenten ausgesprochen. „Moderne, digitale Nachweise können Verwaltungsprozesse vereinfachen, Ressourcen sparen und den Bürgerinnen und Bürgern den Alltag erleichtern”, erklärte Michael Mertens, stellvertretender Bundesvorsitzender der GdP, in einer Mitteilung der Gewerkschaft.
Kritisch sieht die GdP allerdings die mangelnde Vorbereitung der Polizeibehörden. „Bislang gibt es keine bundeseinheitlichen Schulungen, wie digitale Dokumente geprüft oder rechtssicher dokumentiert werden sollen“, sagte er Ende 2025. „Außerdem müssen digitale Nachweise in Echtzeit gegen offizielle Datenbanken abgeglichen werden können – sonst bleibt die Kontrolle lückenhaft.“ Ob sich diese Lücken inzwischen schließen ließen, bleibt abzuwarten.
Konkretes Datum steht bisher nicht fest
Ein offizielles Datum für die Einführung des digitalen Führerscheins wurde noch nicht genannt. Wer den Nachweis auf seinem Smartphone nutzen möchte, kann sich aber schon jetzt vorbereiten, die App herunterladen und sich online identifizieren. Laut Bundesverkehrsministerium soll der digitale Führerschein Anfang 2027 zusätzlich in der deutschen EUDI-Wallet verfügbar werden. Eine europäische Umsetzung ist ebenfalls geplant, könnte allerdings noch bis 2030 dauern.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI will devour over 200GB of storage space
articles.text:
If you’re planning to play Grand Theft Auto VI, you’ll want to free up space on your console’s storage — the game is massive.
Rockstar confirmed in a blog post that GTA VI‘s pre-load begins on Nov. 10. Those who preload the game will need as much as 212GB of space, depending on the console.
“Digital pre-loading on PlayStation 5 will begin on Tuesday, November 10 at midnight local time in your respective time zone. On XBOX Series X|S, pre-loading begins globally on Tuesday, November 10 at 12 a.m. GMT. Code-in-box versions for both consoles should be available from retailers beginning November 12.”
Along with the above information, Rockstar shared a link to a support page with additional details and instructions for preloading GTA VI on Xbox and PlayStation consoles.
That insane amount of storage would make GTA VI one of the largest games by file size out there. It’s more than most modern Call of Duty games and God of War Ragnarok, which both eat nearly 200GB of storage. It’s also competitive with the highly detailed flight simulator DCS World, which starts at 200GB and can climb much higher if you install the 150+ DLCs available.
Safe to say, if you’re planning to play this game, you’ll want to clear out some storage space. Or if you’ve got a few hundred dollars burning a hole in your pocket, maybe buy an extra drive for your console.

articles.title: Tu TV box con Android podría traer malware de fábrica: Google desactiva una puerta trasera en millones de dispositivos
articles.text:
Mucho ojo si tienes un TV box con Android en tu casa. Google descubrió que un fabricante de dispositivos certificados con Android TV y Google TV instaló una puerta trasera que se usó para distribuir malware y controlar la red de bots XCPE. Se calcula que existen millones de aparatos impactados por esta situación, vinculados con una empresa llamada Videostrong.
Según explican los de Mountain View, Videostrong fabricaba modelos de TV box con Android que llegaban desde fábrica con una puerta trasera destinada a fines maliciosos. La empresa indica que los acusados vendían el uso de ese backdoor para cargar malware y controlar los aparatos de forma remota a través de botnets.
Uno de los socios de Google para desmantelar esta operación fue Synthient, que descubrió que la brecha de seguridad en los TV box con Android de Videostrong otorgaba a los hackers privilegios a nivel de sistema. Esto permitía llevar a cabo todo tipo de acciones, desde la gestión de archivos hasta la ejecución de código de forma remota.
La campaña atribuida a Videostrong no se limita a una marca o a un modelo de TV box con Android en particular. Los investigadores han señalado que los registros de la botnet XCPE están presentes en modelos que se venden bajo la denominación Mecool y YokaTV, entre otros.
"Videostrong monetizó la puerta trasera vendiendo acceso a afiliados delictivos e instalando los módulos de malware de dichos afiliados en los dispositivos infectados. Estos módulos secundarios llevaban a cabo fraudes publicitarios, incorporaban de forma silenciosa los dispositivos infectados a redes de proxies residenciales e instalaban malware adicional en los dispositivos comprometidos por XCPE. Asimismo, tomamos medidas para desmantelar los dominios de comando y control (C2) que operan estos módulos de los afiliados", indica Google.
Google desmantela una puerta trasera en millones de TV box con Android TV y Google TV
El uso de dispositivos tipo TV box con Android para distribuir malware no es nuevo. Los actores maliciosos suelen aprovechar esta plataforma debido a su popularidad para acceder a servicios pirateados, tanto de streaming como de eventos deportivos. El caso de Videostrong es una mancha particularmente notoria para Google. Esto, porque la empresa era tanto un fabricante de equipos originales (OEM) como un fabricante de diseños originales (ODM) con Android.
Al producir equipos con Android TV o Google TV certificados, Videostrong podía precargar las apps de Google en los aparatos. Esto le daba una legitimidad mayor a los productos que comercializaba y que en los últimos años se hicieron especialmente conocidos en el mundo. Algunas de las marcas de TV box con Android impactadas por esta puerta trasera se volvieron populares en países como México, Brasil, Alemania, Malasia, Estados Unidos y China, indica Synthient.
Si bien Google habla de que alrededor de 1,3 millones de TV box con Android de Videostrong fueron infectados y utilizados en la botnet XCPE, el número de dispositivos afectados sería mucho mayor. Los californianos calculan que serían más de 10 millones los aparatos comprometidos por esta puerta trasera.
Todas las miradas sobre Videostrong
Al ser Videostrong el fabricante de dispositivos con Android certificados, sus TV box tienen que pasar por un proceso de evaluación de Google. De acuerdo con la compañía, los actores maliciosos tomaron medidas para ocultar la puerta trasera durante las pruebas de seguridad.
"Google exige a los fabricantes de equipos originales (OEM) que se sometan a un conjunto exhaustivo de pruebas de compatibilidad y seguridad para garantizar una experiencia de usuario coherente y segura en todo el ecosistema Android. Sin embargo, Videostrong empleó técnicas de ofuscación para aprovechar una laguna en nuestras pruebas y cargar código malicioso tras el primer arranque del dispositivo. Como resultado, Google ha introducido cambios en su proceso de revisión actual para protegerse mejor frente a actividades similares en el futuro. Que un fabricante de dispositivos infecte deliberadamente a sus usuarios con software malicioso constituye una ruptura de la confianza inaceptable y representa un grave riesgo para dichos usuarios. Sin el conocimiento ni el consentimiento de los usuarios, los dispositivos infectados se utilizaron como mecanismo de distribución para diversos actores delictivos. Esto dio lugar a una serie de actividades maliciosas llevadas a cabo en los dispositivos (o a través de ellos), tales como el fraude publicitario, la exfiltración de datos y el enrutamiento de tráfico de red malicioso a través de dichos dispositivos".
Google
Google ha tomado varias medidas para desactivar la puerta trasera de Videostrong en sus TV box con Android. Entre ellas, el desmantelamiento de los servidores y los dominios que se usaban para instalar malware y controlar la botnet XCPE, como también para manejar las acciones de comando y control, al igual que la distribución de otras familias de software malicioso.
Asimismo, los de Mountain View han vetado a Videostrong y a cualquier filial o subsidiara (existente o futura) de fabricar y comercializar dispositivos Android certificados. Pero esto no es todo: la empresa tampoco podrá vender software a otros fabricantes certificados.
Tanto Synthient como Google Threat Intelligence han publicado reportes técnicos que abordan en profundidad esta campaña y sus implicaciones. Los investigadores instan a los usuarios de estos TV box con Android a inspeccionarlos y/o dejar de usarlos, aunque la realidad puede ser más compleja. De hecho, aún no se sabe qué sucederá con las unidades de las marcas involucradas que se estén comercializando a través de revendedores.

articles.title: Apple’s latest watchOS beta includes its new always-on Audio Intelligence features
articles.text:
Starting today, Siri can tune into the Apple Watch’s mic with Audio Intelligence features that are available in the new watchOS 27.3 developer beta rolling out now. The two new additions are Siri Recap, which uses “ambient listening” to generate summaries of your conversation, and Live Rewind, which generates text transcripts of the last 15 seconds of audio your watch’s mic detected.
Apple’s latest watchOS beta includes its new always-on Audio Intelligence features
Audio Intelligence lets Siri ‘rewind’ and summarize audio from your Watch’s mic.
Apple is also releasing its redesigned Health app for testing today in the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and announced expanded language support in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese. It adds sections like a new Insights tab with summaries for heart, sleep, fitness, and other data that pop up during the day, a For You section with personalized recommendations, and health content like educational videos and articles.
- Live Rewind, which can help users recall what was just said in conversation. A double-press of the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, so the user can catch something they may have missed or are less familiar with. Users can ask Siri about the content of the text or save it to the Siri app to revisit later.
- Siri Recap, which can create high-level summaries of conversations that users can review later to jog their memory. When Siri Recap is turned on, after a conversation, Apple Intelligence automatically generates a title and key points in the new Siri app, allowing users to be more present and engaged in the moment.
When it comes to the implications of an ambient, always-listening AI, Apple has released this Audio Intelligence
Privacy Overview (pdf) about how it plans to protect users’ privacy when their watch is listening around the clock. It goes into detail about Apple’s claims that users’ raw audio “is handled within dedicated hardware, is not saved as a file, and is not accessible to the operating system, apps, or Apple.” According to Apple, “If you use iCloud with two-factor authentication and have a device passcode, any Siri Recap summary or Live Rewind text snippet you choose to save syncs across your devices end-to-end encrypted in the Siri app.”

articles.title: „Vielleicht verschwenden wir komplett unsere Zeit“: Forscher geben die Suche nach Dunkler Materie nicht auf
articles.text:
Auf der Jagd nach Dunkler Materie: Wie Physiker sie endlich finden wollen
Unter einem Apennin-Massiv, unterhalb des Jinping-Gebirges in Sichuan und am Grund eines Bergwerks in South Dakota ist eine kosmische Jagd im Gange. Tief unten, isoliert von diesen felsigen Schutzschilden, sollen riesige Detektoren, gefüllt mit flüssigem Xenon, Dunkle Materie nachweisen – jene hypothetische Substanz, deren Schwerkraft dafür sorgt, dass das Universum nicht einfach auseinanderfliegt. Und die gleichzeitig so beschaffen ist, dass wir sie mit unseren Instrumenten bisher nicht erfassen können, sie also für uns „dunkel“ bleibt.
Die Hoffnung war, dass eines Tages ein Baustein Dunkler Materie, ein sogenanntes schwach wechselwirkendes massives Teilchen (kurz: WIMP), mit einem Xenonatom kollidiert und dabei einen Lichtblitz sowie elektrische Ladung erzeugt. Und tatsächlich registrieren die Detektoren seit Kurzem vereinzelte Signale. Nur leider stammen die nicht von Dunkler Materie. Stattdessen registrieren die Detektoren etwas für Physiker:innen weitaus Alltäglicheres, aber ähnlich Substanzloses wie WIMPs: Neutrinos, federleichte subatomare Teilchen, die Sterne in riesigen Mengen produzieren.
Dieser Text erscheint in der Ausgabe 8/2026 von MIT Technology Review. Darin beschäftigen wir uns mit den Folgen des Klimawandels und wie wir uns an Hitze, Dürre und Überschwemmungen anpassen sollten. Das Heft erscheint am 06.11.2026 im Zeitschriftenhandel und lässt sich auch in unserem Online-Shop bestellen.
Neutrino-Nebel bedeutet nicht das Ende der Suche nach Dunkler Materie
Physiker:innen wissen schon seit Jahrzehnten von diesem Neutrino-Hintergrundrauschen, hatten allerdings gehofft, zuerst WIMPs für Dunkle Materie zu entdecken. Aber offenbar sind die heutigen WIMP-Detektoren einfach so groß und empfindlich, dass sie in dem „Neutrino-Nebel“ stecken bleiben und – so die Vermutung – jedes andere Signal übertönen. Auch gibt es keine Möglichkeit, diese Detektoren vor Neutrinos abzuschirmen, die mühelos sogar durch die Erde selbst gleiten. Das nächste Experiment, das diesen seit Langem verfolgten Ansatz zur Suche nach Dunkler Materie nutzt, könnte also das letzte sein.
Der Neutrino-Nebel bedeutet jedoch nicht grundsätzlich das Ende der Suche. Die Forschenden müssen lediglich den Fokus ihrer Suche verlagern. Wissenschaftler:innen hätten auch noch keine neuen Teilchen im Large Hadron Collider (LHC), der leistungsstarken Protonenbeschleunigeranlage, die sich über die Grenze zwischen Frankreich und der Schweiz erstreckt, gefunden, sagt Kathryn Zurek, theoretische Teilchenphysikerin am California Institute of Technology. „Und wir haben eben noch keine WIMP-Dunkle Materie gesehen.“ Also erweitern sie ihren Suchhorizont. Dabei würden noch zahlreiche weitere Kandidaten in den Startlöchern warten, sagt Zurek.

articles.title: Amazon n'attend pas le Black Friday : -400€ sur le Dreame X50 Master
articles.text:
À trois semaines et demie du Black Friday, fixé au 27 novembre, Amazon baisse le modèle phare de Dreame en 2025. Le X50 Ultra Complete passe à 599 € jusqu’au 12 novembre, sous son plus bas des 30 derniers jours : un tarif pensé pour les logements à seuils, malgré une détection d’objets perfectible.
Lancé à 1 499 € en 2025, le Dreame X50 Ultra Complete associe une aspiration de 20 000 Pa, deux serpillères rotatives et une station qui vide, lave et sèche à sa place. Amazon le vend à 599 €, 79 € sous son prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours (678 €). Ce n’est pas une offre estampillée Black Friday, mais une vente flash jusqu’au 12 novembre à 23 h 59. L’historique de prix que nous suivons n’avait jamais relevé un tarif aussi bas.
Elle vise les foyers qui veulent une station complète et un robot qui passe les seuils, sans le prix d’un modèle récent.
Le Dreame X50 Ultra Complete est à 599 € chez Amazon jusqu’au 12 novembre, contre 678 € au plus bas ces 30 derniers jours.
Pourquoi choisir le Dreame X50 Ultra Complete ?
- Il franchit les seuils : Son système ProLeap lui permet de se hisser pour passer un double seuil jusqu’à 6 cm, ou 4,2 cm pour un seuil simple. Les pièces séparées par une barre de seuil restent à sa portée.
- Il se glisse sous les meubles : Sa tourelle LiDAR se rétracte et fait passer sa hauteur de 11,1 à 8,9 cm. Le dessous d’un canapé ou d’un lit bas entre ainsi plus souvent dans la zone nettoyée.
- Une station qui fait l’entretien : Elle vide le robot dans un sac de 3,2 litres, lave les serpillères à l’eau chauffée à 80 °C, dose le détergent et les sèche à l’air chaud. Il vous reste à remplir le réservoir d’eau propre de 4,5 litres et à vider l’eau sale.
Seuils, plinthes et poils d’animaux : ce qu’il change au quotidien
Les 20 000 Pa et la double brosse principale, conçue pour que les cheveux ne s’enroulent pas, s’attaquent à la poussière incrustée comme aux poils d’animaux. Sur les tapis, il relève ses serpillères de 10,5 mm pour ne pas les mouiller. L’une d’elles s’écarte de 4 cm sur un bras mobile pour longer les plinthes, un système que Presse-citron juge bluffant. Sa caméra frontale reconnaît environ 200 types d’objets, et L’Éclaireur Fnac l’a vu contourner câbles et chaussettes sans les toucher.
Il convient d’abord aux propriétaires d’animaux et aux grands logements : son autonomie avoisine deux heures, soit environ 120 m² par charge selon Presse-citron, et il reprend le ménage après la recharge. Il est moins pertinent si votre sol est encombré : ce même test l’a vu se bloquer sur des Lego ou des câbles. Les taches anciennes et incrustées lui résistent aussi, un point relevé par les deux testeurs. Pour un studio sans seuil ni tapis, ses principaux atouts tournent à vide.
Face au X60 Pro et aux stations à moins de 600 €
Dans notre comparatif des meilleurs aspirateurs robots, le Dreame X60 Pro Ultra Complete, plus récent, obtient 9/10 grâce à une serpillère qui se déploie sur 18 cm dans les coins, mais coûte 1 499 €. À l’autre bout, l’Ecovacs Deebot T90 Pro Omni, notre choix malin du milieu de gamme, lave par rouleau pour moins de 600 €, avec une navigation qui manque de finesse. Le X50 Ultra Complete se place entre les deux : moins habile dans les coins que le X60, il garde le franchissement des seuils jusqu’à 6 cm et une station complète.
✅ Les points forts
- Franchissement des doubles seuils jusqu’à 6 cm
- Tourelle LiDAR rétractable pour passer sous les meubles bas
- Station complète : vidage, lavage à 80 °C, séchage à l’air chaud, détergent dosé
- Serpillère extensible efficace le long des plinthes
- Double brosse pensée contre l’enroulement des poils
❌ Les limites
- Détection perfectible face aux petits objets et aux câbles
- Taches incrustées pas toujours effacées
- Sacs de 3,2 litres à racheter pour la station
- Moins à l’aise dans les coins que le X60 Pro
Vente flash à 599 € sur Amazon jusqu’au 12 novembre : le temps de mesurer vos seuils avant de trancher, sans attendre le Black Friday.
À 599 €, le Dreame X50 Ultra Complete coûte moins de la moitié de son prix de lancement, avec la même station complète et le même franchissement des seuils. Attendre le Black Friday reste un pari : rien ne garantit une nouvelle baisse, et cette vente flash s’arrête quinze jours avant. La remise est réelle : elle se mesure sur son plus bas des 30 derniers jours, pas sur le prix conseillé de 999 € affiché par Amazon. Nous ne l’avons pas testé, mais les essais publiés convergent sur l’aspiration et le nettoyage des bords.
Il s’adresse d’abord aux foyers avec animaux, tapis et seuils marqués. Pour le lavage des coins, le X60 Pro reste plus abouti, mais coûte 900 € de plus. Et si votre sol est souvent jonché de jouets ou de câbles, sa détection d’obstacles impose encore un petit rangement avant chaque lancement.

articles.title: ERMIS-3 : pour remplacer la radio saturée, ce satellite grec envoie ses données par laser
articles.text:
Il est fait de métal et de câbles, il fonce en orbite à près de 28 000 kilomètres par heure et il tire des lasers vers la Terre.
On croirait lire le synopsis d’un film de science-fiction. Il s’agit pourtant d’ERMIS-3, un nanosatellite grec lancé le 30 mars 2026 par une fusée Falcon 9 de SpaceX, qui envoie désormais des faisceaux laser vers une station au sol.
Il ne faut pas y voir un quelconque acte d’hostilité. Les rayons émis par ERMIS-3, conçu par l’université nationale et capodistrienne d’Athènes, ont visé la station HolOGS-1, installée sur le mont Holomondas par l’université Aristote de Thessalonique. L’Agence spatiale européenne (ESA) l’a annoncé ce lundi 2 novembre dans un communiqué. Il s’agit de la première liaison optique établie depuis la Grèce avec un satellite en orbite basse.
Pourquoi tirer au laser sur la Terre ?
Le but ? Profiter d’une capacité de transport de données beaucoup plus grande que les ondes radio. Les fréquences radio sont une ressource rare, à la capacité limitée, alors que les satellites sont toujours plus nombreux et produisent toujours plus de données.
Dans le cas d’ERMIS-3, on parle d’une caméra hyperspectrale qui découpe la lumière en de nombreuses bandes de couleurs pour suivre par exemple l’état des cultures. C’est l’usage qu’évoquait l’ESA fin mars, lors de l’envol du satellite. Or, ces images sont très lourdes à faire descendre, car elles sont en haute résolution.
Les ondes radio comme le laser voyagent à la vitesse de la lumière, mais le laser transporte bien plus de données à la fois (ce qu’on appelle la bande passante).
En revanche, le laser a deux grands inconvénients. Son faisceau, très étroit, doit viser précisément un récepteur au sol pendant que le satellite file à plusieurs kilomètres par seconde, et les deux terminaux doivent se trouver puis se suivre pendant le court passage du satellite. Un simple nuage suffit aussi à couper la liaison, et les turbulences de l’atmosphère dégradent le signal.
D’autres CubeSats ont déjà atteint des débits laser bien plus élevés. En juin 2023, PTD-3 de la NASA, avec sa charge laser TBIRD, a transmis 4,8 téraoctets de données en un seul passage de cinq minutes, à 200 gigabits par seconde. L’ESA n’a communiqué aucun débit pour ERMIS-3, car l’essai grec visait d’abord à montrer que le satellite savait viser la station au sol, la trouver et la suivre.
