articles.title: Anthropic speeds up Claude Code with message threads. But your token bill stays the same.
articles.text:
Anthropic speeds up Claude Code with message threads. But your token bill stays the same.
Anthropic has announced a new feature that aims to speed up long-running Claude Code sessions by reducing the amount of conversation data repeatedly sent to its API, helping developers get responses faster as their coding sessions grow.
Message threads, as it’s called, is available now in public beta for Anthropic’s Messages API and is already enabled by default for “most” Claude Code users, according to an article published by Anthropic on Monday.
The company says that the feature has reduced median time to first token (TTFT) — the time it takes Claude to begin generating a response — by approximately 35% for Claude Code requests containing between 500,000 and 1 million tokens.
Given that it’s now part of the Messages API, the feature also extends beyond Claude Code to developers building their own AI agents, particularly those handling lengthy conversations, repeated tool calls, and large amounts of data.
How message threads works
To understand what’s changed, it’s worth looking at how the Messages API has traditionally handled conversations.
Every time an agent sends a new request to Claude, it includes the entire conversation history. That means all messages and tool calls must be transmitted again, even though the API has previously received them.
For example, a coding agent working through a complex task will likely entail hundreds of API calls. As it reads files and modifies code, the conversation history grows, and by the time that history reaches 500,000 tokens, every subsequent request requires sending those 500,000 tokens again, along with whatever new information has been thrown into the mix.
The API then has to validate and tokenize the incoming data before Claude can begin responding. This rinse-and-repeat processing can add significant latency, particularly during lengthy coding sessions.
And so message threads switches things up by allowing Anthropic to temporarily retain the conversation history on its servers. The first request still sends the complete conversation, including any system prompts and tool definitions. But subsequent requests need only contain new messages and a reference to the previous response.
Behind the scenes, Anthropic reconstructs the full conversation on its servers before passing it to Claude, negating the need for the client to keep uploading the same information. This detail is important, because Claude still processes the entire conversation on every turn — if the history contains 500,000 tokens, the model still receives that context, even though the client has transmitted only the latest messages.
“While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same.”
As such, message threads doesn’t inherently reduce API costs — Anthropic continues to charge for the tokens Claude processes. “While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same,” the company notes.
Developers can, however, combine message threads with Claude’s existing prompt caching feature, which allows previously processed content to be reused at discounted token rates. The two features can work in tandem to reduce latency and processing costs respectively.
Anthropic identifies several use-cases where message threads could be particularly useful. These include long-running coding agents that accumulate file edits and tool results, computer-use agents that repeatedly capture screenshots, and applications handling large volumes of documents or images. In each case, avoiding repeated uploads reduces the amount of data transmitted during a session.
Guillaume Lebedel, co-founder and CTO of AI agent infrastructure company StackOne, took to LinkedIn on Tuesday to illustrate the potential benefits of message threads for computer-use agents, using a simulation to estimate how much data could be saved.
His calculations assume an agent captures one 150 KB screenshot at each step. Without message threads, the 50th request would need to upload approximately 7.5 MB of accumulated screenshots. With message threads, that request would carry just the latest screenshot, approximately 0.15 MB.
Across the entire 50-step session, the cumulative screenshot data uploaded would fall from roughly 191 MB to 7.5 MB — a reduction of approximately 25 times.
While these figures aren’t based on a live API test, they illustrate the potential benefits for agents that repeatedly upload large files. Indeed, Lebedel predicts that computer-use agents could spearhead adoption of the feature, with widespread uptake before the end of the year.
“My bet — computer-use agents adopt it before coding agents do, since a screenshot per step is what makes the resend heavy.”
“My bet — computer-use agents adopt it before coding agents do, since a screenshot per step is what makes the resend heavy, and most have it on by the end of December,” he writes.
How to use message threads
To implement the feature, Anthropic has introduced a new thread parameter to the Messages API. The initial request creates a thread by including thread={"type": "create"}, alongside the full conversation history, system prompt, and any tools being used.
Subsequent requests use thread={"type": "continue", "previous_message_id": first.id}, where first.id refers to the response ID returned by the initial request.
These follow-up requests contain only the new messages. The API retains the earlier conversation and its original system prompt and tool definitions.
Because the feature remains in beta, developers making requests directly must also include the anthropic-beta header with the value message-threads-2026-08-12. In the Python SDK, this can be supplied through betas=["message-threads-2026-08-12"].
Anthropic also provides a simpler approach through its SDK thread helper, which manages the conversation history and API parameters automatically.
Using the Python SDK, developers first create a client with client = anthropic.Anthropic(), before initialising a thread through client.beta.messages.thread(). The latter accepts the model, maximum output tokens and initial system prompt, among other parameters.
Once configured, developers use thread.send() to submit messages. The SDK thread helper automatically creates the thread on the first request, then continues it on subsequent turns, supplying the necessary parameters and retaining a local copy of the conversation history.
The SDK thread helper also adds the required beta header automatically, removing the need for developers to specify it with each request.
Message threads expire
There is, however, one notable limitation in all of this. Message threads expire after just five minutes of inactivity. And as one user observed on X, “Five minutes at the coffee machine and the thread expires.”
Another user went further, writing: “Only 5 minutes for cache expires is almost useless.” The user appears to be referring to the message thread expiry, which is separate from Claude’s prompt caching feature.
“Five minutes at the coffee machine and the thread expires.”
That might seem like an unforgiving restriction for a feature designed to improve lengthy coding sessions, however the implications are perhaps not so dramatic. If a developer steps away for ten minutes, say, the thread will indeed have expired. However, provided the client has retained the conversation history, the SDK helper automatically resends it to establish a new thread when they return. So the first request after a break may therefore take longer, but the coding session can continue without losing its previous context.
For agents operating continuously, the limitation may be even less consequential. Every successful request stored in the thread refreshes the five-minute expiry period, meaning an agent making regular API calls can maintain the same thread throughout a lengthy task.
Developers managing threads directly must handle expiry themselves. An attempt to continue an unavailable thread returns a 404 error, requiring the client to resend the complete conversation and establish a new thread.
There are also some data-handling considerations. Anthropic says thread contents are encrypted and held in server memory without being written to persistent storage. Although threads expire after five minutes of inactivity, their contents may remain in memory for up to an hour after their last use.
The feature is currently ineligible for zero data retention and HIPAA, which could restrict its use in environments with stringent data-handling requirements. Certain context-management capabilities, including on-demand compaction, are also unsupported.
Message threads is available across all Claude models in beta, including through Claude Platform on AWS, Claude in Microsoft Foundry, and Anthropic-managed Claude Models on Google Cloud.

articles.title: Votre smartphone Android va sauvegarder automatiquement vos photos et vidéos sur votre PC
articles.text:
Sauvegarder les photos et les vidéos stockées sur votre smartphone Android sans passer par le Cloud est désormais possible. Google vient de lancer en toute discrétion une nouvelle option pour vous permettre de sauvegarder automatiquement vos photos et vidéos sur votre PC en utilisant la fonction de transfert Quick Share. Cette nouvelle fonctionnalité a été déployée avec la dernière mise à jour des services Google pour Android.
Un backup automatique sur votre PC grâce à Quick Share
Concrètement, cette nouvelle option de sauvegarde a été intégrée dans les paramètres associés à Quick Share. Elle fait partie de la dernière mise à jour des services Google Play estampillée 26.43 dont les notes de version mentionnent une nouveauté offrant la « Sauvegarde automatique des photos et vidéos d’un appareil Android vers Windows à l’aide de la fonctionnalité Quick Share ».
Vous la trouverez ainsi en vous rendant dans les Paramètres > Appareils connectés > Préférence de connexion > QuickShare, sous l’intitulé sauvegarde automatique.
« Les fichiers que vous sélectionnez sur ce téléphone seront automatiquement copiés et stockés sur votre PC, sans passer par le stockage sur le cloud et sans coût additionnel » explique Google dans le détail de l’option.
Android Authority, qui rapporte l’information, avait déjà repéré cette nouvelle option de sauvegarde automatique dans le courant du mois d’avril après avoir décortiqué l’APK des services Google Play. Quelques mois plus tard, nos confrères avaient mis en évidence des éléments prouvant que Google prévoyait d’exclure les smartphones Samsung de cette nouvelle fonctionnalité, une restriction qui a visiblement été étendue aux PC du constructeur coréen.
A priori, la mise en place de la sauvegarde automatique devra être initiée depuis l’application Quick Share sur Windows. Il faudra ensuite s’assurer que le smartphone et le PC soient à proximité l’un de l’autre et qu’ils soient tous les deux connectés au même compte Google. Une fois ces prérequis correctement remplis, Quick Share se charge d’exporter automatiquement les photos et vidéos stockées sur votre smartphone vers le stockage interne de votre PC.
À noter que le déploiement de la mise à jour des services Google Play étant fait de manière progressive peut ne pas être disponible dans l’immédiat sur votre smartphone. Il faudra donc vous armer de patience et penser à vérifier de temps en temps si celle-ci a été déployée sur votre appareil.

articles.title: Robot-tondeuse EGO Power+ Aura-R2 : l'absence d'antenne ne règle pas tout
articles.text:
| Surface de tonte maximale | 6000 m2 | 
| Gestion des zones | 40 | 
| Système de tonte | lames pivotantes | 
| Connectivité | Bluetooth, GSM, Wi-Fi | 
| Pente maximale | 50 % | 
| Hauteur de coupe minimale/maximale | 20 / 90 mm | 
| Dimensions (L x l x H) | 670 x 510 x 310 mm | 
| Masse | 15 g | 
| Batterie | 4.6 Ah | 
| Autonomie | 2 heures | 
| Durée de la charge | 90 min | 
| Largeur de coupe | 24 cm | 
| Réglage de hauteur de coupe | électrique | 
| Gestion des zones annexes | Oui | 
| Antivol | Alarme sonore, Code PIN, Verrouillage position GPS | 
| GPS | Oui | 
| Tonte sous la pluie | Oui | 
| Nettoyage au jet d'eau | Oui | 
L'Aura-R2 de la marque EGO associe navigation RTK et caméras pour entretenir la pelouse sans câble périphérique ni antenne imposée. Nous avons testé le RMR1500E, pensé pour une surface de 1500 m², afin de voir comment cette combinaison se comporte dans notre jardin.
EGO passe à la tonte sans câble périphérique avec sa gamme Aura-R2. Pour se repérer dans le jardin, ces robots-tondeuses utilisent un système baptisé Path IQ, qui associe le positionnement satellitaire RTK à des caméras et la reconnaissance des obstacles par intelligence artificielle.
L'ensemble combine notamment une vision binoculaire, une cartographie visuelle de l'environnement et une estimation des déplacements à partir des images et capteurs de mouvement. Les caméras doivent ainsi aider le robot à conserver ses repères lorsque la réception satellite devient moins favorable.
S'il ne s'agit pas d'un modèle totalement affranchi du RTK, l'absence d'antenne dans le jardin est rendue possible par le NetRTK, qui reçoit les corrections de positionnement directement via le réseau. Une antenne externe est toutefois proposée en option.
La gamme comprend trois versions : le RMR1500E testé ici, annoncé pour 1500 m² et lancé à 2099 € ; le RMR3000E pour 3000 m² à 2499 € ; et le RMR6000E pour 6000 m² à 3749 €. Les deux premiers modèles partagent une batterie de 4,6 Ah, contre 9,5 Ah pour le vaisseau amiral. Ils partagent aussi la même largeur de coupe de 24 cm et gèrent jusqu'à 20 zones de tonte, contre 40 zones pour le RMR6000E.
Tous proposent une hauteur de coupe réglable de 2 à 9 cm et sont annoncés pour des pentes atteignant 50 % à l'intérieur de la zone de tonte. Le pilotage passe par l'app EGO Connect, qui s'appuie sur des connexions Bluetooth, wifi et cellulaire pour la configuration, les commandes à distance et la localisation du robot.
Au déballage, l'Aura-R2 fait plutôt bonne impression. Sa carrosserie grise et noire, ses grandes roues arrière et ses touches de vert lui confèrent un aspect assez massif avec des finitions qui semblent soignées. Les bandes lumineuses sur le dessus et l'éclairage avant ajoutent une petite touche futuriste. Ses 15 kg et la poignée arrière permettent de le déplacer à bout de bras.
La boîte comprend le robot, sa station de charge, des piquets de fixation, l'alimentation et les câbles.
Il faut toutefois sortir un tournevis (non fourni). Le branchement de l'alimentation demande en effet de dévisser le capot de la station pour accéder au raccordement. Le câble fourni mesure 10 m, ce qui laisse une certaine marge pour rejoindre une prise de courant.
Sous le châssis, on trouve un disque de coupe central équipé de trois lames, associé à une plaque de protection. Deux petites roues pivotantes à l'avant complètent les grandes roues motrices arrière. Il n'y a pas de module dédié aux bordures, ni de disque déporté pour aller chercher l'herbe au plus près d'un mur.
La mise en route passe par l'app EGO Connect (Android, iOS). Celle-ci détecte le robot en Bluetooth et explique comment activer l'appairage. Nous n'avons rencontré aucune difficulté à cette étape, ni pour la connexion au wifi. Les indications sont suffisamment claires pour avancer sans avoir à consulter le manuel d'utilisation.
Le choix du positionnement permet ensuite de sélectionner le service NetRTK ou une antenne RTK externe. L'application vérifie alors la disponibilité du signal satellitaire avant d'autoriser la suite de l'installation.
C'est ici que l'absence d'antenne ne doit pas prêter à confusion. Le robot doit en effet toujours recevoir correctement le signal des satellites, y compris depuis sa base. En plaçant la station contre un mur, nous nous sommes heurtés à une erreur et avons dû revoir son emplacement. Il a fallu l'éloigner pour trouver un endroit plus dégagé. Le NetRTK allège donc le matériel à installer et la pollution visuelle d'un poteau, mais ne permet pas de ranger la station dans n'importe quel recoin du jardin.
La première cartographie s'est ensuite déroulée sans difficulté. Le robot se pilote avec deux commandes virtuelles sur le smartphone : l'une pour avancer ou reculer, l'autre pour tourner. On lui fait longer les contours de la pelouse afin d'enregistrer les limites, puis on referme le parcours au point de départ. La méthode est classique et permet de suivre les particularités du terrain. Pour cette première zone, nous n'avons pas eu à nous y reprendre.
Le panneau de commandes supérieur réunit un écran, trois touches et l'incontournable bouton rouge d'arrêt d'urgence. Ces commandes physiques permettent notamment de démarrer la tonte, renvoyer le robot à sa station et valider les instructions. Un code PIN sécurise l'ensemble contre les manipulations malveillantes ou les petites mains trop curieuses.
L'app s'avère toutefois indispensable pour affiner les réglages. Sa page principale affiche la carte, la position du robot, le niveau de la batterie et l'état des connexions. Depuis ce tableau de bord, on peut lancer une tonte ponctuelle, la mettre en pause ou exiger un retour à la base. Pendant le travail, l'interface indique aussi la progression du cycle et la surface déjà couverte.
Le réglage motorisé de la hauteur de coupe constitue un excellent point. S'étalant de 2 à 9 cm par paliers de 5 mm, la plage est suffisamment vaste pour conserver un gazon ras ou laisser davantage de hauteur selon la saison et la configuration du terrain. Ce paramètre peut être appliqué de manière globale ou défini zone par zone.
Les programmes de travail permettent quant à eux de sélectionner les jours, les créneaux horaires et les zones concernées. Il est aussi possible de définir une direction de tonte à chaque parcelle. Deux modes de fonctionnement sont proposés : le standard, qui privilégie la vitesse d’exécution ; et la coupe fine, qui ralentit le robot pour soigner le résultat. Le capteur de pluie, les annonces vocales, les phares et l'éclairage d'ambiance disposent également de leurs propres réglages.
Pour la gestion des obstacles, l'app propose d'activer une sensibilité renforcée (près des limites ou sur l'ensemble du jardin) afin de mieux repérer les petits objets et éléments bas. Les phares avant garantissent de leur côté une perception visuelle efficace en cas de faible luminosité, autorisant ainsi le travail de nuit.
La protection antivol se montre assez complète. En plus du code PIN de sécurité, EGO a prévu un système de localisation du robot, une alarme et une limite de zone de fonctionnement paramétrable. L'application permet en outre de déclencher un signal sonore ou de verrouiller la tondeuse à distance. Des fonctions très utiles pour localiser une machine dérobée ou être alerté dès qu'elle quitte son périmètre.
L'édition de la cartographie s'avère moins convaincante. S'il est possible d'ajouter des zones de tonte, créer des espaces interdits et définir des chemins de liaison, le système oblige à guider le robot au joystick pour tracer ou reprendre le moindre contour. Impossible, par exemple, de réajuster une limite ou de dessiner une zone d'exclusion du bout du doigt sur l'écran, contrairement à ce que proposent certains concurrents.
Nous aurions pu nous accommoder de cette contrainte logicielle si la procédure avait fonctionné à chaque fois. Les véritables complications sont apparues lors de l'ajout d'une zone. En pleine phase d'enregistrement, la communication s'est coupée à plusieurs reprises, nous renvoyant brutalement à l'écran d'accueil. L'interface se figeait alors sur le statut “cartographie en cours”, sans offrir la possibilité de reprendre le pilotage ni de finaliser le tracé. La seule solution de repli consistait à redémarrer physiquement le robot.
Après six tentatives infructueuses, nous avons fini par jeter l'éponge, bien que nous soyons restés à proximité de la machine. Difficile dans ces conditions de déterminer si le problème venait de la liaison Bluetooth, du wifi, du signal de positionnement ou d'un bug du logiciel lui-même. L'association de technologies de navigation vantée par EGO ne nous a malheureusement pas prémunis contre ces interruptions répétées.
Pour le nettoyage, le robot bénéficie d'une certification IP66. Le manuel d'utilisation recommande un nettoyage à la brosse pour les roues, les lames et le châssis, ainsi qu'un passage au chiffon humide pour la carrosserie. De son côté, la FAQ du fabricant autorise le nettoyage au jet d'eau.
Sur notre première zone, l’Aura-R2 effectue sa tonte sans se bloquer. Il circule correctement sur la pelouse et s'engage sans difficulté particulière dans notre passage étroit le long de la terrasse. Nous n'avons pas eu à le dégager ou replacer manuellement pour qu'il termine son parcours. C'est déjà un bon point.
La reconnaissance des obstacles se montre également convaincante dans nos essais. Notre balle de tennis a bien été détectée et évitée. Le robot a aussi identifié le bananier nain présent sur son trajet.
Les approches ne sont toutefois pas toujours aussi délicates. Il lui arrive de buter sur les bords de l'arbuste, ainsi que lorsqu'il négocie les virages serrés près des angles de terrasse. Ces contacts ne l'ont jamais immobilisé pendant notre essai, mais l'évitement ne se fait pas toujours sans toucher. Si la détection est satisfaisante, la manière de contourner certains obstacles peut encore progresser.
Le choix des trajectoires appelle lui aussi quelques réserves. Avec le sens de tonte laissé par défaut, le robot a parfois préféré multiplier les allers-retours sur la largeur d'une zone de 2 à 3 m, plutôt que d'en exploiter la longueur. Il passe alors davantage de temps à faire demi-tour. Puisque l’app permet de choisir l'orientation par zone, mieux vaut ajuster ce paramètre lorsque la disposition du terrain s'y prête.
Le principal problème reste la couverture. À l'issue de notre cycle, certaines portions de pelouse n'avaient pas été correctement traitées, sans qu'un obstacle explique ces oublis. L'application affichait une progression de 100 % alors que des zones ignorées étaient parfaitement visibles sur la cartographie. Le robot a donc terminé sa tâche, mais le résultat sur le terrain restait incomplet et toute la zone n'a pas été tondue intégralement.
Les bordures réclament aussi une reprise manuelle, le disque central ne disposant d'aucun mécanisme particulier pour atteindre l'herbe au ras d'un mur ou d'une terrasse surélevée. Comme sur beaucoup de robots-tondeuses, il faut donc conserver un coupe-bordures pour les finitions.
Enfin, la batterie de notre RMR1500E se vide assez rapidement. Lors d'un relevé, elle est passée de 95 à 61 % pour seulement 34 m² indiqués comme couverts. Ce cycle ne permet pas d'extrapoler une surface maximale par charge, car les demi-tours, la forme de la zone et les manœuvres jouent sur la consommation. EGO indique une durée moyenne de tonte de 110 min et une recharge d'environ 90 min pour ce modèle. Ce temps de charge limite l'attente entre deux sorties.
L'EGO Aura-R2 présente des qualités appréciables avec une reconnaissance des obstacles convaincante, une large plage de hauteur de coupe et une protection antivol complète. Le NetRTK simplifie grandement l'installation, même si la réception satellitaire impose toujours des contraintes d'emplacement pour la station. L'expérience est toutefois pénalisée par des interruptions de cartographie qui nous ont empêchés d'ajouter une zone, ainsi qu’une couverture incomplète dans notre jardin biscornu. EGO doit donc améliorer la stabilité et le comportement de ses app et firmware pour rendre l'ensemble plus fiable. La construction soignée et la capacité à circuler sans blocage constituent néanmoins une base encourageante.
Le Mammotion Luba 3 AWD se distingue par sa navigation associant NetRTK, lidar et vision, son double disque de coupe de 40 cm et une application permettant de modifier facilement les zones directement sur la carte. L'Ecovacs Goat A1600 LiDAR Pro offre pour sa part une navigation indépendante du signal satellitaire grâce à ses LiDAR, ainsi qu'un module coupe-bordures réduisant le travail de finition sur les limites adaptées.

articles.title: UK school estate hit by 3AM ransomware in suspected AI-assisted attack
articles.text:
A 3AM ransomware affiliate targeted a school estate in the UK and successfully encrypted around 37 of nearly 50 machines reached from an unmanaged host.
Researchers at cybersecurity company Bitdefender believe the threat actor may have used AI-generated commands and an automated agentic loop to carry out the operation.
The conclusion is based on a sequence of repeated commands that were slightly modified at each attempt and issued at roughly regular intervals of 40 to 100 seconds.
"We were not able to access the machine the attacker worked from, so we cannot document anything about the language model itself: which model it was, whether it ran locally or remotely, or even whether a person was copying and pasting instructions and results between the implant and the model," Bitdefender explains.
The researchers note that they could only document the behavior, and it looked similar to an agentic loop.
The malicious activity spanned between September 10 and19, but Bitdefender could not establish the attacker’s initial access method.
The threat actor used a modified public PowerShell tool to extract and decrypt credentials stored on three Veeam backup servers, copied a Chrome database containing credentials, and deployed Mimikatz and LSASS memory-dumping tools.
They mapped domain relationships and searched logon-script folders for references to other schools, eventually creating two backdoor domain administrator accounts named ‘library’ and ‘svc_bkpmon.’
After stealing financial data from compromised machines, the attacker configured two-way trusts between three previously separate Active Directory domains to expand their reach.
In the final stage of the attack, they attempted to remove Sophos and Bitdefender protection from reachable hosts, delete system-state backups, and deploy 3AM’s Rust-based encryptor. They succeeded in about 37 cases.
The 3AM ransomware threat emerged in 2023 and came to public attention when an attacker deployed its Rust-based ransomware after LockBit was blocked.
Researchers later linked the operation to the Conti and Royal ransomware gangs, and affiliates have been observed using email bombing and spoofed IT support calls to access corporate networks.
A notable past victim is Kootenai Health, where an August 2024 attack exposed personal information belonging to more than 464,000 patients.
Regardless of the current level of AI tool involvement in 3AM attacks, Bitdefender’s observations suggest the threat actors appear to be experimenting with them heavily.
Earlier today, the NCSC in the UK published this year’s ‘The State of the Cyber Nation’ report, urging critical infrastructure to prepare for AI-powered ransomware attacks by 2028.

articles.title: "Es una cuestión de salud mental": cada vez más padres están pagando hasta 260 euros la noche a niñeras nocturnas
articles.text:
Blanca Yamira Ortiz García tiene 56 años, es puericultora y por cada noche que pasa en casa de una familia con un recién nacido cobra 260 euros, una tarifa que en un buen mes le permite ganar entre 4.000 y 5.000 euros. Su trabajo consiste en que los padres duerman mientras ella se ocupa del bebé, y hay clientas que lo tienen claro: “Para mí es una cuestión de salud mental”. Así lo cuenta un reportaje de Corriere della Sera sobre las llamadas night nannies, o niñeras nocturnas.
Una noche entera de guardia. El turno de Yamira, que ahora trabaja para una familia de Lugano (Suiza), empieza a las 21:00. Entra en la casa, se quita los zapatos, se lava las manos, cambia el pañal al bebé, a menudo lo baña y después se queda despierta a oscuras mientras el resto de la familia duerme. Si el pequeño tiene hambre, es ella quien prepara el biberón, y a la madre solo la despierta cuando toca darle el pecho.
“Yo estoy siempre ahí, preparada para actuar”, reconoce esta puericultora, que en Ecuador llegó a trabajar en un banco y asegura que nunca había ganado tanto como ahora. Eso sí, el oficio tiene su peaje, y ella misma lo resume sin rodeos: “Las puericultoras nocturnas ya no tenemos vida propia, renunciamos a todo para ofrecer este servicio. Desde hace años me despierto cada dos horas por la noche, incluso cuando estoy de vacaciones”.
Puericultoras, no canguros. Y Yamira no es la única. Renata Wetter, de 61 años, es otra de las profesionales con las que habló el diario italiano, y lo primero que deja claro es que no es “ni niñera ni canguro”, porque la puericultura está reconocida en Italia como una profesión auxiliar del ámbito sanitario que exige una titulación. Ella cobra 180 euros por noche y, al igual que Yamira, tiene formación específica para atender a recién nacidos.
¿Y qué las diferencia de una niñera de las de toda la vida? Pues que tienen un papel doble, porque además de cuidar al bebé, algo que también puede hacer cualquier cuidadora convencional, se encargan de que los padres recuperen las horas de sueño que se pierden entre pañales y biberones. Vamos, que lo que venden es tanto el cuidado del pequeño como el descanso de los adultos.
Una idea con recorrido. La figura tampoco es nueva, y en Reino Unido lleva tiempo funcionando. The Guardian le dedicaba un reportaje en abril de 2018 a raíz del estreno de ‘Tully’, la película en la que Charlize Theron interpreta a una madre desbordada que acaba recurriendo a una niñera nocturna. En él aparecía Anastasia Baker, una antigua periodista de la BBC que asegura haber sido la primera en montar una agencia de este tipo, Night Nannies, en 1999, después de tener a su segundo hijo y no encontrar a nadie que ofreciera ese servicio.
Casi dos décadas después, en 2018, su agencia contaba con unas 200 cuidadoras trabajando en Londres y el sur de Inglaterra y había atendido a más de 10.000 familias, con una tarifa habitual de 155 libras por una noche de 21:00 a 7:00. Y el negocio ha seguido creciendo, porque según el reportaje italiano su red supera ya las 500 enfermeras, matronas y niñeras.
También como beneficio laboral. La promesa de dormir del tirón ha llegado incluso a las empresas. Financial Times se preguntaba en un artículo si las niñeras nocturnas eran un beneficio laboral excesivo. Según el resumen que publicó Expat.com en 2024, algunas compañías han decidido pagar este servicio porque las noches en vela pasan factura al rendimiento en el trabajo, y una de las citadas por el diario británico ofrecía cuatro meses de baja de maternidad totalmente pagada y ponía además una niñera nocturna a disposición de quien decidiera volver a trabajar en lugar de agotar parte de ese permiso.
Y es que el descanso tiene un valor que mucha gente está dispuesta a pagar. En una encuesta de OnePoll para la cadena de colchones Mattress Firm publicada a finales de 2018, muchos estadounidenses decían que pagarían casi 300 dólares por una noche de sueño “perfecto”.
Un regalo para la familia. ¿Es entonces un servicio reservado a familias acomodadas? Las tarifas no están al alcance de todos los bolsillos, pero el reportaje italiano describe una demanda que no deja de crecer en Milán y otras ciudades. Además, no todas las familias contratan a estas profesionales durante meses: hay quien se conforma con las primeras semanas. Es el caso de una abogada de 38 años que vive en Milán y que, embarazada de nueve meses, ya ha reservado a dos puericultoras para que se turnen durante la primera semana de vida de su hijo, siete noches seguidas, antes de ir reduciendo el servicio poco a poco.
“Con nuestro primer hijo, mi pareja me regaló un anillo precioso. Esta vez le he pedido que haga un regalo a toda la familia: contratar a una puericultora. Y ya se lo he dejado claro: ‘No quiero anularme como persona ni verme obligada a despertarme ni una sola vez en toda la noche’”, cuenta. Aunque su madre se muestra “escéptica” y considera la decisión “un capricho”, ella asegura que no siente “culpa alguna” y que un entorno positivo beneficia al bebé.
Detrás de todo esto hay también un cambio en cómo y cuándo se tienen hijos. Los datos de Eurostat recogidos por ConSalud muestran que en la Unión Europea siguen creciendo los nacimientos de madres de 35 años o más, lo que posiblemente haga más habitual encontrar a madres primerizas con una carrera asentada y unos ingresos que les permiten pagar este tipo de servicios, a menudo lejos de sus propios padres porque se mudaron por trabajo. Y la tendencia no se queda en Europa, porque en China el negocio de los cuidados de lujo tras el parto ha dado lugar a centros que ya en 2018 cobraban más de 10.000 dólares al mes, y a otros con estancias premium de más de 50.000 euros.
Foto | Ruben Daniel

articles.title: Building ultra-low-latency voice AI applications on AWS | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Building ultra-low-latency voice AI applications on AWS
Conversational AI is transforming how humans interact with technology. From virtual assistants and AI-powered contact centers to real-time translation and accessibility tools, voice-first interfaces are rapidly becoming the default mode of interaction for millions of users worldwide.
Yet delivering a truly natural voice experience remains one of the hardest challenges in AI infrastructure. Users expect human-like responsiveness. Excess latency can break conversational flow and erode trust. To feel natural, AI-generated speech must arrive within the same temporal window as human turn-taking.
This post introduces how Cartesia, an AWS Partner specializing in real-time voice AI, uses purpose-built State Space Models (SSMs) and AWS infrastructure to deliver sub-100ms text-to-speech and speech-to-text at global scale. Developers can build voice experiences that feel indistinguishable from human conversation.
The rise of conversational AI and latency expectations
The demand for real-time voice AI is growing rapidly across industries:
- Contact centers: AI agents handling millions of customer interactions require instantaneous speech generation to maintain natural dialogue.
- Telehealth: Remote patient consultations demand low-latency voice for accurate, empathetic communication.
- Gaming and virtual worlds: Immersive experiences require real-time voice synthesis for non-player characters (NPCs) and player interactions.
- Accessibility: Screen readers and voice interfaces must respond instantly to serve users with visual impairments.
- Inbound and outbound sales: AI sales agents must respond without awkward pauses to qualify leads, handle objections, and keep prospects on the line.
Traditional transformer-based text-to-speech (TTS) models struggle with streaming latency because they process entire sequences before producing output. This architectural limitation creates a fundamental tension: higher quality often means higher latency. A new class of models, State Space Models, resolves this trade-off.
AI for voice: State Space Models (SSM)
State Space Models (SSMs) take a fundamentally different approach to processing sequences than transformers, the architecture behind most of today’s AI. Transformers use a mechanism called attention, which compares every element in a sequence to every other element. As a result, the amount of computation grows quadratically as the sequence gets longer. SSMs instead treat a sequence as a system that evolves continuously over time, processing it step by step and carrying a compact internal state forward. This can be converted into a form computers handle efficiently, keeping the cost low for certain long sequences. This efficiency makes SSMs well suited to real-time, streaming data like live speech.
Key advantages of SSMs for audio processing include:
- High-quality long-range dependencies: Structured SSMs are a form of linear recurrence, but their state parameterization preserves information over long audio sequences, avoiding the long-range signal decay that limits classic recurrent neural networks (RNNs) such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks.
- Constant memory footprint: Unlike transformers that cache all previous tokens, SSMs maintain a fixed-size hidden state.
- Native streaming support: The recurrent structure processes input token-by-token, so it supports true streaming without architectural modifications.
These properties make SSMs uniquely suited for real-time voice applications where both quality and latency are non-negotiable.
How it works: SSMs for real-time voice
Cartesia puts these SSM advantages to work in two production voice models: Sonic for speech generation and Ink for transcription.
Introducing Cartesia
Cartesia is a real-time multimodal intelligence company that has built a voice AI application, purpose-built on State Space Model architecture. Founded by researchers who pioneered SSM advances, Cartesia’s application is designed for streaming inference at the edge of human perception.
The application features two core models, Sonic for text-to-speech and Ink for speech-to-text, both optimized for sub-100ms first-byte latency while maintaining studio-quality output.
Sonic (text-to-speech)
Sonic is Cartesia’s flagship streaming text-to-speech model, delivering ultra-realistic speech synthesis with sub-100ms latency:
- First audio byte in approximately 90ms: Users hear the voice respond almost instantaneously.
- Ultra-realistic voice quality: Natural prosody, emotion, and expressiveness across over 44 languages.
- Voice cloning with minimal data: Create natural-sounding custom voices from 10-second audio samples.
- Streaming-native architecture: Audio begins generating before the full text input is received.
- Context-aware synthesis: Maintains consistent tone and style across long passages.
Sonic is recommended for teams that want the fastest time-to-production with minimal operational overhead. Call the API and receive streaming audio in real time.
Ink (speech-to-text)
Ink is Cartesia’s streaming speech-to-text model, purpose-built for conversational AI applications:
- Native turn detection: Automatically identifies when a speaker has finished their turn, alleviating awkward pauses without a separate voice activity detection (VAD) or end pointing model.
- Context-aware end pointing: Uses semantic understanding to distinguish between mid-sentence pauses and true conversation boundaries.
- Streaming transcription: Emits partial transcripts in real time as the user speaks, so a downstream large language model (LLM) can begin forming its response before the turn ends.
- Noise robustness: Maintains accuracy in noisy environments common in real-world deployments.
- Multi-speaker support: Handles overlapping speech and speaker transitions gracefully.
Together, Sonic and Ink provide the complete voice AI stack needed to build conversational agents that feel human.
Deploying Cartesia on AWS
If you need data sovereignty, latency control, or compliance, you can deploy Cartesia models directly into your own AWS account. Sonic is delivered as an Amazon SageMaker AI model package through AWS Marketplace, which you deploy to a SageMaker AI endpoint running entirely within your virtual private cloud (VPC). Inference data doesn’t leave your account.
The deployment patterns in this section cover Sonic. Ink is currently available through the Cartesia API, which you can purchase through the Cartesia Voice AI Platform listing in AWS Marketplace. Two primary patterns are available for Sonic.
Option 1: Amazon SageMaker AI (AWS Marketplace model package)
Deploying on Amazon SageMaker AI is the fastest path to a managed, in-VPC Sonic endpoint. Sonic ships as an AWS Marketplace model package, so there’s a one-time subscribe step that grants your account an AWS Region-specific model-package ARN. You then create the SageMaker AI endpoint from that ARN, either from the console or with the SageMaker or Boto3 SDK. The following steps follow Cartesia’s official deployment notebook.
Prerequisites
Run from an Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instance or SageMaker Studio.
The AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role needs AmazonSageMakerFullAccess.
To subscribe, your role (and you) need aws-marketplace:Subscribe, aws-marketplace:Unsubscribe, and aws-marketplace:ViewSubscriptions. Otherwise, the account must already be subscribed to the listing.
Before deployment, choose a supported instance type from the model package’s SupportedRealtimeInferenceInstanceTypes field:
- ml.g6e.xlarge or larger
- ml.g7e.2xlarge or larger
- ml.g7.2xlarge or larger
- ml.p5.48xlarge
- ml.p5en.48xlarge
If your chosen instance type’s applied value is below your current usage plus your planned endpoint instance count, you may need to request a service quota increase. See SageMaker AI quotas for details.
Deploy Sonic 3.6 to a SageMaker endpoint
In Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, you can subscribe to its AWS Marketplace model package, create a SageMaker model, and host it on a real-time endpoint. The following four steps show the deployment path.
- In SageMaker AI, open AWS Marketplace resources, then All products. Search for Sonic 3.6 SageMaker and choose the Cartesia listing.
- Choose View purchase options, review the pricing and terms, and subscribe. The subscription grants your AWS account access to the model package. It doesn’t deploy resources.
- Open Deployments & inference > Deployable models, choose Create model, select Use a model package subscription from AWS Marketplace, and select Sonic 3.6 SageMaker. Choose an execution role, then create the model.
- Create a real-time endpoint from the model with a supported GPU instance, such as ml.g6e.2xlarge. The endpoint first appears with Creating status. Wait for InService before invoking it.
The model-package ARN is Region-specific. To verify the Sonic 3.6 package in US East (N. Virginia) with the SageMaker API, run:
After the endpoint reaches InService, invoke it with the SageMaker Runtime InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream API and process the returned audio stream in your application.
Option 2: Self-managed on EC2 GPU instances
Some teams have existing GPU infrastructure, strict networking requirements, or a need to co-locate Cartesia with other services. For these cases, you can run the model container yourself on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) GPU instances. This gives you full control over the runtime, scaling, and network path. It uses Cartesia’s container image, obtained from Cartesia, rather than the AWS Marketplace model package.
Obtain the container image. Request the Sonic container image and licensing terms from Cartesia. Replicate it into your own private Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository so your compute plane can pull it with IAM-scoped credentials rather than reaching out to an external registry at scale.
Choose your GPU instance family. Sonic runs on NVIDIA GPU instances. The G6 (L4) and G6e (L40S) families are the optimal balance for real-time TTS. The earlier G5 (A10G) also works. Match GPU memory and vCPU to your target concurrency and prefer a single-GPU instance per model replica for simplest scaling.
Provision the compute plane (Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS)). For ECS: register a GPU task definition (set the container’s GPU resource requirement, for example, resourceRequirements with type GPU) and run it as a service behind an Application Load Balancer. For EKS: create a GPU node group (or Karpenter provisioner) using the EKS GPU-optimized AMI, install the NVIDIA device plugin, and deploy the container as a Deployment fronted by a Service/Ingress.
Configure networking for low latency. Place inference nodes in a cluster placement group to minimize inter-node latency, keep replicas in a single Availability Zone for the tightest path, and use VPC endpoints for ECR/S3 pulls. For hybrid or on-premises callers, terminate traffic over AWS Direct Connect or a private Network Load Balancer to avoid public-internet hops.
Load model weights efficiently. Store model weights on a shared, low-latency volume (Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) or Amazon FSx for Lustre) mounted across replicas so new pods/tasks start without each re-downloading multi-GB artifacts. Warm the model at container start and expose a health check so the load balancer only routes to ready replicas.
Tune batching and concurrency. Set the container’s max batch size and concurrent-stream limits to match your traffic profile. Higher batch size improves GPU utilization but adds first-byte latency, so tune against your sub-100ms target. Benchmark streams-per-GPU to find the replica capacity you will scale on.
Implement custom auto scaling. Scale on a signal that reflects real load, active audio-stream count or GPU utilization, rather than CPU. On Amazon ECS, use AWS Application Auto Scaling with a custom Amazon CloudWatch metric. On Amazon EKS, use HPA/KEDA driven by a GPU or stream-count metric, with Karpenter (or Cluster Autoscaler) adding GPU nodes as replicas grow.
Add observability and resiliency. Emit latency (time-to-first-byte), stream counts, and GPU metrics to CloudWatch. Run at least two replicas across nodes for availability. Set rolling-update or draining policies so deployments don’t drop in-flight audio streams.
This approach is recommended when integrating Cartesia into an existing machine learning (ML) system, meeting networking or compliance requirements not available through managed services, or optimizing cost with Reserved or Spot GPU capacity. The trade-off is that you own provisioning, scaling, patching, and monitoring that SageMaker would otherwise handle for you.
Learn more: See Amazon ECS task definitions for GPU workloads, managing NVIDIA GPU devices on Amazon EKS, and getting started with GPU-accelerated EC2 instances.
Choosing the right deployment pattern
AWS offers two ways to run Sonic, each suited to a different starting point.
The managed path, using the Amazon SageMaker AI model package from AWS Marketplace, is the default for most teams: you subscribe, deploy to an in-VPC endpoint in minutes, and let SageMaker handle scaling and operations.
The self-managed path, running the model container yourself on EC2 GPU instances, is designed for teams with specific constraints: existing GPU infrastructure, strict networking requirements, or a need to co-locate Cartesia with other services. For these teams, full control over the runtime, scaling, and network path matters more than time to deployment.
The following table summarizes how the two compare.
| Criteria | SageMaker (Marketplace) | EC2 GPU (Self-Managed) | 
| Time to Deployment | Minutes after subscribing | Hours to days | 
| Compute | Real-time endpoint. See SupportedRealtimeInferenceInstanceTypes for supported instances. | EC2 GPU instances | 
| Operational Control | Managed by AWS | Full control | 
| Scaling | SageMaker automatic scaling | Custom scaling policies | 
| Cost Model | Software fee + per instance hour + infra | EC2 (Reserved/Spot savings) | 
| Networking | In-VPC endpoint (network isolation) | Placement groups, Direct Connect | 
| Best For | Fast, managed, in-VPC | Custom infra, max control | 
Beyond deploying Cartesia in your own account, these models are already proven in production inside Amazon services, and few environments are more demanding for real-time voice than a live contact center. Amazon Connect is exactly that proving ground.
In production: Amazon Connect
This section shows how Cartesia’s voice models operate inside Amazon Connect at production scale.
What is Amazon Connect?
Amazon Connect is a cloud-based contact center service that businesses use to set up and run customer support operations that handle inbound and outbound voice calls, chat, and messaging. With pay-as-you-go pricing and deep integration with AWS services, Amazon Connect powers millions of customer interactions daily across industries from financial services to healthcare.
How Cartesia powers the Amazon Connect experience
Cartesia’s voice AI models integrate natively with Amazon Connect to deliver next-generation contact center experiences:
- Instant responsiveness: Alleviate unnatural pauses that erode customer confidence in AI-powered interactions.
- Real-time transcription: Ink provides live transcription with intelligent turn detection for agent-assist workflows.
- Multilingual support: Serve customers in over 44 languages with consistent voice quality and natural prosody.

articles.title: IFC bets on cash-flow lending for African MSMEs
articles.text:
African enterprises are being strangled by short-term dollar debt, over-leveraged balance sheets, and administrative red tape, threatening the continent’s ability to generate employment for its fast-growing youth population.
Delivering his address at the Africa Financial Summit (AFIS) in Luanda on Tuesday, Makhtar Diop, Managing Director of the International Finance Corporation (IFC), issued a blunt assessment of Africa’s structural capital mismatch.
Addressing central bank governors, finance ministers, and commercial bank executives, Diop argued that while the continent’s projected 4.5% economic growth is notable amid global headwinds, it remains insufficient to absorb millions of young entrants into the labour market.
With advanced economies cutting foreign aid budgets and domestic fiscal space severely constrained by inflation and public debt, Diop warned that Africa can no longer depend on external development assistance. Instead, domestic and international savings must be mobilised into productive enterprise through local-currency credit, long-term debt, and equity.
“When we talk to leaders across the continent, they all raise the same challenge: how can we create jobs for our very young population?” Diop said. “If we do not create those jobs, we risk the kind of situation we are already seeing today, fueled by anxiety over climate change, geopolitics, mental health, regional and global pandemics, and other pressures. These challenges weigh heavily on young people, who may take to the streets and demand change. So we need to focus totally and utterly on job creation.”
The real-sector capital mismatch
According to Diop, the fundamental barrier to African competitiveness is not a shortage of domestic savings, but the absence of viable financial instruments to intermediate those funds.
Drawing from consultations with private sector operators across the continent, Diop identified five structural distortions handicapping African businesses:
African firms are ‘forced’ to finance long-term capital investments with short-term bank facilities, undermining corporate durability. Enterprises across the continent are excessively leveraged because risk capital remains scarce at scale. “You can lend to a company, but you build a company with equity,” Diop noted.
Companies continue to incur debt in US dollars while generating revenues in depreciating domestic currencies. Subdued corporate bond issuance prevents local institutional capital, including pension funds, from backing domestic firms. Diop dismissed the narrative that domestic investors lack an appetite for African risk, noting that quality issuances are consistently oversubscribed.
Unpredictable regulatory changes continue to deter multi-year capital deployment. Beyond financial mechanics, Diop called for an administrative overhaul of African civil services, arguing that public bureaucracies often view the private sector with suspicion rather than as an engine of job creation.
“In many countries, public administrations still do not see themselves as being there to serve the private sector,” Diop said. “The feeling among the private sector in many countries is that businesses still have to struggle to make civil servants understand that they are there to serve the country and help create jobs. So, there is a cultural revolution that still needs to happen.”
To bridge the gap between statutory legislation and real-world implementation, Diop proposed establishing permanent national “Private Sector Councils.” These bodies would provide heads of state and finance ministries with a real-time feedback loop on how commercial laws are applied on the ground and recommend rapid corrective interventions.
Ditching collateral for cash flow and fintech
A core pillar of the IFC’s African agenda, Diop stressed, involves dismantling traditional collateral constraints for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs). Historically, African commercial banks have rationed credit based on immovable assets such as real estate, thereby automatically excluding the majority of informal and emerging businesses.
Diop stated that the IFC is actively shifting its focus toward non-bank financial intermediaries, deploying fintech platforms and digital telematics to underwrite borrowers based on observable revenue rather than fixed property.
“We want to move from lending based on collateral towards lending based on cash flow,” Diop said. “Data is the new gold. That is why the fintech agenda is so important for IFC. By using new technologies and the fintech architecture, we will be able to reach many more MSMEs.”
To shield borrowers from exchange rate volatility, the IFC is also expanding its local-currency exposure. Around 35% of the corporation’s continental commitments are currently disbursed in local currencies, with internal targets to increase that share substantially.
Mobilisation targets
Under its “IFC 2030 Strategy,” the World Bank Group’s private-sector lending arm has re-engineered its balance sheet to act as a catalyst for private co-investment.
Five years ago, the institution managed roughly $33 billion in combined financing, mobilising $0.90 of commercial capital for every $1 of its own funds. Today, annual commitments have exceeded $100 billion, with a global mobilisation ratio of 3.4-to-1.
Africa accounts for approximately 25% of the IFC’s total global portfolio. While the corporation’s African mobilisation ratio has climbed from $0.60 to $1.50 per dollar deployed, Diop set a target to scale that ratio to 5-to-1 in the coming years.
To unlock offshore institutional liquidity, the IFC is reallocating personnel directly into major financial capitals, including London, New York, Tokyo, Frankfurt, and Sydney.
Dedicated investor-relations teams are tasked with channelling international sovereign wealth funds and institutional asset managers into African equity funds, infrastructure corridors, and clean energy projects.
Simultaneously, the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), the political risk insurance arm of the World Bank Group, has met its $25 billion guarantee target years ahead of its 2030 deadline, providing risk-mitigation instruments to reassure private investors entering volatile markets.
Deepening continental partnerships
Domestically, the IFC is backing the consolidation of African commercial banking under its Local Champions Initiative, helping indigenous and regional lenders fill the space vacated by multinational European and American banks that have exited the continent over the past decade.
In the host country, Angola, where the government has curbed public debt and brought inflation down to 8.43%, Diop confirmed he will sign two major direct-financing agreements with domestic agricultural companies this week to advance food security and reduce reliance on imports.
Regionally, the institution is collaborating with African multilateral partners. Diop noted that Ethiopis Tafara, IFC’s Vice President for Africa, is leading a joint initiative with Dr Sidi Ould Tah, President of the African Development Bank (AfDB), to coordinate with domestic sovereign wealth funds and institutional asset managers to mobilise internal long-term capital for trade and regional transport corridors.
As global liquidity tightens, the strategic direction outlined in Luanda signals an end to the reliance on traditional concessionary aid. For the IFC and its institutional partners, Africa’s economic future depends on structuring investable, local-currency instruments that convert domestic savings into real-economy employment.

articles.title: OPINION: Healthcare’s pilot culture is holding back HealthTech innovation | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Across Europe, HealthTech companies are developing new technologies that can improve patient care, ease pressure on clinicians and help health services make better use of limited resources. But while these technologies are often successful in getting into hospitals in the pilot phase, many struggle to move beyond that and secure long term adoption.
This is not a new problem. Companies working with large public healthcare organisations, like the UK’s National Health Service (NHS) or Ireland’s Health Service Executive (HSE), are familiar with the issues surrounding new technology implementation. These organisations work at a considerable scale with complex responsibilities and obligations around patient safety and public spending. In short, widespread implementation of new technology, no matter how innovative, can often be met with hesitancy.
And while the caution is understandable, with so many companies unable to get out of the pilot phase, it raises the question of whether processes are designed to welcome innovation or whether they are designed to keep healthcare stuck in its ways.
The problem with pilot culture
Pilots play an important role in healthcare innovation. They allow clinicians to assess whether a technology works in practice, from how patients respond to identifying changes needed before wider implementation. They are the first step to mass adoption of new technologies, but far too frequently, they are also the last step.
Wider adoption of successful pilots can run into issues on many fronts: Who owns the budget needed to buy the technology? Which team is responsible for implementation? How will the technology work with existing systems? Who provides training and support?
These are all questions that should be obvious but are often addressed far too late and end up stopping adoption in its tracks.
Another issue is the fact that the clinicians who champion pilots are often the people most willing to experiment; some can even be evangelistic about new technologies. However, their colleagues may not have the same priorities or passions and so a technology that works well in one department can struggle to get buy-in from the key stakeholders across other departments.
Procurement can favour the familiar
Procurement is another point where promising HealthTech companies can encounter difficulties.
Healthcare procurement carries the huge responsibility of spending public money, meaning they need to find suppliers that are financially sound with products that must meet the appropriate clinical, technical, and regulatory requirements. They need to have complete confidence in what they’re choosing.
A young, unestablished HealthTech company may not garner that confidence, no matter how effective the solution they have developed is. Young companies are also up against it when it comes to meeting the requirements set out by procurement, which are often designed around suppliers with years of experience securing public-sector contracts.
This creates a difficult cycle where a company needs a contract to build its track record, but needs a track record to secure the contract.
Not to mention the fact that procurement’s decisions can often focus mainly on price, so a technology that carries a high immediate cost may struggle to secure approval.
The result of these issues can be an unintended preference for established suppliers, even when a smaller company has a better approach to a clinical problem.
When caution becomes culture
Similar to the case with procurement, healthcare providers have to make sure that what they are offering the public is backed by an incredibly high standard of evidence and accountability. This can create a culture that puts caution ahead of good clinical outcomes and this can actually create risks of its own, as delaying the adoption of useful technology as a result of being overly cautious can have negative consequences for patients, clinicians and public finances not to mention the commercial consequence for Europe.
HealthTech startups need to generate revenue, build a sustainable business and invest in further development. If the route from pilot to procurement remains unpredictable, companies may struggle to plan their growth or attract the investment required to expand.
For many it may push them to look to markets where purchasing decisions are more straightforward, meaning healthcare organisations risk losing access to innovations developed close to home, while European companies lose opportunities to build global businesses from their early clinical successes.
Build the route to scale from day one
There are practical steps healthcare systems can take to improve the path from pilot to adoption.
First, the people responsible for implementation and procurement should be involved early. An enthusiastic clinician on-side is valuable, but a pilot also needs buy-in from finance, IT, operations, procurement and those who will support the technology after launch. They can’t be overlooked.
Second, pilots should be designed with scale in mind. Before a trial begins, the organisation and supplier should agree what success looks like, which outcomes will be measured and what evidence would justify wider deployment. They should also consider training, integration, support costs and the effect on existing workflows.
Third, procurement requirements should better balance risk, costs and the long-term benefits of proposed technology. And the evidence new healthcare companies are required to give should be proportionate to the contract and the potential consequences of failure. The size and the experience of the company should not determine the outcome if the solution they are offering is genuinely helpful to clinicians and/or patients.
Finally, healthcare organisations should learn from their own pilots. Sharing results, including unsuccessful projects and the reasons behind them, can reduce duplication and help other teams make better decisions when it comes to their own pilots. Working in silos doesn’t help anyone.
Innovation needs a destination
The NHS has previously recognised the importance of tackling the problems with pilot culture through innovation guidelines, which help innovators navigate the routes towards wider use.
In Ireland, the HSE’s Framework for Health Innovation was also introduced this year with the explicit aim of creating a more consistent pathway from local ideas and pilots to lasting impact across the health system.
These initiatives point towards the same underlying need: successful experiments must have a realistic route into everyday healthcare.
Europe has the talent and entrepreneurial ambition to build world-class HealthTech companies. Giving those companies a credible route from evidence to adoption will help ensure their innovations have the opportunity to make a meaningful difference.

articles.title: Refrigerator cyberattack spreads to many European countries, spoiling food worth thousands
articles.text:
What we know so far: Last month's cyberattack on French grocery store refrigerators became an expensive reminder of the risks of relying on the Internet of Things for critical infrastructure. New attacks this week show that several European countries face the same vulnerabilities, with lax security practices and obsolete systems the likely culprits.
A cyberattack on internet-connected refrigeration systems ruined food at grocery stores in at least seven European countries on Monday, with one Belgian Delhaize store estimating its losses at €100,000. The attack mirrors the one that hit French grocers in mid-October, exposing gaping security holes.
Grocery stores and chains in Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden, Finland, and Estonia reported that refrigerators had been set to defrost, in some cases raising temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), spoiling food and leaving many shelves empty. The French attack set cooling systems to the same temperature and caused damages estimated in the tens of millions of euros.
An ICA store manager in Stockholm told Reuters on Monday that employees didn't notice the attack, which hit at 2am local time, until hours later, by which point "everything" was destroyed. Other targeted businesses include Delhaize in Belgium and Luxembourg, Carrefour and De Laet & Van Haver in Belgium, Coop in Sweden, and more.
It remains unclear who was responsible for the attacks. No one has claimed responsibility, and at least some affected stores have security vulnerabilities so deep that practically anyone could have accessed their systems.
The refrigerators attacked in France were operated by Danfoss, and the incident came two months after security researchers at Claroty warned of multiple vulnerabilities in the company's controllers. Danfoss also supplied the affected units in at least some of Monday's attacks, though Belgian installer Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's refrigeration, was also involved.
Security researcher Kevin Beaumont says several thousand Danfoss management systems are directly reachable from the internet with essentially nonexistent login security. In his words, the username is "admin" and the password changes daily to the current date. Claroty's research points to a hidden daily code derived from the date that bypasses the real password, a flaw Danfoss has since patched.
Furthermore, many affected systems were running outdated firmware, and some can't receive patches at all because they are end-of-life, a common risk with IoT devices. Shodan.io shows thousands of exposed Danfoss units, more than half in France, with others in South Africa and elsewhere.
Whether a sophisticated state actor or a bored individual was behind the attacks, they serve as another lesson in IoT pitfalls. Some also fear that similar incidents could form part of a broader effort to destabilize a country's infrastructure.

articles.title: CrowdStrike Reportedly Paying $495 Million for AI Security Firms Fiddler, Dreadnode
articles.text:
CrowdStrike on Tuesday announced agreements to acquire AI agent observability firm Fiddler AI and AI security testing company Dreadnode, in deals reportedly worth a combined $495 million.
CrowdStrike has not disclosed the financial terms of either acquisition. According to The Wall Street Journal, which reported the deals ahead of the official announcements, the cybersecurity giant is paying roughly $400 million for Fiddler and about $95 million for Dreadnode.
CrowdStrike said both purchases will be paid mostly in cash, with a portion in stock subject to vesting conditions. The deals are expected to close in the fourth quarter of CrowdStrike’s fiscal year 2027, which ends on January 31, 2027.
Fiddler was founded in 2018 and is based in Palo Alto, California. In January, it announced a $30 million Series C round that brought its total funding to $100 million.
The company’s technology monitors AI agents and explains the decisions they make. CrowdStrike says Fiddler will add pre-deployment evaluation of agents, tracing of their reasoning and tool calls, and detection of behavioral drift and hallucinations in production.
It will also log agent activity for compliance audits and track token usage and spending. CrowdStrike plans to sell the technology as Falcon Observe.
Dreadnode, founded in 2023, develops offensive AI security tools. The startup raised $14 million in Series A funding in early 2025.
According to CrowdStrike, Dreadnode’s platform lets users describe in plain language what they want to test. It then runs more than 100 known AI attack strategies, including jailbreaks, prompt injection, and multi-turn and agent-specific attacks.
The tests target AI models, agent reasoning loops, applications and MCP servers. Findings are ranked by severity, mapped to frameworks such as the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, MITRE ATLAS and the NIST AI RMF, and fed to CrowdStrike’s Falcon Guardian AI detection and response product as policy recommendations.
The Dreadnode team, led by CEO Brad Palm, will join CrowdStrike’s Cyber Superintelligence Lab. Dreadnode-based testing capabilities are expected to become generally available in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027.
Alongside the acquisitions, CrowdStrike introduced an AI Kill Switch in Falcon Guardian that allows authorized administrators to halt a misbehaving AI agent, prevent it from restarting, and cut off its network access.
CrowdStrike has made several security acquisitions over the past year. In January, it announced plans to buy identity security firm SGNL for $740 million and browser security company Seraphic for a reported $420 million. In September 2025, it agreed to acquire AI security firm Pangea.
