articles.title: Yvonne Bajela is bringing $17M in fresh capital to Europe's startup scene | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Yvonne Bajela knew it was time to launch her own fund. She spent more than a decade as a VC, most recently at LocalGlobe and Impact X Capital Partners, where she made bets on now-unicorn companies like the fintech Wise, the insurance company Marshmallow, and robotaxi Mooves.
On Tuesday, she announced that her own fund, Evertrue Capital, officially closed an oversubscribed $17 million Fund I.
“After more than a decade backing founders who bet everything on their ideas, it felt like time to make a bet of my own,” she said. “I wanted the independence to act on those convictions and build something that reflected my own approach to investing.”
The firm, which has already backed seven companies, will focus on early-stage investing across the U.K. and Europe. The average check size will be around £350,000, she said, with plans to back at least 20 companies over the next three years.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, she said this AI boom helped her realize that this was the right time to launch her own fund. Not only has it changed the economics of launching a company, she said, but it has created new opportunities for early-stage investors like herself. “The ability to build has been democratized,” she said. “But the ability to build something enduring remains rare.”
As TechCrunch has previously reported, the U.K.’s startup scene is having a moment. King’s Cross, for example, is one of the world’s top AI hubs, while companies like Revolut, Synthesia, ElevenLabs, and the Bezos-backed CuspAI are redefining what it means to scale and attract success in the U.K. market. For someone like Bajela, this moment means there is an opportunity to snap up investments in the next generation of top British talent early. “I think more globally significant businesses will emerge from a wider range of starting points,” she said.
However, this is also a tough market for emerging fund managers. In the U.S., it has been described as a barbell market where capital is concentrated at the top and among firms led by those who already have solid track records. Things may be slightly rosier in the U.K., as PitchBook data through the end of September shows that emerging fund managers in this region raised $7.4 billion, already surpassing the $6.2 billion they raised in all of 2025.
Still, Bajela said fundraising was a grind. The hardest rejections weren’t necessarily the outright nos. “They were the ones that came after months of conversations and significant time invested, only for the answer to ultimately be no,” she said. “Time is one of the most valuable resources a founder has, and a prolonged process without clarity has a real cost.”
Still, she said the fund nabbed five institutional backers, including the British Business Bank and Basecamp, the fund-of-funds of the investment firm Phoenix Court, which is also home to LocalGlobe. Evertrue was part of the £400 million British Business Bank’s Investor Pathways capital initiative, which saw it distribute £90 million to 10 first-time fund managers. Bajela said Evertrue wanted to raise around $13 million but saw a lot of investor interest. She decided to turn down additional investors rather than expand the fund size.
“Fund size is a strategic decision, not a measure of success in itself,” she said. “I wanted enough capital to build meaningful positions in my highest-conviction investments without creating pressure to deploy capital simply because it was available.”
Around 80% of Evertrue’s LPs are U.K. based, with the rest scattered across Europe, Asia, and the U.S. She said her international LP base represents the relationships she’s built “over more than a decade investing across markets.” It also reflects the fund’s global ambition, she said, especially since so many British founders keep their eyes on a U.S. expansion; more than half her portfolio already operates in the U.S.
Evertrue will invest mainly across AI and fintech, she said, adding that she’s “particularly interested in people with a unique insight into a problem, an unusual ability to execute, and the ambition to build something much bigger than their initial product.”
“I also pay attention to the distance a founder has traveled, what they’ve overcome, and how that has shaped their perspective,” she continued.
She’s lived in Japan as a senior investment manager at Mitsui and started her career as an analyst at Goldman Sachs. Throughout her career, she said she’s seen how “widely distributed ambition and talent are.”
“I want Evertrue to be known for the quality of the founders I back and the businesses they go on to build.”

articles.title: Waymo cars already appearing on Toronto streets despite worries
articles.text:
Self-driving taxi service Waymo has officially hit Toronto streets just weeks after the company’s Oct. 16 announcement that it would begin testing its autonomous vehicles on local streets.
It’s a potential major step forward in the way people move around Toronto, but Waymo’s Canadian launch still has a tough road ahead to navigate, between regulatory hurdles and serious concerns from officials at City Hall and the taxi industry.
On the eve of Waymo’s big announcement, lobbyist Aidan Grove-White, of StrategyCorp, logged a call to Adam Chaleff, the mayor’s Director of Legislative Affairs & Issues Management. Another StrategyCorp lobbyist, Alex Bernst, attended an Oct. 22 meeting with City staff from the Strategic Policy & Initiatives and Policy & Innovation units of the Transportation Services department.
Matt Elliott first reported on these lobbying files in his City Hall Watcher newsletter, though no further details about the phone call and meeting are publicly available.
And while talks are ongoing behind closed doors, resistance to the new technology has been a bit more public.
Mayor Chow is wary about the new technology, and in an interview with the Toronto Star, her press secretary, Braman Thillainathan, said that “Any move toward autonomous vehicles must not put people out of work or undermine workers’ livelihoods.”
“The mayor will not support Waymo if it costs jobs, drives down wages for other workers, or contributes to precarious work in our city,” added Thillainathan.
Kristine Hubbard, Managing Director at Beck Taxi and an outspoken critic of the rideshare industry, raised concerns over a video that surfaced on Monday showing a Waymo vehicle (albeit with a human driver) turning through a pedestrian crossing.
Love how the pedestrian walk sign was lit but you go ahead WHAT ARE WE DOING
— Kristine Hubbard (@KristineHubbard) November 2, 2026
Hubbard tells blogTO that Waymo’s arrival “is a very timely issue as we discuss the traffic crisis that faces our city.”
“Simply put: there are too many cars on our roads,” says Hubbard, adding that the U.S. tech company’s expansion north of the border comes at a time when “we attempt to protect Canadian sovereignty, we have yet another billion-dollar American company ready to take ownership of our roads.”
“The false promises of fewer cars on the streets are the echo of all of the lies told by companies like Uber when they entered the market. We have more cars, higher emissions, and the largest poverty-paid workforce in history as a result of inaction from the provincial and municipal governments.”
Though data suggests Waymo’s robotaxis are less prone to accidents than human drivers, Hubbard argues that, based on social media evidence shared on Monday, “Roads are less safe.”
“As we saw from social media posts, Waymo is not even trying to be a safer option as they gather data through surveillance of our City.”
Hubbard noted that Waymo vehicles were spotted on the eve of news that food bank visits are on the increase, and argues that “Taking jobs from Ontarians is certainly not a safe option.”
Waymo has argued that its technology is safer than human drivers, and the company has stressed that vehicles will not even operate autonomously until local roads have been fully mapped.
Waymo explained in October that it will be “taking a rigorous, phased, safety-first approach starting with high-definition mapping of local street networks and testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel” before the cars can go driverless.
Other locals welcome the new technology, noting that autonomous vehicles have lower collision rates than human-driven cars.
So excited to ride Waymos in Toronto. Even more excited to have drivers who are safer than humans on the roads!
— Alex Glista 🇨🇦🇪🇺 (@AlexanderGlista) November 2, 2026
Would you drive in a Waymo? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title: OpenAI says ChatGPT is catching up to Google in search
articles.text:
In many circles, “Ask Chat” has replaced “Google it,” and that’s reflected in a new announcement from OpenAI: the volume of search queries run through ChatGPT now equals 20 percent of the volume run through Google.
OpenAI says ChatGPT is catching up to Google in search
ChatGPT processes one-fifth the volume of search queries as Google, per OpenAI.
Adam Fry, OpenAI’s consumer product lead for ChatGPT, made the announcement at a press event on Monday. He said the company defines a search as any time a user inputs a query that results in a web search, as opposed to tasks like defining a term or a simple how-to explanation. (Fry did not specify the source of the Google search volume number.)
Having one-fifth as many searches as Google is still a long way from overtaking it, but for comparison, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said during Google’s 2023 antitrust trial that Bing had about 3 percent of the search engine market share after trying for more than a decade. During the trial, Google described AI as a potential disruptor, arguing ChatGPT was poised to seriously compete with it — now, OpenAI seems to agree. (OpenAI likely uses Microsoft Bing for a significant part of its searches, along with its in-house search index, although there is still some speculation that it routes some queries through Google.)
The news comes amid an ongoing search engine shake-up, as Google continues to reduce conventional referrals to third-party sites and invests heavily in AI tools — not just AI Overview but also additional generative AI capabilities, including personalized search results with visualizations and charts. But as search queries increasingly route through OpenAI and other AI labs’ services, other companies are investing in the same types of AI-focused search experience, even if they call it something else: for OpenAI, it’s “Intelligent UI,” or creating a visual and interactive interface within a chatbot response. “That’s where the future of this technology goes. You’re talking to a canvas,” Fry said.
Much like Google, OpenAI sees a potential path to profitability through ads, particularly as it approaches an IPO potentially slated for early next year. OpenAI has defended its ads in the past, and Fry told reporters they hadn’t produced a lasting backlash. “Ads have not negatively impacted the product or the usage of the product,” he said, adding that “most people do not seem to mind ads in the product.”
OpenAI announced last month that the company would begin introducing images of sponsored products and services in ChatGPT rather than just a company’s name, logo, and a link to its product like before.
“Ads have maybe shown us that we could be doing this more, actually,” Fry said.

articles.title: Amazon closes AI creator's account after he attempts to buy seven Nvidia DGX Spark mini-PCs — Epic CEO Tim Sweeney says his regular orders were canceled before arrival after he tried to buy two GPUs
articles.text:
Amazon closes AI creator's account after he attempts to buy seven Nvidia DGX Spark mini-PCs — Epic CEO Tim Sweeney says his regular orders were canceled before arrival after he tried to buy two GPUs
Amazon’s closure email cites a verification process and offers no reason.
AI creator Nick Saraev says on X that Amazon closed his account after he tried to buy seven Nvidia DGX Spark AI mini-PCs. The closure email cites a verification process and gives no reason. Epic CEO Tim Sweeney chimed in that his regular orders would go through, then get canceled before arrival, after he tried to buy two GPUs.
Saraev puts it plainly that “Amazon just closed my account” and that “Buying even modest amounts of compute immediately puts you on a watchlist.” He was “4 orders deep,” and Amazon will no longer allow him to buy DGX Sparks.
The shared screenshots indicate those orders were all canceled, with each stating, “Your order was canceled. You have not been charged for this order.” Although he does not give a unit count, the screenshots indicate he tried to buy seven DGX Sparks in total. All show the same listing, with 128GB of memory and 4TB of storage.
Amazon’s support account did respond to his earlier post, about three hours before his closure post, offering a review. The shared email shows that Amazon had “made the final decision” to close his account after review; no reason was given. However, it did mention “previous attempts to verify your account,” and he says he did go through the verification process, but seven DGX Sparks is a significant amount that might draw suspicion. Either way, Amazon’s Conditions of Use reserve the right to “refuse service, terminate accounts” or “cancel orders in its sole discretion.”
He’s not alone in running into trouble with the company. Sweeney says that “Amazon didn’t cancel my account but continued accepting all my regular orders and canceling them just prior to arrival dates, after I tried to buy two NVIDIA GPUs. Rather bizarre.” Nvidia GPUs are often used for local inference. Saraev replied that everyone would “appreciate a bit more transparency.”
Also, in September, Dracones89 on the Nvidia developer forum shared that one Amazon account was hit with “suspicious activity locks” while trying to buy a pair of Asus GX10s; the user ended up with two DGX Sparks from Micro Center instead. Another X user, @PurzBeats, wrote, “They canceled the order when I tried to buy my 5090, twice.” This is a different trajectory than the OpenClaw days of Mac minis, when buyers faced long delivery waits rather than canceled orders or closed accounts.
With local inference remaining of high interest to many, particularly AI influencers, the event is potentially disturbing, especially after recent comments about self-owned DRAM by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. While this time it was a guy who helps entrepreneurs and small businesses implement AI and claims 500K on YouTube and 700K on Instagram, the slope is slippery, although Saraev’s orders are hardly typical.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The 128GB DGX Spark has an MSRP of $6,950, but it may be found at 20% or more over that: two Amazon listings showed $8,499.99 and $9,499.99 when we checked today, which would put seven at roughly $59,500 to $66,500. Both showed Prime delivery tomorrow, so the hardware is still on sale there.
Hardware has been climbing in price, largely due to rising memory costs. As open-weight models have become more popular, so has local AI inference. The combination may make retailers uneasy, as you’re dealing with high ticket prices and there has been uncertainty about the safety of models as they have improved, with open-source AI agent tools reportedly being used in multiple recent cybersecurity incidents.
Micro Center, a different retailer, required one buyer to sign an Advanced Computing Product Purchaser Declaration with photo ID, end user, and an install location, just for a workstation with an RTX 5090. This form specifically forbade exporting or reselling the hardware, which might give a little insight into Amazon’s reasoning, too. Amazon’s conditions also say customers “must comply with all U.S. or other export and re-export restrictions.” China and the U.S. remain locked in a fight over exports of AI hardware.
Amazon hasn’t explained itself, but the attention this is getting may motivate a more detailed response. Right now, it’s a warning signal to users looking to buy significant amounts of hardware for AI work, at least from traditional online retailers. Brick-and-mortar stores, like Micro Center, may crack down further to prevent workarounds designed to export the hardware illegally.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: 'Now is the time for employers to be open about what they track and why': Employees say more bosses are using tracking software — and want it to be publicly declared
articles.text:
'Now is the time for employers to be open about what they track and why': Employees say more bosses are using tracking software — and want it to be publicly declared
Worker tracking software isn't actually all that effective
- Owl Labs argues that tracking workers' activities doesn't show how they're working
- 82% of workers believe employees should have to disclose the use of monitoring tools
- The biggest opportunity to improve productivity comes from upgrading hybrid meeting tech
New research has claimed almost three in five (59%) UK workers say their company is using monitoring software to track their activity both across basic attendance but also computer activity like mouse movements, keyboard usage and meeting participation.
And a further four in five (82%) believe that employers should have to disclose their use of monitoring software – something that's not currently required by law.
But despite a rise in workplace monitoring software, likely driven by a surge in post-pandemic hybrid working, the report from Owl Labs argues that tracking doesn't actually provide any meaningful insight into work at all.
Is your employer tracking how and when you work?
According to the data, the most commonly monitored activities are login/logout times (32%), number of meetings attended (22%), screen and mouse movement (17%) and keyboard usage (15%) – however, workers are already finding workaround to falsely appease tracking metrics.
For example, more than a quarter (28%) of UK workers admit so-called phantom meeting attendance, where they mark a meeting as 'attended' or even attend it without paying attention, and then catch up later via notes and summaries. It's something that managers (33%) are more likely to do than non-managers (15%), the report found.
The study also pointed to an increase in AI avatar interest, with 50% of managers and 21% of non-managers considering using an avatar to attend meetings on their behalf – further making meeting attendance metrics less important.
Hybrid work's impact on workplace tracking
Owl Labs also revealed some losses in efficiency as a result of hybrid working, but ironically, having workers placed across multiple locations isn't the issue. It's the tech they're being handed out.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Around three in four (73%) UK workers reported losing time because of technical difficulties during hybrid meetings, with audio problems generally the most significant. Teams spend on average six minutes to get a hybrid meeting started.
The report implies that spending money on better AV tech to support hybrid meetings may create a better outcome than simply deploying software to see who's attending those (suboptimal) meetings.
What does tracking software mean for workers?
Owl Labs CEO Frank Weishaupt urges companies to be more transparent about what they're tracking with their workers, helping improve trust between workers and higher up.
"With the Government reviewing how workplace monitoring should be regulated, now is the time for employers to be open about what they track and why," Weishaupt added. "Trust and reliable technology are what keep people productive, and what keep them in the business."

articles.title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
articles.text:
How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
Borrowing from disciplines like economics could help AI safety researchers control AI models, even if they don’t understand them.
A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.
As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.
Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution—a sort of moral code.
The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions, and mislead their evaluators.
Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage.
An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay.
In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.
A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).
Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.
The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.
A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?”
Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.
During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.
There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.
Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.
Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.”
One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.
It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.
“Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior.
Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.)
Whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” says Hazan. A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it?
“It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he says of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.

articles.title: Privacy commissioner says Bill C-22 must change to protect Canadians | BetaKit
articles.text:
Canada’s privacy commissioner is recommending that the Senate make changes to Canada’s controversial proposed lawful access legislation, Bill C-22.
The news: Speaking before the Senate’s standing committee on national security on Monday, privacy commissioner Philippe Dufresne told senators that his office had drafted several proposed changes to Canada’s proposed Bill C-22, also known as the Lawful Access Act.
If passed into law, Bill C-22 would give law enforcement, as well as national security agencies like the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS), more power to monitor and collect personal communications and data.
From the source: “The current bill incorporates significant improvements over previous versions,” Dufresne told the committee. “These are positive measures, but in spite of these improvements, extra amendments are still necessary to better protect the privacy of Canadians.”
The context: Recommendations from the privacy commissioner included narrowing the definition of which information can be collected and the range of people it could be obtained from, as well as more clearly defining what constitutes publicly available information. Dufresne also recommended a carve out for healthcare-related data or privileged information, and asked that electronic service providers be able to “trigger a preemptive, arm’s length assessment” on how a particular access order would impact their operations.
Notably, Dufresne advocated for legal principles around proportionality and necessity to be integrated into the bill. In the legal field, those terms refer to core legal principles that limit state power and evaluate the legality of rights-restrictive actions. Dufresne told senators that right now “there is no overarching requirement that all obligations imposed under the Act be both necessary and proportionate.”
Final thought: Bill C-22 has earned the ire of both civil liberties organizations and much of Canada’s tech ecosystem, prompting companies like Signal to say they would halt operations in Canada were it to become law. The Munk School’s Citizen Lab and the Electronic Frontier Foundation have argued that the bill infringes on privacy rights and creates a de facto surveillance state.
Bill C-22 passed the House of Commons earlier this year and is currently before the Senate. Some senators, such as Senator Yuen Pau Woo, have expressed doubts about passing the bill in its current form. 
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.

articles.title: Reddit is adding more ads
articles.text:
Reddit is testing ads on another area of its platform: search. With this update, ads will appear within your search results “based on a range of factors, including contextual relevance to a search query,” according to Reddit.
Reddit is adding more ads
Searching for an ‘espresso station’ on Reddit could surface ads for espresso machines, beans, or mugs.
That means searching for “espresso station” could present you with ads for espresso, machines, beans, or mugs, while a search for a “home office setup” may yield ads for monitors, desks, or office chairs. Reddit currently shows ads across its feeds in a variety of formats, including images, videos, sponsored posts, and AMAs. It also shows ads within threads.
Reddit has announced a number of changes to its platform over the past several weeks, including new Following and For You feeds and limiting who can access “Old Reddit.” The company most recently announced plans to make Reddit a “logged-in-only experience” to fight Google’s AI scraping, contributing to its stock declining 29 percent.
Reddit says it’s piloting the new search ads with a select number of advertisers to start.

articles.title: Digital fraud slows African banks’ cross-border expansion
articles.text:
A surge in cybercrime across African banks and fintechs is forcing financial institutions to retreat to domestic markets, stalling cross-border integration and leaving continental initiatives like PAPSS and AfCFTA underutilised.
An escalating wave of digital fraud has emerged as the primary operational deterrent to cross-border financial integration in Africa, with 88% of commercial banks and fintech companies reporting increased electronic financial crimes.
The finding, detailed in the sixth edition of the African Financial Industry Barometer presented at the Africa Financial Summit (AFIS) in Luanda, highlights a growing security crisis that is prompting lenders to abandon cross-border ambitions in favour of domestic retrenchment.
Published jointly by Deloitte and Jeune Afrique Media Group, the survey gathered responses from financial leaders across 20 African nations.
Although overall industry confidence remained steady at 8 out of 10, matching the previous year’s rating, operational caution has intensified significantly as institutions struggle to secure digital channels against cross-border fraud.
Africa is confident in its financial future. So why is integration stalling?
Financial institutions rate the industry’s outlook highly, yet many are consolidating at home, regional initiatives are struggling to deliver, and digital fraud is rising. Explore the contradiction in the 2026 African Financial Industry Barometer.
Confidence is high. Expansion is another matter.
African financial leaders remain broadly optimistic. But confidence varies significantly between institutions already operating across borders and those focused on domestic markets.
Confidence depends on where you operate
Scores are out of 10. The categories include both institution types and business segments; they are not mutually exclusive groups.
Where do institutions want to grow?
Select a strategy to see what the survey says about expansion priorities.
Domestic consolidation was the most commonly identified growth strategy, particularly among banks and insurance companies.
Some local institutions favour regional alliances instead of establishing wholly owned operations abroad.
Fintech operators are the group most inclined towards organic regional expansion, despite their exposure to digital fraud.
Multi-market financial groups continue to consider acquisitions to strengthen existing regional footprints.
These percentages represent reported strategy preferences and are not parts of a single whole. Separately, 25% reported no regional expansion plans.
Three integration projects. Limited tangible progress.
AfCFTA, PAPSS and the African Exchanges Linkage Project are intended to make cross-border commerce, payments and investment easier. Survey respondents see slow implementation. Select a project to compare the findings.
AfCFTA
African Continental Free Trade Area — designed to deepen intra-African trade and regional economic integration.
HOW RESPONDENTS ASSESS IMPLEMENTATION
What stands out: Only 7% report tangible progress, despite the agreement’s continent-wide ambition.
PAPSS
Pan-African Payment and Settlement System — designed to support intra-African cross-border payments in local currencies.
HOW RESPONDENTS ASSESS IMPLEMENTATION
What stands out: PAPSS has the highest reported tangible progress of these three projects, but institutional participation remains limited.
The PAPSS participation problem
Beyond perceptions of progress, the survey asked institutions about their connection plans.
These are selected response categories, not a complete breakdown of all respondents.
AELP
African Exchanges Linkage Project — intended to connect participating African stock exchanges and facilitate cross-border investment.
HOW RESPONDENTS ASSESS IMPLEMENTATION
What stands out: AELP records the weakest progress assessment. Separately, 56% of respondents report no concrete benefits from the project.
The risks behind the retreat
Digital fraud is rising, cybersecurity remains a major concern, and the infrastructure needed to deploy defensive AI tools is uneven. Select a risk category to explore the findings.
Digital fraud is increasing
Share of surveyed institutions reporting an increase in digital fraud.
The tension: Fintechs are among the institutions pursuing regional expansion, yet banks and fintechs also report particularly widespread increases in digital fraud.
Cybersecurity tops the risk agenda
Share identifying cybersecurity as a major operational concern. This is distinct from reporting an increase in digital fraud.
Why this matters: Cross-border activity introduces additional operational and counterparty complexities, making security capacity especially important.
AI could help detect fraud. Deployment is harder.
85% recognise the impact of AI for fraud detection, but institutions report significant barriers to implementation.
The contradiction: Institutions recognise AI’s potential, but data, security and talent constraints complicate its practical deployment.
Confidence in Africa’s financial future is not the same as confidence in operating across its borders. The survey reveals a gap between industry optimism, actual integration progress and the operational capacity needed to connect African markets.
How to read this data
Source: Sixth African Financial Industry Barometer, presented at AFIS 2026 by Deloitte and Jeune Afrique Media Group. The survey gathered responses from financial leaders across 20 African countries.
Confidence: Scores use a 0–10 scale. Institution categories and business segments can overlap.
Growth strategies: Respondents could identify different approaches. Percentages should not be added together.
Integration: AfCFTA, PAPSS and AELP percentages reflect surveyed institutions’ assessments of progress. They are not independent measurements of actual transaction volumes, trade flows or market connectivity.
PAPSS participation: The connected, onboarding and no-plans figures are selected categories, not a complete distribution.
Risks: Increased digital fraud, cybersecurity concerns and AI adoption barriers are different survey measures. They should not be interpreted as equivalent or as proof that fraud alone caused institutions to avoid regional expansion.
Domestic consolidation over cross-border expansion
Rather than deploying capital into regional corridors, financial institutions are prioritising their domestic bases.
When asked about growth strategies, 49% of respondents identified consolidating their existing national markets as their primary objective.
Regional partnerships and alliances followed at 42%, while only 37% favoured organic expansion into other African jurisdictions. Formal cross-border mergers and acquisitions registered 32%, and a quarter of all surveyed institutions stated they have no plans for regional expansion.
Strategic postures reflect distinct operational priorities across sectors. Commercial banks and insurance companies are focusing almost exclusively on domestic consolidation, seeking to avoid unfamiliar legal and counterpart risks abroad.
Fintech operators represent the primary group pursuing organic regional expansion, even as they face the highest incidence of digital fraud. Pan-African banking conglomerates continue to pursue selective acquisitions to defend their established multi-market footprints, while purely local institutions favour bilateral partnerships as a low-capital route beyond their domestic borders.
This divergence in strategy is mirrored in institutional sentiment. Multi-country institutions reported confidence scores of 8.53 out of 10, and regional banking groups gained 0.75 points to reach 8.00.
Capital markets registered the sharpest rise in optimism, increasing from 6.50 to 8.57. Conversely, purely domestic institutions saw their confidence drop to 7.33, while the insurance sector declined by 0.90 points to 7.45.
José Barata, Managing Partner and Banking Sector Lead at Deloitte Angola, noted during the presentation that institutional scale heavily dictates market sentiment.
Barata explained that while confidence remains high among multinational and regional groups with established structures, purely local and national players report lower confidence, indicating that capital allocation decisions require a closer assessment of specific institutions and their operating environments.
Flagship integration projects face an adoption stall
The inward turn of the financial sector is taking a visible toll on continental integration initiatives, including the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), and the African Exchanges Linkage Project (AELP).
Only 7% of respondents reported tangible commercial progress resulting from AfCFTA, with 69% stating that implementation is moving too slowly, and another 24% viewing the agreement as stalled.
The AELP, designed to interconnect stock exchanges across the continent to unlock regional portfolio investments, recorded even weaker sentiment.
Just 4% of respondents reported tangible progress from the linkage project, while 53% described its pace as too slow and 43% considered it at a complete standstill. Fifty-six per cent of respondents reported experiencing no concrete benefits from the platform.
Adoption metrics for PAPSS, the African Union-backed payment network developed to clear intra-African trade in domestic currencies, indicate severe structural friction.
Although 19% of institutions acknowledged tangible operational progress, 57% stated that rollout has been too slow, and 24% considered it stalled.
More critically, 45% of surveyed institutions reported having no plans to connect to PAPSS. Only 11% are actively connected, with an additional 12% currently working through onboarding.
Across the wider survey, 41% of respondents reported deriving no commercial benefits from either AfCFTA or PAPSS.
Lenders attribute this hesitation to unmitigated counterparty liabilities, clearing uncertainties, and an absence of harmonised dispute-resolution systems.
In the absence of regulatory alignment across jurisdictions, cross-border operations must comply with competing anti-money-laundering, customer verification, and capital repatriation rules, thereby driving up administrative costs.
Barata stressed that software and infrastructure cannot bridge this gap without systemic alignment, observing that regional integration requires more than a stated intention to operate across borders.
He emphasised the necessity of interconnected payment networks, practical settlement protocols, stronger regulatory cooperation, and the foundational financial mechanisms required to process cross-border transactions safely.
The $775 billion capital mobilisation gap
The operational retreat is compounding the continent’s internal capital mobilisation shortfall. Citing OECD figures from the African Financial Markets Initiative, the report highlights that African pension funds and insurance firms hold an estimated $775 billion in institutional assets. However, this pool of domestic savings remains largely disconnected from long-term real-economy requirements.
While 64% of respondents are actively engaged in financing small and medium-sized enterprises, 41% reported no involvement in funding affordable housing developments.
Africa has $775 billion in institutional assets. Why isn’t more reaching the real economy?
Africa’s pension funds and insurers hold an estimated $775 billion in assets. But financing for businesses, housing and infrastructure remains constrained. Explore the gap between available institutional capital and its deployment.
This is an estimated stock of institutional assets — not cash sitting idle, and not an amount that could immediately be redirected into new projects.
How can more long-term African savings support productive investment without undermining pension obligations, insurance liabilities or investment risk standards?
The money exists. But it isn’t a single pot.
The $775 billion estimate brings together long-term assets managed by pension and insurance institutions. These investors have different obligations, liquidity needs and investment mandates. Select a category to understand why that matters.
What does $775 billion actually mean?
It describes an estimated asset pool managed by institutions across Africa. The survey does not provide a verified allocation of this total between pensions, insurers, infrastructure, SMEs and housing.
Pension funds invest to meet future retirement obligations. Infrastructure and other long-duration assets may fit some portfolios, but investments must satisfy rules on risk, diversification, liquidity and expected returns.
Insurance portfolios must support claims-paying capacity and regulatory capital requirements. Their investment choices depend on the duration and predictability of liabilities, as well as the risk and liquidity of available assets.
The $775 billion estimate demonstrates the scale of institutional assets. It does not tell us how much is uncommitted, how much is invested outside Africa, or what proportion could safely finance additional domestic and regional projects.
Financial institutions are not equally engaged.
The survey reveals a difference between financial institutions’ participation in SME financing and affordable housing. These figures measure institutional engagement, not the share of the $775 billion allocated to either sector.
Indicates reported institutional engagement, not the volume of SME credit.
Measures non-participation, not the size of the housing finance deficit.
Explore the two financing markets
Select a sector to see why institutional participation does not automatically translate into sufficient financing.
That indicates substantial institutional activity, but it does not reveal how much finance SMEs receive, the terms on which it is offered, or how much unmet demand remains. Lending risk, information gaps and the availability of suitable financing instruments can constrain access.
Housing finance can require long-duration funding and reliable repayment structures. Land administration, project preparation, affordability and credit risk can affect investment viability. The survey’s non-participation figure does not quantify the funding shortfall.
Three ways to make long-term capital more investable
Mobilising institutional assets is not simply a matter of directing funds towards new sectors. Investors need suitable instruments, manageable risks and confidence in how projects are governed. Explore three possible approaches.
Give institutions more suitable assets to buy
Deeper bond markets, investment funds, securitisation structures and infrastructure securities could create more investable opportunities for pension funds and insurers.
The goal is not to force capital into particular projects, but to develop instruments whose risk, maturity, liquidity and returns are compatible with institutional mandates.
Make viable projects less risky to finance
Credit guarantees, first-loss capital, blended-finance structures and development-finance participation can sometimes reduce the risks borne by private investors.
Such mechanisms still have costs and require careful design. They cannot turn fundamentally unviable projects into sustainable investments.
Strengthen the foundations of investment
Reliable financial reporting, transparent procurement, enforceable contracts and credible project governance can improve investors’ ability to assess and manage long-term risks.
Better project preparation and regulatory clarity may help expand the pipeline of opportunities that meet institutional investment standards.
These are potential policy and market mechanisms, not quantified forecasts of how much of the $775 billion they could mobilise.
Having a large pool of institutional assets does not mean having an equally large pool of capital available for new investment. Mobilising more of Africa’s long-term savings requires bankable projects, suitable financial instruments and credible safeguards for investors.
About the data and what it does not show
Source: Sixth African Financial Industry Barometer, AFIS–Deloitte 2026. The survey includes financial institutions across 20 African countries.
Institutional assets: The $775 billion figure is an estimated combined stock of pension and insurance assets. It is not a measure of idle funds or immediately investable capital.
SME financing: The 64% figure represents institutions reporting significant engagement in SME financing. It is not the percentage of institutional assets allocated to SMEs.
Affordable housing: The 41% figure represents institutions reporting no engagement in affordable-housing financing. It is not the proportion of unmet housing-finance demand.
Limitations: The available findings do not quantify how the $775 billion is divided among asset classes, how much is invested abroad, or how much could be redirected into new projects.
Policy options: The final panel describes possible mechanisms for mobilising investment. These are explanatory approaches, not measured outcomes from the survey.
An executive quoted in the barometer observed that Africa does not lack savings but rather lacks sufficient mechanisms to channel them into productive investments at scale.
Barata reinforced this assessment, stating that the primary challenge is not a shortage of capital, but the absence of functional channels through which funds can be directed toward productive enterprise.
He noted that policymakers and institutions must address investment risk, deepen local markets, and build the confidence required to deploy domestic capital into the productive economy.
To unlock this capital, executives surveyed by Deloitte and AFIS recommended three interventions: opening national markets to reciprocal capital flows, mitigating investment risk through guarantees and blended-finance vehicles, and enhancing corporate governance alongside transparent financial reporting.
The report notes that these measures are interdependent and argues that opening markets without mitigating underlying financial risks will fail to attract institutional investors.
Escalating fraud and an acute talent deficit
The worsening operational risk profile presents an immediate obstacle to these reforms. Cybersecurity now ranks as the primary operational threat for 51% of surveyed institutions, rising to 79% among commercial banks and 63% among fintech firms.
Digital fraud was reported to have increased across 66% of the general industry, escalating to 88% among banks and fintech operators.
Barata pointed out a contradiction in how institutions perceive this operational environment. He explained that while approximately two-thirds of institutions surveyed previously identified digital fraud as a substantial risk, many continue to perceive their individual exposure as relatively low.
He warned that as digital service delivery expands, exposure to fraud and cyberattacks increases concurrently.
This security exposure is intensified by a widening skills deficit, with 41% of institutions identifying technical talent shortages as a critical risk, an 11-percentage-point increase year-on-year.
External variables have added to the pressure, with 48% of leaders citing geopolitical instability as an operational risk, up six percentage points, and 41% reporting sustained margin compression due to domestic inflation and currency depreciation.
AI ambitions constrained by infrastructure deficits
To counter rising fraud volumes and streamline verification tasks, financial institutions are turning to artificial intelligence.
Practical interest is concentrated heavily in defensive applications, led by fraud detection at 85% impact recognition, process optimisation at 84%, predictive analytics and business intelligence at 74%, and product personalisation at 69%.
Overall, six of the seven AI use cases evaluated in the survey registered impact recognition above 60%, with only 15% of executives citing the lack of a clear commercial case as an adoption barrier.
The challenge instead lies in institutional infrastructure. Deficiencies in data quality were cited by 56% of respondents as a barrier to AI deployment, matching the 56% who cited cybersecurity and data privacy concerns.
Technical skill deficits were identified by 44%, and regulatory uncertainty was noted by 33%. Barata remarked that the sector has shifted from experimental applications to execution, with executives focused on deploying automated tools in practice to improve credit underwriting, secure operations, and demonstrate operational returns.
The complete AFIS-Deloitte African Financial Industry Barometer is scheduled for full publication between late January and February.
The preliminary findings suggest that waiting for universal regulatory alignment across all 54 African nations is impractical.
The report recommends pursuing practical gains through bilateral regulatory corridors, institutional capacity enhancements, and sector-targeted frameworks, highlighting the insurance industry as an accessible starting point for cross-border alignment.
The underlying requirement for meaningful integration remains operational security. Until national regulators, central banks, and financial institutions build the technical frameworks necessary to curb the surge in cross-border fraud, the continent’s $775 billion in institutional capital reserves will remain confined within domestic borders.

articles.title: Mega-Börsengang in Gefahr? Warum Anthropic trotz Rekordzahlen Investoren schreckt
articles.text:
Anthropic IPO: Warum der größte Börsengang aller Zeiten ins Wanken gerät
Läuft alles, wie seit Monaten von manchen Börsianer:innen erwartet, könnte in den kommenden Tagen der größte Börsengang aller Zeiten über die Bühne gehen. KI-Anbieter Anthropic soll dabei eine Bewertung von rund zwei Billionen Dollar anstreben. Doch zuletzt hat sich die Hype-Stimmung rund um die KI-Branche deutlich abgekühlt. Und auch die neuesten Zahlen von Anthropic bieten durchaus Potenzial für Zweifel.
Anthropic: Umsatz bremst sich ein
Zwar hat der Claude-Entwickler für das abgelaufene dritte Quartal 2026 einmal mehr ein rekordverdächtiges Umsatzplus gemeldet. Gegenüber dem Vorjahresquartal stieg der Umsatz um 1.127 Prozent auf 16,96 Milliarden Dollar. Doch zuletzt hat sich das Umsatzwachstum damit stark eingebremst, wie CNBC schreibt. Nach 132 Prozent und 144 Prozent in den ersten beiden Quartalen kletterte der Q3-Umsatz gegenüber dem Vorquartal „nur“ um 47 Prozent.
Darüber hinaus musste Anthropic im abgelaufenen Dreimonatszeitraum einen Verlust von 23,29 Milliarden Dollar hinnehmen. In den neun Monaten des Jahres 2026 summierte sich das Minus damit auf 104 Milliarden Dollar. Auch wenn ein Großteil davon aus Neubewertungen von Wandelanleihen und Derivaten stammt – im dritten Quartal blieb auch unter dem Strich ein operativer Verlust von 567 Millionen Dollar. Im Quartal zuvor hatte noch ein Gewinn von 974 Millionen Dollar zu Buche gestanden.
895 Milliarden Dollar an Verpflichtungen
Ebenfalls auf die Stimmung potenzieller Investor:innen drücken dürfte die Offenlegung des Umfangs von Kaufverpflichtungen und Mietverträgen, die vor allem für den Ausbau von Rechenleistung und Infrastruktur gedacht sind. Diese Verpflichtungen belaufen sich nämlich auf gut 895 Milliarden Dollar. Der Großteil dieser geplanten Ausgaben soll schon in den kommenden fünf Jahren anfallen.
Darüber hinaus wies Anthropic in der aktuellen Mitteilung auf Risiken für seine vertraglich vereinbarten Rechenkapazitäten hin. Möglich sei, dass die Partner keine Finanzierung für den Kauf von KI-Chips erhalten. Die kreditfinanzierte Expansion der KI-Branche und die zugleich ausbleibenden Anzeichen für den massiven Investitionen entsprechende Einnahmen hatten dafür gesorgt, dass die Aktien großer Tech-Firmen zuletzt kräftig nachgaben.
IPO-Preisspanne noch nicht bekannt
Geht es um die mögliche Preisspanne für die im Rahmen des IPO auszugebenden Aktien, hält sich Anthropic weiter bedeckt. Bloomberg zufolge rechnen Investor:innen mittlerweile eher mit 1,4 bis 1,5 Billionen Dollar statt der zwei Billionen Dollar, die zuvor im Raum gestanden hatten. Doch auch damit würde das KI-Unternehmen den Börsengang von SpaceX deutlich übertreffen, der 86,2 Milliarden Dollar eingebracht hatte und als bisher größter IPO gilt.

articles.title: Introducing India-based inference for Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Introducing India-based inference for Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock
Kimi K3 is a multi-modal, open-weight foundation model (FM) that provider Moonshot AI reported achieved frontier-level coding and general agentic intelligence at release.
In addition to global and US-based inference, Amazon Bedrock now supports in-country inference in India for Kimi K3: unblocking local workloads with strict data residency requirements. Customers like Ultrahuman are already seeing the benefits in production:
        “Jade, an AI Health and Wellness assistant in the Ultrahuman app, answers questions in plain language using each person’s own Ring and glucose data, across more than 14,000 conversations a day. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock let us add a leading open-weight model through the API we already use, with health data staying inside AWS and Mumbai as a fallback Region. With prompt caching, we’ve cut LLM costs by 80 percent and made multi-turn chats 85 percent faster.”
— Aditya Patawari, VP Engineering, Ultrahuman
In this post, we explain the different global and geographic inference options available, and share code for an example use case: optical character recognition (OCR) and understanding of Indic-language documents, with follow-up question answering in code-mixed Hinglish.
Choose where inference can run
Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock is offered through cross-Region inference profiles. You can invoke the model from any of a wide range of AWS Regions (the “source”). Amazon Bedrock then securely processes your request in one of multiple possible “destination” Regions.
Cross-Region inference is fully managed by AWS: Data is encrypted in transit between Regions and remains on the AWS network, never traversing the public internet or requiring you to set up any multi-Region virtual private cloud (VPC) infrastructure.
The inference profile ID you invoke controls which destination Regions are eligible:
| Profile | Model ID | When to choose it | 
| Global | global.moonshotai.kimi-k3 | Recommended for most use cases: lowest cost and most broadly available | 
| India geographic | in.moonshotai.kimi-k3 | Inference processing must stay within Mumbai and Hyderabad Regions | 
See the Amazon Bedrock Kimi K3 model card for up-to-date information on available inference profiles, which AWS Regions they can be called from, and what destination Regions they can use for inference.
Example walkthrough: Indic-language document understanding
Let’s consider an example use case: reading a scanned Hindi document, extracting structured data, and answering follow-up questions in mixed Hindi and English (Hinglish).
This need is common in Indian financial services and public sector workflows where know your customer (KYC) forms, utility bills, and similar documents must often be digitized. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock can directly read and reason about images, including those containing multilingual text. It offers a potential solution with no separate OCR or translation service required.
Prerequisites
The full source code for this example is available on GitHub.
To follow along, you need:
- An AWS account.
- Python 3.11 or later installed, with internet access to install the required PyPI packages.
- The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed, with credentials configured with sufficient AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to invoke the Kimi K3 model through the India inference profile.
For example, to use Kimi K3 through the ap-south-1 Mumbai Region with India geographic inference, the following IAM policy grants sufficient access. Replace the {ACCOUNT_ID} placeholders with your AWS account ID:
For more information about permissions, see Prerequisites for running model inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. If your organization restricts AWS Regions, ask your administrator to review the geographic cross-Region inference IAM and SCP guidance. Keep the source Region permitted and allow routing to both India destinations, using a profile-scoped exception where appropriate. The Responses API guide also describes required default-project access.
Get started with the inference APIs
As detailed on the model card, Amazon Bedrock supports multiple APIs for invoking Kimi K3, all under the Bedrock Runtime endpoint:
| API | Request and response format | 
| Chat Completions | OpenAI-compatible messages input and assistant-message output. | 
| Responses | OpenAI-compatible input and structured output items. | 
| Converse | Standardized messages, content blocks, and inference parameters across supported models. | 
| InvokeModel | Model-specific JSON request and response bodies. | 
Because the OpenAI-compatible APIs are recommended for this model, we use those in this example and connect through the openai Python Library.
Amazon Bedrock supports generating API keys for integrations that require them. However, AWS recommends using short-lived credentials instead where possible. The AWS token generator Python library derives a short-term API key-like token from the standard AWS CLI credential chain.
If you use a named profile for your AWS CLI, you might need to set the AWS_PROFILE environment variable first. After CLI credentials are set up, you can invoke the model with the following code:
Here, region (ap-south-1 Mumbai) specifies the source Region to which the request is made. The inference profile in.moonshotai.kimi-k3 ensures that inference is processed in Indian Regions only.
A broad range of features like streaming, tool calling, and structured outputs are supported across both the Chat Completions and Responses APIs. See the OpenAI Python API Reference for more examples.
Analyze images
Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock supports images as well as PDFs and a range of other file types. You can send input files to the model directly by base64-encoding. For OCR or other use cases where small details are important, consider setting the image detail parameter to high. This improves accuracy, at the cost of more input tokens consumed per image.
In some cases, we’ve seen higher output quality for Kimi K3 when images are provided before text inputs. We suggest experimenting with request ordering. Consider the following example code:
To demonstrate, we generated an image of a synthetic electricity bill in Hindi.
Given this image input, the model can answer questions by pulling data directly from the document with no separate digitization step required. For example:
Q: Bill kitne ka hai aur last date kab hai? Late hua toh kitna dena padega?
A: Bill ka total ₹2,217.20 hai, aur last date 20/10/2026 hai. Late hua toh ₹2,261.54 dena padega.
Build a structured extraction pipeline
Beyond general question-answering, you can create structured document processing workflows by using static prompts to extract a consistent set of expected fields across many documents.
To apply firm constraints on output structure (rather than best-effort prompt-guided generation), Kimi K3 supports structured output on Amazon Bedrock either through function calling or by providing a JSON Schema output format. These options are described in more detail in the OpenAI documentation (for OpenAI-compatible APIs) and the Amazon Bedrock User Guide (for native Converse/InvokeModel APIs).
In the full sample code repository, we’ve provided an end-to-end pipeline that:
- Transcribes the document in its original script (OCR).
- Extracts key fields as JSON using a configurable schema, with dates normalized to ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD), Devanagari digits (for example २८८) converted to Western digits (288), and names transliterated into English.
- Writes a short English summary.
- Answers multi-turn follow-up questions in Hinglish (Hindi written in Latin script, mixed with English) about the same document.
For the same synthetic Hindi electricity bill in the preceding figure, the pipeline returns structured fields such as the following (abbreviated):
We’ve also included a KYC form example and an open-ended schema-free mode, where the model selects the most useful fields itself for any other document type. All provided sample documents are synthetic, with fictional names and addresses and masked identity numbers.
Download the sample code from GitHub to explore further and try it out on your own images.
As with any automated extraction, you should verify the outputs are reliable for your specific use case before relying on them for important decisions. Consider adding post-validation logic or a human review step for critical workflows.
Optimize price-performance, service tiers and caching
Tune your system prompts and schemas against example documents for reliable extractions. Amazon Bedrock Advanced Prompt Optimization (AdvPO) provides a fully managed option to optimize prompt templates based on reference examples.
Amazon Bedrock service tiers give you control over price-performance on a per-request basis. For less latency-sensitive cases, you can select the flex tier to enjoy a 50 percent discount on default standard pricing. For latency-critical scenarios, you can select “priority” to request higher queue priority at a higher price. See the pricing page for details.
Use cases with long, seldom-changing content in their input prompts can also benefit from prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock. Make sure the static content (system prompt, tool descriptions, and so on) appears at the beginning of the input, before dynamic sections like the current image and question.
Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock supports both discounted pricing for cache hits, as well as an explicit caching mode. In the default implicit caching mode, the service attempts to automatically cache and reuse repeated prompt prefixes between requests with no user action required. However, you can improve performance by selecting the explicit mode and specifying ‘breakpoints’ of cacheable content in your input, boosting cache hit rate, response speed, and cost savings.
The following example shows explicit prompt caching with the Responses API. For more information, see prompt caching in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide:
Monitor usage
Amazon CloudWatch metrics are automatically generated for Kimi K3 under the AWS/Bedrock namespace, giving visibility of the invocation rate, token counts, cache usage, latency, errors, and throttling.
Model invocation logging is opt-in and can optionally contain prompts and outputs. Review access, retention, and storage location settings before enabling it.
Logs and metrics are stored in the source Region where you submitted your request, regardless of which destination Region might have processed it in cross-Region inference. You can optionally enable AWS CloudTrail data event logging to log model invocations in CloudTrail, which records requests’ destination Region as an additionalEventData.inferenceRegion field.
Clean up
Kimi K3 is billed on a per-token basis, so these code samples don’t provision any persistent AWS resources to clean up. If you created a new IAM Role or User to explore with, or added extra permissions to your existing User/Role, remember to delete them when you’re finished.
Conclusion and next steps
In this post, we explored how Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock provides on-demand intelligence capable of understanding mixed Indic and English languages. It now supports fully in-country data processing in India (AWS Mumbai and Hyderabad Regions) through the in.moonshotai.kimi-k3 inference profile.
Try it today in the Amazon Bedrock console or through the inference APIs. Check out the model card for more information, and visit AWS re:Post to find answers or ask the community about Amazon Bedrock.

articles.title: España necesita recuperar la confianza en sus trenes y cerrar dos años el AVE Madrid-Barcelona se postula como el primer paso
articles.text:
El pasado viernes 30 de octubre, en su última declaración ante los medios de comunicación, Óscar Puente apuntó a que la línea Madrid-Barcelona podría cerrar dos años para renovarse por completo. La idea se puso encima de la mesa tras las críticas que cuestionan cómo se ha gestionado la renovación en el corredor andaluz, marcado por dos gravísimos accidentes (Adamuz y Urda) en apenas nueve meses.
¿Qué ha pasado? "Lo estamos valorando, pero no sólo por una cuestión de seguridad". Estas fueron las palabras, recogidas por La Vanguardia, de Óscar Puente el pasado viernes 30 de octubre durante la rueda de prensa. Respondiendo ante los medios sobre el accidente del pasado día 28 de octubre en Urda (Toledo), el ministro de transportes confirmaba que la posibilidad de cerrar la línea Madrid-Barcelona estaba encima de la mesa.
Hoy, 3 de noviembre, ha reiterado que no hay ninguna decisión tomada pero que optar por "el sistema alemán" (cerrar la línea por completo para realizar la renovación) es "algo que se tendrá que valorar llegado el momento".
¿Por qué? La línea Madrid-Barcelona va a renovarse por completo. Esta línea de alta velocidad es la que más pasajeros mueve y hace ahora un año se presentó un programa para renovarla por completo. La idea es reducir el tiempo de viaje entre ambas ciudades por debajo de las dos horas.
La intención es modernizar por completo la infraestructura y eso conlleva cambiar las traviesas actuales por "aerotraviesas", un invento español que debería reducir el vuelo de balastro al paso del tren y permitiría alcanzar velocidades punta de 350 km/h. Además, es necesario actualizar el sistema ERTMS de nivel 1 a nivel 2 y construir nuevas estaciones para redirigir el flujo del tráfico.
No. Es la respuesta que, de momento se ha dado desde Cataluña. "Si es posible hacer la inversión afectando lo mínimo al servicio, es lo deseable por parte de todo el mundo", ha señalado Salvador Illa, presidente de la Generalitat de Cataluña y compañero de partido de Óscar Puente.
La respuesta señala a una negativa desde Cataluña de manera diplomática a frenar el tráfico ferroviario entre las ciudades. De hecho, Illa ha tratado de quita hierro al asunto señalando que lo de Puente es una mera "reflexión" y que, eso sí, las labores se tienen que hacer "siempre con criterios de máxima seguridad y afectando lo mínimo al servicio".
Un lío. Cerrar la línea Madrid-Barcelona unos dos años es un verdadero lío en materia de movilidad. De hecho, la línea está viviendo uno de sus peores momentos desde que se inauguración, con el puente aéreo absorbiendo parte del tráfico de quienes no se fían de viajar en tren. Bien por seguridad, bien por comodidad o bien por puntualidad.
Ahora mismo, la red que en sus primeros días movía unos dos millones de pasajeros al año ahora mueve 15 millones. Justo después del accidente de Adamuz, la red vivió un pequeño conato de colapso, lo que afectó directamente al transporte de mercancías y trabajadores y a una alternativa rodada por carretera que también colapsó.
En El Confidencial alertan de que el sector turístico ya asegura que hay unos 100.000 millones de euros en juego, ahora que el 82% de los desplazamientos entre las ciudades se realizan por tren. El cierre, incluso, afectaría directamente al crecimiento de la economía del país.
¿Es necesario? La gran duda de si es o no necesario cerrar el corredor ha llegado un año después de su presentación. Entonces se defendía hacer las obras de remodelación por la noche para afectar lo mínimo al tráfico. Pero en estos 12 meses, España ha vivido dos graves accidentes que ha tenido sus consecuencias en cómo se contempla la obra.
La renovación de la línea Madrid-Sevilla se ha extendido en el tiempo. El sistema ERTMS-2 que se va a instalar en lugar del actual LZB ya debería estar en marcha pero no ha sido así. La caída del sistema LZB es una de las principales causas que motivaron el accidente de Urda (Toledo) la semana pasada.
Quienes defienden el cierre total alegan mayor seguridad a la hora de trabajar y una intervención más corta. Que ningún tren circule para que, cuando puedan volver a hacerlo recuperen el tráfico al 100% de la capacidad. Desde los sindicatos defienden que estas renovaciones ayudarían a trabajar más rápido y con mayor seguridad ya que los empleados que han trabajado en la línea Madrid-Sevilla no siempre tenían los conocimientos y experiencia suficientes.
Una línea tocada. Lo peor para el Madrid-Barcelona es que esta línea ha vivido un severo declive en el último año. En noviembre de 2025 se defendía dar un salto cualitativo alcanzando velocidades de paso nunca vistas en España. Hoy, el sistema de alta velocidad al completo genera dudas entre los pasajeros.
En el verano de 2025, los trenes AVLO de Talgo se fisuraron en esta línea. En ese momento empezó un cruce de reproches entre Adif, Talgo y Renfe. Unos aseguraban que el problema era de los trenes y otros echaban la culpa a las vibraciones de la infraestructura.
En enero de 2026, tras el accidente de Adamuz (Córdoba), lo primero que se hizo fue bajar la velocidad de paso en el Madrid-Barcelona. Las vibraciones volvían a estar enel punto de mira. Examinar las vías a conciencia provocó retrasos inesperados y la eliminación de los últimos turnos del día. Hoy, casi un tercio de los kilómetros entre Madrid y Barcelona están limitados a 30 km/h. El accidente de Urda ha vuelto a poner encima de la mesa las dudas sobre el mantenimiento que se está haciendo en la alta velocidad española.
Foto | André Marques

articles.title: Nigeria’s LemFi expands beyond remittances with app rebuild, new products - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian cross-border fintech LemFi has rebuilt its app and launched a new global brand as it expands beyond remittances into savings, credit and eSIM services.
Founded in 2021 by Ridwan Olalere and Rian Cochran, LemFi lets more than two million customers send money to more than 30 countries across Africa, Asia, Europe and beyond. It processes around US$2 billion in transactions every month.
The company has now introduced savings and credit services in the UK, with other markets to follow, as well as eSIM connectivity that allows customers to buy mobile data in more than 100 destinations without changing SIM cards or paying roaming charges.
To support the expansion, LemFi has re-architected its app from the ground up so that multiple products across different countries sit within a single account. It has also launched a new brand platform, “Ambition has no passport”, which will roll out across its global markets.
“We started LemFi because sending money home was broken. What we learned is that the harder problem starts after the transfer,” said Olalere. “Our customers are building careers and businesses in one country while supporting people in another, and the financial system treats them as if they can only exist in one place at a time. We have rebuilt LemFi to work the way their lives do.”
LemFi has raised more than US$85 million to date from investors including Highland Europe, Left Lane Capital, Palm Drive Capital, Endeavor Catalyst and Y Combinator.
