articles.title: Introducing Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities
articles.text:
Introducing Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities
You run security at your organization. It’s 7:00 am, and you’re having breakfast. You receive a ping: a new critical vulnerability has been disclosed. Your team scrambles to compare vendor advisories, read technical research, check which systems run the affected software, and answer familiar questions from the business: are we affected, and what are we doing about it? Another disclosure arrives before that work is finished.
AI is changing both the volume and speed of critical vulnerability discovery. It can analyze large codebases at scale and surface deeply nested flaws that may have existed for years without being found through human review. That discovery momentum will put more pressure on security teams to understand the impact of each disclosure on their infrastructure.
To help security teams prepare, today we’re introducing Zero Wire: a public vulnerability intelligence feed on Cloudflare Radar, bringing the clarity of a news wire service to critical security developments. It helps security leaders and practitioners understand significant vulnerabilities and decide what to do next.
How it works
Zero Wire lives inside Cloudflare Radar under the security section.
Each briefing brings together a plain-language explanation of the vulnerability, who should investigate it, recommended actions, and links to the evidence and vendor guidance. The format is deliberately simple: an index card with what you need to know, without the drama. A CISO should be able to understand the issue quickly and ask the right questions. An engineer should be able to follow the same briefing to the technical guidance needed to investigate and remediate it.
We also offer a pre-compiled prompt you can use with your agent to assess the impact on your infrastructure. Cloudflare contributes security research, observations from our network, and practical knowledge of the controls that can help reduce exposure. The information is useful whether or not you are a Cloudflare customer.
Zero Wire brings that context together with authoritative external sources, giving readers a starting point for assessment and a place to return as an issue develops.
Our focus
Rather than a catalog of every CVE, Zero Wire complements vendor advisories and vulnerability databases, linking readers to the evidence and technical guidance needed to act. Zero Wire focuses on critical CVEs in Internet-facing software, such as vulnerabilities in web applications, the runtimes and libraries they depend on, and services exposed to the Internet, where a proxy can help mitigate exploitation.
We select significant issues that security teams need to understand and assess. Each briefing explains the potential impact, which deployments should be investigated, what is known about exploitation, and the available mitigation and patching guidance. A vulnerability’s severity and evidence of active exploitation are distinct: readers need both to make informed decisions.
A dedicated Cloudflare protection, such as Web Application Firewall (WAF) rules, is not a prerequisite for inclusion. Some issues require vendor updates or changes beyond the traffic Cloudflare can inspect. Where Cloudflare controls can help, we explain their scope and configuration requirements.
A walk through Zero Wire
Start on the Zero Wire homepage. Each card introduces an issue, identifies associated CVEs where applicable, and summarizes why it matters and what to do. You can search for a published briefing using a CVE or issue name, and follow technology tags to related entries. One briefing can cover several related CVEs when understanding them together makes the response clearer.
Find what needs attention
The homepage separates briefings into two categories. “Needs attention” brings together issues requiring active assessment or action, including those with known exploitation or developing guidance. “Reference” keeps briefings available when guidance has stabilized. Moving to “Reference” does not mean every affected system has been patched: an older vulnerability can still matter to an organization that has not completed remediation.
The status and last-checked date help you interpret each card. Known exploitation, an ongoing investigation, and an available vendor fix describe different things. Read them alongside the briefing’s evidence rather than treating them as a verdict on your own environment.
Understand what happened and who should investigate
When you open a briefing, the overview tells you what happened, why it deserves attention, and which teams should investigate. The explanation connects the technical issue to its practical consequences, such as service disruption or risk of data exposure.
For example, the recent php2shell vulnerability concerns flaws in the PHP runtime. That distinction matters for teams running applications such as WordPress or Magento: updating application code or a plugin alone does not repair the underlying runtime. The briefing helps readers identify the right system owners and directs them to the PHP security guidance for affected versions and remediation.
Turn the briefing into an action plan
What to do now gives your team a short set of next steps. Depending on the issue, that can mean identifying affected deployments, checking versions with a hosting provider, applying vendor updates, reviewing suspicious activity, or keeping compensating controls in place while patching.
The purpose is to make the next conversation concrete. For a PHP deployment, ask which runtime is actually running, whether the vendor’s fix has been applied, and who owns the update. Follow the linked vendor advisory for detailed applicability and remediation instructions, which can change as the investigation develops.
Assess your exposure with an AI agent
In this section, we share a prompt that can be used with your AI agent to quickly assess the impact on your infrastructure. The prompt asks for a read-only assessment of deployed software, relevant vendor fixes, exposure, and compensating controls, with per-asset evidence, unknowns, and next actions. It helps your team investigate its own environment; copying the prompt does not itself scan or change systems.
Check the evidence and follow what changed
To help you learn more about the vulnerability, each briefing links to external documents such as CVE records, research, and relevant exploitation evidence, including CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. These sources answer different questions. A vendor advisory establishes affected versions and remediation guidance. An exploitation report provides evidence of attacker activity.
If applicable to a briefing, Cloudflare can add context about traffic seen on our network, for example by showing traffic matching WAF rules that indicates exploitation attempts. Those distinctions matter. Observing an attack attempt does not establish that a particular organization was compromised. Equally, a lack of observed attempts on Cloudflare’s network does not establish that exploitation is absent elsewhere. Briefings distinguish what the sources establish from what remains unknown.
Where available, charts add context to that evidence. The php2shell briefing shows the volume of HTTP requests matching Cloudflare WAF managed rules over time. Note that requests matching these rules are not a count of compromised systems or successful exploits; the chart aims at providing practitioners a sense of what the focus level is by threat actors on a particular vulnerability.
Finally, update chronology records important developments, such as new advisories or changes to the evidence and response guidance. Together with the last-checked date, it helps returning readers understand what has changed since their previous visit.
Understand Cloudflare’s role
The Cloudflare section provides links to whether we offer compensating controls or provide a way to mitigate the vulnerability impact on your infrastructure.
If a particular CVE can be addressed with a WAF rule, the briefing reports its availability and essential configuration requirements. When applicable, paid Plans and free Plans links take customers to the relevant dashboard configuration. The next step is explicit: “Review your WAF configuration to determine whether you are protected”. A link allows you to review your security posture, it does not automatically enable a rule or verify a deployment.
Note that a WAF mitigation is a compensating control for the traffic it covers, it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Blocking the requests can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. The security teams should always follow the vendor remediation guidance.
Stay informed with Zero Wire
A useful vulnerability briefing should leave you with a clearer understanding of the issue and a concrete next step. Day Zero brings those essentials together: what happened, who should investigate, what to do now, and where to find the evidence.
Visit Zero Wire vulnerability intelligence, share the relevant briefings with the teams responsible for your systems, and return for new entries and updates. When the next disclosure arrives, we want you to spend less time assembling the basic facts and more time acting on them.
Follow Cloudflare Radar on X @CloudflareRadar and Bluesky @radar.cloudflare.com for updates.

articles.title: Por qué la segunda oleada de ‘hackeos’ a las neveras en supermercados avisa de los riesgos que vienen
articles.text:
Por qué la segunda oleada de ‘hackeos’ a las neveras en supermercados avisa de los riesgos que vienen
Los ataques prueban que, en un mundo hiperconectado, las infraestructuras críticas son vulnerables. Esta vez fueron los supermercados, mañana puede ser un hospital
Decenas de supermercados de al menos siete países europeos amanecieron este lunes con parte de su género estropeado. Un ciberataque subió la temperatura de las cámaras frigoríficas de varios establecimientos, en algunos casos hasta los 50 grados, echando a perder productos frescos y congelados. Los países más afectados fueron Bélgica y Suecia, pero también se registraron problemas en Luxemburgo, Países Bajos, Irlanda, Estonia y Finlandia.
Lo llamativo del caso es que pasó exactamente lo mismo hace tan solo tres semanas, esta vez en Francia. Tanto en ese incidente como en el de este lunes, los ciberdelincuentes lograron entrar en el software usado para controlar a distancia los sistemas de refrigeración, para subir a continuación la temperatura de las cámaras frigoríficas.
Los ciberataques a las neveras dicen mucho sobre la situación de vulnerabilidad en la que está la sociedad. Y plantea varios interrogantes: ¿Qué ha pasado exactamente? ¿Cómo es posible que suceda algo así dos veces seguidas? ¿Qué implicaciones tiene este ciberataque? ¿Cómo se puede prevenir? Estas son algunas respuestas (y varias dudas) a estas cuestiones.
Qué se sabe del ciberataque
El ciberataque no se ha lanzado sobre el software de las cadenas de supermercados afectadas. “Por lo que sabemos, se ha dirigido sobre los controladores y supervisores de refrigeración comercial conectados a internet”, explica David Arroyo Guardeño, científico titular del Grupo de Investigación en Ciberseguridad y Protección de la Privacidad (GICP) del CSIC. “El vector de ataque, como en tantas ocasiones, explota interfaces de acceso con fallas de autenticación o autorización. También se han identificado redes de mantenimiento remoto desactualizadas gestionadas por subcontratas locales de climatización y mantenimiento de frío comercial”, indica el informático.
La empresa en el centro del huracán es la danesa Danfoss, una multinacional especializada en sistemas de refrigeración y climatización industrial. El ataque ha sido técnicamente sencillo ―no se ha usado inteligencia artificial (IA) ni parece que haya requerido mucha preparación―, pero ha tenido un gran impacto por haber afectado al sector de la distribución.
Quién ha sido
Es pronto para saberlo. Nadie ha reclamado por el momento la autoría del ataque, ni hay ninguna pista que lleve a conclusiones válidas en este ámbito. “La agencia de ciberseguridad francesa (Annsi) y los servicios de inteligencia de los países afectados lo están tratando como cibersabotaje para colapsar la cadena de suministro alimentaria, y barajan tanto la hipótesis de hacktivistas pro-estatales con fines de guerra híbrida y desestabilización en países europeos como la de grupos criminales oportunistas explotando paneles de control mal configurados”, señala Arroyo.
Qué implicaciones tiene
Los ciberatacantes han demostrado que tienen la capacidad para interceptar las cámaras de frío. Eso debería tomarse como una advertencia. Esta vez han sido supermercados, ocasionando pérdidas económicas a algunas empresas comerciales. Pero la situación podría ser mucho peor. Por ejemplo, inutilizando sistemas de refrigeración de vacunas en un contexto de pandemia. De ahí que deba leerse como una advertencia.
El acontecimiento muestra varias cosas. Para empezar, el hecho de tener miles de sistemas conectados hace que la superficie de ataque (es decir, los dispositivos o procesos susceptibles de ser hackeados) sea cada vez mayor. Los expertos en ciberseguridad suelen decir que la mejor forma de proteger algo contra un ciberataque es no conectarlo; cualquier archivo o programa conectado a internet puede tener algún fallo.
Algunos de esos sistemas conectados controlan procesos físicos esenciales, como la cadena del frío, el suministro energético o las infraestructuras hídricas. Eso significa que, si se descubre una vulnerabilidad (o fallo) en el software con el que se opera alguno de esos sistemas, se puede explotar desde cualquier lugar del mundo con conexión a internet.
Por qué en Europa
Esta vez ha sido en Europa, pero no siempre es así. El Pentágono ha revelado esta semana que está investigando como ciberataque unos fallos registrados en agosto en las cámaras frigoríficas de varias bases militares estadounidenses.
No es el único ciberataque que han sufrido infraestructuras críticas estadounidenses este año. En julio, una serie de ataques afectaron a instalaciones relacionadas con el suministro de agua potable en al menos siete Estados de EE UU. Solo en Atlanta, por ejemplo, los grifos de 300.000 hogares dejaron de surtir agua durante horas después de que alguien (todo apunta a hackers iraníes) saboteara a distancia una estación de bombeo, lo que dificultó el suministro. Hubo ataques similares también en EE UU en 2021 y 2023.
El incidente no tuvo efectos en la salud de los ciudadanos, más allá del llamamiento en algunas localidades a hervir el agua para minimizar el riesgo de contaminación. Pero, igual que el ciberataque de las neveras podría haberse dirigido a las medicinas, los atacantes podrían haber tratado de envenenar el agua subiendo los niveles de cloro, como de hecho ya intentaron hacer en Israel hackers iraníes hace tres años.
Qué otros ataques similares ha habido
Uno de los primeros ciberataques con efectos sobre las infraestructuras críticas de un país de los que se tiene constancia lo sufrió Ucrania. Entre 2015 y 2016, con la anexión de Crimea todavía caliente, Rusia lanzó uno de los ataques más sofisticados que se recuerdan contra infraestructuras energéticas. El virus BlackEnergy dejó sin calefacción a varias ciudades ucranias en pleno invierno, inutilizando de forma sincronizada varias centrales energéticas del país. Según se supo más tarde, el ataque llevó al menos 19 meses de planificación y trabajo a las fuerzas militares rusas.
Aunque ese ataque se lanzó en un contexto de ciberguerra, fue un primer aviso para el mundo: desde un ordenador a miles de kilómetros se puede afectar a la vida de millones de personas.
Cómo se puede evitar que vuelva a pasar
Desde que existe la informática, existen los ciberataques. Y la IA está potenciándolos. La única forma de intentar contrarrestarlos es aumentar la inversión en ciberseguridad. “Tenemos una actividad ciber de altísima intensidad en estos momentos. Los descubrimientos de vulnerabilidades mediante IA, concretamente de zero days [los fallos de código que no ha identificado nadie, ni los propios desarrolladores de ese código], están aumentando muy considerablemente la superficie de exposición. La polarización y el clima político son otro componente que actúa de claro carburante”, resume Arroyo.
En el caso del ataque a las neveras, todo apunta a que una correcta actualización de sistemas podría haber hecho mucho más difícil que alguien pudiera intervenir en la cadena de frío de los alimentos.

articles.title: Cities Worldwide Build and Scale AI Services With NVIDIA Physical and Agentic AI
articles.text:
Cities generate enormous amounts of data from cameras, sensors and operational systems, but turning it into useful action — for planning, maintenance and public services — remains a challenge.
Physical and agentic AI offer new ways to close that gap, from digital twins for infrastructure planning to vision and service agents, while keeping local governments in control of how sensitive data is processed and used.
Building on initiatives announced at GTC Berlin, NVIDIA and its partners are expanding physical AI and AI agents to cities worldwide. Shared computing infrastructure gives city departments, neighboring municipalities and local developers a common foundation to build on — extending services without each organization having to acquire and manage resources of their own.
Agentic AI for Cities
From resident services to vision agents, cities are adopting NVIDIA agentic AI to deliver faster, more responsive public services. City teams don’t need a massive infrastructure investment to get started building these AI services: depending on the workload, NVIDIA RTX workstations or a small GPU system may be enough.
In Spain, 1MillionBot combines open source ALIA models trained at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center with NVIDIA Nemotron and other models in resident-service agents for Madrid Digital (Comunidad de Madrid), Administració Oberta de Catalunya and 150+ deployments across Spain, handling municipal procedures, appointment requests, urban-planning incidents and service inquiries.
In the San Francisco Bay Area, LiveX is bringing its AI City vision to life with NVIDIA Cosmos world models and Nemotron open models, and Omniverse and Metropolis libraries on NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs. The interactive, conversational AI hosts understand people’s needs, provide answers and take action, and can be tailored to local languages and service needs in airports, hospitals, local events and other public spaces.
Vision AI agents can turn existing city camera feeds into operational insights, helping teams identify mobility and safety issues and coordinate emergency responses across city services.
In Wrocław, Poland, K2K is building shared AI infrastructure using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Cosmos world reasoning models, and NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) to transform existing camera streams into actionable intelligence for mobility, safety and event response — using the same infrastructure across several city functions.
In Malaysia, ITMAX bundles infrastructure and agentic AI applications into long-term managed services for cities, including for traffic management. Built with reference to Cosmos, Nemotron and the Metropolis VSS blueprint, ITMAX’s SamurAI V2 vision agents are scaling on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs to support 17,000+ cameras by 2027. ITMAX integrates TeraSim, an open source traffic simulation platform from Laplace Intelligence, to test signal timing, reducing peak-hour corridor travel times by up to 26%.
Plan and Operate Critical Infrastructure With Digital Twins
Beyond public-facing services, digital twins can help cities expedite infrastructure planning, minimizing disruption to local communities. City digital twins can also serve as a real-time operational simulation to facilitate faster decision-making.
At Dangote’s Lekki refinery in Nigeria, Honeywell Technologies’ Forge Plant Cognition uses Nemotron-powered AI agents to understand operational data. A digital twin of the plant and its processes, built using Omniverse libraries, is also planned to support simulation and training. The platform, built on Dell PowerEdge servers with NVIDIA RTX PRO accelerators, helps operators identify bottlenecks, anticipate equipment and process issues, and optimize plant performance.
In Taiwan, Linker Vision and Dutch architecture firm MVRDV are using NVIDIA Omniverse and Nemotron to build environmental, social and governance agents that can assess the environmental impact of various urban planning scenarios, simulating 15-year outcomes of an urban forest canopy in 10 minutes — increasing design iteration speed from two weeks per iteration to less than an hour.
Build a Broader Local AI Ecosystem
Cities can extend AI to more services by building on infrastructure already in place and adding capacity. Shared resources and managed services can help extend those capabilities across departments and municipalities.
At Morocco’s Tanger Med port, Cires Technologies is expanding a sovereign AI factory for planned applications in worker safety, congestion analysis, cargo routing and port operations. Cires Technologies is also building an ecosystem of application providers to develop local models and applications for ports and cities.
Beyond city services, Barcelona Supercomputing Center’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme gives startups access to sovereign computing, technical support and training. BSC AI Factory also supports research and innovation for startups — spanning agriculture, medical imaging, knowledge access and speech services.
Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress, running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona, where NVIDIA Vice President of EMEA Paolo Guglielmini will deliver a keynote address followed by a panel moderated by Charbel Aoun, director of smart city and spaces for EMEA at NVIDIA.

articles.title: Arnis turns any place on Earth into a Minecraft world
articles.text:
Arnis turns any place on Earth into a Minecraft world
Louis Erbkamm built the first prototype in his free time. Now GitHub Copilot helps him maintain it alone.
Louis Erbkamm knows his way around Arnis, the smallest town in Germany, but he’s never set foot in it.
I know where the shops are. Where the boats are… I know the city pretty well, but I haven’t been there yet.
Louis Erbkamm, maintainer of Arnis
Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors.
Two weeks and a slow prototype
Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school.
That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow.
Arnis has a lot of buildings, it has streets, it has waters, it has all kinds of different elements that are useful to test with.
Louis
The project didn’t have a name yet, so it borrowed the town’s unique moniker.
A community that brings its own ideas
When Arnis added elevation, its worlds stopped being flat, and geospatial specialists from all over showed up with ideas on how best to integrate it. They started discussions on their own, and Louis says that’s exactly what he needed.
Bigger calls happen in the open too: before porting Arnis from Python to Rust, Louis opened discussions on GitHub to hear different perspectives. Contributors have since translated Arnis into about 20 languages and built major features of their own.
The best thing that has happened to me is essentially this big community on GitHub to see actually people from all kinds of different fields coming together to work on something that I started as a side project.
Louis
How a trash bin gets into Minecraft
Some features start on a walk. Louis noticed how many trash bins there were in his city, and there were none in his generated worlds.
Minecraft has no dedicated bins, so he took the question to the community, and together they found a block that fit. Placing one follows the same path as everything else: for the area a user selects, Arnis queries OpenStreetMap for every mapped element, then looks up each element’s coordinates and type.
If an element isn’t mapped, Arnis can’t place it. For structures too detailed for the map to describe, like the Statue of Liberty in New York, or Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro, Arnis converts 3D models into Minecraft blocks.
One maintainer, a stack of pull requests
As the sole maintainer, Louis reviews every pull request himself, and they stack up. He usually spends evenings or weekends working on Arnis, which means the community has to wait for him to be done with work for the day.
He uses GitHub Copilot to get an overview of open issues and bugs from the latest release, see how many people are running into them, trace where a bug came from in the codebase, and create a fix. Since he brought AI into the project, he says, code reviews and documentation have both increased.
I could delegate those annoying and boring tasks to Copilot, while I could still have a look at those really cool topics that are related to the development of it.
Louis
Sub-agents that look for regressions
Big features arrive as big pull requests.
Louis opens a large pull request in the GitHub Copilot app for a first overview and a performance review, with Copilot running in the background looking for small changes that would cut memory usage or generation time.
It takes just one wrong calculation in street lights, for example, to make the generation time of an entire city much slower.
Louis
He also keeps a mental list of the areas of the codebase that need extra care whenever someone changes them, and he has written the same warnings out by hand over and over.
I’m starting a few sub agents with the GitHub Copilot app to have a look specifically at those cases, and to come up with corner cases to test to make sure that we do not introduce any regressions into new releases.
Louis
He likes that the terminal, his files, the code changes and the pull request all sit in one app next to the chat.
An unexpected classroom
Louis’s favorite use of Arnis is in schools, where teachers have generated their city or a neighborhood park.
Some turn it into a contest: every student starts from the same generated area, improves a nearby park or playground using Arnis and Minecraft, and the class looks at the results together.
Where Arnis goes next
Recent releases have gone beyond the bounds of Earth, adding the Moon and Mars. Louis wants Arnis to stay easy to use while getting closer to reality, with more detail in less time, and he would like to see it in more schools.
Start with your hometown
Download Arnis from github.com/louis-e/arnis, pick a place on the map, choose where to spawn, and click Start Generation: within a few minutes, the world is ready to open in Minecraft. Louis suggests a place you know, like your hometown or somewhere memorable you’ve been, such as the Grand Canyon or Niagara Falls. Then look for what’s missing.
So maybe you see a bench that was not generated even though it is there.
Louis
Map it on OpenStreetMap, or tell Louis if it’s a bug and he will fix it.

articles.title: ChatGPT : les agents IA Dots deviennent plus puissants et encore plus autonomes — Frandroid
articles.text:
L’intelligence artificielle à votre service, même quand vous n’êtes pas devant votre PC ou votre smartphone. Voilà comment on pourrait résumer les Dots d’OpenAI, ces assistants IA utilisant chacun un ordinateur dans le cloud, à qui vous attribuez un nom, un avatar et une mission.
Une fois lancé, votre Dot travaille pour vous en permanence en se connectant à 4 000 applications via les plugins de ChatGPT, que vous lui parliez ou non. Il validera seul certaines décisions et vous demandera votre accord pour les plus importantes. Et pas besoin de lancer une application ou une interface Web : depuis fin octobre 2026, vous pouvez parler à un Dot depuis iMessage et Google Messages.
Quelques jours plus tard, le 2 novembre, Thibault Sottiaux de chez OpenAI annonce que les Dots vont prendre en charge plus de modèles de langage, dont les puissants GPT-6 Astra et GPT-6.1 Terra. D’autres seront intégrés au fil des mises à jour.
Les Dots peuvent choisir entre les modèles IA les plus puissants d’OpenAI
En réponse à son propre message sur X (Twitter), l’ingénieur précise que « votre Dot choisira le modèle le plus adapté à la tâche, en s’appuyant sur différents modèles pour les différentes parties du travail ». Vous n’avez donc strictement rien à faire pour obtenir les résultats, en théorie, les plus optimaux possibles.
Pour le moment, seuls les détenteurs d’un abonnement ChatGPT Pro aux États-Unis et au Canada peuvent utiliser les Dots. Aucune information concernant une éventuelle sortie internationale n’a été communiquée à ce stade.

articles.title: Ozempic eletrônico? Empresa chinesa cria dispositivo para controlar apetite
articles.text:
A chinesa BrainCo está desenvolvendo um dispositivo vestível que pretende suprimir o apetite por meio de estímulos cerebrais. A empresa apresenta a tecnologia como uma possível alternativa aos medicamentos para obesidade à base de GLP-1, como Wegovy e Zepbound.
A sócia fundadora Nyx He prevê o lançamento nos próximos dois a três anos, inicialmente na China, com posterior expansão para os Estados Unidos. Segundo a Bloomberg, a proposta ainda está em desenvolvimento e busca levar a tecnologia de interface cérebro-computador ao mercado de perda de peso.
Como funcionaria o GLP-1 eletrônico
O dispositivo utilizará uma interface cérebro-computador (BCI, na sigla em inglês) para estimular sinais neurais relacionados ao controle do apetite. A BrainCo pretende usar essa tecnologia para influenciar os mecanismos cerebrais envolvidos na sensação de fome.
Durante entrevista no evento Bloomberg Tech London, He descreveu o projeto como uma “versão eletrônica dos medicamentos para obesidade à base de GLP-1”. A comparação, porém, representa a proposta comercial da própria empresa, e não uma equivalência terapêutica já demonstrada.
A abordagem também é diferente da utilizada pelos medicamentos disponíveis no mercado. Wegovy e Zepbound imitam hormônios metabólicos envolvidos na regulação do apetite. A BrainCo, por sua vez, pretende atuar por meio de estímulos cerebrais, sem depender de medicamentos.
Até o momento, a empresa não apresentou publicamente resultados que demonstrem a eficácia do dispositivo na redução do apetite ou na perda de peso. Também não foram divulgados detalhes suficientes sobre os mecanismos de estimulação ou os resultados de testes com a tecnologia.
A companhia avalia diferentes modelos de comercialização, incluindo versões específicas para uso médico e outras destinadas diretamente aos consumidores.
Outros dispositivos desenvolvidos pela BrainCo
Sediada em Hangzhou, na China, a BrainCo já trabalha com tecnologias de neuroterapia, próteses e robótica. Entre seus produtos estão fones de ouvido com interface cérebro-computador não invasiva, comercializados para tratar condições como autismo, transtorno do déficit de atenção e hiperatividade (TDAH) e insônia.
Os equipamentos coletam e decodificam sinais neurais e, em alguns casos, também conseguem estimulá-los. A empresa desenvolve ainda próteses de mão que permitem a amputados e pessoas com deficiência controlar dedos artificiais por meio de sinais cerebrais.
Entre as principais frentes de atuação da companhia estão:
- Fones de ouvido BCI voltados ao tratamento de distúrbios neurológicos;
- Próteses de mão controladas por sinais cerebrais, que permitem atividades como tocar piano e praticar caligrafia;
- Fornecimento de mãos robóticas para a indústria chinesa de robôs humanoides.
Embora tenha concentrado suas atividades em tecnologias não invasivas, a BrainCo poderá explorar futuramente abordagens que dependam de implantes cerebrais, segundo He.
Empresa mantém planos de expansão internacional
A atuação da BrainCo nos Estados Unidos ocorre em meio ao aumento do escrutínio geopolítico sobre tecnologias de interface cérebro-computador. Entre as propostas em discussão estão restrições americanas a investimentos em empresas chinesas do setor.
Apesar desse cenário, He afirmou que a companhia continua registrando forte demanda por suas próteses e mãos robóticas no mercado americano e espera que o crescimento se acelere.
“Ainda observamos uma enorme demanda por nossos produtos, tanto pelas mãos robóticas para humanoides quanto pelas próteses de mão para amputados”, declarou a executiva.
Em janeiro, a Bloomberg News informou que a BrainCo havia apresentado um pedido confidencial para realizar uma oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO, na sigla em inglês) em Hong Kong. He não quis comentar os planos de abertura de capital nem a possibilidade de captar recursos adicionais antes da listagem.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Over 100 European Stores Hit as Supermarket Fridge Attacks Return
articles.text:
More than 100 stores in several European countries saw their fridges and freezers heat up overnight from Sunday to Monday, and several retailers have blamed a cyberattack. The incidents closely resemble the attacks that disrupted European supermarkets three weeks ago.
The affected businesses, ranging from major chains to small butcher shops, are in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden. Some units were set as high as 50°C (122°F), and problems have also been reported in Finland, Italy and Portugal.
Nobody has taken responsibility for the attacks. Investigators have not established whether the two waves are connected.
The first wave hit France overnight from October 11 to 12. Around 700 supermarkets had their refrigeration units forced into defrost mode, including Intermarché, Carrefour, Coopérative U and Monoprix stores. Food was spoiled, and the attacks reportedly caused fires.
CERT-FR, the incident response team of France’s cybersecurity agency ANSSI, initially linked the compromises to Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series controllers. A day later, it expanded its alert to cover Copeland and Dixell XWEB systems. Danfoss said most of the hacked units were legacy products it no longer updated.
Exposed Danfoss, Copeland controllers hijacked in new attacks
The technique appears to be the same. Stephan Moelans, CEO of Belgian refrigeration firm Sabcobel, told the Belga news agency that the attackers forced the units’ evaporators into defrost mode, as happened in France.
According to Moelans, a software update is not enough to fully resolve the weakness, and the affected equipment also needs to be physically modified.
Dutch broadcaster NOS reported that, as far as is known, the targeted devices were made by Danfoss and Copeland. An Estonian refrigeration supplier said the units attacked there were older Danfoss models.
Danfoss said that on October 13 it had told its customers to cut their systems’ internet connections and to reconnect only through a secure network. “Most stores took action at that time, but a small number did not,” a company spokesperson told NOS.
Security researcher Kevin Beaumont said people he spoke with had confirmed that every freezer hit on Monday had a management interface reachable from the internet. According to Beaumont, many of the devices are end-of-life and have no available patch.
Officials have not publicly explained how the attackers got in.
Deception security firm Lupovis told SecurityWeek that, between October 20 and 30, it saw suspicious activity aimed at its Danfoss AK-SM refrigeration controller sensors, including sensors in some of the affected regions. Most of the login attempts relied on factory-default credentials that Danfoss documents publicly, while others appeared to be trying to fingerprint specific Danfoss controller components.
“The activity peaked on 26 October, and importantly, we had not observed this behaviour on these sensors before 20 October. All authentication attempts were rejected by our sensors,” said Lupovis CEO Xavier Bellekens, adding that the timing is noteworthy.
Censys has found just over 1,000 Danfoss StoreView interfaces reachable online worldwide. “France continues to lead Danfoss StoreView exposures globally, followed by Belgium and the US,” the internet intelligence firm said.
The number of exposed StoreView instances in France has fallen sharply, from 1,825 before the October attacks to 220 at the time of Censys’ latest analysis.
By matching firmware build dates, Censys estimates that 41% of the French instances still online run a patched version. It counted 138 exposed instances in Belgium, 51 in the Netherlands and 50 in Sweden, of which 68%, 37% and 58%, respectively, appear to be patched.
Only a handful of exposed instances were seen in Luxembourg, Ireland and Estonia. Censys did not indicate whether any patched devices were among those compromised on Monday.
Belgium among hardest hit
Belgium appears to have taken the biggest hit. Delhaize said an IT incident disrupted refrigeration at several dozen of its stores, Carrefour counted 15 affected locations out of more than 700, and Colruyt said five franchised Spar shops were attacked.
An IKEA store in Mons was hit as well, and the Belgian federal prosecutor’s office has opened an investigation.
In Luxembourg, four Delhaize outlets were affected. In Ireland, SuperValu pulled chilled and frozen products from 13 stores where one specific refrigeration model was impacted.
Swedish grocer ICA confirmed that a limited number of its stores were impacted, while Coop reported problems at a handful of locations. An ICA store manager said they had to throw out significant amounts of food.
In the Netherlands, Danfoss said the systems of at least 17 businesses were hit, mainly butcher shops and small grocers.
Finnish retailer Kesko said a few of its smaller stores had temperature disruptions. In Italy, the operator of several Coop-branded supermarkets in Sicily alerted the national cybersecurity agency, and in Portugal, the Mosqueteiros group confirmed incidents at seven Intermarché stores.
EU agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen called the attacks a deliberate bid to disrupt the food supply chain and erode consumer trust. “The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply concerning,” he said.
Hansen said the bloc’s food security is not under threat for now, but he acknowledged the food that had to be thrown away and the harm to businesses.
